Preface



For a long time I wanted to build the systematic knowledge of what it means to work as an AI
Solution Architect: how to reason across the layers of an AI system — from tokens and models to
workloads, systems, infrastructure, and fleets — so that a vague requirement can be turned into a
defensible architecture. I kept looking for the resource that would lay all of that down in one coherent
thread. What I found were deep dives into single layers — models, serving, infrastructure, agents —
but no single spine that connected them into the one thing an architect actually does: chaining a real
workload to a defensible solution.
    That feedback loop — curiosity, question, research, model, write — is the engine of this book:
writing the reasoning down forces every assumption, quantity, and trade-off to become explicit, and
exposes the gaps that deserve further measurement. The AI field moves fast, and I am still learning
too. This handbook is a continuously evolving reference — developed and shared layer by layer,
decision by decision, from the token up to the fleet. If it helps others build the same systematic
mental model, then it has outdone what I had planned it for.
Start here. For the working method, begin at Ch. 1 (The Token) and follow the canonical workload
through Chs. 16–20 (TCO and the fleet, where the numbers pay off), returning to the policy sections
later. The following Preface sections — the thesis, reading paths, the evidence discipline, and the
currency policy — are the reference layer: valuable to a careful reader, but skimmable on a first
pass. The full provenance/taxonomy rule set also lives in the Sources, Method, and Reproducibility
chapter, so the Preface need not be read in full before starting the chapters.


The thesis

The book has one thesis, and it is the spine of every chapter:

      Given an ambiguous problem, how do I systematically arrive at a defensible AI
      architecture?

    The canonical method — the decision loop that Chapter 22 makes explicit — is previewed in the
Preface, then assembled piece by piece. Chapters 1–21 acquire the tools: tokens, workloads, model



                                                   vi
vii                                                                                               Preface


structure, arithmetic intensity, memory, parallelism, serving, benchmarking, TCO, fleet operations,
and the factory gate. Chapter 22 then synthesizes those tools into the professional reasoning loop
that runs through the whole book, placed late not because it belongs at the end but because the
reader needs the technical vocabulary first to see it operate on a real workload.
      That loop — which every chapter echoes — runs from requirements and workload characterization,
through constraints and candidate architectures, to benchmarking, bottleneck analysis, optimization,
total-cost reality checks, and a final red-team challenge. Parts I–V walk through the technical substrate,
layer by layer. Part VI turns to the discipline itself: how one learns to reason across those layers.


How the book is organized

The six parts mirror the layers an architect reasons across:

      • Part I — The Token. Models and mechanisms, from a single token to the memory and compute
        arithmetic that prices every decision.

      • Part II — The Workload. The job the system does: workload characterization and measuring
        what matters.

      • Part III — The System. Memory, compute, communication, parallelism, and serving.

      • Part IV — The Architecture. Designing, benchmarking, engineering, and costing a system.

      • Part V — The Fleet. Operating AI at scale, and agents.

      • Part VI — The Architect. The spine made explicit, plus a patterns library.

      A worked canonical scenario — an enterprise retrieval-augmented question-answering work­
load on a 70B-class model — runs through the book, so every mechanism is anchored in concrete,
reproducible arithmetic rather than abstraction. One caveat, so the book is not misread: this sce­
nario is a teaching instrument, not a claim about what an AI workload is. Real workloads span a
wide design space — long-context RAG (KV/memory-bound), high-throughput chat (decode-bound),
batch inference (utilization/cost-bound), reasoning (test-time-compute-bound), agentic (concur­
rency/variance-bound), embeddings, vision, fine-tuning, training — and each shifts which quantity
dominates. The canonical scenario picks a single, tractable, input-heavy RAG case and carries it
through so the reasoning stays continuous; a real deployment will sit somewhere else in that space,
and the chapters are written to give the reader the arithmetic to re-derive the bounds for their point.


How to use this book

The chapters build on one another, but not every reader needs them in order. A few reading paths,
depending on where the reading begins:
Preface                                                                                              viii


      New to inference systems. Parts I → II → III sequentially — the token, then the
      workload, then the system. This is the path that builds the vocabulary the later chapters
      assume.
      Practicing architect. Start with Ch. 22, the reasoned loop, then use Parts I–V as the
      quantitative reference it calls on.
      Infrastructure specialist. Parts III–V (system, architecture, fleet) directly; skim I–II for
      the workload framing.
      Customer-facing solution architect. Parts II, IV, and VI — scoping a workload, de­
      signing an architecture, and the professional discipline.
      Frontier-model reader. Appendix A alone, but only after Chs. 3, 7–11, so the total-vs-
      active, KV, and serving mechanism the appendix leans on are already in hand.


The operational decision checklist

The full reasoning loop is earned in Chapter 22, but its shape is useful from the first page. When
a workload arrives, the same six questions recur in the same order; the chapters that follow each
answer one of them. Keep this list in view while reading — it is the spine made operational.

      1. What is the workload? — tokens in/out, rps average and peak, concurrency, latency
      SLOs. (Ch. 4)
      2. What fits on one host? — weight residency, KV per token, the concurrency floor.
      (Chs. 3, 7)
      3. Which phase binds? — prefill compute or decode bandwidth, at this operating point.
      (Chs. 2, 8)
      4. How many hosts? — the fleet sized from the per-host bound, with headroom and
      failover. (Chs. 16–17)
      5. Who serves it, and how? — batching, parallelism, P/D disaggregation, scheduling.
      (Chs. 10–11, 20)
      6. Is it the right call? — TCO, the red-team challenge, the recorded decision. (Chs. 16,
      22, 25)

    The six questions are cross-cutting: each is first raised in one part and cashed out across the
others — Q1 in Part II, Q2–3 across Parts I and III, Q4–5 across Parts III–V, and Q6 in Parts IV and VI.
The technical justification for why the loop has this shape — and where it breaks — is Chapter 22;
this checklist is the early, operational view of the same loop.

figure 1: The architect’s decision loop — the book’s spine. A vague requirement is carried through
workload characterization, constraints, candidate architectures, benchmarking, bottleneck analysis,
TCO, and a final red-team challenge before an architecture is committed. Stage 03 (“Validate &
Defend”) produces a provisional recommendation — the candidate that survives benchmarking and
TCO — and stage 04 (“Commit”) subjects it to the red-team challenge before the final choice is
recorded; the recommendation is therefore provisional until it has been challenged. Two loops are
drawn: the inner (green, left) returns a failed benchmark or TCO validation from “Validate & Defend”
back to “Design & size” to re-derive the candidate; the outer (red, right) returns from “Commit” to
“Understand” when the committed architecture reveals a requirements revision is needed.

The Architect’s Evidence Discipline

Every load-bearing quantitative claim in this book carries Axes 1 and 2 as an inline pair; the Axis-3
measurement status rides along with claims whose measurement status is known, not with every
claim. Keeping these axes separate is itself a discipline. A claim carries the labels directly (inline,
e.g. [1P][DERIVED]) or via an identified table or section that states them (e.g. a worked-example
table whose header or footnote gives the provenance and status for every row). Purely illustrative
or rhetorical numbers that no later calculation depends on may carry the labels in the surrounding
prose rather than inline; the Sources, Method, and Reproducibility chapter defines these exceptions
unambiguously. The provenance axis records where the number came from: [1P] first-party (the
model vendor’s own spec), [canonical scenario] the book’s own internally defined workload and
model (Ch. 4, Table 4-2), [ILLUSTRATIVE] a non-canonical worked-example or scenario input
chosen to make a calculation concrete, [2°] reputable second-hand (textbook, survey, independent
benchmark), or [LAB] measured on the author’s own home-lab hardware (illustrative of mechanism,
not production). The epistemic-status axis records what was done to it: FACT directly stated by the
source, DERIVED computed by arithmetic from stated inputs, ASSUMPTION a deliberately chosen
scenario input (paired with a scenario provenance — [canonical scenario] or [ILLUSTRATIVE]),
HYPOTHESIS reasoned but not yet validated, or UNRESOLVED a question the book leaves
open. A label pair always combines one item from each of the first two axes, e.g. [1P][DERIVED]
or [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]; the third axis — measurement status (ANALYTICAL /
ILLUSTRATIVE / MODELED / MEASURED, or UNMEASURED where the stage is not yet determined)
— rides with that pair or stands alone, and is defined in full in the Sources, Method, and Reproducibility
chapter.
     One mapping is worth stating explicitly, because it is easy to get wrong: the canonical scenario
(Ch. 4, Table 4-2) keeps its own provenance. Within that [canonical scenario] provenance the
epistemic-status axis splits every value into exactly two cases. An input or parameter assumption — a
traffic level, a latency target, a price, a token count — is [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION].
A value arithmetically derived from those assumed inputs — an execution occupancy, a tokens-per-
second rate, a cost-per-request, a tokens-per-dollar figure — is [canonical scenario][DERIVED].
A vendor hardware constant (e.g. the H100 footprint) is [1P][FACT], never [ILLUSTRATIVE].
[ILLUSTRATIVE] is reserved for a non-canonical hypothetical worked example (a “what-if” that
is not the canonical scenario): its inputs are [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] and its derived
results [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]. The ASSUMPTION/DERIVED split tells a reader whether a
number was chosen or computed; the [canonical scenario]/[ILLUSTRATIVE] split tells them
whether it is the book’s fixed reference set or a one-off what-if.
     Two habits matter most. First, arithmetic belongs on the epistemic-status axis, not the provenance
axis: a worked example computed from a model card is [1P][DERIVED], never [2°] just because
arithmetic was done. Second, the conclusions an architect draws are only as defensible as the units
behind them — so every major worked example ends with a unit check and a sanity check (does this
Preface                                                                                              xii


result stay inside the physically possible?). That habit is part of the discipline, not an appendix. The
full statement of this scheme, including how each label is verified, is in the Sources, Method, and
Reproducibility chapter.
    Evidence cutoff and edition date. This edition is build v20260913 (2026-09-13). The single
evidence cutoff for it is 2026-08-30: model, vendor, and hardware claims are stated as of that date,
and the “As of 2026-08” markers in the body refer to this same cutoff. Primary sources (arXiv reports,
model cards, vendor pages) were accessed as of the build date; each is cited with a stable identifier in
the References chapter. Fast-moving model and vendor assertions (Appendix A in particular) are

changed after 2026-08-30 is not silently updated in this edition; a later build revalidates the fast-

rather than inheriting the prior value.
    Dated addenda remain outside that snapshot. Appendix A, A.6 carries a boxed 2026-09-27 ca­
pability probe under revision v20260913+addendum-20260927. The separately dated 2026-10-28
technology notes in the body and Appendix A carry revision v20260913+addendum-20261028.
These notes distinguish inspected sources and code from locally reproduced measurements. Neither
addendum silently updates the original August comparisons or the First-hand Sources list.
    Build identifier and generation. The build identifier v20260913 is the content edition: it names the
source snapshot and evidence cutoff that the text reflects. Re-rendering that same source to a PDF
on a later date (e.g. a proof generated in October) does not change the content edition and does not
extend the evidence cutoff; it only changes the PDF’s generation timestamp, which is recorded in
the document metadata and is not evidence. A change to the content requires a new build identifier,
which invalidates the prior edition and is recorded in the release log — except a dated post-cutoff
addendum carried under its own revision identifier and listed in the Appendix addenda row.
    Release log. The revision that produced this PDF is recorded at the end of the Sources, Method,
and Reproducibility chapter, in the “Edition history” panel, along with the source revision (commit),

Reading conventions

Three conventions keep the book consistent and honest about its own limits.
    Terminology. For the capacity arithmetic in this handbook, GPU memory and VRAM are
used generically for accelerator-local memory; HBM refers specifically to high-bandwidth-memory
implementations, which is what the worked examples assume. TTFT, time-to-first-token and prefill
latency likewise; RAG and retrieval-augmented-generation are the same. Where a distinction is
architecturally load-bearing — prefill versus decode, total versus active parameters, model capacity
versus system capacity — the book holds it sharply. Synonyms are a readability concession; load-
bearing contrasts are never relaxed (Ch. 2, 8, 17).
    Hardware is a generic stand-in. The worked arithmetic is anchored to concrete constants
xiii                                                                                            Preface


— for example, an H100 GPU’s 0.989 PFLOPS BF16 dense tensor-core peak and 3.35 TB/s HBM
bandwidth, with an 8×H100 host used as the canonical deployment unit — because arithmetic needs
concrete anchors. Those values are a current high-end accelerator, presented as an example, not a
prophecy: the H200, B100/B200 and later generations change the constants, not the method. Re-derive
the constants from the current hardware sheet; the roofline (Ch. 8) and the canonical arithmetic
(Ch. 7) keep the method independent of any single generation. Forward-looking numbers are marked
ILLUSTRATIVE.
       Quick reference. For a day-to-day cheat-sheet: Chapter 26 (§2.1) carries a workload-to-strategy
decision matrix, and Chapter 25’s Architecture Decision Record is a reusable template to copy into a
repository. Those, plus the evidence discipline above, are worth re-reading first whenever a chapter
feels dense.


A note on currency

The mechanisms in this handbook — tokens, memory floors, rooflines, parallelism, KV arithmetic —
are durable; they do not change as the industry moves. But the frontier does move, and a handbook
for architects should carry the latest technology information. The Appendix therefore surveys the
frontier open-weight architectures of 2026, mapped back to the mechanisms and decisions explored
in the body of the book — and closes on the question that is more durable than any single architecture:
where should the intelligence live.

The Token




    1
chapter 1.


It All Starts With the First Token




The Architect’s Question

Before we can size a model, a context window, or a serving budget, we have to know what the input
actually is. After this chapter we should be able to reason about an AI system’s smallest unit of
cost and meaning — the token — and to translate between human units (a sentence, a page, a
word) and the machine unit every architecture decision is priced against. This is the first rung of
the token→fleet spine: everything downstream (memory, compute, latency, cost) is ultimately a
statement about tokens.


1.1. Concept

A token is the atomic unit of text that a language model reads and writes. It is not a word, not
a character, and not a byte — it is whatever the model’s tokenizer decided to carve the text into.
A single token can be a whole word (handbook), a common subword (hand), a single character,
a short punctuation+space pair, or in worst cases a fragment of a character. (This chapter scopes
to text-tokenized autoregressive models. Modern multimodal systems also use non-text token-like
representations — image patches, audio frames — that are not produced by a text tokenizer; for those,
“token count” is a different quantity from text-token count and does not map one-to-one onto model
compute the way it does here.)
    The disconnection from human units is the first thing an architect has to internalize: cost and
capacity in an LLM are measured in tokens, not words or characters, because the workload
accounting is token-based — embedding lookup, attention arithmetic, KV cache memory, and decode
time are all counted in tokens. That does not mean every operation has a fixed per-token price: the



                                                 2
3                                                                          It All Starts With the First Token


cost per token varies by phase (prefill vs decode), by operating point (batch size, context length), and
by hardware utilization, and attention work grows nonlinearly with context. The token is the unit
we count and budget in; the per-token cost is what the later chapters derive. This chapter exists to
make that switch automatic.


1.1.1. Tokenization

Tokenization splits a string into an ordered list of integer IDs from the model’s vocabulary (typically
tens of thousands, up to ~256k entries). The split is data-driven: learned from a large corpus, byte-
pair encoding (BPE) repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent byte/subword pairs until the
vocabulary is built, so the boundaries are wherever the corpus statistics happened to fall — not where a
grammarian would put them. Two practical consequences follow. First, text is generally recoverable
from its token IDs under the specified tokenizer (the detokenizer inverts the encoding), but the
segmentation does not correspond cleanly to words or semantics: the characters of architecture
and architect may or may not share a token depending on corpus frequency. The encode/decode
round-trip is usually lossless for the byte-level mapping, but the token boundaries are not semantically
meaningful. Second, token counts are not proportional to character counts in any fixed way.
[1P][FACT] A high-frequency English word is often one token (verifiable on most vendor tokenizer
demos — e.g. common words like the, we, run render as single tokens); a rare technical term, a long
digit string, or dense code is frequently several. The “one token ≈ 4 characters” rule of thumb is
for rough estimation of general-English prose, never a law — we confirm against the model’s own
tokenizer before pricing anything.


1.1.2. Context window

The context window is the maximum sequence length the model can condition on at a given
generation step — that is, the total of the retained input/prefix and the tokens generated so far. It is a
hard service constraint at the configured limit: exceed it and the request fails or must be truncated.
(This is the engine-configured maximum, not a law of physics — some models use sliding-window or
rolling attention that retains only a bounded recent context, and a few support positional-scaling or
provider-side context extension, so the model’s positional capability and the serving stack’s configured
cap can differ; the distinction is developed in Ch 7 and Ch 22.) Current-gen models commonly ship
windows ranging from roughly 8K up to a million-plus tokens, varying by model and vendor ([1P]
[FACT] vendor model cards, e.g. 128K/1M+ windows as of 2026); the advertised number is a fixed,
checkable property of the model we choose — verify it on the card, never assume it from the family
name. Note there are three related but distinct limits: the model-advertised maximum (the card’s
window), the engine-configured maximum (what the serving stack is set to allow, which can be lower
to bound memory), and the request-level available input budget (the advertised window minus the
reserved generation budget and any positional-scaling or provider-API cap). The context window
is one of the first numbers we will be quoted, and one of the easiest to overcommit against. But it
It All Starts With the First Token                                                                   4


is a configured maximum, not a per-request charge: a 9.2K request in a 128K window is computed,
cached, and billed on the ~9.2K tokens actually used, not on the full 128K. What the window does
bound is the worst case — the memory a single request could reserve and the admission capacity the
engine must hold — and some engines reserve or pre-allocate against that maximum (a policy choice
that varies by engine), while others allocate only for the tokens actually processed. So the window
sets the ceiling on reservation and admission, not the floor on per-request cost; the cost tracks the
tokens actually cached and billed (developed in Ch 7 and Ch 16).

1.1.3. Embeddings

Text enters the model as token IDs, but the model does arithmetic on vectors. The first such vector
is the token embedding: a learned lookup table maps each discrete token id to a dense vector
in a high-dimensional space, and the transformer operates on those vectors. Two distinct widths
must not be conflated: the token-embedding width (the model’s hidden dimension, e.g. 4096 for
LLaMA-7B, 8192 for LLaMA-2/3 70B and for the canonical 70B reference, 12288 for a GPT-3-class 175B
model) and the retrieval-embedding width (the dimension of a sentence/document embedding
produced by a separate encoder for RAG, typically 384–1536 for dedicated retrieval models, or the
full hidden dim if the LLM itself is used as the encoder). The “128 to a few thousand” range applies to
retrieval embeddings; the token embedding width is architecture-dependent and for modern LLMs
is illustratively in the 4096–16384 range (not an exhaustive bound across all models). Two other
vector objects are distinct from the token embedding and should not be merged with it: positional
encodings (which encode a token’s position in the sequence, added to or modulating the embedding)
and contextual hidden states (the per-layer, per-position activations the transformer produces,
which depend on the whole context, not just the token id). The token embedding maps each discrete
token id to a learned continuous vector; relationships in that learned space emerge from training but
should not be interpreted as a simple human-semantic distance metric.
    For the architect the practical facts are: embeddings live in a lookup table sized vocab × dim,
they account for a real but small slice of a model’s parameter count (a 100k × 4096 table holds 100,000
× 4,096 ≈ 409.6M ≈ 0.4B params — a rounding error next to a 70B model, but not zero), and they are
the first thing a vocabulary mismatch or a re-tokenized prompt can silently change.

1.1.4. Attention

Attention is the mechanism by which each token’s representation is recomputed as a weighted blend
of the representations of all tokens before it in the context. The weights come from a similarity
(query·key) between the current token and every prior token, normalized, and used to mix the value
vectors. It is the mechanism that makes a model “pay attention to” relevant earlier tokens when
producing the next one.
    The architect-relevant fact: attention’s cost scales quadratically with context length in the
full-attention regime — the number of input×output position pairs grows as L². That quadratic term
5                                                                       It All Starts With the First Token


is the single biggest reason context windows feel expensive, and it is the pivot for every optimization
downstream (sparse/linear attention, KV caching, retrieval to keep context short).
    One precision matters before the mental model hardens: the L² term is a prefill cost — it describes
computing attention across all position pairs in one pass over the full input. During decode, each
generated token attends once to the growing prefix, so the per-token step is a linear cost in context
length, and the length shows up as a growing KV cache memory footprint (per-token key/values)
rather than as per-step compute. The practical read is therefore “long context is quadratic in prefill
compute, and linear-but-memory-growing in decode” — a distinction as important as the quadratic
fact itself, and one we return to in Chapter 2 (compute gears), Chapter 7 (memory arithmetic) and
Chapter 8 (roofline). Keeping prefill and decode separate is what prevents the over-simple “long
context = quadratic inference” once we optimize context in later chapters.
    One architectural consequence to hold now: which layers emit a per-token cache is a property of
the attention architecture, not the context length alone — dense attention emits a key/value per token
on every layer, while hybrid/linear-attention layers (Mamba-style state, linear-attention kernels) hold
a constant-size recurrent state that does not grow with length. A third family — compressed per-
token KV: MLA-style latent attention, grouped-query attention (GQA) and multi-query attention
(MQA) head sharing — still stores a per-token entry, so its cache does grow with token count, but
at fewer bytes/token than full MHA. These are distinct mechanisms: constant-state (no per-token
growth) versus reduced-width per-token (per-token growth, smaller footprint). This is why “the KV
problem” and its fixes are really a model-architecture question (Ch. 3) that lands as a memory question
(Ch. 7) — and why the token layer is the right place to have met it. We only need the concept here;
the mechanism inventory is Chapter 3’s, the arithmetic Chapter 7’s.

1.1.5. KV cache as a concept

When the model generates one token at a time, it recomputes the same prefix repeatedly unless it
saves the intermediate results. The KV cache (key–value cache) is the stored key and value tensors
for every token in the context, so that generating the next token only computes attention against
the new token rather than re-deriving the whole prefix. It is the reason “long conversations are
expensive in memory, not just in compute.”
    KV cache size per token scales with


                  KVper-token = 2 × nlayers × nKV heads × dhead × bytes-per-value

    (one key and one value per layer per KV head). For full multi-head attention (MHA) the
KV heads are all the query heads, so n_KV heads × d_head = d_hidden and the formula reduces
to the simpler introductory form 2 × n_layers × d_hidden × bytes-per-value. The general
form matters once we meet grouped-query (GQA) and multi-query (MQA) attention, which
share a small number of KV heads across many query heads and can make the cache several times
smaller than the full-MHA figure (Ch. 7) — so d_hidden alone is not the correct KV width for those
It All Starts With the First Token                                                                    6


architectures. It is on the order of ~256 KiB (0.26 MB) per token for a 7B-class model (32 layers,
d_hidden 4096, full-MHA) and ~1.25 MiB (1.31 MB) per token for a 70B-class model (80
layers, d_hidden 8192, full-MHA) at 8-bit precision. The arithmetic is the formula above with
one byte per value: 2 × 32 × 4096 = 262,144 B and 2 × 80 × 8192 = 1,310,720 B. That 8-bit figure is
the raw tensor byte-halving of the BF16 value — exactly 50% (1.31 MB vs 2.62 MB). So FP8 KV = raw
tensor byte-halving = 1.31 MB/token (exactly 50% of BF16). Any block-allocation/metadata overhead
is NOT vendor-measured here and must be filled by a deployment benchmark. The vLLM FP8-KV
blog post’s often-quoted ‘54%’ is a decode inter-token-latency (ITL) slope, not a memory ratio, so it is
not a memory-footprint coefficient here. At 9.2K tokens the raw byte-halving figure gives ~12.06 GB
(not ~13.4 GB — the figure one gets by assuming ~11% block/metadata overhead on top of the raw
tensor bytes). A different engine or a GQA/hybrid-attention model has a different per-token footprint,
so re-derive it for the target stack (the geometry and the “do not generalize” caveat are in Ch. 7).
[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] Either way, a long context (say 32K tokens) alone can be tens of GB of
memory. A first non-obvious architectural lesson hides here: MoE expert sparsity alone does not reduce
per-token KV state. A Mixture-of-Experts model activates only a fraction of its neurons per token,
which saves compute, but the attention layers still process every token densely and emit a key/value
per token — so MoE shrinks compute-per-token, not memory-per-context. What actually determines
KV memory is the attention architecture and cache policy, not the expert count: GQA/MQA shrink
the per-token K/V width, hybrid/linear/compressed-latent attention change how much context is
retained, sliding-window caps some layers’ retained context, and quantization (FP8) reduces the
bytes per element without stopping the linear growth. This is a controlled comparison — it holds the
attention geometry, context length, and cache dtype fixed; an MoE model that also uses GQA or a
different attention mechanism can have a much smaller KV footprint than a dense full-MHA baseline.
The distinction — compute-sparsity vs memory-sparsity — is one an architect has to get exactly right,
and it is why “the KV problem” is an attention-architecture question more than a model-size question
(developed fully in Ch. 3 and Ch. 7). We deliberately keep this to concept + order of magnitude here;
Chapter 7 (Memory) does the verified arithmetic against the canonical scenario.



1.2. Mental Model

    A token is best understood as a metered unit of model I/O, the way electricity is metered by
the kilowatt-hour — important not because a single kilowatt-hour is meaningful by itself, but because
every downstream cost and capacity number is denominated in it. (It is a computational/textual unit,
not a unit of thought: two tokenizers can render the same semantic content in different token counts,
and a reasoning model can spend very different compute per visible token.)
    A useful image for the full pipeline:
       Text → tokenizer → discrete IDs → embedding → vectors → attention recomputes
       each token → KV cache remembers the prefix → generate one token at a time.

    Reading the mnemonic: read “remembers the prefix” as persistent state, not as a processing stage —

    We do not need to hold all of this as a practitioner. The durable mental model is: tokens are
the interface between a human’s request and a machine’s arithmetic, and anything we are
asked to size or price in an LLM system reduces, one way or another, to “how many tokens, in what
context, with what precision.”
1.3. Worked Example

    The canonical scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2 — the one set of numbers every chapter cites) is an
enterprise Q&A system: ~2,000 registered users, ~10 requests/s average, prompt of ~1,200 tokens plus
~8K retrieved context (~9.2K input), ~300-token output, on a 70B-class dense model. We reuse those
numbers everywhere, so let us read one concrete property off them here.
    Worked example, not reference. If average request is ~9.2K input + ~300 output ≈ 9.5K tokens per
request, and traffic is ~10 req/s, then the system ingests:
    • Input tokens/s: 9,200 tokens/req × 10 req/s = 92,000 tokens/s (peaks higher at ~40 req/s →
      ~368k).
    • Output tokens/s: 300 ×10 = 3,000 tokens/s output.
    • Roughly 30× more input tokens than output tokens in this workload (9.2K ÷ 300).

    (All figures trace to the canonical scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2); none are measurement claims.)
    This ratio — input-heavy — is a hypothesis that memory (KV cache) and prefill dominate this
system’s cost rather than decode, not a conclusion token counts alone establish. Decode’s serial
nature, per-step weight reads, batching, cache residency, and the latency SLO can still dominate
capacity economics even on an input-heavy workload; the token mix is the first signal, and the
measured per-phase utilization and goodput (throughput that meets the SLO; Ch 7, Ch 8, Ch 14)
are what confirm it. We will not act on it here; Chapter 7 (Memory) and Chapter 8 (Compute) do.
The point of the worked example in this chapter is to fix the unit: every one of those numbers is a
statement about tokens, and we can now say it without translating from words or pages.


1.4. Measurement

    For this concept chapter, measurement is about counting tokens correctly, because a miscount
at the input silently misprices everything downstream. Three things an architect can actually check:
    1. Actual token count, not the rule of thumb. Run the model’s own tokenizer on representative
       prompts. The “4 chars ≈ 1 token” heuristic is for estimation only; real counts differ by language,
       formatting, code, and tokenizer version.
   2. Input vs output split. Measure both legs of the request (prompt tokens and generated tokens),
       because they land on different bottlenecks — input on memory/prefill, output on decode —
       and on different cost line items.
   3. Peak vs average context. Log the distribution of context lengths, not just the mean. A
       workload that averages 9.2K input tokens but peaks far higher (illustrative variant, say 32K)
       has a very different KV cache and latency profile.

    This measurement habit is the token-layer answer to the book’s recurring question, “what would
I actually measure here?” — we measure token counts and their distribution, at the edge, before any
architecture decision is made.


1.5. Common Mistakes
    • Assuming one token ≈ one word. A token is often a word fragment, not a whole word: a
       high-frequency English word is frequently one token, but a longer or rarer word is usually
       split into several subword tokens, and code, numerics, and non-Latin scripts routinely run
       2–5× the naive word-count estimate. The mapping is tokenizer-dependent (it depends on the
       corpus the tokenizer was trained on), so the “one token ≈ 4 characters” rule of thumb is for
11                                                                       It All Starts With the First Token


       rough estimation of general-English prose only — confirm against the model’s own tokenizer
       before pricing anything.
     • Ignoring the input/output asymmetry. Treating a request as “one unit” hides that input-
       heavy workloads tend toward high prefill compute and KV-capacity pressure, while output-
       heavy ones are decode-dominant (run-time per generated token) — opposite bottlenecks with
       opposite fixes. (Note: “capacity pressure” is a memory-capacity constraint, not a memory-
       bandwidth bound; see Ch 4/8.)
     • Quoting context window as free capacity. The window is an upper bound, not a recom­
       mendation; using it fully is expensive. Keeping a 9.2K average inside a 128K window still costs
       for the length we actually use.
     • Trusting a vendor’s tokenizer count without checking. Tokenizer versions change and
       report differently; measure on our traffic, not the marketing figure.


1.6. Architecture Consequence

     Whatever we learned here, file it under “can I size an input before I buy capacity?” Concretely,
the decision this chapter enables is: estimate tokens-per-second (input and output separately), and
therefore tokens-per-second capacity and cost, before choosing a model or a serving configuration. It is
the load-bearing input to model selection (Ch. 5), the memory budget (Ch. 7), the compute budget
(Ch. 8), and the token economics (Ch. 16). No downstream chapter runs without a token count to
price against — this one gives us the unit.
1.7. What We Still Don’t Know

     As of 2026-08: tokenizer internals are rarely published in full, so exact per-token behavior for
a given model is often only empirically observable, not specified (— tokenizer construction details,
e.g. exact BPE merge rules for commercial models, are not fully public). Whether a fully learned,
near-optimal tokenization for our domain can beat the generic vocabulary by a repeatable, quantified
margin is still an open, workload-dependent question. And the interaction between tokenizer choice
and downstream reasoning quality is not yet crisply characterized — we flag it as an open area rather
than a settled fact.
1.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: The Internal Q&A Tool, From First Principles

(Chains the continuous scenario — this is its first appearance.)
     An architect is pulled into an early-stage design conversation about a new internal Q&A tool.
There is no model, no server, no budget — just the raw ask: “We have thousands of employees who
want to ask questions over our internal documents.” Before any architecture can be defended, we
have to turn that vague desire into a machine-denominated statement.
     From the token-level work alone (which we worked through in this chapter), the architect can
already establish: the unit is tokens; the request shape will be prompt + retrieved context + output;
It All Starts With the First Token                                                               12


the workload is input-heavy; and the first number to lock down is tokens-per-request, because every
downstream decision (which model fits, how much memory, what latency is possible) is priced
against it. The specific sizing — turning “thousands of employees” into ~2,000 registered users, ~10
req/s, ~9.2K input tokens — is Chapter 4’s job (workload anatomy). Here the point is narrower and
sharper: we can now speak the system’s currency, and that is a prerequisite for every architecture
question that follows.

What Actually Happens During Inference




The Architect’s Question

After this chapter we should be able to reason about the two fundamental modes of LLM inference —
prefill and decode — and to identify which system constraint each mode exposes. We should be able to
compute the bandwidth and FLOP demands of a given workload, compare them against real hardware
limits, and understand why, at the canonical low-batch operating point, decode is HBM-bandwidth-
bound while prefill is compute-bound — and that this is a regime statement, not a universal rule: at
other batch sizes and context lengths the binding constraint can shift (the qualification is developed
in §2.2 and Ch 8). This distinction directly shapes architectural decisions: whether we need more
GPUs, whether we can disaggregate prefill from decode, and how we size memory and compute
in a fleet. After this chapter we should see inference not as a single monolithic cost but as two
opposite-bound processes that require different levers.


2.1. Concept

Inference is the process of turning a sequence of input tokens into a sequence of output tokens using
a trained neural network. In an autoregressive model, every generated token requires a fresh forward
pass, but the computation split between the prefix (the prompt) and the suffix (the generated output)
is fundamentally different.
   Prefill is the first pass over the prompt. The model reads every token of the input context,
computes attention over the entire prefix, and produces the first output token. During prefill, the
model attends over all input positions, so the attention work grows with the square of the context
length. (The full prefill also has a substantial linear-in-L component — the weight-matmul FLOPs,



                                                 13
What Actually Happens During Inference                                                                 14


2N L — which does not grow quadratically; the quadratic term is the dense-attention pairwise
component, developed in Ch 8 and Ch 22.)
    Timing convention (used throughout the book). We attribute the first sampled token to prefill:
prefill = processing the prompt + sampling token 1, and decode = the per-token loop that begins
with token 1 as its first input and produces token 2 onward. This is the standard TTFT convention —
time-to-first-token includes the first token’s sampling, so the first token is the last output of prefill,
not the first output of decode. (Some engines split this differently — e.g. counting the first token’s
forward pass as the first decode step — but the difference is one token’s worth of latency, and every
formula and figure in this book uses the convention above.)
    Decode is the per-token generation that follows. After prefill, each new token only attends to the
cached keys and values from the prefix plus all previously generated tokens. In the batch-1-equivalent
weight-streaming model we use for this first-pass arithmetic, the per-step cost has two parts: the
weight-read (the entire model weight matrix from HBM, constant in context length because the
auto-regressive pass reuses the same parameters every step) and the attention over the growing
KV cache (linear in context length, since each new token attends to all cached keys/values). At the
canonical operating point the weight-read dominates, so the per-step cost is approximately constant
in context length — but that is a regime statement, not an identity; the attention term grows with
context and is the one that eventually binds at long context (Ch 8, Ch 22). (In a real serving stack,
batching and weight-read amortization change this per-request picture substantially; that is the
subject of later chapters.)
    The critical architectural insight, at the canonical low-batch operating point: prefill tends to be
compute-bound (high arithmetic intensity — the whole prompt is processed in one parallel pass),
while decode tends to be bandwidth-bound (low weight-reuse efficiency — the 140 GB weight matrix
is re-read every step for a single token). These are the typical bottlenecks, and confusing them is the
most common architectural misstep. But neither is a universal physical law: the characterization is
an operating-point property of model × workload × kernel × hardware (batch size, attention length,
and kernel fusion all shift it), and the roofline framework in Ch 8 is what identifies which regime a
given kernel actually sits in.
    One detail the figure makes explicit is when a token’s K/V enters the cache. The first decode
step, precisely: (a) prefill populates the cache with the prefix K/V and samples the first token; (b)
that first token is the input that seeds the decode loop (the green initialize path in Fig 2.1); (c) each
decode step takes one input token, runs the transformer on it — which computes and appends
that input token’s K/V to the cache — attends over the cached K/V, and samples the next token
from the logits; (d) the sampled next token is the output of this step and the input of the following
step, whose forward pass then computes and appends its K/V. A token’s K/V therefore enters the
cache on the step in which it is the input, not on the step in which it is sampled.

    This is the figure the rest of the book builds on. Each later chapter develops one part of it. Chapter
3 (model) asks what the blocks compute and how the KV cache is sized; Chapter 6 (metrics) measures
which phase is the bottleneck; Chapter 7 (memory) prices the KV cache precisely; Chapter 8
(compute) derives the FLOPs and roofline that make prefill compute-bound; Chapter 10 (parallelism)
splits the model across the devices the pipeline traverses; Chapter 11 (serving) schedules many
of these pipelines; Chapter 15 (performance) diagnoses which phase actually hurts; and the fleet
chapters price the host count the loop demands. Because the two phases stress different resources,
the structure of the whole book rests on this single split.
    Where the Q/K/V and KV cache live in this picture (the bridge to Ch. 3/7). The transformer
layer computes, for each token, three learned projections — query (Q), key (K) and value (V).
Attention scores are the similarity of a query to every prior key; the scores weight the values, which
are blended into the token’s new representation. What matters for architecture: K and V for a token
do not change once that token has been processed. The query for a later token attends against
them, but rewriting them would be redundant work. So decode does not recompute the prefix’s K/V
— it reuses the stored K and V from prefill. That is the KV cache: not an optimization bolted on, but
the direct consequence of which projections are reusable and which (the query) is always new. It
is also why KV memory grows with sequence length (one K and one V per token, per layer), why
attention architecture and precision (GQA/MQA, KV quantization) change the bytes-per-token of
what is really a memory problem, and why kernel choices like FlashAttention change the traffic, not
the footprint. Ch. 3 and Ch. 7 do the arithmetic; this figure is where the causal thread starts.

    The discipline the book applies everywhere: every optimization is a hypothesis about which
resource it shifts and what it trades away. FlashAttention moves the bottleneck from bandwidth
toward compute (fewer HBM round-trips); KV quantization trades capacity for a small precision
loss; prefix caching trades prefill compute for cache residency; continuous batching trades latency
for utilization; P/D disaggregation trades a homogeneous pool’s simplicity for separate compute- vs
bandwidth-optimized pools. When the book introduces a technique, it will name the resource it
targets and the resource it costs — that is the difference between reasoning and a vendor catalog. The
optimization decision map (Ch. 15) is this framework read backwards: from an observed symptom to
the resource that is likely starved.
    The causal chain (how the chapters hold together). The book is one argument, not a set of
topics. The thread is:
    tokens determine sequence length → sequence length determines KV growth and attention work
→ KV growth determines memory pressure → attention and model execution determine compute
and bandwidth demand → those resource demands determine latency behavior → latency and
concurrency determine scheduler requirements → scheduler behavior determines serving efficiency
→ serving efficiency and SLOs determine host count → host count and model topology determine
interconnect and fleet architecture → fleet architecture determines cost, resilience, placement, and
operational complexity.
    Every chapter is one link of that chain, and each deepens the same mental model from Ch. 2
rather than restarting it. By the time the argument reaches Ch. 11 (serving) or Ch. 17 (fleet), the
concepts were introduced in Ch. 2 — Ch. 2 gave the shape, the later chapters give the numbers and
the decisions. If a chapter ever feels like “here is another concept,” it has broken the thread.

2.2. Mental Model

     Inference is two fundamentally different physical processes, distinguished by what limits them.
     In the canonical operating point — a long prompt with high arithmetic intensity —
prefill is compute-bound. It is like a massive industrial fire hose drawing one enormous burst
of water out of a reservoir: the flow is huge, and the time it takes is limited entirely by the raw
horsepower of the pump (compute/FLOPs) pushing the water. The pipe is wide open, but the motor
is working at its absolute limit — and the burst delivers the first glass of water, the first token. (This
is an operating-point property, not a fixed identity: a low-intensity prefill or a tiny prompt could
shift it toward the bandwidth side — Ch. 8 makes the dependence on model × workload × kernel ×
hardware explicit.)
     In the canonical operating point — low batch — decode is bandwidth-bound. It is like
pushing the water of that same 140,000-liter reservoir (140 GB) through a standard garden hose: the
whole volume must flow every 25 milliseconds just to deliver one glass of water — one generated token.
The pump (compute) is more than powerful enough, but the diameter of the hose (HBM bandwidth)
physically cannot move that volume of water in that time frame. (Again an operating-point property,
not an identity: at high batch decode can become compute-bound.)
     When we ask “is this workload compute-bound or bandwidth-bound?” the answer depends
entirely on which physical constraint we are hitting: the horsepower of the engine, or the diameter
of the pipe.
What Actually Happens During Inference                                                             20


    Figure convention (used throughout the book). Arrows in the diagrams carry different
meanings by context, and the reader should not assume one universal reading: a data-flow arrow
(Fig 2.1, 11.3) shows tokens or activations moving; a dependency arrow shows “must be decided
before”; an influence arrow (Fig 4.1) shows “constrains/informs”; a causation arrow (Fig 6.1) shows
“drives / causes”; and a conceptual-association arrow (App. A.4) shows “relates to.” Where a figure’s
arrows are ambiguous, the caption states the intended reading.
2.3. Worked Example

    To make the distinction concrete, let us walk through the canonical enterprise Q&A scenario
from canonical scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2): a 70B-class dense model in FP16, 1 host with 8×H100 GPUs,
prompt of 1,200 tokens + 8K retrieved context (~9.2K input), 300-token output, TTFT budget 1.2 s
(retrieval ~120 ms + prefill), TPOT budget ~25 ms/token. All numbers are derived from the canonical
scenario; none are measurement claims. Where the book writes Analytical bound — not a benchmark,
it marks a first-order model check under a stated bounding assumption, not a measurement of actual
serving throughput. Scope of the single-host premise. Throughout this chapter and the arithmetic
chapters that follow, “1 host with 8×H100” is a per-host / per-request feasibility container: it
asks whether one host can meet the per-request latency and memory SLO (TTFT 1.2 s, TPOT ~25
ms, KV residency) for a single in-flight request. It is not a claim that one host serves the canonical
10 rps average / 40 rps peak arrival rate. The per-request arithmetic here answers “does one host’s
compute/bandwidth/memory satisfy one request’s latency budget”; the capacity question — how
many such hosts to absorb λ = 40 rps, where in-flight concurrency λ·W ≈ 344 at the ~8.6 s service
time — is answered later (Ch 16–17), and is a different computation that must not be conflated with
per-request feasibility. Keeping the two questions separate is the difference between sizing a host
and sizing a fleet.

    Worked example arithmetic details:

    • Decode bandwidth. In auto-regressive decode, generating one token requires a full forward
      pass of the 70B parameter matrix. At FP16 (2 bytes per parameter), the weight footprint is
      W = N ×2 = 140 GB. This is the aggregate model-wide weight traffic — but note the unit
      of comparison carefully. Name it precisely: this 140 GB is the logical model-weight footprint
      used as a first-order HBM traffic approximation (what later chapters call the canonical
      weight-stream approximation). It is the footprint that results from reading every parameter
      once per decode step in a dense model with no reuse, not a claim about physical HBM traffic
      in a real engine. Physical traffic depends on residency, caching hierarchy, fusion, batching,
      quantization, sharding, and implementation, and rises or falls accordingly. For a hypothetical
      single-device implementation holding the entire FP16 model, the aggregate model-weight
      traffic per decode step is ~140 GB; on a tensor-parallel deployment both weight residency
      and this traffic are sharded across GPUs, so the relevant comparison is per-GPU shard traffic
      against per-GPU HBM bandwidth, plus communication overhead. (A 140-GB FP16 model
      cannot reside on a single 80-GB H100 anyway, so the whole-model-on-one-GPU comparison
      is deliberately hypothetical.) With a TPOT budget of ~25 ms per token, the aggregate required

    • Prefill FLOPs. The prefill pass computes attention over the 9.2K input tokens and produces
      the first output token. The parameterized-linear FLOP floor for a dense transformer forward
      pass is well approximated as 2 × params × tokens (the factor of 2 accounts for multiply-add
      per parameter per token). Call this what it is: the parameterized-linear FLOP floor, 2N L,
      excluding explicit attention-score/value aggregation and other non-matmul overhead.
      The full-attention component is not captured by 2N L — it grows ~quadratically with sequence
      length (Ch 22), so for a 9.2K-token prefill 2N L is a lower bound on total compute, not the
      whole story. Thus:




     prefill FLOPs = 2 × N × L = 2 × 70 × 109 × 9.2 × 103 ≈ 1.288 × 1015 ≈ 1.29 PFLOP

assumptions. The prefill phase is compute-bound for the separate reason given in Table 2-1: arithmetic
intensity ~9.2K FLOP/byte > ridge ~295 [canonical scenario][DERIVED]. Note the direction of this
argument: exceeding the theoretical peak proves the target is impossible on a single H100 under the
stated model, but it does not imply any rate below the peak is achievable — real kernels land well
under MFU 100%. Meeting the latency SLO therefore calls for multiple GPUs (model parallelism or
data parallelism) or more efficient attention implementations.

2.4. Measurement

     How do we know whether a given workload is prefill-dominant or decode-dominant in practice?
Three practical measurements:
     1. Divide the TTFT into retrieval + prefill. Measure the retrieval latency (vector search,
       document fetch) separately from the prefill latency (prompt processing). In the canonical
       scenario, retrieval takes ~120 ms, leaving ~1.08 s for prefill on a 9.2K-token prompt. If prefill
       exceeds this budget, the bottleneck is compute or memory, not retrieval.

     2. Log TPOT against current sequence length, at controlled batch/concurrency. Track the
       time-per-token as the generated sequence grows. This is a scaling curve, not a binary verdict.
       An increasing TPOT as the sequence lengthens reveals growing KV-attention cost — each
       new token attends over a longer KV sequence, and decode attention work and KV cache traffic
       generally grow with sequence length even though cached K/V projections are not recomputed.
       A relatively flat TPOT suggests weight streaming (a fixed per-step cost — reading the full
       140 GB weight matrix each step) remains dominant. TPOT does not have to stay constant;
       batching, kernel choice, occupancy, and scheduling can make the observed curve complicated,
       so measure it rather than asserting a trend.

     3. Measure actual HBM utilization vs FLOP utilization. Using GPU profilers (NVIDIA Nsight,
       vLLM stats), watch the fraction of peak HBM bandwidth consumed versus the fraction of peak
       FLOPS consumed. If HBM utilization is near 100% while FLOPS utilization is low, the kernel is
       bandwidth-bound (typical of decode). If FLOPS utilization is near 100% while HBM utilization
       is low, the kernel is compute-bound (typical of prefill).

     These measurements cost nothing but a profiler attach and a few representative requests — and
they prevent the architect from applying the wrong optimization lever.


2.5. Common Mistakes

     • Treating prefill and decode as the same bottleneck. A dangerous mistake is assuming that
       what slows prefill will also slow decode, or vice versa. Prefill FLOPs scale with input length;
       decode bandwidth is constant per token. Confusing the two leads to over-provisioning compute
       for a bandwidth-bound workload, or under-provisioning compute for a compute-bound one.

     • Assuming one H100 suffices for 70B inference. The arithmetic in §2.3 shows that a single
       H100 cannot meet the decode bandwidth demand (5.6 TB/s vs 3.35 TB/s) nor the prefill compute
       demand (1.19 PFLOPS required vs 0.989 PFLOPS peak, from 1.29 PFLOP / 1.08 s). Attributing
       70B serveability to a single GPU ignores the opposite bottlenecks and produces an architecture
       that fails latency SLOs.
What Actually Happens During Inference                                                                 26


    • Ignoring the input/output token asymmetry. A workload with 9.2K input tokens and
      300 output tokens imposes a substantial prefill compute burden despite producing relatively
      few output tokens — output-token count alone does not determine serving cost or resource
      pressure. The two legs of the request have different cost structures and different optimization
      paths: decode is repeated per output token and dominates wall-clock latency (at the canonical
      ~25 ms/token, 300 output tokens take ~7.5 s of decode vs a ~1.08 s prefill budget), while prefill is
      a large one-shot burst of compute and dominates the compute burden (the 9.2K-input attention
      pass). Quoting only per-token latency or only throughput/s hides this distinction.

    • Using manufacturer-peak bandwidth/FLOPS without mapping to real kernels. H100
      3.35 TB/s HBM3 is the theoretical peak; actual sustained bandwidth for weight-read kernels
      may be 60–80% of peak. H100 989 TFLOPS BF16 dense is the tensor-core peak; actual matmul
      throughput depends on kernel fusion, batching, and precision. Citing raw numbers without
      kernel context is an anti-catalog error — the number must be matched to the actual serving
      kernel in use.


2.6. Architecture Consequence

    The opposite bottlenecks of prefill and decode have immediate architectural consequences:
    • With prefill in the compute-bound regime → optimization levers: kernel fusion (flash-
      attention, scaled-dot-product attention with fewer reads), model parallelism (splitting the
      70B parameters across GPUs), more GPUs in parallel, or prefill-specific servers that dedicate
      hardware to the bursty preload phase. Lowering precision (FP8, or BF16 in place of FP16)
      does not reduce the underlying algorithmic operation count (the usual 2 × params × tokens
      FLOPs are approximately unchanged — the matmuls still multiply the same matrices); rather it
      reduces the precision, lowers the bytes transferred/stored, and can raise the effective accelerator
      throughput (8-bit tensor cores run at higher peak rate).

    • With decode in the bandwidth-bound regime → optimization levers: continuous batch­
      ing (vLLM, PagedAttention) to amortize weight reads across many tokens in flight, KV cache
      offloading to SSD or system memory, P/D (prefill/decode) disaggregation (separate pools of
      GPUs for prefill bursts vs. decode steady state), and higher-bandwidth memory topologies
      (NVSwitch, HBM3e).

    The key architectural decision this enables: can we disaggregate prefill and decode onto
different hardware? If prefill needs more FLOPS and decode needs more bandwidth, a single
homogeneous GPU pool is suboptimal. A two-pool architecture — a prefill cluster optimized for
compute (more GPUs, higher FLOPS) and a decode cluster optimized for bandwidth (faster HBM,
larger NVLink domains) — is therefore an architecture worth testing. Whether it actually needs fewer
GPUs is not established by the asymmetry alone: it depends on achievable utilization, duplicated model
27                                                                What Actually Happens During Inference


residency, KV-transfer cost, interconnect topology, workload shape, burstiness, and the hardware
assigned to each pool, all of which must be measured. (The asymmetry makes it a candidate worth
benchmarking, not a concluded win.) This is the central theme of Chapter 11 (Serving) and the
prefill/decode-disaggregation pattern (Ch 12, candidate b).


2.7. What We Still Don’t Know

     • Sustained HBM bandwidth for weight-read kernels. The 3.35 TB/s H100 figure is a
      theoretical peak; real serving kernels (vLLM, TGI, transformer-engine) may achieve different
      sustained rates depending on kernel fusion, graph optimization, and batch size. — a hypothesis
      to be measured on real hardware before it is cited.

     • Effect of continuous batching on the 2 × params × tokens approximation. Continuous
      batching amortizes weight reads and improves hardware utilization, scheduling efficiency,
      and aggregate goodput — but it does not reuse one request’s transformer activations to avoid
      the forward-pass work of another unrelated request, so it does not reduce the mathematical
      FLOP count per request. Compute that is re-used across requests sharing a common prefix is
      a different mechanism: prefix caching (or KV reuse), which skips the re-prefill of a shared
      prefix and thereby does cut real forward-pass work for that portion. The magnitude of the
      prefix-cache hit rate at fleet scale is not yet pinned down. — to be benchmarked with realistic
      concurrency patterns.

     • Cross-technology bandwidth numbers. Name the SKU, not the memory class: the H200
      (HBM3e successor to the H100) is 4.8 TB/s, B200-class HBM3e is ~8 TB/s, and AMD MI300X is
      ~5.3 TB/s. How these compare to the 5.6 TB/s decode demand shifts the GPU count equation
      but does not change the fundamental bandwidth-bound vs compute-bound classification.
      [1P][FACT] — vendor-published specifications as of the 2026-08-30 cutoff; verify against the
      specific generation in use.

     • Effect of quantization on decode bandwidth vs prefill FLOPs. Int4 or FP8 quantization
      reduces the weight bytes (e.g., 70B at FP8 = 70 GB instead of 140 GB), which directly lowers the
      HBM read demand in decode; it does not reduce the algorithmic operation count of the matmuls
      (the 2 × params × tokens FLOPs are approximately unchanged), though lower precision can
      raise the effective throughput of the tensor cores at which those ops run. The direction of the
      shift is clear (decode bandwidth improves; prefill ceiling rises in effective rate), but the precise
      trade-off point where decode becomes compute-bound rather than bandwidth-bound depends
      on the quantization scheme and hardware support. — workload-dependent.
What Actually Happens During Inference                                                           28


2.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: TTFT and the Prefill/Decode Split

The architect is still in the early design conversation about the internal Q&A tool described in
Chapter 1. The team has settled on a 70B-class dense model for accuracy, and they have a rough
traffic estimate: ~2,000 registered employees, each roughly as active as the canonical scenario (~10
requests/s average, peaks ~40 rps), with prompts of ~1,200 tokens of internal documents plus ~8K
retrieved context and ~300 tokens of answer.
    From the unit-and-token work of Ch 1 alone, the architect can already state the hard numbers:
each request carries ~9.2K input tokens and ~300 output tokens. At 10 rps average, the system
must sustain ~92,000 input tokens/s in prefill and ~3,000 output tokens/s in decode. At 40 rps peak,
those numbers jump to ~368,000 and ~12,000 respectively. The architect can also state the two
opposite bottlenecks: prefill will be compute-bound (~1.29 PFLOP per request at 9.2K input), and
decode will be bandwidth-bound (a ~140 GB/token weight-read requiring ~5.6 TB/s sustained over
each ~25 ms decode step). The team’s immediate architectural choice is whether to build a single
homogeneous GPU cluster or to separate prefill and decode pools — the differing bottleneck profiles
make disaggregation worth evaluating, though whether it uses fewer GPUs must be measured rather
than assumed (Ch 11).
    Before passing this workload to Chapter 4 (workload anatomy), the architect locks in one more
number: the tokens-per-request split. This is the currency every downstream chapter will price
against, and it has already been established as ~9.2K input + ~300 output per request. The rest of
the design — model fitting, memory budget, latency budget, cost — can now proceed in token-
denominated terms.
chapter 3.


Understanding the Model




The Architect’s Question

After this chapter we should be able to reason about what a model’s parameter structure means
for deployment: dense versus Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), total parameters versus active parameters
per token, and what each implies for compute budgets and memory budgets. We will meet the
mechanisms (how MoE routes, how attention weights are computed) not to learn how to train a
model but so that, as architects, we can look at a model card and immediately know whether the
quoted parameter count is what we actually pay for at inference time, and whether the KV cache
will grow as expected. After this chapter we can ask: given a workload and a model architecture, what
is the real residency and compute cost per token?


3.1. Concept

The parameter allocation regime of a model determines how many of its weights are touched on
each forward pass. This regime is not a property of the model family name alone; it is a consequence
of the training objective and the routing mechanism.

    • Dense models activate all parameters for every token. A 70B dense model reads all 70B
      weights (or close to it) for every token, because every layer’s full hidden dimension participates
      in every attention and feed-forward computation. The parameter count on the model card is
      the inference cost count.
    • Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models route each token to a fraction of the total parameters. A
      MoE model may have 236B total parameters (an illustrative figure) distributed across eight
      experts, but only the top-2 (or top-1) experts are activated per token. The quoted total parameter



                                                    29
Understanding the Model                                                                              30


      count includes the unused experts; the active parameter count per token is the fraction that
      routing selects.

    The architect-relevant distinction: total parameters ≠ active parameters per token. This
inequality is the single most important number to read from a model card when sizing a deployment,
because it directly changes the compute cost per token. However, the KV cache does not share this
privilege — we will show why MoE sparsity saves compute but not memory.


3.1.1. Alternative inference: the token is not the execution step

Dense versus MoE describes parameter allocation. Autoregressive versus diffusion generation de­
scribes a different axis: how the model constructs an output and which intermediate states it revisits.
A diffusion language model can itself be dense or MoE. The active-parameter count still matters,
but final output tokens no longer count the model’s work on their own. We also need the sequence
of model evaluations, the positions recomputed in each evaluation, and the point at which output
becomes final. The mechanisms below are first-party to their papers and released code; the accounting
interpretation is derived.


From corruption to learned generation

A diffusion model learns to reverse a specified corruption process. In a continuous denoising diffusion
model, the forward process progressively adds noise to data. Training constructs corrupted examples
and teaches a model to predict information needed for the reverse process, such as the added noise
(Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models). At generation time, sampling starts from a simple prior
and repeatedly applies learned reverse updates. The forward process is not an inference pipeline
that first corrupts the requested answer: the answer is not available during generation. The forward
process defines the learning problem. [1P][FACT]
    Score-based formulations express related dynamics through the score, the gradient of the log
density of perturbed data (Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equa­
tions). The associated reverse-time stochastic differential equation and probability-flow ordinary
differential equation provide different sampling trajectories. In the ideal formulation they can share
time-marginal distributions; this does not make their finite-step numerical errors, randomness
or network-evaluation counts identical. A deterministic solver can still require many sequential
evaluations. [1P][FACT]
    Text requires a discrete construction because token IDs are categories, not continuous pixel values.
Discrete diffusion defines corruption through transitions between categorical states. Uniform token
replacement and an absorbing MASK state are different choices (Structured Denoising Diffusion
Models in Discrete State-Spaces). In masked diffusion, training hides selected tokens and learns to
recover them from the visible sequence. MDLM (Simple and Effective Masked Diffusion Language
Models) and LLaDA (Large Language Diffusion Models, generation code) connect this procedure to

diffusion likelihood objectives; it is not merely a fixed-rate masked-language-model loss with a new

learn transport and can iteratively rectify the coupling (Flow Straight and Fast). Straight training
interpolants do not guarantee that any trained model has perfectly straight generation trajectories
or equal-quality one-step sampling. The shared systems question is repeated model evaluation along
a path. The objectives and samplers remain distinct. [1P][FACT]
Understanding the Model                                                                               32


A language-generation trajectory

A basic masked language sampler allocates an output canvas containing unresolved positions. Each
evaluation predicts token distributions using the current canvas and the prompt. The sampler accepts
some predictions and leaves other positions unresolved. A confidence policy may accept several
positions at once, so generation need not advance strictly left to right. In the inspected LLaDA base
sampler (observation 2026-10-28), already accepted token IDs are retained; remasking low-confidence
candidates does not mean that every accepted token is repeatedly edited. The configured output
capacity and evaluation schedule still determine work even when later display logic removes an EOS
suffix. [1P][FACT]
    Parallel predictions are not free joint reasoning. Several position-wise predictions from one
canvas evaluation are conditioned on the old canvas, not necessarily on one another’s newly sampled
values. Individually plausible tokens can form an implausible combination. Confidence thresholds,
extra rounds and verification can improve this tradeoff, but they change the amount of work and
may change task quality. A lower iteration count is therefore not a quality-neutral implementation
improvement by default. [1P][FACT]
    The inference loop is also not an agent loop. An agent turn may invoke a model, inspect a tool
result and decide its next action. A diffusion round updates an internal output state. An autoregressive
model with a long chain of thought remains autoregressive. A diffusion draft model can also propose
blocks for an autoregressive verifier, as in DFlash; that combination does not turn the verifier’s target
distribution into a fully diffusion-based language model. [1P][FACT]


State reuse follows dependency boundaries

The ordinary causal-cache argument depends on a fixed prefix. Later output tokens cannot change an
earlier token’s causal hidden state. Under bidirectional attention, an unchanged token ID can acquire a
different representation when another canvas position changes. Its previous K/V tensors can therefore
be stale even though its spelling is unchanged. Approximate cache policies exploit empirical stability,
delayed caching or selective refresh; those policies require quality and refresh-cost measurements.
Fast-dLLM and dKV-Cache are concrete examples, not proof that ordinary autoregressive caching
transfers unchanged. [1P][FACT]
    A block-causal model creates a stronger boundary. Earlier finalized blocks cannot depend on later
blocks, while the active block can use bidirectional attention internally (Block Diffusion). The runtime
can reuse correctly finalized prefix state and repeatedly recompute the active block. Finalization
must make cached state correspond to the accepted block contents; accepting token IDs alone is not
always enough. DiffusionGemma (model card, Google release post) uses a related separation between
cached encoded context and a mutable decoder canvas, then encodes the completed canvas before
continuing. These are architectural boundaries, not a universal property of the word “diffusion.” [1P]
[FACT]

    Not every language diffusion process starts from MASK or only fills holes. Uniform-state renois­
ing can begin with ordinary token states. Editing models can replace accepted tokens or perform
insertion/deletion operations within a bounded block. LLaDA2.2 (paper, checkpoint) restores its
configured block length after such operations; this is not an unbounded global canvas. A stopping rule
may test unresolved positions, stability, confidence, EOS or an iteration limit. These are operational
termination rules, not proofs of semantic correctness. [1P][FACT]
    The architectural consequence is conditional, and it is the reason this section sits in the model-
understanding chapter rather than in a serving chapter. Parallel positions can improve matrix
utilization at low request concurrency, but repeated evaluation can increase total compute and
communications. Block size changes both parallel work and the delay before commitment. A useful
deployment comparison therefore fixes the task-quality requirement first, then measures the inference
schedule, peak state and committed-output latency together. The token remains the application
interface; the execution trace connects that interface to resources. [DERIVED]
    A note on provenance: the total-versus-active distinction arises from the training regime. In
dense pre-training, every token sees the full model gradient; in MoE pre-training, a routing loss
directs each token to the most relevant expert(s), and the unused experts receive no gradient for that
step. The routing mechanism itself (top-k, importance sampling, learned gates) is an architectural
decision that outlives training and becomes a deployment fact.


3.2. Mental Model

    A model’s parameters form a resource pool that is allocated differently depending on the routing
regime.
    • In a dense model, the pool is fully allocated every time. If the model is 70B params in FP16, we
      need 140 GB of weight memory available for every token. There is no “spending less” — the
      full 140 GB is the residency floor.
    • In an MoE model, the pool is fractionally allocated. The total pool may be large (reflecting
      the model’s capacity and training compute), but what we actually wire up per token is a slice.
      With top-2 routing from 8 experts, roughly 2/8 = 25% of the total parameter mass is active per
      token. This fraction saves compute (fewer FLOPs) but the attention layers still see every token,
      so the KV cache still grows with context length just as in a dense model.

    The durable mental model: total parameters set the ceiling; active parameters per token
set the floor. The architect must track both numbers.
