      dominates on TCO. Fine‑tuning should be a deliberate choice triggered by a sustained query
      volume, not a default.


5.6. Architecture Consequence

    Whatever we learned here, file it under “can I size the workload before I pick a model?”
Concretely, the decision this chapter enables is:
   • Estimate tokens‑per‑request (input and output separately), and therefore tokens‑per‑second
      capacity and cost, before choosing a model or a serving configuration.
    • Use the selection surfaces (quality, latency, KV cost, cost/token, retrieve‑vs‑generate) to narrow
      the model space from the full vendor catalog to a handful of viable candidates.
    • For RAG workloads, select the embedding model and generation model as a two‑part decision,
      not a single choice. The embedding model is chosen at ingestion time (compute‑light, stor­
      age‑bound); the generation model is chosen at serving time (compute‑bound, latency‑bound).

    This consequence feeds directly into the fine-tuning-for-specific-workloads pattern and the RAG
pattern (both cataloged in Ch 26, Patterns Library): the architect first characterizes the workload,
then lets the characterization speak the model selection, not the other way around.


5.7. What We Still Don’t Know

    HYPOTHESIS: the interaction between embedding dimension and retrieval quality across diverse
enterprise domains is not yet characterized with reproducible benchmarks. Early evidence suggests
768 dim is a sweet spot, but the quality difference between 768 and 1024 dim varies by corpus genre
(legal vs. engineering vs. creative), and no public study quantifies this domain‑dependence.
    HYPOTHESIS: the break‑even point between RAG + guardrails and fine‑tuned models as a
function of query volume and domain specialization is model‑ and domain‑dependent: it is set
by the Q∗ equation above (training + storage cost over the quality uplift), not by a universal rule of
thumb. Any quoted break‑even volume is a derived scenario value; more data points and a measured
∆Q are needed before it can be stated as a general principle.
    HYPOTHESIS: guardrail latency (PII redaction, refusal checking) on generated 300‑token outputs,
~2–8 ms/request on CPU in the illustrative scenario; measure on the target stack (the figure depends
on the guardrail implementation and hardware).
    Each of these flags is an open empirical question a team should resolve against its own target
workload — resolved by measurement into [1P][FACT] or [2°][FACT], promoted to [1P][DERIVED]
or [2°][DERIVED] where the resolution is arithmetic, or dropped — rather than left as an untested
assumption.

     An architect is assembled for a design review of the enterprise Q&A tool described in Chapter
4 — the canonical workload (Ch 4, Table 4-2). The team has agreed on the retrieval architecture:
vector search with embeddings, 768‑dim all‑mpnet‑base‑v2, late‑interaction (MaxSim) retrieval over

     • 768‑dim embeddings give adequate retrieval quality at ~1 GFLOPs per embedding, with ~3.1
       GB index storage for a 1 M‑chunk corpus (vs ~1.5 GB at 384‑dim) — a persistent footprint that
       scales with corpus size, alongside the 70B base model.
     • 9.2K input at ~2.62 MB/KV‑token costs ~24.1 GB of cache (initial) on the 70B generation model,
       well within the 8×H100 node’s 640 GB HBM. The prefill TTFT of ~1.08 s plus retrieval (~120
       ms) sits at the 1.2 s TTFT budget, with the p95 ≤ 2 s SLO giving the real margin.
     • The 30× input‑vs‑output ratio means this system is prefill‑dominated; model selection must
       weigh KV cache cost and prefill throughput more heavily than decode throughput.
     • The base‑model + RAG + guardrails paradigm produces the lower modeled TCO under the
       illustrative cost and quality assumptions used in this worked example (see the parametric Q∗
       break‑even above). This is not a general 10× cost relationship — the actual ratio depends on
       the domain‑specific quality uplift and the query volume, and must be measured rather than
       assumed.

     The architect now has a concrete model shortlist: 768‑dim all‑mpnet‑base‑v2 for the retrieval
leg, and the 70B FP16 base model for the generation leg (dense — the MoE challenger from Ch 3
was rejected on residency and KV grounds), served on 8×H100 with vLLM continuous batching. No
fine‑tuning is needed at this scale. The architecture decision record (to be written in Chapter 25) will
reference this characterization and the selection surfaces that drove it.

Measuring What Matters: From Telemetry to
Architecture Decisions




The Architect’s Question

After this chapter we should be able to walk into a running inference system, read its metrics, and
answer a deceptively hard question: is this system meeting its obligations, and if not, which lever do
we pull? Teams commonly instrument the wrong thing — model capability and offline quality —
and then are blind when a real workload misbehaves. This chapter builds the metric hierarchy that
turns raw telemetry into architecture decisions: what to log, what each number means, how to read a
latency distribution instead of a mean, and how to tell bandwidth-bound from compute-bound purely
from the counters. After this chapter, “the system felt slow” becomes a falsifiable, diagnosable claim.


6.1. Concept

6.1.1. The Metric Hierarchy

Not all numbers are equal. We organize serving telemetry into three layers, each answering a different
question and each consumed by a different role:

   1. Workload metrics — what the system is being asked to do. Requests per second (rps), the
      token profile (input length, output length, context length), and concurrency. These are the
      independent variables; we do not control them, we characterize them. For the canonical
      enterprise-Q&A RAG workload these are fixed by canonical scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2): ~10 rps
      average with ~40 rps peaks, ~9,200 input + ~300 output tokens per request, TTFT 1.2 s / TPOT
      ~25 ms.



                                                  85
Measuring What Matters: From Telemetry to Architecture Decisions                                       86


   2. Serving metrics — how well the system performs under that workload. Time-to-first-token
      (TTFT), time-per-output-token (TPOT), inter-token latency, and goodput (tokens produced
      that actually meet the SLO). These are the dependent variables; they are what the SLO is
      written against.

   3. Resource metrics — why performance is what it is. HBM bandwidth utilization, FLOP
      utilization / model FLOPs utilization (MFU), KV cache occupancy, memory pressure, and
      queue depth. These reveal the binding constraint.

    The discipline this chapter works toward: never jump from a workload metric straight to a
serving metric, or a serving metric straight to a hardware conclusion. The causal direction is
workload → resource demand → serving behavior (the workload’s token profile drives the resource
demand; the resource supply shapes how the model behaves). Diagnosis runs the other way: a slow
response (serving) is diagnosed by asking whether the kernel is bandwidth- or compute-bound
(resource), which is only meaningful given the token profile (workload). Skipping a layer produces
superstition — “it’s slow, let’s buy GPUs” — instead of a mechanism.


6.1.2. Why the Wrong Metric Persists

Teams default to measuring what they already have dashboards for: model quality (accuracy, ROUGE,
benchmark scores) and average latency. Both are dangerously incomplete. Quality is the goal and
a feasibility gate — a fast or cheap architecture that fails the quality bar is disqualified before
performance even matters — but it is not the bottleneck that explains a resource or latency failure
once quality is acceptable; that is the role of the serving metrics. Average latency is a single scalar
that hides the tail that actually violates SLAs. The entire thesis of this chapter is that the metric that
drives an architecture decision is usually not the metric the model card advertises.


6.2. Mental Model

The three metric layers form a diagnostic chain, like the layers of the OSI stack in miniature:

    • Workload is the traffic — what we are asked to do.
    • Serving is the service — how well we did it.
    • Resource is the engine — how hard the machine is working, and on what.

    (The listing order here is by role — independent inputs, dependent outputs, explanatory engine.
It is not the causal order: causation flows workload → resource → serving, which is how Fig 6.1
stacks them top to bottom. The two orderings are different and both intentional.)
    When something breaks, we read upward: a p95 TTFT breach (serving) forces us to look at
the resource layer first (resource: is prefill queuing because we’re FLOP-bound?) and then the
token profile (workload: did context length grow?). The causal direction follows the system, not
87                                     Measuring What Matters: From Telemetry to Architecture Decisions




                                         Workload metrics

                                    rps · token profile · concurrency



                  causation                                                        diagnosis

                                         Resource metrics

                               GPU util · memory · bandwidth · KV cache




                                          Serving metrics

                                         TTFT · TPOT · goodput


      causation ↓ (workload → resource → serving) | diagnosis ↑ (serving → resource → workload)




       figure 6.1: The metric hierarchy as a diagnostic chain [ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual]
 The three metric layers and the bottom-up diagnostic path from a p95 TTFT breach to its root cause.
Causation runs downward (workload → resource demand → serving behavior); diagnosis runs upward
                    (serving symptom → resource evidence → workload/context).
Measuring What Matters: From Telemetry to Architecture Decisions                                       88


the diagnosis: the workload generates resource demand, and the resource supply shapes serving
behavior — so when numbers are healthy, the chain confirms our architecture was right.
    The mental model also warns against one number standing in for many different things.
“Throughput” without a qualifier is meaningless: is it requests per second, tokens per second, or
goodput — tokens per second that arrived before the SLO deadline? We commit to always qualifying.


6.3. Worked Example

6.3.1. Latency Is a Distribution, Not a Mean

A very common measurement error is reporting (and SLO-ing) the average latency. Fig 6.2 shows a
synthetic request stream: the body of requests follows a log‑normal distribution centered near 0.8
s (99% of observations), with a 1% straggler cluster at 5.0 s. That combination is deliberately not a
two‑point “99% at 0.8, 1% at 5” distribution; it is a realistic spread, so the percentiles below are read
off the plotted histogram rather than guessed. The plotted stream is a synthetic sample of N = 10,000
requests — 99% drawn from a log‑normal with median 0.8 s, 1% a straggler cluster at 5.0 s — and the
percentiles are read by linear interpolation on the sorted sample. The mean of that stream is

                               E[L] ≈ 0.99 × 0.8 + 0.01 × 5.0 ≈ 0.84 s

— looks fine. But the distribution actually has a long tail: p50 ≈ 0.80 s, p90 ≈ 0.94 s, p95 ≈ 0.99 s, and
p99 ≈ 1.33 s. The mean hides the tail; percentiles expose it — but notice how far one has to go to
expose this tail. Under the canonical p95 TTFT SLO of ≤ 2 s, even p99 (≈ 1.33 s) still looks healthy.
The 5 s stragglers are the top 1% of the stream — they sit between the 99th and 100th percentile,
so a p99 line alone does not bring them into view. Only the p99.9 / maximum reading (or the full
distribution) surfaces them. This is the sharper lesson: a tail can hide not just behind the mean but
behind any single percentile, and the choice of which percentile to SLO against matters. It is why we
log the full distribution and also watch the outlier fraction (how much probability mass sits beyond
the SLO line), not just one percentile.
    Why the mean is not a signal. The same request stream of 99% @ 0.8 s + 1% @ 5 s reported as a
single number looks healthy (mean ≈ 0.84 s; the figure’s exact simulated stream mean ≈ 0.85 s — the
0.84 is the two-point analytic approximation), yet p99 paints a very different picture under a 2 s SLO.
Log the distribution; SLO against the percentile.
    Apply this to the canonical workload. We budget TTFT ≤ 1.2 s (retrieval ~120 ms + prefill ~1.08
s) with a p95 ≤ 2 s. Suppose a flash crowd (the ~40 rps peak) causes prefill requests to queue. If on
average the batch is well-behaved, p50 TTFT might sit at ~1.0 s. But the jobs that arrive behind
~1–2 same-time prefill requests each pay the full 1.08 s prefill of the job(s) ahead of them, so p95
TTFT drifts to ~2.5 s. The average says “fine”; the p95 says “we just violated our SLO.” We hence
log p50, p90, p95, and p99 independently and run the SLO against the percentile, never the mean.

6.3.2. Goodput vs Raw Throughput

Deploying a higher-throughput configuration can reduce goodput. Concretely: suppose we enable
larger dynamic batching to raise raw tokens/s from 50 tok/s to 70 tok/s, but the batch window pushes
p95 TTFT from 1.8 s to 2.3 s — above the 2 s SLO. The extra 20 tok/s are produced, but they land in the
tail that misses the SLO, so goodput does not grow. Raw throughput is up 40%; goodput (tokens that
met the SLO) is effectively unchanged in this case, because the batch of SLO-compliant tokens didn’t
grow. (The general relation is goodput = raw_rate × compliant_fraction: if the compliant fraction
falls from 96% to 94%, goodput is 50×0.96 = 48 vs 70×0.94 = 65.8 — it rises despite the p95 breach.
The “unchanged” claim holds only when the extra tokens all land in the SLO-missing tail, i.e. the
compliant fraction drops proportionally to the raw-rate gain. A p95 breach is a configuration-level
acceptance signal; request-level SLO-goodput is a separate measurement and must be computed
from the compliant fraction, not inferred from the p95 alone.) Goodput is the metric the customer
experiences; raw throughput is what the GPU achieves. The architect optimizes goodput. This is
why “faster” hardware or bigger batches do not trivially mean a better system.


6.3.3. Detecting the Regime: Bandwidth-Bound vs Compute-Bound

The most decision-relevant resource question is: is this layer bandwidth-bound or compute-bound?
We recall the arithmetic from Chapter 2:

    • Decode is HBM-bandwidth-bound at low batch. Generating one token needs a full forward
      pass over the 70B weights of the canonical 80-layer, hidden-8192, full-MHA 70B reference
      = 140 GB (FP16) of reads per token — a batch-1-equivalent idealized weight-streaming read
      (one request’s full weight pass), not a measured bytes-physically-read figure. Within a ~25
      ms TPOT budget that demands 140 GB / 0.025 s ≈ 5.6 TB/s (batch-1-equivalent) of HBM
      bandwidth, against an H100’s ~3.35 TB/s peak [1P][FACT]. Scope warning: this 5.6-vs-3.35
      TB/s comparison is an illustrative single-device roofline argument, not the canonical
      8×H100 host’s actual deployment verdict. Two scope notes keep this honest. First, 5.6 TB/s
      is the aggregate model-wide weight-read rate for a hypothetical single-device implementation;
      under tensor parallelism (the canonical 8×H100 host) the 140 GB is sharded, so each GPU
      only needs ~0.70 TB/s against its own 3.35 TB/s — the single-device 5.6>3.35 bound does not
      itself show a per-GPU bandwidth shortfall. Second, the deeper and shard-invariant reason
      decode is memory-limited is its low arithmetic intensity (the ratio of FLOPs to bytes moved,
      ~1.0 FLOP/byte here) — far below the ~295 FLOP/byte roofline ridge point that separates
      memory-bound from compute-bound kernels (the roofline and its ridge are developed in Ch 8;
      this chapter only needs the qualitative point that a low intensity starves the compute units
91                                        Measuring What Matters: From Telemetry to Architecture Decisions


       for weights). That is what makes compute units starve for weights regardless of sharding. So
       the honest statement is: decode is memory-bound because its intensity is low and batching
       raises it, not merely because an aggregate 5.6 TB/s exceeds one GPU’s 3.35 [canonical scenario]
       [DERIVED]. (This is an operating-point property, not an identity: at high batch decode climbs
       the intensity slope and can become compute-bound.)

     • Prefill is compute-bound at the canonical long-prompt operating point. The reason
       prefill lands on the compute plateau of the roofline is its high arithmetic intensity: the FLOPs per
       byte moved are far above the ~295 FLOP/byte ridge point (developed in Ch 8), so the compute
       units — not the HBM weight stream — are the binding resource. Only after establishing that
       regime do we check the deadline: the prefill pass for 9,200 input tokens costs ≈ 2 ×70e9 params
       × 9.2e3 tokens ≈ 1.29 PFLOP, which against the ~1.08 s prefill budget implies a required rate of
       ≈ 1.19 PFLOPS — above a single H100’s ~0.989 PFLOPS dense BF16 peak (1.19 > 0.989). But that
       1.19-vs-0.989 comparison is a single-device deadline/capacity illustration, not the evidence
       that prefill is compute-bound: on the canonical 8×H100 host the aggregate peak is ~7.9 PFLOPS,
       so the host comfortably satisfies the rate — the “single H100 can’t prefill a 9.2K prompt in 1.08 s”
       conclusion is about whether one arbitrarily-chosen GPU can meet the deadline, not about the
       kernel’s roofline regime. Prefill being compute-bound (rather than bandwidth-bound) follows
       from its high arithmetic intensity, not from the 1.19-vs-0.989 comparison. [canonical scenario]
       [DERIVED]

     At the resource layer, the tell is utilization: a decode kernel pinned at ~95% of HBM bandwidth
but ~30% of FLOPs is bandwidth-bound; a prefill kernel with ~90% FLOP utilization is compute-bound.
The same hardware, the same model — the boundary flips between prefill and decode. This
is precisely why Splitwise/DistServe (and Mooncake’s KV-centric disaggregation) split prefill from
decode onto different pools: the bottleneck-regime difference justifies it. [S4][1P][FACT] (source
keys: each [S#] names one entry in the References chapter, where [S3]–[S7] resolve; Ch 11 lists
[S1]–[S6] inline.) These percentages are hypothetical telemetry signatures used to illustrate how to
read utilization — not a measured benchmark find from any trace. They are representative operating-point
values (a low-intensity decode kernel at high HBM-utilization/low FLOP-utilization, a high-intensity
prefill kernel at high FLOP-utilization), useful to classify a kernel’s regime; an actual deployment’s
percentages come from its own counters, and a real utilization reading (observed vs. theoretical peak
vs. required minimum) must be distinguished from these example values. See Ch 8 for the underlying
intensity/roofline arithmetic that shows why these regimes occur.

6.3.4. Reading Telemetry Into a Decision

A concrete dashboard-read → decision trace. We see: p95 TTFT climbing (serving), KV cache hit
ratio low (resource: memory), and prefill queue depth growing (serving). Workload is unchanged.
Reading up the chain: low prefix-cache hit means many independent 9.2K prefixes are being prefill-
processed from scratch on the ~40 rps peak — each ~1.29 PFLOP saturating FLOPs. The decision:
enable prefix / RadixAttention-style caching (SGLang) or Automatic Prefix Caching (vLLM) so shared
retrieved-context prefixes are reused instead of re-prefilled, cutting effective prefill FLOPs and TTFT.
[S3][1P][FACT] Prefix caching is a compute-saving move, not a latency tuning — and the telemetry
told us that.


6.4. Measurement

Three practical habits anchor the architect:
93                                       Measuring What Matters: From Telemetry to Architecture Decisions


     1. Instrument the hierarchy, not just the app. Deploy counters at all three layers from day
       one — rps and token profile (workload); TTFT/TPOT/goodput percentiles (serving); HBM
       bandwidth, FLOP/MFU, KV cache occupancy, queue depth (resource). A system that only logs
       serving metrics cannot tell why; one that only logs resource metrics cannot tell what it was
       asked.

     2. Always qualify “throughput.” rps ≠ tokens/s ≠ goodput. The same number, three stories.
       State the SLO window (p95 ≤ 2 s TTFT) before quoting any rate, or the rate is meaningless.

     3. Log the distribution. Capture p50/p90/p95/p99 for every latency metric, and the full token-
       length distribution (a 32K-tail context is a different workload than a 9.2K average). The mean
       is a summary, not a signal.

     These habits answer the book’s recurring question — what would we actually measure here? —
with three layers of counters at the edge, before any architecture decision is committed.


6.5. Common Mistakes
     • SLO-ing the average. A ~0.85 s mean (the figure’s simulated stream; the two-point analytic
       approximation gives ~0.84 s — the figure’s displayed value is used here) hides a 5 s tail. SLO
       against p95/p99, and watch the outlier fraction, not the mean.
     • Optimizing raw throughput when the SLO windows it. Bigger batches raise raw tokens/s
       but can push TTFT past its deadline, zeroing goodput. Optimize goodput.
     • Jumping straight to “buy more GPUs.” A bandwidth-bound decode and a prefill-cost
       problem need different fixes; without the resource layer we guess.
     • Treating hardware peak as a ceiling we can hit. H100’s 3.35 TB/s is the theoretical HBM
       peak; real memory-bound kernels realize a fraction of it. Design headroom against real utiliza­
       tion, not the spec sheet.
     • Conflating model-quality metrics with serving metrics. Accuracy is the goal; TTFT is
       the constraint. A slow, accurate model fails its SLO just as surely as a fast, wrong one.


6.6. Architecture Consequence

     The metric hierarchy directly dictates architecture. For the canonical workload:
     • Bandwidth-bound decode + compute-bound prefill ⇒ P/D disaggregation (Split­
       wise/DistServe/Mooncake) is the remedy at scale, because squeezing both regimes from one
       resource pool fights itself. [S4][1P][FACT]
     • Repeat-prefix RAG ⇒ enable prefix caching (RadixAttention/APC), which turns repeated
       9.2K prefills into cached lookups and defends the p95 TTFT against the 40 rps peaks. [S3][1P]
       [FACT]
Measuring What Matters: From Telemetry to Architecture Decisions                                     94


    • KV cache pressure ⇒ quantize or offload KV. FP8 KV = raw tensor byte-halving = 1.31
      MB/token (exactly 50% of BF16) [canonical scenario][DERIVED]; any block-allocation/meta­
      data overhead is NOT vendor-measured here and must be filled by a deployment benchmark.
      (The vLLM FP8-KV blog’s ‘54%’ is a decode-ITL latency slope, not a memory ratio.) And
      vLLM KV-offloading (its own 2026-01-08 blog [S7][1P][FACT]) cuts TTFT by 2–22× in a par­
      ticular warm-cache-hit/reuse benchmark, not a generic cold-cache improvement — both are
      memory-layer fixes the telemetry would call for when KV occupancy nears capacity.
    • Speculative decoding where decode bandwidth is the wall — DFlash reports over 6×
      lossless acceleration, up to 2.5× over EAGLE-3, in its paper’s evaluated configurations [S5]
      [1P][FACT] — because it reduces weight reads per accepted token. These are paper-reported
      results, not portable serving-speed figures: treat them as performance claims to re-measure on
      the target workload, not as a guaranteed speedup.


6.7. What We Still Don’t Know
    • Goodput in production is rarely published. The research corpus gives strong qualitative
      and some quantitative anchors (Mooncake 525% simulated throughput / 75% more requests
      [S4][1P][FACT], DFlash >6× [S5][1P][FACT]), but portable end-to-end goodput figures across
      real enterprise RAG workloads remain [UNRESOLVED].
    • Prefix-cache hit rates in mixed workloads are workload-dependent; the actual reduction
      in prefill FLOPs from APC/RadixAttention for a given document-retrieval distribution is
      [UNRESOLVED].
    • Tail-latency drivers under batching interact: batch size, arrival burstiness, and KV frag­
      mentation each affect p99 differently, and their joint effect is [UNRESOLVED].


6.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: The Post-Lunch Slowdown: Reading Telemetry
     Up the Chain

An on-call architect is paged: “the internal Q&A tool got slow after lunch.” The dashboard shows
rps at the ~40 rps peak (workload, up from the 10 rps baseline), p95 TTFT at 2.4 s against a 2
s SLO (serving, breached), and KV cache occupancy at 85% with low prefix-hit ratio (resource,
memory/FLOP pressure). Following the chain rather than guessing, the architect reads: a concurrency
spike (workload) with repeated full 9.2K prefills (low prefix hit) is saturating prefill FLOPs (compute-
bound). The architecture is memory- and compute-sane at the 10 rps design point but was never sized
for the lunch peak. The fix is not “buy GPUs immediately” — it is to enable prefix caching to collapse
the repeated prefills, which the telemetry shows will address the actual mechanism. The architect
re-checks the dashboard an hour later: p95 TTFT back under 2 s, goodput restored — because they
measured the right thing at the right layer.

chapter 7.


Memory Is the First Constraint




The Architect’s Question

After this chapter we should be able to answer the architect’s fundamental constraint question: does
the model and its context fit in the memory floor before we ask whether it can compute or communicate?
We will build the arithmetic for the KV cache from first principles, reconcile it with the canonical ~1.3
MB/token figure from Chapter 1, and contrast inference residency (weights + KV) with fine-tuning
residency (weights + gradients + optimizer states). The goal is to make “does it fit?” a concrete,
quantified check — not a back-of-the-envelope guess. Throughout, the arithmetic anchors to the
canonical enterprise-Q&A RAG scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2): ~10 rps average / ~40 rps peak traffic served
by a 70B FP16 model on an 8×H100 host. KV cache per-token figures are given at the referenced
precision throughout: ~1.3 MB/token at 8-bit (this is Chapter 1’s reference figure), ~2.62 MB/token
(exactly 2.5 MiB/token) at FP16 — and the canonical scenario’s KV constant is the FP16 2.62 MB/token
figure, not the 8-bit ~1.3 MB/token number.


7.1. Concept

Memory is the first constraint because every LLM workload begins with a residency check: can
the model and its active data structures be placed on the target hardware? The KV cache is the
primary expression of this constraint during inference: it grows linearly with context length, and its
size depends on the model’s layer count, hidden dimension, and the precision chosen for key and
value storage. Unlike FLOPs, which scale with operations per token, the KV cache occupies memory
continuously for the lifetime of a request — it is always resident, always consuming HBM bandwidth
for every re-read. The architect must therefore size two distinct memory loads: the static weight



                                                   96
97                                                                         Memory Is the First Constraint


footprint and the dynamic KV footprint that varies with prompt length. Quantization (FP8, FP4, 2-bit
asymmetric) reduces both, but the KV cache is the one component whose reduction must be quoted
per precision, not as a uniform factor: FP8 KV realizes ~50% in serving today (raw byte-halving),
while 4-bit KV’s raw bound is a full 4× (2.62 → 0.66 MB/token at this chapter’s geometry) — realized
savings land between, once per-block scale/offset metadata and per-token variation are counted —
rather than the single 2×–4× that weight-only quantization applies to weights. The residency floor
is therefore set by weights + KV (+ activations, in fine-tuning), and the architect’s first question is
whether this sum fits on the target GPUs. This is why “does it fit?” is the architect’s primary gate:
before we ask whether the model can compute or communicate, we must first establish that the
working set — weights plus the context-dependent KV state — resides on-GPU. If it does not, every
subsequent decision (offload, recompute, page) is a degradation, not a cost-optimization.
     The residency floor has two distinct regimes. For inference, the floor is weights + KV: the model’s
static parameters plus the context-dependent key/value tensors that grow with every token added to
the prompt. In fine-tuning, the floor rises further to weights + gradients + optimizer states, because
every parameter update requires its own momentum and velocity vectors (Adam) or per-parameter
scaling (LAMB/RMSProp). The contrast between these two floors — inference ~164.1 GB for a 70B
model at FP16 with 9.2K input (140 + 24.1; the 9.5K-max is 164.9 ≈ 165 GB) [canonical scenario]
[DERIVED], fine-tuning exceeding 1 TB [canonical scenario][DERIVED] — is the architect’s central
memory-takeaway.
     We keep two terms rigidly distinct in this chapter, and the distinction is the antidote to “does it
fit?” mistakes:
     • Residency floor = weights + KV. This is the minimum memory the model’s parameters and
       active KV tensors must occupy for a single request. It is what the numbers in this chapter quote
       (~140 GB weights + ~24.9 GB KV ≈ 165 GB at 9.5K max).
     • Practical host requirement = weights + KV + runtime/workspace + safety margin. Deploying
       a model on a GPU requires additional VRAM for CUDA kernels, activation buffers, NCCL
       (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library) communication, a warmup/KV-allocation safety
       pool, and (on a multi-GPU host) tensor- or pipeline-parallel copies. On the canonical 8×H100
       host this runtime/workspace term is ~64 GB, turning the ~165 GB residency floor into a larger
       deployment footprint. [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] The ~64 GB is a planning reserve, not
       a measured constant; a representative split is ~8 GB CUDA context/driver + ~16 GB activation
       buffers (batch + intermediate tensors) + ~8 GB NCCL communication buffers (tensor-parallel
       all-reduce staging) + ~32 GB warmup/KV-allocation safety pool. The exact value must come
       from a deployment benchmark on the target stack (Chapter 14); the 436 GB KV budget (640 −
       140 − 64) shifts by the same amount if the measured reserve differs.

     When the text says a workload “fits” or “does not fit,” we are always talking about the residency
floor first; the practical host requirement is a superset that must be checked before committing
hardware. Conflating the two is exactly what produces a “165 GB fits in 160 GB” error.
Memory Is the First Constraint                                                                       98


7.1.1. Count state by lifetime, not by the model label

The weights-plus-KV floor in this chapter describes the autoregressive baseline. A diffusion language
runtime needs a state-lifetime inventory before the same capacity calculation can be applied. We
distinguish resident weights, reusable context state, mutable canvas state, peak activations and logits,
kernel workspace, and runtime allocations. These categories must be disjoint at the instant being
measured; two names for the same buffer do not create two memory costs. [DERIVED]
    The KV tensor byte formula remains valid for actual K/V tensors. What changes is the proof
that those tensors can be reused: Chapter 3’s dependency figure shows why unchanged token IDs
are insufficient under bidirectional refinement. A block-causal boundary can make an earlier prefix
immutable. Approximate cache policies instead trade refresh work against quality. Memory capacity
and cache validity are separate checks. [1P][FACT]
    Repeated sequential evaluations need not multiply peak memory by the number of rounds when
inference releases temporary buffers after each round. Retained histories, previous-round logits for
self-conditioning, or simultaneous verification views change that lifetime calculation. As a shape-only
example, a 256-position canvas over a 262,144-entry vocabulary needs 256 × 262,144 × 4 = 268,435,456
bytes, or 256 MiB, for one FP32 logits tensor at batch one. This excludes probabilities, sampling
workspace, retained logits, attention buffers and the rest of the model. It is not a measured model
footprint. [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION][DERIVED]
    This distinction affects admission control. A runtime may have enough capacity for prefix state yet
fail when many requests enter a high-workspace refinement phase together. Weight precision alone
cannot certify fit: the inspected LLaDA sampling code (observation 2026-10-28; LLaDA generation
code) can use FP64 sampling intermediates even when the network weights use a lower precision.
The deployed sampler’s live tensor shapes and lifetimes decide the practical requirement. [1P][FACT]
for the inspected code; the admission consequence is [DERIVED].
    None of this changes the canonical autoregressive budget above — it changes what must be
inventoried before that budget’s arithmetic is reused for a different generation mechanism.


7.2. Mental Model

    The KV cache is per-request state that persists across autoregressive decode steps for
the lifetime of the active sequence — unlike weights, which are loaded once and reused across
requests, the KV cache is allocated per request and grows with every token added to the context. A
9.2K prompt on a 70B model at FP16 carries ~24 GB of KV state that must remain on-GPU for the
entire prefill + decode sequence. If it does not fit, the serving stack must page, offload, or recompute
— each option degrades latency or throughput. The durable mental model is: every token we add to the
context exacts a fixed memory toll, and that toll is paid in HBM every time the GPU re-reads the cache
during decode. This is why context length is the single most powerful lever on inference memory
pressure, and why “does it fit?” is the architect’s primary gate.
99                                                                        Memory Is the First Constraint


7.2.1. Persistent state is architecture-specific

The KV formula in this chapter describes keys and values retained across autoregressive steps. A
whole-clip denoiser has a different lifetime model. Its latent video changes after each scheduler
update, so video keys and values cannot simply be retained as immutable prefix entries for every
later step. The inspected Wan2.2 path recomputes attention from the current clip representation
(observation 2026-10-28; Wan2.2 sampling loop, attention defaults causal=False, window_size=(-
1,-1)). Static prompt embeddings can remain reusable, but that is not the growing autoregressive
cache. [1P][FACT]
     The corresponding fit test includes resident weights and encoders, latent and scheduler state,
per-layer activations, attention workspace, temporary conversion buffers, and VAE reconstruction.
The peak is the maximum of the live allocations at each stage, not the sum of all tensors ever created.
Tiled or chunked reconstruction can reduce a decoder peak without reducing the denoiser’s token
count. CPU offload can reduce GPU residency while adding host-memory and transfer requirements.
A model that loads successfully has not yet passed the largest-shape inference test. [1P][FACT]
for the documented implementation mechanisms; the budget interpretation is [ILLUSTRATIVE]
[DERIVED].
     The canonical KV table below is untouched: it prices the autoregressive text path this chapter
sizes. The boundary changes which state function we plug into “does it fit?” for a different generator
— the same decision, a different inventory.

      Note on “does it fit?”: this residency check answers a single-request question — does ONE request’s
weights + KV fit in the pool? It says nothing yet about how many such requests fit concurrently. For that,
an architect must subtract the runtime/activation/workspace floor (~64 GB on the 8×H100 host) from
the 640 GB pool before sizing KV. We compute that concurrent capacity — the ~436 GB KV budget and
~17.5 requests/host (byte-accurate 17.51; conservative integer floor 17) — in Chapter 17. Keep the two
numbers separate: the ~500 GB headroom (Ch. 4/7, single-request) and the ~436 GB KV budget (Ch. 17,
concurrency) answer different questions.
      Attention-family sensitivity note. The ~2.62 MB/token (2.5 MiB) figure is the full-MHA (multi-
head attention) upper bound: n_KV-heads = n_query-heads, and n_KV-heads × head_dim = hidden_
dim, i.e.


                              KVMHA per-token = 2 × nlayers × dhidden × B

      Real 70B-class dense models commonly use grouped-query attention (GQA): LLaMA-2 70B,
for instance, has 64 query heads but only 8 KV heads, so per-token KV shrinks by the head ratio to

    — about 8× smaller. For the canonical 9.2K context that is ~3 GB of KV instead of ~24 GB, and
the fleet-sizing arithmetic of Chapter 17 changes accordingly (many more concurrent requests fit for
KV). We keep the full-MHA bound as the canonical conservative residual because an architect should
size against the worst case the chosen model actually presents — the honest move is to read the model
card’s KV-head count and substitute it into the GQA formula above. The framework is unchanged;
only the constant changes. (kv_gqa_variant_mb is recorded in canonical-workload.yaml.)
    The figure shows one group’s geometry: 8 query heads funnel into a single shared K/V head.
Because GQA caches only one K/V per group (8 K/V per token) instead of one per query head (64
K/V per token), the per-token KV falls ~8× — from ~2.62 MB/token (full MHA) to ~0.33 MB/token.
That is the takeaway: many query heads can share a few K/V heads, and the cache shrinks by exactly
the 8:1 head ratio. Head count is the real dial: substitute the model’s KV-head count into 2 × layers
× KV_heads × head_dim × bytes.

7.3.1. A smaller-model counterexample: fit is a gate, not a prediction

An illustrative 8-billion-parameter model stored entirely in FP16 has raw weights of 16 GB. Assume
32 attention layers, eight KV heads per layer, a head dimension of 128 and two bytes per KV element.
This is a separate GQA example, not the handbook’s canonical 70B attention layout, and none of its
constants feed the canonical tables in this chapter. The KV storage per resident token is 2 × 32 × 8 ×
128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes.
      At 9,500 resident tokens, one sequence needs 1.245184 GB of raw KV. With an explicitly assumed
4 GB reserve for runtime state and workspace, the analytical budget is 21.245184 GB. A nominal 24
GB device passes this preliminary capacity gate. It does not yet pass an allocation or serving test. The
reserve is an assumption, and the calculation excludes unmodeled conversion peaks, fragmentation
and additional sequences. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
      The counterexample is equally important. Ideal four-bit storage for 70 billion weights is already
35 GB before scales, alignment, unquantized layers, KV or workspace. Neither a 24 GB nor a 32 GB
card holds that unsharded tensor. Two 24 GB cards provide 48 GB in total, but a working placement
still needs supported sharding and a feasible budget on each rank. Shared client memory adds another
constraint: the installed system capacity must also serve the operating system and other devices.
It is not a guaranteed GPU allocation. Device capacities are first-party specifications (Intel Arc
Pro B70 datasheet, B65 datasheet, Arc Pro B60 datasheet, retrieved 2026-10-28); the 35 GB figure is
[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] from them.
      Capacity and bandwidth answer different questions. Reading the illustrative 16 GB of weights
once at the B60’s nominal 456 GB/s takes at least about 35.1 ms in a simple weights-only streaming
model; at the B70/B65 nominal 608 GB/s the corresponding value is about 26.3 ms. These are analytical
byte-transfer floors, not measured token latencies. They ignore attention, KV traffic, launch overhead
and communication, and they assume the nominal bandwidth is achieved. Batching or reuse can also
change the bytes moved per output token. Passing the capacity gate therefore justifies a measurement,
not a throughput or cost claim. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]

7.3.2. A dense model with a mixed history-state budget

The history budget has two terms, and the second one is not a KV cache. Each recurrent update
replaces a fixed-shape summary of previous tokens, while a separate attention layer retains token-
indexed keys and values. The states below are shown at successive times; the recurrent snapshots
are not all retained together. The schematic does not claim that every operation within the model
has constant memory or constant execution time.
      The full-attention component of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B illustrates the transfer from a configuration
to a memory estimate. Its language configuration has 16 full-attention layers, four KV heads per
layer, and a head dimension of 256 (released configuration, retrieved 2026-10-28). With BF16 KV
storage, the raw component is:
      2 × 16 × 4 × 256 × 2 = 65,536 bytes per cached token.

      At 262,144 cached tokens, this component occupies 16 GiB. This analytical result assumes one
sequence and unsharded raw tensors. It excludes the recurrent and convolution states of the other
48 language layers, visual processing, runtime buffers, and allocation overhead. It is neither the
complete request footprint nor a measured concurrency limit. [1P][FACT] for the configuration;
[DERIVED] for the storage.
      At 131,072 tokens the same component is 8 GiB. Doubling history therefore adds 8 GiB to
this component under the stated assumptions; it does not double every memory object in the
request. In notation, the simplified history budget is M_history(L) = L × 65,536 bytes + M_
recurrent, where M_recurrent covers fixed-shape recurrent and convolution state for this decode
path. Temporary prefill workspaces remain outside that expression. These are derived storage
estimates, not measured allocations. [DERIVED]
      The serving consequence follows from the state lifetimes. Capacity planning needs both terms,
including any replication or sharding imposed by the engine. A prefix checkpoint for an intermediate
position must preserve the time-recurrent state corresponding to that position, not merely a list of
attention pages. A preempted or branched request can require additional snapshots, and speculative
rollback needs the correct pre-draft state. Bounded live decode state therefore does not imply free
checkpointing or unrestricted prefix sharing; the implementation determines which extra copies are
retained. [DERIVED]
      Recurrence across depth is a separate cache problem. Huginn revisits a recurrent block within
one token’s execution, and its model card requires HuginnDynamicCache so later block calls do not
overwrite earlier iterations’ K/V (Huginn model card, KV-cache Details, recurrent-depth paper). That
iteration-aware attention cache does not establish a bounded time-recurrent state footprint. Its own
retention or sharing policy belongs in the resource budget. [1P][FACT] for the card; [DERIVED] for
the accounting distinction.
      Less history traffic can relax one memory bottleneck without removing the weight-read or
compute bottleneck. A recurrent token mixer and a full-attention layer also expose different prefill
execution opportunities. Their kernel mix and sequence-length dependence must be measured
separately before transferring a decode-state estimate into a throughput forecast. The architectural
decision is which state representation the engine can maintain correctly at the required concurrency,
not which family label sounds smaller.
      The original memory-fit decision remains; the state function inserted into that decision changes.
A full-MHA comparison is meaningful only under its stated geometry and precision, and it is
not a universal upper bound for arbitrary recurrent-depth execution. This is a different model’s
configuration carried as its own assumptions — the canonical 80-layer, hidden-8192, full-MHA
numbers in this chapter are unchanged by it.

+ optimizer, a substantially higher floor. Note the ~1,120 GB is the parameter/optimizer floor (weights
+ gradients + Adam m/v/master), which is fixed by model size and precision. The actual training peak
is higher and is not inferable from that floor alone: it also includes activation memory (scales with batch
size × sequence length × hidden dim, and is the dominant term for long-context or large-batch runs),
temporary kernel workspace, allocator fragmentation, and checkpointing buffers. A host that fits the

1,120 GB floor can still fail to fit a given training run if its activation peak exceeds the remaining HBM —
so the fit verdict for training must be checked against the measured peak for the specific batch/sequence
configuration, not the parameter floor. (QLoRA’s ~50–70 GB figure is likewise a floor: it holds the 4-bit
base + adapters + a small optimizer, and its activation peak still depends on the run’s batch and sequence
length.)

7.3.3. Quantization describes several different choices

“Four-bit model” leaves several architectural questions open. Which tensors use four-bit values? How
are those values chosen? What do the four bits represent? Where are scales stored? Which kernel
consumes the resulting tensors? The figure below separates these questions. A calibration method, a
tensor encoding and a checkpoint container can participate in the same deployment; they are not
competing answers to one question.
      AWQ and GPTQ primarily address error control during post-training weight quantization. AWQ
uses representative activations to identify important channels and chooses equivalent channel
scaling that reduces the error introduced by quantizing weights. “Activation-aware” describes the
information used by the method; it does not mean that activations are also stored in four bits. The
paper’s exploratory observation about protecting a small fraction of salient weights is not a definition
requiring those weights to remain FP16. Its scaling method seeks protection without that irregular
mixed-precision storage. [1P][FACT] (AWQ, §3).
      GPTQ instead uses approximate second-order information to compensate for quantization error
in the remaining weights as quantization proceeds. Its original implementation targets weight
quantization, not activation quantization. Neither method name uniquely specifies a group size, scale
dtype, zero-point layout, permutation or checkpoint packing. Those fields are needed to reproduce
both accuracy and memory use. Calibration data must represent the intended workload; a method’s
reported behavior on one evaluation does not establish behavior on another distribution. [1P][FACT]
(GPTQ, §2–4).
      A container answers a different question. GGUF stores model metadata, tensor descriptions,
tensor types and aligned tensor payloads. It is not a single numerical precision. Its tensor-type field
permits different encodings within one model. Consequently, a comparison labeled “AWQ versus
GGUF” confounds an error-control method with a file format unless both sides are expanded into
complete deployment configurations. The useful comparison specifies the method, tensor encodings,
mixed-precision exceptions and execution backend. The same caution applies to safetensors: storing
tensors in a recognized container does not establish that a loader understands their quantized schema.
[1P][DERIVED] (GGUF specification, pinned revision, retrieved 2026-10-28).
      A compact configuration record can keep the axes separate:
Memory Is the First Constraint                                                                   108

packed tensors and checkpoint container describe different parts of a deployment, and loading still
requires a kernel-required runtime layout with compatible dispatch. Unsupported combinations
may be rejected; fallback is not guaranteed. Mechanism and storage accounting, not an accuracy or
throughput comparison.

      The record is more durable than a list of product names. It also exposes a missing assumption
before a memory estimate becomes a hardware recommendation.


Shared scales change the storage calculation

OCP MXFP4 1.0 uses E2M1 four-bit values, with one eight-bit E8M0 scale shared by a block of
32 values. E8M0 represents a power-of-two scale. The common one-dimensional NVFP4 scheme
also uses E2M1 values, but shares an E4M3 local scale over 16 values and uses an additional FP32
tensor-global scale. Neither scheme uses an affine integer zero point in this comparison. The local
scale’s encoding and granularity change the set of representable values and its adaptation to a
block’s dynamic range; smaller groups also require more scale bytes. This is a mechanism difference,
not an automatic accuracy ranking. [1P][FACT] (OCP MX 1.0, §4–6; NVIDIA NVFP4 explanation,
2025-06-24).
      The next figure holds the number of logical values constant. The same 32 four-bit values require
16 payload bytes in either scheme. MXFP4 adds one local-scale byte, producing 17 bytes per 32 values,
or 0.53125 B/value. Common 1D NVFP4 adds two local-scale bytes, producing 18 bytes per 32 values,
or 0.5625 B/value, before the tensor-global scale. For a tensor with N values in complete blocks, this
example’s compact NVFP4 storage is 0.5625N + 4 bytes. The four global-scale bytes are shared across
the tensor, not repeated for each block. [1P][DERIVED]
      These rates are not the total footprint of a model. A mixed-precision model retains some tensors
at higher precision. A file adds metadata and alignment gaps. A runtime may pad dimensions,
reorder scales, create extra representations or reserve workspace. The memory ledger therefore
separates checkpoint bytes, resident tensors, load/repack peak, activations, KV cache and workspace.
A checkpoint that fits on disk may still fail during loading, and a successfully loaded checkpoint
Memory Is the First Constraint                                                                    110




figure 7.4: Four-bit payloads and shared scale storage: both rows represent 32 E2M1 values, MXFP4
adding one local-scale byte (17 B per 32 values) and common 1D NVFP4 two (18 B per 32 values) plus
a separate FP32 scale per tensor. Bars are proportional only for payload and local-scale bytes. Totals
exclude padding, headers, extra copies and high-precision exceptions. Derived storage accounting,
not an accuracy or throughput comparison.
111                                                                        Memory Is the First Constraint


may not leave enough memory for the intended context and concurrency. The exact runtime layouts
remain implementation-dependent. [1P][DERIVED]

Worked example: scale overhead is small but not zero

A 4096 × 4096 weight matrix holds 16,777,216 values. The shape is illustrative; the byte results
follow the stated layouts. BF16 payload occupies 33,554,432 bytes. MXFP4 with complete 32-value
blocks occupies 8,912,896 bytes. Common 1D NVFP4 with complete 16-value blocks and one FP32
global scale occupies 9,437,188 bytes. The difference comes from the chosen scale representation
and grouping, not a different number of four-bit payload values. Both calculations exclude padding,
additional scale copies and non-weight tensors. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
      An integer scheme can produce a different bill again. With groups of 128, an illustrative INT4
layout containing an FP16 scale and a packed four-bit zero point per group uses 8,716,288 bytes
for the same matrix. Replacing the packed zero with an FP16 scaled-zero increases that layout to
8,912,896 bytes. Equal total bytes do not make this integer scheme numerically equivalent to MXFP4.
The example explains why an estimate needs the actual scale and zero layout rather than “four bits
plus a little overhead.” It does not choose an accuracy or speed winner. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
      For a separate resource sensitivity, a 70B-parameter teaching model that stores 98% of parameters
in MXFP4 and 2% in BF16 — fractions deliberately chosen, not a real checkpoint inventory — needs
39.24375 GB of compact weight storage rather than 140 GB. Retaining this chapter’s full-MHA, BF16
KV assumptions (80 layers, KV width 8192, 9,500 tokens per sequence) leaves raw KV at 24.90368 GB
per sequence. In a 640 GB aggregate pool with a fixed 64 GB reserve, the storage-only integer ceiling
rises from 17 sequences to 21, not in proportion to the weight compression. The added KV budget
does not prove that the ranks can place it or that 21 requests meet the latency SLO. Workspace,
fragmentation and per-rank balance still need measurement, and the reserve itself may change.
[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
      The causal consequence is narrower than “quantization solves memory.” Weight compression
frees one term in the memory ledger. If KV dominates the remaining footprint, context length
and concurrency can still bind. Weight precision and KV precision remain separate decisions, with
separate scale calibration, attention-kernel support and quality validation. KIVI’s separate treatment
of key and value statistics is one example of a KV-specific method, not a consequence of choosing an
AWQ weight checkpoint. [1P][FACT] (KIVI).

activations, gradients and optimizer state. [1P][FACT] (OFP8; SmoothQuant; QLoRA).


7.4. Measurement

    Four practical measurement habits follow from the arithmetic above:
   1. Compute KV cache per-token cost for the model. The per-token KV footprint of a fully-
      cached (MHA) attention head is



                         KVper-token = 2 × nlayers × dhidden × bytes-per-value

    (one key and one value per layer, each dhidden wide), evaluated at the chosen precision. For a
70B model at FP16 the answer is 2 × 80 × 8192 × 2 B = 2,621,440 B ≈ 2.62 MB/token (exactly 2.5
MiB/token; 2,621,440 bytes is 2.62144 decimal MB). At 8-bit the per-token value halves to ~1.31
113                                                                          Memory Is the First Constraint


MB/token (~1.25 MiB; the Ch.1 reference). Do not assume the 1.3 MB/token figure applies at FP16 —
it does not; it is an 8-bit number. When evaluating a model where the hidden dimension or layer
count differs from LLaMA-70B, recompute the constant factor — a model with 64 layers and 8192
dim will have ~2.1 MB/token at FP16 (2 × 64 × 8192 × 2 B = 2,097,152 B), while a model with 100
layers and 12288 dim will have ~4.9 MB/token (2 × 100 × 12288 × 2 B = 4,915,200 B).


      2. Log peak context length, not just average. A workload that averages 9.2K input tokens
        but has a long tail toward 32K or 128K will have a very different KV cache profile. Log the
        95th-percentile context length and re-run the KV arithmetic; the memory floor may shift from
        fitting on 2×H100 to needing 8×H100. This is especially important for RAG workloads, where
        the retrieved context may average 8K but occasionally peak at 32K+ for technical documents.

      3. Measure inference residency as weights + KV, not weights alone. It is common to see the
        140 GB weight footprint (70B FP16) fit across two 80-GB accelerators and conclude that 160
        GB is sufficient. But 140 GB of weights leaves only ~20 GB before runtime/workspace and KV
        are added; at 9.2K input the KV cache adds ~24.1 GB, pushing the total to ~164.1 GB — already
        over the 160 GB aggregate, so the model does not fit on two accelerators once KV is counted.
        Always include KV when we state the memory floor for inference.

      4. Account for KV quantization when reporting residency. If the serving stack uses FP8
        KV, the per-token KV cost drops from ~2.62 MB to ~1.31 MB (raw tensor byte-halving, exactly
        50% of BF16 = 2,621,440/2 = 1,310,720 B = 1.25 MiB), and the 9.5K max residency falls from
        ~165 GB to ~152 GB (weights 140 GB + KV 12.45 GB). State both the BF16 and FP8 residency
        numbers, because the choice of KV dtype changes the hardware requirement decisively. Note
        the accounting basis: the ~1.31 MB/token figure is the raw tensor byte-halving of the same
        MHA tensors (one byte per K/V element, exactly half of BF16’s two bytes); it is NOT a vendor-
        measured serving footprint, and any block-layout or per-token scale/offset metadata overhead
        is not included. Do not generalize a fixed ratio to all FP8-KV deployments: the realized
        per-token footprint depends on the engine version, cache-block layout, scale/offset metadata,
        allocator rounding, and the accounting boundary (logical payload vs allocated cache vs observed
        resident memory), so re-derive it for the target serving stack rather than inheriting a multiplier.
        (For reference, the 9.5K total at this byte-halving basis is ~152 GB — still above a single H100,
        but now within 2×H100, 160 GB.)


7.5. Common Mistakes

      • Assuming KV cache size scales sub-linearly. The KV cache grows linearly with context
        length. Doubling the context from 9.2K to 18.4K doubles the KV memory, all else equal. There
        is no automatic compression unless the attention mechanism itself is hybrid or sparse.
Memory Is the First Constraint                                                                     114


    • Using the 8-bit KV figure (~1.3 MB/token) at FP16. Chapter 1’s ~1.3 MB/token is explicitly
      at 8-bit precision. At FP16, the per-token KV cost is ~2× that, ≈2.62 MB/token (2.5 MiB — §7.4).
      Mixing the two figures produces wrong residency calls.

    • Ignoring the weight + KV residency contrast. Quoting only the weight footprint (140 GB
      for 70B FP16) and claiming it fits on one H100 (80 GB) is a category error. Weights alone exceed
      one H100; KV must be added.

    • Quoting one KV-quant reduction for every precision. KV cache quantization must be
      read per bit width: FP8 KV ≈50% of BF16 (raw byte-halving) is what serving stacks realize
      today, while 4-bit KV’s raw bound is a full 4× (2.62 → 0.66 MB/token here; 0.52 → 0.13 for a
      7B, §12.3) — realized savings land between, once block/scale metadata is counted. (The vLLM
      “54%” figure is a decode inter-token-latency slope ratio, not a memory ratio.) Weight-only
      quantization’s 2×–4× applies to weights; do not transfer an expectation across precisions or
      across tensors without naming the bit width.

    • Overlooking the fine-tuning residency floor. Full fine-tuning of 70B requires ~1.12 TB with
      Adam optimizer states — roughly 1.75× the 8×H100 host. This is not a temporary overhead; it
      is the permanent memory floor for the training duration.


7.6. Architecture Consequence

    The memory floor is the first constraint every architecture decision respects, because unlike
compute or bandwidth it cannot be moved by better kernels — it is fixed by weights + KV + (for
training) optimizer state. Several concrete consequences follow for the canonical enterprise-Q&A
workload:
    • Model residency decides host count. A 70B FP16 model (140 GB weights) at the 9.5K max
      context (9.2K in + 300 out) needs ~24.9 GB of KV cache (FP16), so the max end-of-generation
      residency ≈ 165 GB — it does not fit on a single 80 GB H100, nor within the 160 GB aggregate of
      2×H100 (160 GB < 165 GB). By aggregate memory capacity it needs ≥ 3×80 GB (240 GB) — but
      note this is an aggregate-HBM lower bound on card count, NOT a validated 3-way tensor-
      parallel configuration: whether three 80-GB cards actually admit a 70B model depends on
      head/layer shard divisibility, KV-head routing, TP=3 support, workspace/communication layout,
      and per-rank fragmentation, none of which the aggregate sum establishes. A practical TP
      topology (e.g. TP=4 or TP=8) must be checked against the serving engine and model geometry
      before three cards are treated as deployable. The canonical single host of 8×H100 (640 GB) is not
      justified by basic capacity alone — three 80 GB GPUs already clear the 165 GB residency floor;
      the 8×H100 host is chosen for compute, bandwidth, topology, concurrency, implementation
      constraints, and headroom. [canonical scenario][DERIVED]
115                                                                         Memory Is the First Constraint


      • KV cache quantization buys back memory, not compute. FP8 KV ≈ 50% of BF16 (raw
        byte-halving), dropping the 9.5K max residency from ~165 GB toward ~152 GB. This is a
        memory lever, orthogonal to bandwidth/compute fixes — the architect pulls it when the KV
        floor, not decode bandwidth, binds.

      • Fine-tuning is a different memory regime than inference. The same model that serves in
        ~165 GB demands ~1,120 GB under full Adam fine-tuning (weights 140 GB + gradients 140 GB
        + Adam m/v/master states 840 GB) — roughly 1.75× the 8×H100 host. This is why the architect
        separates the serving fleet from the training fleet: the memory floors differ by an order of
        magnitude. [canonical scenario][DERIVED]

      • Context length is the largest controllable KV lever. Doubling context from 9.2K to 18.4K
        doubles KV (~24.1 GB → ~48 GB); 128K context drives KV to ~335 GB, which forces quantization
        or model parallelism. The architecture must set a context-length ceiling to keep the served
        model within host memory. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]

      In short: the architect sizes the host by weights + KV at the longest supported context, treats KV
quantization as a spare memory dial, and keeps inference and training on separate memory-planning
tracks.


7.7. What We Still Don’t Know

      • Per-model KV state beyond K/V — the additional per-head state and per-layer scale/offset
        metadata some attention implementations store alongside keys and values. The 2 × layers
        × n_KV-heads × head_dim × bytes formula prices the K/V entries themselves (§7.3 covers
        GQA/MQA exactly by substituting the model card’s KV-head count), but the extra per-token
        bytes an implementation adds on top of K/V are not derived in this chapter and must be
        established per architecture and serving stack.

      • Quality loss from aggressive KV quantization (2-bit KIVI, or sub-4-bit schemes) at very long
        context lengths (128K+, MoE experts). The primary sources anchor FP8 KV ≈50% of BF16 (raw
        byte-halving) at near-zero quality loss, but 2-bit asymmetric patterns and their interaction
        with RoPE and sliding-window layers are not fully mapped.

      • Whether per-request KV caching can be partially offloaded to CPU DRAM during decode
        without TTFT impact, beyond the vLLM KV Offloading Connector’s 2–22× TTFT reduction
        range [S7][1P][FACT], which is highly prompt-size-dependent. The community is converging
        on tiered KV storage (GPU resident hot set + CPU/DRAM cold set), but the latency trade-offs
        at concurrency > 1 are not yet primary-anchored.

      • Frontier 2026 has begun re-engineering the KV constant factor, not just quantizing
        it. All four 2026-class open architectures attack KV cache size at the attention layer itself, on
Memory Is the First Constraint                                                                         116


      top of the per-token footprint this chapter derives: DeepSeek-V4’s hybrid CSA+HCA reports
      KV cache at only ~10% (Pro) / ~7% (Flash) of DeepSeek-V3.2 at 1M-token context [1P: arXiv
      2606.19348]; GLM-5.3-Flash’s sparse+linear hybrid reports ~4.4× smaller per-layer average
      BF16 KV cache than GLM-5.3 [1P: Z.ai GLM-5.3-Flash release article, 2026-08-26]; Kimi K3’s
      Kimi Delta Attention + Attention Residuals targets information flow across long sequences
      [1P: arXiv 2607.24653]; Qwen3.8-Flash-Next combines Gated DeltaNet (compress history) with
      Qwen Sparse Attention (micro-block indexing) for long-context cost [1P: HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-
      Flash-Next]. For the architect this is a decisive shift: the KV arithmetic in this chapter (per-token
      × context) is not a fixed constant across model generations — a 2026 hybrid-attention model
      can hold dramatically more context per byte of KV than the canonical 70B/8×H100 framing
      assumed. Size the host against the specific model’s KV scheme, not a universal constant.

    • The impact of MoE routing on KV cache: does each token really emit a full key/value per layer
      across all experts, or does routing activate only a subset? The total-vs-active and MoE-vs-dense
      facts of Ch 3 (total parameters ≠ active parameters per token; MoE gives compute sparsity, not
      weight-residency sparsity) confirm that attention layers process every token densely and emit
      key/value per token, so MoE sparsity does not reduce KV — but the constant factor for MoE
      models (e.g., number of experts per layer) needs per-model validation.



7.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: Sizing Memory First for the 5,000-Employee Wiki

An architect is asked to design an internal Q&A system over the company’s document repository.
The initial ask is vague: “We need to let all 5,000 employees ask questions over our internal wikis.”
Before any architecture can be defended, the architect must turn this vague desire into a machine-
denominated statement using the chapter’s core constraint.
    From the unit-and-token work of Ch 1 alone, the architect can already establish several facts.
The unit is tokens; the request shape will be prompt + retrieved context + output; the workload is
input-heavy (retrieved context dominates); and the first number to lock down is tokens-per-request,
because every downstream decision (which model fits, how much memory, what latency is possible)
is priced against it.
    Running the KV arithmetic: if each request uses ~9.2K input tokens (the canonical ~1,200 prompt
+ 8K retrieved) plus ~300 output tokens, the request grows to a 9.5K max KV sequence by the end
of generation. The KV cache per request at 70B FP16 is ~24.9 GB (max, 9.5K), against ~24.1 GB for
the initial 9.2K-prefill residency. The weight footprint is 140 GB. Total max inference residency is
≈165 GB, which does not fit within the nominal 160 GB aggregate HBM of 2×80 GB H100s; practical
deployment therefore requires additional capacity, lower precision, or a larger GPU configuration. It
fits comfortably within the 640 GB aggregate HBM of an 8×H100 host. If the context is extended to
32K (e.g., wider document retrieval), the KV cache rises to ~84 GB, pushing total residency to ~224
GB — still fitting in 8×H100 but requiring a multi-GPU node.

      The architect can now speak the system’s currency: tokens, KV bytes, and the residency floor.

chapter 8.


Compute




The Architect’s Question

After chapters on tokens, workloads, and memory, the architect naturally asks: how much compute
does this actually require, and at what point does the hardware cease to be the limiting factor? This
chapter gives us the FLOP-scale arithmetic, the arithmetic-intensity roofline, and the utilization
framework that lets us answer that question without guessing. We will move from per-token FLOPs
to prefill PFLOP counts to sustained MFU on real hardware, and then to the roofline that tells us
whether a given layer is compute-bound or memory-bound — the difference that decides whether
we should reach for batching, quantization, or a different hardware generation. Throughout, the
arithmetic anchors to the canonical enterprise-Q&A RAG scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2): ~10 rps average
/ ~40 rps peak traffic, with 70B FP16 weights and an 8×H100 host. KV cache per-token figures are
referenced at FP16 (~2.62 MB/token, i.e. 2.5 MiB) unless an 8-bit (~1.31 MB/token, 1.25 MiB) variant is
explicitly stated.


8.1. Concept

Compute in a language model is priced in floating-point operations, or FLOPs. Every matrix mul­
tiplication, every attention weight update, every activation function evaluation contributes to the
total. The architect’s first principle is that FLOPs scale linearly with parameter count and context
length, but the efficiency with which those FLOPs are executed depends on the hardware ridge point
and the arithmetic intensity of the kernel.
    For a dense transformer layer, the dominant cost is the matrix multiplication — query-key,
value-aggregation, and MLP projections. In FP16, a single multiply-add counts as two FLOPs. The



                                                 122
123                                                                                             Compute


per-token cost is therefore approximately 2 ×N FLOPs where N is the number of active parameters.
This is the arithmetic baseline: every token processed costs roughly two floating-point operations
per parameter.


8.1.1. Fewer sequential evaluations can mean more total work

Implementation observations: 2026-10-28. The work counters below are illustrative, not measured perfor­
mance.
      For an iterative language generator, the approximately 2N projection-cost rule applies to processed
positions, not just final output tokens. Let Pj be the active parameter count and Qj the positions
evaluated in network evaluation j. A projection-dominated work proxy is

                                                         ∑︂
                                         Fprojection ≈        2Pj Qj .
                                                         j

      The trace also needs attention pair counts, output-head work, routing, sampling, refresh and
verification. For a full dense-attention evaluation over length L, attention work grows quadratically
with L. For K active queries over a cached prefix of length C, the attention main term grows with
K(C + K), before the architecture’s head and layer factors. Reducing the number of recomputed query
positions does not eliminate reads of a long prefix. [DERIVED]
      Consider an explicitly illustrative 7B-active-parameter model that emits 256 tokens in 32-token
blocks and uses eight decoder evaluations per block. There are eight blocks, hence 64 sequential
decoder evaluations. The decoder nevertheless evaluates 256 × 8 = 2,048 output positions. Its projection
proxy is 2 × 7B × 2,048 = 28.672 TFLOP. A simplified output-only AR counter evaluates 256 positions
and gives 3.584 TFLOP. The block example has one quarter as many sequential evaluations but eight
times as much output-side projection work. These are different quantities, not contradictory results.
[ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION][DERIVED]
      This arithmetic omits prompt encoding, context attention, block-finalization encoding, the output
head, refresh, classifier-free guidance, verification and communication. It also simplifies the book’s
first-token-from-prefill convention. It compares counters, not equal-quality models, and predicts
neither a fourfold speedup nor an eightfold end-to-end slowdown. A network-evaluation count must
include extra verification passes and the shapes of any combined guidance branches, rather than
count only outer sampler rounds. [DERIVED]
      Why might the higher-work path still finish earlier? Processing more positions together can reuse
loaded weights across more matrix rows and improve low-batch utilization. Why might it lose under
load? Optimized AR request batching can already supply those rows, while refinement continues to
repeat work. Distributed execution also repeats tensor-parallel collectives and any expert dispatch
required by each evaluation. The number of sequential rounds and the total communicated bytes
can move in opposite directions. [DERIVED] The low-concurrency case is vendor-reported rather
Compute                                                                                            124


than re-measured here: Google’s DiffusionGemma card reports low-batch generation speed while
warning of quality and high-QPS limits (DiffusionGemma card). [1P][FACT]
   MoE adds a working-set issue. Active parameters per token do not equal the union of experts
touched by all positions in a parallel block. LLaDA2.2 explicitly limits a block’s expert pool before
per-token routing (LLaDA2.2 technical report, retrieved 2026-10-28). That bounds an execution
working set; it does not make the other resident experts disappear. The useful measurements are
expert-union size, dispatch bytes, load imbalance and collective time, alongside active FLOPs. [1P]
[FACT]; measurement consequence [DERIVED]
   The resulting fleet decision follows measured service demand. At a fixed task-quality and latency
target, GPU-seconds, successful-request throughput and resident state determine capacity. Output
tokens divided by denoising steps do not determine the number of hosts. [DERIVED]

8.1.2. The roofline diagnostic

But FLOPs alone do not tell the full story. The hardware can only execute FLOPs if data is available
— weights, activations, and KV cache all compete for the same HBM bandwidth. The arithmetic
intensity (FLOP/byte) determines whether a kernel is compute-bound (intensity above the ridge
point) or memory-bound (intensity below). This roofline model is the central diagnostic tool of this
chapter: it tells us, for any given layer and precision, whether increasing FLOPs will actually reduce
latency or whether we are already starved for bytes.

      Three different “bounds” — keep them apart. Throughout this book, three words
      that all contain “bound” mean three different things, and conflating them is a real error.
      Compute-bound means performance is limited primarily by arithmetic throughput (the
      kernel sits above the ridge; it is starved for FLOPs). Memory-bandwidth-bound (what
      the roofline calls “memory-bound”) means performance is limited by memory-transfer
      bandwidth (the kernel sits below the ridge; it is starved for bytes moving per second).
      Memory-capacity-constrained (equivalently KV-capacity-constrained) means feasible
      concurrency or context is limited by how much data fits in HBM — not by how fast
      it moves. The canonical RAG workload illustrates all three without overlap: prefill is
      compute-bound (high intensity), decode is bandwidth-bound (low intensity), and long
      input raises KV residency, which capacity-constrains how many requests can be resident
      at once. “Input-heavy” does not by itself mean “memory-bound” — it tends to raise
      prefill compute and KV-capacity pressure, two distinct effects. When the book says
      “memory-bound” without qualification, it means bandwidth-bound in the roofline sense;
      capacity pressure is stated explicitly.
125                                                                                                Compute


8.1.3. A resource model survives a backend change; an implementation may not

Backend-documentation observations: 2026-10-28. They do not establish feature availability at the
edition’s 2026-08-30 cutoff.
      The compute and memory equations apply across accelerator vendors. Their constants belong
to a specific device and execution path. A peak INT8 dense TOPS figure does not describe BF16
throughput, a sparse peak does not describe a dense workload, and aggregate device memory is not
one allocation pool. The useful comparison starts with the model’s operators, resident bytes and
communication pattern. It then asks which kernels implement those operations on the candidate
hardware (Arc Pro B70 datasheet, Arc Pro B65 datasheet, Gaudi 3 Accelerator white paper). [1P]
      In PyTorch, torch.xpu names the Intel GPU device backend (PyTorch XPU getting-started
note, pinned revision 5c48869). It does not name every Intel accelerator. Intel Gaudi uses a
separate hpu path and software stack (Gaudi PyTorch porting guide, which allocates tensors as
torch.device("hpu")). A client NPU can use the OpenVINO NPU plugin rather than the GPU
backend (OpenVINO GenAI documentation). Even within Intel GPU inference, an engine-native SYCL
path can bypass PyTorch (llama.cpp SYCL backend documentation, pinned revision 8ca4060). oneAPI
libraries, SYCL execution and Level Zero provide different parts of the software path; none supplies
a serving scheduler by itself, and Habana’s collectives run through their own HCCL library (HCCL
API reference). [1P][FACT] for the stack boundaries; the portability consequence is [DERIVED].
      This distinction changes a portability decision. A device API can be available while a required
model operator or cache layout is not. Source-level portability therefore reduces one part of mi­
gration work. It does not establish feature parity, numerical equivalence or sustained performance.
[DERIVED]
      The chapter unfolds in four parts. First, the core arithmetic: FLOPs per token, prefill PFLOP
counts, and H100 sustained utilization. Second, the roofline: why early layers are compute-bound
while later layers and decode are memory-bound. Third, the canonical scenario arithmetic: 70B on
8×H100, TTFT 1.2 s, TPOT ~25 ms. Fourth, the mini-case: a continuous deployment scenario that
threads the prefill/decode divide.


8.2. Mental Model

      FLOPs are like the distance a car can travel on a gallon of fuel: it tells us the system’s capacity,
not how long the trip will take. The trip time is determined by the ridge point: if the arithmetic
intensity is below the ridge, adding more FLOPs won’t help because we are waiting for data. If we are
above the ridge, we are limited by how fast the compute can chew through operations. The roofline
chart — peak TFLOPS on the vertical axis, FLOP/byte on the horizontal — is the map that resolves
this. Where our kernel lands on that chart decides whether we should profile memory bandwidth or
compute throughput.
      Read this ladder together with the roofline: the roofline’s vertical axis (peak TFLOPS) and horizontal
