figure 8.1: Where inference computation and data movement actually live. The hierarchy runs from
the smallest/fastest/closest resource (registers, tensor cores, on-chip SRAM) to the largest/slower/far­
ther (HBM, GPU interconnect, other GPUs). Inference work maps onto it: matrix multiply runs on
the tensor cores; model weights and the KV cache are predominantly HBM-resident; FlashAttention
restructures attention to tile through on-chip memory and cut HBM traffic; tensor-parallel (TP)
communication crosses the GPU interconnect; pipeline-parallel (PP) communication moves activa­
tions between pipeline stages. The gradient of speed↔capacity↔distance is why compute, memory
bandwidth, memory capacity and interconnect bandwidth are distinct architectural constraints —
each is a different level of this ladder. Schematic note: the vertical ordering is a relative speed/ca­
pacity/distance ranking, not a measured timing scale — the gaps between levels are not to scale, and
the same physical resource (e.g. HBM) can appear at different logical positions depending on the
access pattern. [ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual]
127                                                                                           Compute


axis (FLOP/byte) are both determined by where on this hierarchy the work sits. A kernel is compute-
bound when its FLOPs run on the tensor cores and data fits in on-chip memory (high arithmetic
intensity); it is bandwidth-bound when it must stream large tensors from HBM faster than the bytes
can move (low arithmetic intensity). So the “bound” classification of Ch. 8 is not a property of the
model alone — it follows from where the model’s weights and the KV cache happen to be resident,
and how much of the computation a kernel can keep on-chip. Ch. 15’s FlashAttention discussion is
exactly this ladder in action: keep more of the tile on-chip, move fewer bytes between HBM and the
compute units.
8.3. Worked Example: Canonical Scenario Arithmetic

      The canonical scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2) is an enterprise Q&A system: the canonical 80-layer,
hidden-8192, full-MHA 70B reference (a 70B-class dense model), FP16 weights (~140 GB), 1 host with
8×H100-class GPUs (80 GB each), average prompt 1,200 tokens + 8K retrieved context (~9.2K input),
300-token output, TTFT budget 1.2 s (retrieval ~120 ms + prefill), TPOT budget ~25 ms/token.
      Scope. “1 host with 8×H100” here is a per-host / per-request feasibility container (does one host
meet one request’s latency and memory SLO). It is not a claim that one host absorbs the 40 rps peak
arrival rate — as Ch 17 derives, that peak puts in-flight concurrency λ·W ≈ 344 at the ~8.6 s service
time, far above one host’s KV-residency ceiling (C ≈ 17.5, conservative integer floor 17), so the fleet
needs ~21 hosts (Ch 17’s floor-17 screen). The compute/roofline arithmetic of this chapter answers
the per-request and per-host-shard question; the fleet question is a separate multiplication that Ch
17 performs (with the cost basis in Ch 16). We keep them distinct because each requires measuring
against a different quantity (a latency budget vs an arrival rate).
8.3.1. FLOPs per token

For a 70B-parameter dense model in FP16, the per-token forward FLOP count is approximately:


                      FLOP/token ≈ 2 × N = 2 × 70 × 109 ≈ 140 GFLOP/token

      [DERIVED: 2 FLOPs/parameter × 70 ×10⁹ params; standard dense-forward arithmetic, which is
the same 2×N rule that gives, e.g., a 175B dense model 2 × 175 × 10⁹ ≈ 0.35 TFLOP/token]
      This applies to both prefill and decode: each token that enters the forward pass costs ~140
GFLOP. The distinction between prefill and decode is not in the per-token FLOP count but in the data
movement pattern — prefill reads the full context once, while decode re-reads weights per token.
      The implementation examples in this paragraph were inspected on 2026-10-28. The 2P estimate
(two FLOPs per parameter — the 2 ×N rule above) applies to the parameterized matrix work in a
specified execution path. It does not account for all history-dependent attention, indexing, routing,
or repeated-depth computation. A shared core executed several times reuses weights but repeats
arithmetic. A phase-dependent architecture can also activate different paths during prefill and
decode. The parameter estimate therefore needs a phase and an execution count before it enters
the roofline analysis. (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash technical report; Huginn model card and Geiping et al.,
Compute                                                                                             128


arXiv:2502.05171 for recurrence-aware cache and per-token adaptive compute). [1P][FACT] for the
phase-dependent mechanisms; the execution-count qualification is [DERIVED].


8.3.2. A small execution-budget example

An illustrative work model makes the distinction precise. Let C be fixed work outside a repeated core,
F the work of one core pass, and r the executed pass count. Ignore decision overhead for this first
estimate. Total work is C + rF; the unique core weight inventory remains unchanged as r changes.
If C = 1 work unit and F = 2 work units, four passes cost 9 units and three passes cost 7. Omitting
one of four passes removes 25% of core work but only 2/9, approximately 22.2%, of total work. The
units are illustrative operation-budget units, not milliseconds, FLOPs measured on a device, or a
model benchmark. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
    Selecting pass 3 after executing pass 4 still costs 9 units in this model. A real stopping check
adds overhead, and lower work does not guarantee proportionally lower wall time. Small batches
can underfill kernels. State movement, synchronization and memory stalls can dominate. A quality-
preserving reduction in actual core executions is necessary evidence for a compute saving; a selected
exit index alone is insufficient. [DERIVED]
    Communication follows the executed path as well. If each core pass uses tensor-parallel collectives,
repeating the core repeats those collectives unless a specific implementation changes the schedule.
Weight sharing does not share their results across different hidden inputs. If MoE routing is also
present, expert dispatch adds a separate traffic term; it cannot be inferred from the number of depth
passes alone. Neither a shared parameter count nor a lower active-parameter count establishes the
communication time. The deployment record must identify placement, parallel strategy, tensor sizes
and the actual overlap achieved. [DERIVED]

              prefill FLOPs ≈ 2 × N × L = 2 × 70 × 109 × 9.2 × 103 ≈ 1.29 PFLOP

8.3.4. Sustained vs. peak: H100 MFU

NVIDIA H100 SXM5 lists ~1,979 TFLOPS FP16 Tensor Core peak “with sparsity” and ~989 TFLOPS
FP16 peak without sparsity [1P: NVIDIA H100 datasheet]. In practice, sustained model FLOPs
utilization (MFU) for a well-tuned transformer workload typically runs at 30–40% of peak on H100
[2°: industry benchmark reports, derived from real kernel profiles]. At 35% MFU:


                  sustained = peak × MFU = 989 TFLOPS × 0.35 ≈ 346 TFLOPS

    [1P][2°][DERIVED: vendor peak (1P) × typical MFU (2°) — the MFU range is a secondary, empirical
figure, so the sustained value inherits the provenance of its weakest input, the 2° MFU, while the
peak is first-party]
    Scope matters here. The 346 TFLOPS figure is the sustained rate of a single H100, and the 2,471
tokens/s derived from it is therefore a per-GPU number. The canonical host is an 8×H100 node, so
we must not multiply demand by a per-GPU rate as if it were per-node. Track the scope explicitly as
we scale.
    Per GPU (one H100 at 35% MFU):

                                                   346 TFLOPS
                 prefill tokens/s (per GPU) =                    ≈ 2,471 tokens/s
                                                 140 GFLOP/token
    [DERIVED: sustained FLOPS ÷ per-token FLOPs; per-GPU scope]
    Per host (8×H100, idealized before TP communication, imbalance, and kernel/system overhead):


                 prefill tokens/s (per 8×H100 host) = 8 × 2,471 ≈ 19,800 tokens/s

    or, equivalently, 8 × 346 TFLOPS ≈ 2.77 PFLOPS sustained ÷ 140 GFLOP/token. [DERIVED:
per-GPU × 8; idealized aggregate, first-order only]
    For 10 rps with 9.2K input tokens each, the prefill demand is ~92,000 tokens/s (from the canonical
workload). At ~19,800 tokens/s per host, we would need roughly:

                                  tokens/s demand     92,000
                       nhosts =                     =        ≈ 4.6 →∼ 5 hosts
                                  tokens/s per host   19,800
    [DERIVED: token demand ÷ per-host prefill throughput; idealized aggregate]
    At the peak 40 rps (368,000 tokens/s) the same arithmetic gives ~18.6 → ~19–20 hosts. This
aligns — independently — with the KV-residency / Little’s-Law fleet sizing derived in Chapter 17, with
the cost basis in Chapter 16 (~21 hosts at peak, ~$155,816.93/mo self-host ≈ $24.97/1K — illustrative
131                                                                                                 Compute


included-cost, Ch 16), which is a useful cross-check that the two fundamentally different constraints
(prefill FLOP throughput vs. KV residency/service time) point at the same order of fleet.
      Honest boundary on both numbers. The per-GPU 2,471 tokens/s is itself an analytical
figure at an assumed 35% MFU — not a measured throughput. The 8× aggregate (~19,800/host)
is a theoretical first-order estimate that assumes perfect tensor-parallel scaleout: it does not
account for TP communication, per-rank load imbalance, kernel inefficiency under a given batch, or
scheduling/system overhead. It is an upper-bound analysis value, not a servable goodput. Actual
reachable prefill throughput must come from benchmark goodput under the target workload (Chapter
14). Treat both numbers as scope-disciplined models, never as measured capacity.
      This rough sizing illustrates that prefill is FLOP-bound at this scale — the compute requirement is
the primary constraint, and memory bandwidth (HBM at 3.35 TB/s per H100) is sufficient to keep the
compute fed if the kernel is efficient. The ridge point for dense FP16 on H100 is ~295 FLOP/byte (989
÷ 3.35); the arithmetic intensity of a mature attention kernel sits near or above this ridge, meaning
the kernel is compute-saturated rather than bandwidth-starved once the batch is large enough.

8.3.5. Decode: bandwidth-bound at low batch

Reading the roofline (summary of Fig 8.2): the dense-FP16 ridge at ~295 FLOP/byte (H100: 989 TFLOPS ÷
3.35 TB/s) separates the compute-bound region (right) from the memory-bound region (left). Prefill sits
far above the ridge — its arithmetic intensity is set by the sequence length (weights read once, reused
across all tokens), so it is compute-bound; decode at batch=1 sits at the far left of the chart (~1 FLOP/byte,
~295× below the ridge) and is memory-bound. Batching and quantization shift kernels rightward toward
the ridge; the distinction between the two phases is the single most important reading of this chart.
      For decode, the per-token FLOP cost is the same ~140 GFLOP, but the arithmetic intensity drops
sharply. Each decoded token re-reads all 70B weights from HBM (a batch-1-equivalent weight-
streaming read). A 70B FP16 weight matrix is 70 ×10⁹ × 2 B = 140 GB — one full pass reads 140 GB
(batch-1-equivalent), not 280 GB. (The naïve “2 ×70 ×10⁹ × 2 B ≈ 280 GB” double-counts the FP16
footprint: the leading “2” is already inside the 2-bytes-per-element, so writing 2 ×70 ×10⁹ × 2 B counts
the weight bytes twice. Any KV/output-projection reads are a separate, smaller term on top, not a
second full weight footprint.) The effective arithmetic intensity is therefore:

                                                      140 GFLOP
                       arithmetic intensitydecode ≈             ≈ 1.0 FLOP/byte
                                                        140 GB
      [DERIVED; a lower-bound bandwidth model — real kernels also read activations and KV, so
measured intensity is typically below this and heavily dependent on fusion and cache residency]
      This is well below the H100 dense-FP16 ridge of ~295 FLOP/byte, meaning single-stream decode
is overwhelmingly memory-bandwidth-bound. Throughput improves with batching because the
weight-reread amortizes across tokens — decode intensity ≈ batch size (weight-only), so at batch=32
the effective intensity is ~32 FLOP/byte, still ~9× below the 295 ridge (compute-bound decode needs
batch ≈ 295, or quantized weights, which halve bytes and double intensity), and TFLOP/s utilization

                                           is memory-bound.
133                                                                                         Compute


increases accordingly. KV-read caveat: the weight-only intensity above omits the per-sequence KV
re-read (~24 GB at the canonical 9.2K context, FP16 full-MHA). Including it, the decode intensity
is (140·B)/(140 + 24·B) FLOP/byte, which saturates at ~5.8 FLOP/byte as B→∞ — far below the 295
ridge. So with the KV term, decode stays bandwidth-bound at every batch size; the “batch ≈ 295”
figure is the weight-only first-order estimate (valid when the KV re-read is small relative to the
weight stream, e.g. short contexts or KV quantization). This is why continuous-batching systems
(Orca, vLLM) prioritize batch growth: it is the primary lever for pushing decode arithmetic intensity
toward the ridge (on the weight-only term).
      Scope note on the single-device roofline here: the 140 GB weight-read and the per-GPU ~3.35
TB/s HBM bandwidth are single-GPU quantities, so the ~1.0 FLOP/byte intensity and the “memory-
bandwidth-bound” label above are a per-kernel / single-device roofline argument. It is not a verdict
on the canonical 8×H100 host’s actual bandwidth adequacy — under tensor parallelism the 140
GB weight matrix is sharded across GPUs, so each GPU streams only its own shard (~0.70 TB/s
against its own ~3.35 TB/s, Ch 6). The classification (low-batch decode is bandwidth-bound) is shard-
invariant because it follows from the low arithmetic intensity, not from the aggregate weight-read
rate exceeding one GPU’s bandwidth.


8.3.6. The execution path determines the applicable roofline

Quantizing stored weights reduces one source of memory traffic, but the selected kernel determines
the arithmetic. In a fused weight-dequantization path, a kernel reads compressed weights and converts
them for higher-precision multiplication. A native block-scaled path instead requires compatible
low-bit operands, scale layouts and device instructions. An emulation path may reconstruct higher-
precision weights before GEMM. These paths can load related checkpoint representations while
having different traffic, compute and workspace costs. Their operation counts and supported peak
rates cannot be mixed in one roofline. Fig 7.3 makes this execution gate explicit. [1P][DERIVED]
      In the Chapter 7 mixed-weight sensitivity — a teaching model storing 98% of parameters in
MXFP4 and 2% in BF16 — a dense 2N useful-operation convention and one complete weight stream
give about 3.567 FLOP/B at batch one, compared with 1 FLOP/B for BF16 weights. This is a weight-
only analytical intensity, not a 3.567× throughput prediction. It excludes activation and KV traffic,
conversion, additional scale traffic and communication. At large batch or during prefill, a GEMM
may already be compute-bound; during long-context decode, attention and KV access can dominate.
A lower weight-byte count therefore changes a candidate bottleneck, not the measured end-to-end
bottleneck by definition. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
      Communication needs a separate ledger. Compressed checkpoint loading can reduce distribution
bytes if compressed files are transferred. It does not automatically compress activation all-reduces,
expert all-to-all traffic or optimizer communication. Fewer devices might become feasible after a
memory reduction, but that is a new parallelism configuration with different compute, memory
and interconnect limits. Communication savings cannot be credited before the transmitted tensor
Compute                                                                                         134


types, placement and collective schedule are known. [1P][DERIVED] (The distinction follows the
weight-only scope of GPTQ.)


8.4. Measurement

   Three measurable quantities anchor compute sizing:
   1. Per-token FLOP count. Measure by flops profiling (e.g. NVIDIA Nsight Compute) on the
     target model and precision. The 2×N rule is a useful prior, but actual count varies by layer
     depth, activation choice (SiLU vs. ReLU), and whether kernel fusion combines matmuls.

   2. Sustained MFU. Profile TFLOP/s achieved divided by peak TFLOP/s for the target hardware
     and precision. A well-tuned transformer on H100 FP16 typically lands in the 30–40% range;
     below 20% suggests a memory or communication bottleneck that should be diagnosed before
     scaling.

   3. Arithmetic intensity (FLOP/byte). Compute as achieved FLOPs divided by bytes transferred
     (weights + activations + KV read/write). Compare to the hardware ridge point (H100 dense
     FP16: ~295 FLOP/byte; H200: ~989 TFLOPS ÷ 4.8 TB/s ≈ 206 FLOP/byte — H200 keeps H100’s
     GH100 die and its dense FP16 peak, trading a bigger/faster HBM3e for bandwidth; GB200:
     higher on both terms (faster dense BF16 peak and ~8 TB/s HBM), so its BF16 ridge is higher,
     and its NVFP4 ridge higher again). If intensity is below the ridge, the kernel is memory-bound;
     above, compute-bound.

   A compute roofline does not include every exposed distributed stall. A communication kernel can
consume SM and HBM resources while appearing to overlap a matrix multiplication. The joint trace
must therefore distinguish model computation, collective work, exposed waiting and computation
slowed by contention. Peak interconnect bandwidth cannot be added to peak compute to predict the
combined schedule; Chapter 9 separates their mechanisms and measurement boundaries. [DERIVED]


8.5. Common Mistakes

   • Assuming 2×N FLOPs/token is exact. It is a baseline derivation; actual per-token FLOPs
     vary with layer depth, activation fusion, and kernel fusion. Profile before quoting.

   • Treating prefill and decode as having the same FLOP/byte profile. Prefill reads the full
     context once and is FLOP-bound; decode re-reads weights per token and is memory-bound.
     The arithmetic-intensity roofline distinguishes them.

   • Using peak TFLOP/s as sustained throughput. Peak includes sparsity or BF16/FP8 variants
     that may not be available in the chosen precision. Use the FP16 number without sparsity (≈989
     TFLOPS on H100) as the baseline for dense compute sizing.
135                                                                                            Compute


      • Ignoring the batch-size dependence of arithmetic intensity. A single-token decode batch
        has very low intensity; batching raises it. Always state the batch assumption when reporting
        TFLOP/s or tokens/s.

      • Confusing H100 sparsity-inclusive peak (1,979 TFLOPS) with dense peak (989 TFLOPS).
        The 2× sparsity figure appears in vendor data sheets but most transformer workloads do not
        activate sparsity. Quote the dense figure unless the kernel is specifically sparsity-enabled.


8.6. Architecture Consequence

      The compute arithmetic and roofline have direct consequences for system design:
      • If prefill is FLOP-bound (as it is for 70B+ models with long contexts), the primary opti­
        mization is batching — larger prefill batches do not remove the per-request attention work
        (each sequence still has its own attention computation); they improve accelerator utilization by
        forming larger matrix operations, amortizing weight and execution overhead across requests,
        and raising achieved FLOP/s. The relevant lever is the achieved efficiency (MFU) of the prefill
        kernel, not a change to the per-request FLOP count. System design should therefore provision
        for batchable prefill (continuous batching, Orca, vLLM continuous batching) as the first-order
        throughput lever.

      • If decode is memory-bound (single-stream, low batch), the primary optimization is batching
       — decode arithmetic intensity ≈ batch size, so even modest batch sizes (8–16) raise it to ~8–16
        FLOP/byte (batch 16 → ~16, still ~18× below the 295 ridge), improving TFLOP/s utilization
        without reaching compute-bound; compute-bound decode needs batch ≈ 295, or quantized
        weights, which halve bytes and double intensity. KV cache quantization (FP8, int8) also reduces
        bytes per token, raising effective intensity. P/D disaggregation (prefill on GPUs, decode on a
        separate pool) can rebalance: prefill’s FLOP demand is served by compute-optimized GPUs,
        while decode’s bandwidth demand is served by wide-memory GPUs or even CPU offload.

      • If the workload’s intensity crosses the hardware ridge (e.g. a workload at ~250 FLOP/byte
        is memory-bound on H100’s ~295 ridge but compute-bound on H200, whose FP16 ridge is ~206
        FLOP/byte — 989 TFLOPS ÷ 4.8 TB/s — from its higher HBM3e bandwidth), the same workload
        may shift from memory-bound to compute-bound, changing the optimal hardware choice.
        The shift comes from the lower ridge, not from precision: a higher ridge moves the boundary
        right and makes compute-bound harder (H200’s ~412 FLOP/byte ridge in dense FP8 — ~1.98
        PFLOPS ÷ 4.8 TB/s, never the sparsity-inclusive ~4 PFLOPS (§8.5) — would do the opposite),
        and precision scaling moves intensity and ridge together (bytes halve → intensity doubles;
        peak doubles → ridge doubles), so FP8 alone does not change the classification. This is why
        the H200 represents an inflection point where inference and training hardware lines begin to
        converge [1P: NVIDIA H200 SXM datasheet].
Compute                                                                                             136


    In practice, the architect measures arithmetic intensity for the target workload and precision,
locates the kernel on the roofline chart, and then selects hardware and batching strategy accordingly.
The roofline is the diagnostic; the architecture decision follows.


8.6.1. From video dimensions to repeated attention work

The same derive-then-decide move applies to a workload that evaluates all of its token positions
together rather than one per step: the budget below is derived from counted dimensions, not from a
duration label.
    A worked example makes the new work unit concrete. We use Wan2.2 TI2V-5B in its text-to-video
path, not the A14B expert model. Its configuration specifies a dense transformer with hidden width
3,072, 30 layers, and 24 attention heads. The VAE has 48 latent channels and temporal/spatial strides
of 4, 16, and 16. The denoiser patches the latent video by (1,2,2). The release’s “720P” example is
precisely 1,280 × 704 pixels, 121 frames, at 24 frames/s. The dimensions, rather than the marketing
resolution label, determine the budget. [1P][FACT] (Wan2.2 TI2V-5B configuration, pinned revision
1ea34ff, retrieved 2026-10-28; Diffusers transformer config).
    Fig 8.3 shows the data path. The prompt passes through UMT5-XXL. An optional image follows
a separate reference-conditioning path. The T2V calculation below does not add that I2V branch
to its state budget. Initial noise spans the entire latent video. Each scheduler step calls the denoiser
on this representation; VAE decoding follows the final update. [1P][FACT] (sampling loop, pinned
revision 1ea34ff, retrieved 2026-10-28).
    For this aligned shape, the temporal latent count includes the first-frame convention:
                  ⌊︃ ⌋︃

   At this shape the attention core requires 9,144,709,939,200 FLOP per layer, or about 9.145 TFLOP.
Across 30 layers it requires about 274.341 TFLOP per branch evaluation. The inspected upstream loop
evaluates conditional and unconditional predictions separately at each of its 50 default scheduler
timesteps (same pinned revision 1ea34ff). That is 100 single-sample branch evaluations, giving
about 27.434 PFLOP of attention-core work over the trajectory. This is not the whole model’s FLOP
count and is not a GPU execution time. A runtime may batch the two branches into one forward call
without removing their two-sample arithmetic. [1P][DERIVED] (configuration; sampling loop).
   The memory calculation has an equally important boundary. One hypothetical BF16 hidden
tensor contains N × d × 2 = 167,608,320 bytes. Materializing one BF16 score tensor for 24 heads
would require 24 × N 2 × 2 = 35,721,523,200 bytes, or about 33.268 GiB. This is a hypothetical
implementation choice, not a claim that FlashAttention allocates such a tensor. Tiled exact attention
avoids retaining the full score matrix while still performing the pairwise work. The upstream code
creates initial latent noise in FP32, so assigning BF16 to every live tensor would also undercount
state. [1P][DERIVED] (attention module; sampling loop).
   The sensitivity explains the architectural consequence. Extending 121 to 241 frames changes the
temporal latent count from 31 to 61. Token count rises by about 1.968×; the dense pairwise term rises
by about 3.872×. Doubling both spatial dimensions gives four times the tokens and sixteen times
the pairwise work. These are algebraic sensitivities, not claims that either larger workload meets
the release’s quality or memory envelope. A request limit expressed only in clip-seconds misses this
distinction. [1P][DERIVED]
   At 24 frames/s, 121 frames also exposes a measurement convention. The final frame’s timestamp
is 5 seconds after the first. A constant-frame-duration container spans 121/24, or about 5.0417
seconds. A service contract needs one convention. “Five-second clip,” “121 frames,” and “27,280 latent
tokens” describe related but different quantities. [DERIVED]


8.7. What We Still Don’t Know

    • Arithmetic intensity of fused kernels. Most roofline estimates treat attention or MLP as
      separate matmuls, but in practice frameworks fuse multiple operations into a single kernel.
      The effective FLOP/byte of a fused attention+MLP kernel is not well cataloged in primary
      sources and would require profiling on the target hardware to anchor.

    • MFU across precisions and sparsity. The 30–40% H100 FP16 figure is a rule of thumb; actual
      utilization depends on architecture, kernel quality, and batch config. A systematic MFU atlas
      across H100/H200/GB200, FP16/BF16/FP8, dense/MOE would be a valuable reference.

    • Arithmetic intensity of emerging attention mechanisms. Linear attention (DeltaNet,
139                                                                                             Compute


        MLA), compressed attention (CSA, HCA), and hybrid sparse patterns have different FLOP
        profiles and data movement. Their roofline position is not yet established in primary sources.

      • Frontier 2026 has begun to answer this. DeepSeek-V4’s hybrid CSA+HCA attention reports
        that, at 1M-token context, single-token inference drops to ~27% of the FLOPs (Pro) / ~10%
        (Flash) and KV cache to ~10% / ~7% of DeepSeek-V3.2 [1P: arXiv 2606.19348]. In its 2026-08-
        26 release article, Z.ai compares GLM-5.3-Flash with GLM-5.3: it reports 3× less attention
        compute per head per layer and a 4.4× smaller average BF16 KV cache per layer. These
        are normalized attention metrics, not whole-model FLOP or total-cache ratios. These are [1P]
        first-party vendor figures, not yet independently reprofiled on our own hardware — which
        is exactly the arithmetic-intensity measurement an architect should still do before trusting a
        vendor’s roofline claim for their own workload.

      • How quantization shifts the ridge. Moving from FP16 to FP8/int8 changes peak TFLOP/s
        and bytes-per-operand, shifting the ridge point. The net effect depends on the quantization
        scheme (element-wise vs. per-tensor, dynamic vs. static) and whether the kernel is re-tuned
        for the lower precision.


8.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: Continuous Deployment Scenario

An architect is brought into an ongoing deployment of a 70B-class Q&A system on 8×H100 GPUs.
The system is serving ~10 requests/s average with ~9.2K input + 300 output tokens per request,
and the TTFT budget is being missed: p95 TTFT is 2.8 s, exceeding the SLO of 2 s. The TPOT of 28
ms/token is within spec, but the prefill delay is the bottleneck.
      The temptation is to reach for a roofline and “prove” prefill is memory-bound. That reasoning is
wrong here, and the error is worth naming: it is spread by treating prefill like token-by-token decode.
In decode, each new token re-reads the weight matrix from HBM, so the arithmetic intensity is ~1
FLOP/byte — genuinely memory-bound. In prefill, the weight matrix is read once and reused across
the whole sequence; the sequence dimension supplies the matrix-matrix reuse. Prefill’s effective
intensity is (2 × N × L) / (N × 2 bytes/param) = L = 9,200 FLOP/byte at the canonical 9.2K
context — ~1.5 orders of magnitude above the ~295 FLOP/byte dense-FP16 ridge. At that operating
point prefill is compute-bound, exactly as the rest of this chapter teaches.
      So a high TTFT is not evidence of a bandwidth problem. The architect does the correct thing:
profile the prefill kernel and determine which of several distinct causes is actually limiting it, rather
than assuming memory. The profile separates four candidates:
      • Compute-bound — the GEMMs are saturated at high MFU; more FLOPs/ops per token would
        not help, but better kernel efficiency (flash-attention, fused MLP) would.
      • Communication-bound — tensor/pipeline parallelism crosses the NVLink/Host fabric; data
        movement, not math, is the ceiling. The fix is a different parallelization or a smaller cross-GPU
        footprint.
Compute                                                                                              140


    • Launch / occupancy-limited — the kernel is too small or the grid under-fills the SMs;
      increasing batch or improving occupancy raises utilization without adding hardware.
    • Attention / memory constrained (within prefill) — the quadratic attention term, not the
      linear weights, grows with context; at 128K+ contexts this term dominates prefill cost (at 32K
      it is already ~+60% — the 4·n_layers·L²·d term, Fig 22.1), so the fix is to reduce the attention
      term (flash-attention, sparse/linear attention), not to batch harder.

    The architect measures MFU to choose among these. If the prefill kernel is running at 12% MFU,
the problem is occupancy or launch — grow the batch or fuse kernels. If MFU is already near ~40%
and the kernel is compute-saturated, then prefill is compute-bound and more batch just queues
more work without reducing per-request TTFT; the lever instead is kernel efficiency, attention-term
control, or P/D disaggregation so prefill’s FLOP profile is served by compute-optimized GPUs while
decode’s bandwidth profile runs on wide-memory GPUs.
    The recommendation is therefore: profile first (MEASURE, do not assume), and only then pick the
intervention. Batching helps when prefill is occupancy-limited; kernel fusion helps when GEMMs are
under-saturated; attention-term control and disaggregation help when the bottleneck is the quadratic
attention term or the compute/bandwidth mismatch between phases. The workload’s true roofline
position, not an assumed “memory-bound prefill,” dictates the fix.




    Prefill PFLOP also grows with context: 2 ×70B × L tokens scales linearly — ~0.29 PFLOP at 2K → ~4.6
PFLOP at 32K — so the longer the window, the larger the one-time compute cost of loading it. Sustained
throughput (tokens/s) is what matters for continuous serving, and at the canonical 9.2K point the prefill
is ~1.29 PFLOP (Table 8-1).
chapter 9.


Communication




The Architect’s Question

Before we can place a model across multiple GPUs or across a cluster, we need to know what the
interconnect can — and cannot — move. This chapter asks: given a model size, a parallelism strategy,
and a traffic pattern (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter), what is the communication time, and
does it dominate the compute budget? We will size the hidden bottleneck that often goes unnoticed
until the job stalls.



9.1. Concept

Implementation citations in this chapter were inspected on 28 October 2026 for the separately dated
addendum, outside the 30 August snapshot. They identify documented or source-inspected paths, not a
tested combined environment or a refresh of the August hardware comparisons.
    Communication in a distributed LLM system follows the deployed topology, not a universal
vendor hierarchy. A server may connect its accelerators through PCIe, a dedicated scale-up fabric,
integrated Ethernet links, or a combination of paths; NVLink and NVSwitch are NVIDIA’s examples
of such a path, while Gaudi organizes a different integrated-network topology (Gaudi 3 white paper,
retrieved 2026-10-28). Across hosts, Ethernet/RoCE or InfiniBand may carry the traffic, subject to
the actual adapter, routing and transport support. Each layer still has a distinct bandwidth ceiling, a
distinct latency profile, and a distinct cost per gigabyte, so the architect must match the collective
operation to the layer where the bandwidth is sufficient: moving the same data over a slower
layer adds minutes to training time or inference latency for no computational benefit. The relevant



                                                 141
Communication                                                                                    142


quantities are directional bandwidth, latency, contention, and the physical traffic of the chosen
collective — a product name alone supplies none of those measurements for a deployment.
   A collective operation describes how data from a group of ranks becomes a result; it does not
specify a network, an algorithm, or a hardware vendor. A rank is an index within a communication
group, not a synonym for a server — one server can host several ranks, and several independent
groups can occupy the same devices. The communicator identifies the participants and the context
in which their operations match (MPI 5.0 standard; NCCL communicator API, retrieved 2026-10-28).
   The collective operations that dominate multi-node training and inference are:

    • all-reduce: each rank contributes an equal-shaped tensor; a reduction such as the elementwise
      sum is returned to every rank. Averaging additionally requires division by the rank count;
      the collective does not imply that division. Data-parallel training commonly uses gradient
      reductions, while tensor-parallel inference uses activation reductions.
    • all-gather: every GPU contributes a tensor; every GPU receives the concatenation of all
      fragments. Used when a model split across nodes needs the full weight or KV cache locally.
    • reduce-scatter: ranks contribute equal-shaped tensors, reduce corresponding elements, and
      receive distinct partitions of the reduced result. Each output partition has 1/N of the input
      tensor’s elements. Unlike all-gather, this operation also performs a reduction; it is not its
      mathematical inverse.

   The bandwidth each collective consumes depends on three factors: the data volume (bytes), the
number of participating nodes (N), and the interconnect’s effective bandwidth in the presence of
contention. A 70B FP16 model is 140 GB, and its FP16 gradient is the same size — the §9.3 worked
example all-reduces that 140 GB gradient tensor. The 140 GB is a logical input size, not the physical
traffic of the collective. For an eight-rank point-to-point ring, each rank sends 245 GB and receives
another 245 GB (§9.3). A one-way transfer of the logical 140 GB alone would take 56 s at an assumed
effective 2.5 GB/s; the ring’s send volume instead gives 98 s. The bandwidth denominator must use
the same direction convention as the counted bytes.

      Behind these three workhorses sits one contract. For a fixed-count all-reduce, each rank con­

the result. SUM returns a sum — averaging requires division by the group size or an explicitly selected
averaging operation, at any group size, not an implicit property of the operation. The reduction
operation, dtype, element count, communicator, and operation order form a single contract, and
matching buffer byte counts alone are insufficient (MPI 5.0 standard; NCCL API header, pinned
to v2.32.3-1, retrieved 2026-10-28). Table 9-2 states the full set of operations this chapter’s traffic
arithmetic can encounter within one group.

9.2. Mental Model

    The concentric-ring model represents increasing communication distance in the actual topology,
not a mandatory sequence of fabrics. An accelerator accesses its local HBM first. Inside a server,
PCIe or a dedicated scale-up fabric connects devices; NVLink and NVSwitch are examples for the
NVIDIA configuration in Table 9-1, not universal server components. Across servers and racks,
Ethernet/RoCE or InfiniBand can carry traffic according to the deployed links, adapters, and routing.
A useful placement keeps frequent exchanges within a measured low-latency group where possible
and budgets any traffic that crosses its boundary. Physical distance alone does not establish a
bandwidth ranking: rail count, topology, contention, and transport support remain part of the
measurement.
    Directionality comes before division. H100’s advertised NVLink bandwidth is 900 GB/s bidirec­
tional per GPU, or 450 GB/s per direction (NVIDIA H100 datasheet). This per-GPU port aggregate is
not a measurement of a particular topology’s bisection. A one-way 140 GB transfer at the directional
peak takes about 0.31 s [1P][DERIVED]. A collective also incurs reduction, synchronization and
routing work:
145                                                                                      Communication



                                                                  bytes
                                     Tcollective ≈ α × nsteps +
                                                                    β
      where α is the per-step latency, β is the achieved bandwidth under an explicit directional con­
vention, and nsteps is the number of communication steps. The byte term must count that algorithm’s
physical traffic rather than substitute the logical tensor size. This expression is a simplified model;
overlap, reduction work and collective offload can change the critical path. For a flat one-way 140 GB
transfer, the nominal 25 GB/s of one HDR port gives a best-case 5.6 s; an assumed practical-effective
2.5 GB/s Ethernet path gives 56 s. The eight-rank ring in §9.3 instead sends 245 GB per rank: about
0.54 s at the H100 directional peak, 6.1 s at an assumed effective two-rail 40 GB/s, and 98 s at 2.5
GB/s. These are analytical comparisons, not measured NCCL results; deployment choices require
§9.4 measurements.
      The reduce-scatter and all-gather rows of Table 9-2 become concrete in Fig 9.2, which follows
one SUM through a balanced four-rank ring. Reduce-scatter leaves a different reduced fragment at
each rank, and all-gather then replicates those already-reduced fragments — gathering the original
inputs instead would not produce the same result. The two phases are also the traffic §9.3 counts:
each phase sends (N − 1)/N of the tensor per rank, which is where 122.5 GB per phase, and 245 GB
per rank, comes from at eight ranks and 140 GB (MPI 5.0 standard; nccl-tests performance definition,
pinned, retrieved 2026-10-28).
      Floating-point SUM adds another constraint. Its mathematical expression is unchanged when
an implementation changes the reduction tree, but finite-precision addition can produce different
bits, and the MPI standard explicitly recognizes this effect (MPI 5.0 standard). A reproducibility
claim therefore needs a scope: inputs, dtype, rank count and mapping, algorithm, kernels, and
hardware/software versions. A fixed random seed does not by itself establish bitwise collective
reproducibility.
      The software path above those physical rings has several distinct decisions, and Fig 9.3 separates
them from the setup path. The framework chooses a communication group and operation; its backend
connects that request to a collective implementation; the implementation chooses an algorithm and
uses device execution and transport facilities; those facilities share HBM, device links, PCIe, NICs, and
switches — the layers of Table 9-1. Changing a transport can leave the collective semantics unchanged
while changing which resource limits the operation (NCCL API header, pinned to v2.32.3-1; NCCL
transport selection, pinned; oneCCL MPI transport, pinned to 2022.1.0; oneCCL OFI transport, pinned,
retrieved 2026-10-28).
      MPI is a standard, not one library and not a CPU-only transport: Open MPI, MPICH, and Intel MPI
are implementations, and GPU-aware implementations can accept supported device buffers, so eligible
configurations can move their payload without staging it through host memory. Device-pointer
recognition, direct RDMA, operation support, and stream integration are separate capabilities — none
follows automatically from the phrase “GPU-aware.” The fair comparison is specific: Open MPI’s
v5.0.x CUDA documentation supports device buffers for several blocking collectives yet explicitly

restricts nonblocking reduction collectives on the documented CUDA-aware UCX path (Open MPI
CUDA-aware support), while MPICH v5.0.2 documents CUDA, HIP, and Level Zero build support —
a build statement, not a guarantee for every datatype, provider, or persistent device-buffer operation
(MPICH v5.0.2 README, retrieved 2026-10-28). A nonblocking MPI request allows overlap; it does
not guarantee independent background progress, and a correct MPI program must tolerate weak
progress (MPI 5.0 standard).
      A typical NCCL call instead submits work to a CUDA stream: stream order connects the collective
to preceding producers and later consumers, a consumer on another stream needs an explicit
dependency, and network paths can use CPU proxy threads, so GPU-oriented communication does
not imply zero host resource use (NCCL stream semantics; NCCL proxy source, pinned to v2.32.3-1).
The submission-versus-completion contract itself is measurement business, taken up in §9.4.
      MPI and NCCL can coexist: NVIDIA’s own example uses MPI to launch and coordinate ranks and
distribute the NCCL unique ID, then calls NCCL for the tensor reduction (NCCL MPI example). The
presence of mpirun or MPI_Bcast in an application therefore does not identify the collective payload
path; conversely, an MPI implementation may itself carry GPU payload, and oneCCL’s transport
layer includes MPI as well as OFI paths (oneCCL MPI transport, pinned; oneCCL OFI transport,
pinned). Bootstrap, collective algorithm, and transport require separate labels.
      A ring is one execution strategy, not the meaning of all-reduce. A balanced point-to-point
ring pipelines fragments through reduce-scatter and all-gather — the structure Fig 9.2 shows —
while trees can reduce synchronization depth, hierarchical algorithms can keep much of the traffic
inside a fast local group, and pairwise exchanges serve a different redistribution pattern in all-to-all
(NCCL ring implementation, pinned to v2.32.3-1; NCCL cost model, pinned). Channels add parallel
communication paths, and protocols such as NCCL’s LL, LL128, and Simple govern lower-level
movement and synchronization (NCCL environment variables); a protocol name is not an algorithm
or a physical fabric.
      The useful choice depends on message size and topology. For small messages, launch and per-step
latency can dominate — the per-step latency term of the model above; for large messages, sustained
directional bandwidth and load balance matter more — its byte term. Communication kernels may
compete with model kernels for SMs, HBM, and cache, while network progress consumes host
and NIC resources, so more overlap can reduce exposed waiting yet slow the computation being
overlapped. The architecture decision follows the combined critical path, not a library name or an
isolated bandwidth score.
9.3. Worked Example

      For a communication-only illustration, a 70B model has 140 GB of FP16 weights. We separately
assume an FP16 gradient tensor of logical size M = 140 GB at each rank. Chapter 10 instead
assumes FP32 gradients, so its logical tensor is 280 GB. Neither a 140 GB weight tensor nor this
gradient buffer fits on one 80 GB GPU. Even two 80 GB GPUs fitting the weights would not establish
training-state fit: gradients, optimizer state, activations and workspace also require memory. A real
Communication                                                                                        150


deployment must specify partitioning and chunking before applying this model. For the arithmetic
below, eight logical ranks perform a point-to-point ring without collective offload. Each phase sends
(N − 1)M /N = 122.5 GB per rank; reduce-scatter followed by all-gather therefore sends 245 GB
and receives another 245 GB per rank. These are endpoint traffic counts, not a claim that the full
buffer can be allocated on an H100. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
    Option A — H100 NVLink directional-peak model. The advertised 900 GB/s is the sum of
both directions at each GPU endpoint. The corresponding peak in one direction is 450 GB/s. We use
that directional peak to obtain an ideal ring time, not an achieved bandwidth or a memory-feasible
eight-replica training deployment. A flat one-way transfer alone would take

                                                 140 GB
                                      Tflat =            ≈ 0.31 s
                                                450 GB/s
    The ring sends 245 GB and receives another 245 GB per rank. With concurrent send and receive,
its ideal time is Tring ≈ 245/450 ≈ 0.54 s. Equivalently, 490 GB of sent-plus-received traffic divided
by 900 GB/s gives the same time. Reduction, synchronization, contention and staging can increase
the elapsed time. The ring accounting follows the NVIDIA nccl-tests performance definition. [1P]
[DERIVED]
    Option B — InfiniBand across eight logical ranks. HDR InfiniBand delivers 200 Gb/s per
link (≈ 25 GB/s before link coding; NDR doubles this to 400 Gb/s). InfiniBand uses a 64b/66b line
code, so the useful payload sits a bit below the line rate. A ring-all-reduce or tree-all-reduce across 8
nodes will see lower effective bandwidth due to multi-hop forwarding and congestion. A realistic
effective throughput is roughly 40 GB/s (aggregated across 2 HDR rails/ports per node — the multi-rail
effective bandwidth referenced in §9.2 and Fig 9.1). Using the ring model:

                                         N −1 M     7 140 GB
                             Tring ≈ 2           =2           ≈ 6.1 s
                                          N Beff    8 40 GB/s
    Option C — 25 Gb/s Ethernet (RoCE2) across 8 nodes. 25 Gb/s ≈ 3.125 GB/s unidirectional.
With protocol overhead and multi-node tree contention, a practical effective bandwidth might be 2.5
GB/s. Ring model:

                                                 7 140 GB

    Under these stated assumptions, the InfiniBand time is about 11× the ideal NVLink ring time,
and the Ethernet time is about 180×. A synthetic iteration containing 100 serialized collectives of this
size would spend about 54 s, 610 s or 9,800 s respectively in communication. These totals exclude
overlap and computation; they do not predict a real training iteration without its collective schedule.
[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
    The worked example also highlights why model parallelism and pipeline parallelism exist: when
a single GPU cannot hold the model, splitting it across nodes moves the communication from the
151                                                                                      Communication


inner rings to the outer rings, and the architect must budget the extra seconds per collective against
the savings from fitting a larger model.
9.4. Measurement

      Measuring communication in situ is harder than counting tokens, because the bandwidth numbers
above are peaks; real systems see lower effective bandwidth due to congestion, operating-system
interference, and protocol overhead. Three practical measurements an architect can make:
      1. Correctness and completion. A known-input test establishes the operation, dtype, element
        count, communicator, reduction, root, rank order and output partition. Floating-point compar­
        isons use a documented tolerance; bitwise repeatability is a separate result. Device producers
        must finish before the collective reads their buffers, and consumers must observe completion
        rather than host submission. A CUDA-stream submission returning successfully does not by
        itself establish that its result is ready on another stream (NCCL stream semantics).

      2. Collective performance on feasible buffers. A microbenchmark uses resident per-rank
        allocations that fit after runtime reserves, including any separate input/output buffers and
        scratch space. The logical 140 GB example in §9.3 is not a request to allocate 140 GB on one 80
        GB GPU. The test matrix spans small activation messages and larger gradient buckets, group
        sizes and node mappings. Each result records the stack, topology, transport, selected algorithm,
        warmup, sample count, repeated trials and timing boundary. Host enqueue time differs from
        device-completed latency. The original elapsed time stays beside algbw and busbw; the latter is
        an algorithm-specific normalization, not a physical-link byte counter (nccl-tests performance
        definitions). A point-to-point link test answers a different question from a collective test.

      3. Service impact under contention. The same shapes run in the actual compute and arrival
        schedule, first in isolation and then with concurrent traffic. Profiler traces separate exposed
        communication stalls, hidden communication and compute slowed by shared-resource con­
        tention. Summing all collective durations can overstate the exposed cost, while subtracting
        all overlap can understate it. TTFT, ITL, errors and SLO-goodput establish the serving con­
        sequence; training uses device-completed iteration time and its critical path. A large-buffer
        bandwidth result alone does not establish either outcome (Chapter 14).

      Collective tests must also exercise the backend the workload actually uses. NCCL tests describe
an NCCL path; they do not certify XCCL or HCCL. The examined vLLM XPU configuration selects
the XCCL backend with recent PyTorch (vLLM XPU platform source, pinned to revision 5df63a7),
while Gaudi exposes HCCL (Habana HCCL API reference, retrieved 2026-10-28). The test record
therefore needs rank placement, data type, message size, transport, and a sent/received bandwidth
convention. For Gaudi’s documented 24 × 200 Gb/s port total (Gaudi 3 white paper), the nominal
arithmetic is 600 GB/s per direction or 1,200 GB/s bidirectional aggregate — derived nominal figures,
and neither is an achieved all-reduce bandwidth. [1P][DERIVED]
Communication                                                                                             152


    The key invariant: always measure on the same hardware and software stack that the production
job will use. A benchmark run on a clean VM with no other traffic will overstate the achievable
bandwidth compared to a crowded cluster.
    Failure tests complete this contract. Missing ranks, mismatched counts or collective order, network
faults and process exits can block a group. Framework watchdogs, asynchronous library errors and
request deadlines need one recovery policy. An asynchronous success code does not establish
correctness after communicator failure; recovery must be exercised at the framework and service
boundary (NCCL communicator errors and abort).


9.5. Common Mistakes

    • Assuming peak bandwidth is sustained. PCIe Gen5 x16 peaks at ~64 GB/s, but a single
      all-reduce never saturates the full link because the traffic is split across multiple GPUs and
      multiple links. Measured effective bandwidth is typically 40–60% of peak; design against the
      measured number, not the spec sheet peak.

    • Placing all-reduce on Ethernet without a bandwidth budget. A 70B model gradient
      all-reduce at 25 Gb/s Ethernet (≈ 2.5 GB/s practical-effective) takes ~56 s per step (a flat lower
      bound; ~98 s with the ring factor, §9.3). If the training runs 1,000 iterations, that is ~56,000 s (15.5
      hours) spent exclusively in communication. Always compute the per-iteration communication
      cost before committing to a lower-bandwidth fabric.

    • Ignoring contention from other traffic. NVSwitch can carry many concurrent channels,
      but if other collectives (e.g., all-gather for optimizer state) are running simultaneously, the
      bisection bandwidth is shared. Measure with the full production workload pattern, not an
      isolated micro‑benchmark.

    • Using InfiniBand as a default without checking the cost–performance ratio. InfiniBand
      HDR 200 Gb/s gives ~25 GB/s unidirectional, which is sufficient for many workloads, but
      the price per GB of optics and cables is 5–10× that of Ethernet. If the communication time is
      acceptable on RoCE2, the cheaper fabric may be the better architectural choice.

    • Overlooking protocol overhead. RoCE and InfiniBand use the same 64b/66b line coding but
      differ in framing and header sizes. An NDR 400 Gb/s InfiniBand link delivers a ~380 Gb/s class
      useful payload; a 200 Gb/s RoCE2 link delivers ~180 Gb/s. The difference matters when we are
      computing per-second throughput for a fixed data volume.


9.6. Architecture Consequence

    The interconnect choice is not a detail to be decided after the model, the parallelism strategy, and
the hardware are selected — it is a first-class design variable that shapes all three. If the architecture
153                                                                                       Communication


calls for data-parallel training of a 70B FP16 model across 8 nodes, the all-reduce bandwidth dictates
whether the nodes are connected by InfiniBand, 200 GbE, or even 100 GbE. If the budget can
accommodate NVLink‑connected hosts, keeping the all-reduce on-node gives an ideal ring time
about 11× below the assumed InfiniBand case and about 180× below the assumed RoCE case (§9.3).
These ratios apply to this communication-only model, not to end-to-end throughput.
      The architecture consequence also flows in the other direction: a tighter communication budget
(e.g., target <0.5 s per all-reduce) may force a particular parallelism strategy. We might choose model
parallelism (pipeline parallelism, tensor parallelism) to keep the per-collective data volume smaller, or
we might accept a slower fabric and reduce the frequency of collectives (e.g., gradient accumulation
steps between all-reduce calls). The interconnect bandwidth number is the anchor that makes these
trade-offs quantifiable.
      Finally, the architecture consequence extends to cost. A cluster of 8×H100 servers connected
by NVSwitch is the highest upfront capital expenditure, but it delivers the lowest per-iteration
communication time, which translates to higher throughput per dollar over the life of the cluster. A
cluster connected by 200 GbE RoCE has lower capital cost but higher per-iteration communication
time, which may increase the total cost of ownership if the training job runs for many weeks. The
architect must balance capex vs. opex by way of the communication arithmetic shown in this chapter.
9.7. What We Still Don’t Know

      • Contention patterns under mixed workloads. The benchmark numbers above assume a
        dedicated collective on a quiet fabric. In a production fleet, other traffic (user requests, other
        training jobs, KV cache movement) shares the same links. The effective bandwidth under
        realistic multi‑job congestion is not yet characterized with a standard suite, and the interaction
        between all-reduce and RoCE/Ethernet best‑effort traffic can cause tail latency spikes that are
        difficult to predict.

      • Adaptive collective algorithms. New collectives (e.g., gradient compression, sparse all-
        reduce, error‑bounded approximations) claim to reduce the data volume at the cost of a small
        accuracy loss. The bandwidth arithmetic changes when the data volume is 30 GB instead of
        140 GB, but the latency per byte may increase because of compression/decompression steps.
        The net effect on iteration time is workload‑specific and not yet settled.

      • Optical interconnects and the next generation. NVLink‑Switch and the next‑generation
        switch fabrics are pushing node‑level bandwidth higher (toward 1.8 TB/s aggregate), and
        optical intra‑rack fabrics (400 Gb/s–800 Gb/s per lane) are entering data centers. The arithmetic
        base — the relative magnitudes of PCIe, NVLink, Ethernet, InfiniBand — is stable in the near
        term, but the absolute numbers will shift as new silicon and cable technologies ship. Keep the
        framework; update the constants.

      • Cross‑domain generalization. Most published bandwidth measurements use square matrices
Communication                                                                                        154


      (all-reduce of a gradient tensor). Diagonal dominant tensors, sparse gradients, or structured
      compression may exhibit different effective bandwidths because the traffic pattern across links
      is less uniform. The arithmetic framework applies, but the constants need re‑measurement for
      the specific tensor shape.

the host stream API, not a claim that every accelerator or NIC supports every device-side mechanism.
    oneCCL’s official UXL repository was not archived at retrieval, and its default branch was master-

identifier, not its release year (oneCCL releases). That tag exposes a C API and a plugin architecture
(ccl.h, pinned to 2022.1.0); its legacy plugin connects to the existing C++ collective implementation,
and its tree contains MPI and OFI transports (legacy plugin, MPI transport, and OFI transport, all
pinned to that tag, retrieved 2026-10-28). SYCL/Level Zero describe the device execution and memory
path; MPI/OFI describe transport choices at another layer, and actual device-buffer support still
depends on the selected plugin, transport, build, and system configuration.
    Queue semantics are part of that contract. The inspected 2022.1.0 legacy plugin expects an
in-order SYCL queue for its queue path; its CPU branch with a null stream waits on an event,
and other branches contain queue waits or host tasks (legacy plugin source, pinned). The broad
description “asynchronous GPU collective” cannot replace those path-specific completion rules, and
similar-looking function names do not establish matching error, lifetime, or recovery semantics. The
C API has a concrete plugin error boundary: in the inspected tag its wrapper converts caught C++
exceptions into onecclPluginException, and a communicator without a finalize or abort callback
causes the corresponding API to return onecclNotImplemented — a conditional code path, not a
claim that every plugin lacks recovery callbacks (oneCCL API source, pinned). A synchronous return
code also does not establish completion of previously queued device work; runtime failures and the
selected plugin’s recovery behavior remain separate obligations.

9.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: Naming the Parallelism Before the Arithmetic

An architect is asked to design a 70B inference service for a population of 10,000 users. The request
frequency and arrival trace have not yet been supplied. The team considers replicating an eight-GPU
tensor-parallel engine or partitioning one engine across 32 hosts. The communication scheme can be
assessed before the fleet count is known, but a user population alone cannot determine that count.
   The per-request all-reduce is not the right model for inference, and neither is a blanket “all-
gather the full weights every decode step.” It matters which parallelism is in play: ordinary tensor
parallelism (TP) shards each weight matrix across the GPUs, and every decode step exchanges only
the activations (not the weights) via collective ops like all-reduce/all-gather of the small activation
tensors — weight matrices stay resident and are read in place, they are not re-fetched each step. A
different scheme, FSDP-style weight gathering (used in training, and in some sharded-inference
arrangements) does all-gather weight shards before the forward pass. So the architect must name
the scheme before doing the arithmetic. Concretely, for the canonical 8×H100 host the meaningful
per-step data movement is a TP all-reduce of the per-layer activations (tens of MBs, not GBs) plus
the KV cache fragment exchange in disaggregated serving — e.g. ~35 GB of KV moved over NVLink
(~0.08 s at 450 GB/s per direction, §9.2) when a P-D sequence transfers a ~13K-token context (35 GB
÷ 2.62 MB/token ≈ 13.3K) between prefill and decode pools. The distinction changes the answer by
orders of magnitude: re-fetching 140 GB of weights each step is pathological (that is a design smell,
an anti-pattern to flag, not a baseline); exchanging activations or KV fragments is the normal case
that fits comfortably within NVLink.
   The architect proposes keeping each tensor-parallel engine within an eight-GPU host where
memory and operator support permit. Additional independent replicas can then absorb greater traffic
without extending tensor parallelism across hosts. Activation exchange still consumes bandwidth
and synchronization time; it is not free. Cross-host partitioning becomes a separate candidate when
a model or its required request state cannot fit within the chosen host, or when measurements
demonstrate another benefit. A prefill/decode split also needs a measured KV-transfer path; NVLink
timing only applies when that path is actually available.
   Scope note. People, request arrivals and resident requests are different populations. The 10,000-
user setup needs a request-frequency assumption or trace before Chapter 17 can determine occupancy
and fleet capacity. The separate canonical 10/40 req/s workload can use the established Chapter
17 planning analysis. If a deliberately different storage scenario specifies 10,000 simultaneous full-
context resident requests, the ideal whole-context limit of 17 slots per host gives ⌈10,000/17⌉ = 589
hosts before throughput, runtime overhead, placement, SLO headroom and failure reserve. That is a
157                                                                              Communication


request-storage lower bound, not a user-derived deployment recommendation. More replicas do not
by themselves require cross-host model partitioning. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
chapter 10.


Parallelism: Splitting the Model Across
Machines




The Architect’s Question

After this chapter we should be able to answer the inevitable scaling question: a single GPU cannot
hold this model or keep up with this workload — how do we split the work across many GPUs, and
which split is right? We will build the arithmetic for why a model outgrows one GPU, then study
the five parallelization strategies — tensor, pipeline, data, expert, and sequence parallelism — plus a
serving-only sixth (P/D disaggregation, which has no training counterpart), and develop a rule for
choosing among them based on the model’s weight-residency, the workload’s batch shape, and the
interconnect speed. After this chapter, “we scaled it out” becomes a precise claim about what was
split and why.


10.1. Concept

The central idea: parallelism is splitting one of the three things a model occupies — its weights,
its layers, or its data — across multiple devices. Before reading on, one framing note that
prevents a common source of confusion: the parallelism toolkit differs between training and
inference, and “data parallelism” means different things in each mode. In training, DP means
replicated weights plus gradient all-reduce every step (plus FSDP, which shards and re-gathers
weights/optimizer state); the communication load is at the gradient-sync point. In inference, DP
simply means running independent model replicas to raise throughput — there is no gradient sync
at all, because each request is served by one replica. There is also an inference-specific family —
context/pipeline partitioning, expert parallelism, and P/D disaggregation (splitting the prefill stage



                                                 158
159                                                         Parallelism: Splitting the Model Across Machines


from the decode stage into separate pools) — which has no training analogue. The rest of this section
defines the strategies, and §10.3 applies them to inference (the book’s canonical serving context)
unless a strategy is explicitly training-only.
      The strategy names tell us what gets split:

      1. Tensor parallelism (TP) splits a single layer’s weights across GPUs. Each GPU holds a slice
        of the weight matrix and exchanges partial results through the TP group’s interconnect. These
        layer-level dependencies require sufficient measured bandwidth and low latency; NVLink
        is one implementation, not an algorithmic requirement. TP is intra-layer. (Inference: shards
        weights; per-step exchange is activations, not weights — see Ch. 9.)

      2. Pipeline parallelism (PP) splits the model’s layers (stages) across GPUs. GPU 1 runs layers
        1–10, GPU 2 runs 11–20, and so on; activations flow forward, gradients flow backward. PP is
        inter-layer, communication-light, but idle bubbles appear at stage boundaries. (Inference: can
        split decode stages; bubbles hurt latency-sensitive serving more than training.)

      3. Data parallelism (DP) — different in the two modes. Training: replicates all weights on every
        GPU, feeds each a different batch, all-reduces gradients after each step; communication-heavy
        only at the gradient-sync point, but each GPU must hold the full model. Inference: independent
        replicas each serve a disjoint set of requests; no gradient sync; throughput scales linearly until
        KV or memory binds (Ch. 17).

      4. Expert parallelism (EP) shards the experts of a Mixture-of-Experts model across GPUs and
        routes each token to the GPU holding its experts — an all-to-all exchange per token. EP is
        MoE-specific. (Used in both training and inference for MoE models.)

      5. Sequence/context parallelism (CP) splits the sequence dimension across GPUs, useful for
        very long contexts where the KV cache or attention activations exceed one GPU. (Inference-
        centric; the serving analogue of training sequence parallelism.)

      6. P/D disaggregation (inference) — separates the compute-bound prefill stage from the
        bandwidth-bound decode stage onto different GPU pools so each can be sized and scaled
        independently (Ch. 11). This has no training counterpart and is a serving-only strategy.

      These are not alternatives; production systems compose them (e.g. DP across nodes × TP within
a node × PP across a few nodes; or TP+CP within a decode pool + a separate prefill pool). The
architect’s job is deciding which dimension to split first, and in which mode (training vs inference)
the parallelism is being applied.
      The strategies are not either/or. Fig 10.1 shows the three canonical patterns side by side. Tensor
parallel shards one layer’s weight matrix across GPUs — activations are replicated, and each GPU’s
partial sums are all-reduced at layer-level dependencies in the illustrated layout. Those frequent
exchanges make measured collective latency and throughput margin important. Pipeline parallel

cuts the layer stack into stages on different GPUs — hidden states cross stage boundaries point-to-
point, an idle bubble appears as the pipeline fills and drains, and the communication can span nodes
if the stage-boundary transfer meets its budget. Data parallel replicates the whole model and splits
the batch — in training every replica all-reduces its gradient each step; in inference the replicas
are independent, each serving a disjoint slice of requests with no sync at all. Expert and sequence
parallelism (EP/CP) are additional axes that reuse the same machinery. The three primary patterns
compose (e.g. DP across nodes × TP within a node × PP across a few nodes) — which dimension
binds determines which to split first.


10.2. Mental Model

      Each strategy is best distinguished by what it trades bandwidth for. Tensor parallelism exchanges
layer results to distribute weight residency but adds synchronization dependencies. Pipeline paral­
lelism transfers stage-boundary activations and accepts bubbles as the price of not holding all layers
on one GPU. Training data parallelism trades gradient bandwidth for replicated weights; inference
replicas have no gradient synchronization. In either mode, each replica’s assigned devices must fit
its state.
      The useful mental model is a resource triangle: we have weights (memory), activations (work),
and data (batch). Each strategy moves one corner off a single GPU at the cost of communication.
When a GPU runs out of memory, we reach for TP/PP (weight splitting). When a GPU is idle waiting,
we reach for DP/CP (more work per GPU). When the model is too big to replicate, TP wins over DP.
The binding constraint chooses the strategy.

10.3. Worked Example

10.3.1. Why the Canonical 70B Doesn’t Fit One H100

The canonical model is 70B FP16 dense = 140 GB of weights [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] (reality
check: 70 ×10⁹ params × 2 bytes). A single H100 has 80 GB of HBM [1P][FACT]. The arithmetic is
immediate:

    • The weights alone don’t fit on one H100:



                                     140 GB weights > 80 GB HBM

    We need at least 140/80 ≈ 1.75 → ≥ 2 GPUs just to hold the weights (and that’s before KV
cache, which adds ~2.62 MB/token at FP16 (2.5 MiB) — the 9.2K-token canonical prompt needs ~24.1
GB more (initial KV)). [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
    The canonical 8×H100 host (640 GB total) fits the weights + KV comfortably, which is why the
single-host baseline in earlier chapters works. But if the model grows (say to 400B) or owns more,
the split becomes mandatory:
163                                                           Parallelism: Splitting the Model Across Machines


10.3.2. Tensor Parallelism: Splitting Weights Across GPUs

With tensor parallelism, the 140 GB weight tensor is partitioned across GPUs. Two H100 GPUs
would hold 70 GB of weights each, before KV state, activations and runtime overhead. A simplified
tensor-parallel forward pass exchanges partial activations rather than gathering the full weights.
For an eight-rank ring, one equal-sized all-reduce per layer and no overlap, the bandwidth term
is Ttp ≈ nlayers × 2(N − 1)/N × Mact /Bdir . Here Mact is the full logical activation tensor in bytes
contributed by each rank to one collective; for a dense activation it is token count times hidden
dimension times bytes per element. The actual number and shapes of collectives depend on the
partitioning and kernels. Bdir is directional effective bandwidth, not the sum of send and receive
peaks. H100 advertises 900 GB/s bidirectional per GPU, corresponding to a 450 GB/s peak in each
direction; achieved bandwidth requires measurement. Step latency, contention and reduction work
are additional costs. [1P][DERIVED]
      Tensor parallelism keeps weight shards resident and exchanges layer results. In a row-parallel
linear layer, ranks compute partial outputs from their local weight shards; a reduction combines
those partial outputs. Other layouts can use reduce-scatter and all-gather instead.1 The buffer shape,
communication precision, group size and number of collective calls determine the byte budget.
Ordinary TP decode does not fetch the full model weights over the network again for every token.
      Consider a small illustrative decode step with 16 active sequences, one new token per sequence,
hidden width 8,192, two-byte BF16 communication and eight TP ranks. Assume two output all-
reduces per transformer block — attention output and MLP — 80 blocks, no sequence parallelism,
and a balanced point-to-point ring. (The bandwidth term above counts one collective per layer;
this budget’s two-per-block assumption is why the call count below is 160 rather than 80.) These
are explicit teaching inputs, not a measured model configuration. [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]
[ANALYTICAL]
      Each all-reduce has a logical input of


                              M = 16 × 8,192 × 2 = 262,144 B = 256 KiB.

      The ring moves 1.75M = 448 KiB per rank sent and another 448 KiB received — the physical
volume moved exceeds the logical payload above.2 Across 160 calls (two per block × 80 blocks),
each rank sends 70 MiB and receives 70 MiB in that one decode step. The ideal byte term is about
0.163 ms at the 450 GB/s directional bandwidth above, or 2.936 ms at an assumed 25 GB/s; neither is
