    The token population is the rows processed in this step, not the full historical context length.
Prefill may process many more rows. A different sequence-parallel layout, fused kernel or offload
path changes the operation and its schedule. The budget therefore begins with the deployed layer
trace, not a fixed “bytes per model” rule. This distinction also changes the economics: a faster nominal
fabric may not reduce the host count if launch overhead, compute or memory residency remains
binding.


10.3.3. Pipeline Parallelism: Splitting Layers, Accepting Bubbles

Pipeline parallelism puts stage P on GPU P . The cost is the pipeline bubble: while the first micro-
batch fills the pipeline and the last one drains, stages sit idle. With P stages and m micro-batches,
the steady-state ideal speedup over a single serial pass is:

                                                         m·P
                                      ideal speedup =
                                                        m+P −1
    The P −1 term in the denominator is the bubble: the pipeline fills and drains exactly once per
m-batch pass, so P −1 stage-slots are wasted out of the m · P slots each stage would otherwise work.
With P = 4 stages and m = 8 micro-batches, ideal utilization is

                                 8·4    32
                                      =    ≈ 2.9 ×          (out of 4×)
                                8+4−1   11
    — a meaningful bubble. Fewer stages or more micro-batches shrink it: with m = 32,

                                         32 · 4    128
                                                 =     ≈ 3.66 × .
                                      32 + 4 − 1    35
    The lesson: PP is communication-light (each stage only moves activation boundaries across the
fabric) but always pays a bubble that grows with stage count. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]


10.3.4. Data Parallelism: Replicating, Then Syncing Gradients

Data parallelism replicates the 140 GB model on every GPU. For the gradient all-reduce: if the model
has 140 GB of weights and we sync gradients after each step across G GPUs, each GPU sends its
gradient tensor once per step. The gradient bytes are


                  grad bytes = Nparams × bytes/param = 70 × 109 × 4 B ≈ 280 GB
165                                                              Parallelism: Splitting the Model Across Machines


      per step (FP32 gradient; the all-reduce moves the gradient once, not weights+gradients). As in
Chapter 9, a ring all-reduce moves 2 NN−1 times the per-rank gradient through each rank, so for
N = 8 the per-rank traffic is 1.75 × 280 ≈ 490 GB and the sync time is Tring = 2 NN−1 bytes/Beff .
At 25 GB/s (single 200Gb/s link) that is 490 / 25 ≈ 19.6 s per step — far too slow if the step takes
~1 s. At the H100 NVLink directional peak of 450 GB/s, the same ideal ring estimate is 490/450
≈ 1.09 s. The 900 GB/s bidirectional sum cannot divide a send-only traffic count; this remains a
communication model, not proof of training-state fit. The sync cost, not compute, often caps DP at
small scale unless the interconnect is fast. [1P][DERIVED]
      The 280 GB is the logical FP32 gradient for a full model replica, not a feasible single-H100
allocation. In hybrid DP×TP training, a DP communicator can join matching parameter shards from
different replicas. Its per-device buffer size and participating ranks replace the full-replica logical
inputs above; the TP group within each replica is a different communicator (NCCL communicator
definition). Chapter 9’s separate 140 GB example assumes FP16 gradients, so the two examples must
retain their different precision bases.
      Two more communication objects complete the picture. For expert parallelism, the population
is routed token copies rather than TP partial outputs. With eight EP ranks, 256 local tokens per
rank, top-2 routing, hidden width 8,192 and BF16, an illustrative uniform routing model produces 8
MiB of route rows per rank. Seven eighths go remote: dispatch sends and receives 7 MiB per rank.
An equal-sized combine doubles those totals to 14 MiB sent and 14 MiB received. This excludes
metadata, padding, compression, route deduplication and load skew. A hot destination can dominate
completion even when the average byte budget fits. Specialized dispatch/combine implementations
may exploit structure that a fixed-count all-to-all does not expose.3 [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
[ANALYTICAL]
      FSDP changes the object again. Its communication can gather a module’s parameter shards before
computation and reduce-scatter that module’s gradients afterward. An illustrative 64 MiB unit split
eight ways requires 56 MiB sent and 56 MiB received per rank for a balanced ring all-gather; the same
full-size gradient gives the same per-rank reduce-scatter volumes. This is a unit-sized calculation,
not a claim that every forward gathers the whole model or every optimizer state.4 [ILLUSTRATIVE]
[DERIVED][ANALYTICAL]


10.4. Measurement

      Four habits anchor the architect:
      1. Measure weight residency before choosing a split. bytes = params × bytes_per_
          param lands first; it decides whether TP/PP (memory) or DP (replication) is even possible.
      3
       Dispatch/combine structure in DeepSeek DeepEP at pinned revision f6aa38fe06cd4a0489e7730365d4e0114970a2f3
(retrieved 2026-10-27): https://raw.githubusercontent.com/deepseek-ai/DeepEP/f6aa38fe06cd4a0489e7730365d4e0114970a2f3/
README.md
     4
       FSDP _fully_shard implementation, PyTorch v2.9.0 tag (retrieved 2026-10-27): https://raw.githubusercontent.com/
pytorch/pytorch/v2.9.0/torch/distributed/fsdp/_fully_shard/_fully_shard.py
Parallelism: Splitting the Model Across Machines                                                                166


   2. Measure the actual collective path. For the H100 example, 900 GB/s is the bidirectional peak
        sum, not a directional or sustained rate. Compare measured collective completion times at the
        deployed message shapes, rank placement and contention. A cluster’s bandwidth depends on
        its links, rail count and topology; the fabric name alone does not determine the gap.

   3. Measure the bubble and the step time. For PP, log the fraction of idle GPU time (bubble) vs
        compute. For DP, time the gradient all-reduce as a fraction of step time — if it exceeds ~20%, it
        caps scaling.

   4. Measure communication overlap. The best systems overlap all-reduce with the next for­
        ward/backward compute. Log the non-overlapped comm time — that is the true cost, not the
        raw bytes.


10.5. Common Mistakes

    • Splitting with DP when the model doesn’t fit. DP replicates weights; if 140 GB > 80 GB,
        one DP replica doesn’t even fit one GPU. Reach for TP/PP first.

    • Using TP without budgeting its exchanges. The same byte term is larger at 25 GB/s than
        at 450 GB/s, but whether it binds depends on message shape, call count and exposed latency.
        Tensor parallelism requires a communication path fast enough for its per-layer exchanges:
        NVLink is one implementation, not a requirement of the algorithm.5 PCIe or another fabric is
        viable only when measured collective cost leaves sufficient latency and throughput margin —
        a measurement requirement, not a claim of universal performance for any fabric. The feasible
        split also depends on each rank’s memory and supported kernels; a slower link can erase a
        capacity gain even when the weights fit.

    • Ignoring the pipeline bubble. PP’s idle stages waste real utilization; the bubble grows with
        stage count. It is not free.

    • Quoting peak interconnect spec as sustained. NVLink 900 GB/s is aggregate peak; real
        all-reduce achieves a fraction. Budget headroom.

    • Treating parallelism as an either/or. Real systems compose DP×TP×PP; the question is
        which dimension binds, not which one to use.

10.6. Architecture Consequence

      The parallelism strategy is forced by the binding constraint, and that constraint is usually
memory for large models:
      • A model that exceeds one GPU’s memory must split weights → TP (within a node, over
        the fabric that actually connects its GPUs — the requirement is measured collective latency
        and throughput margin, not a vendor fabric name) or PP (across nodes, low comm). Which
        one depends on whether the model fits a node: fits one node → TP among its GPUs; spans
        nodes → PP across them, with TP inside each node.

      • A workload with high throughput demand (like the canonical ~10 rps / 40 rps) → inde­
        pendent inference replicas after the state fits each replica’s assigned devices. The canonical 70B
        fits across an 8×H100 node through intra-host model parallelism; additional replicas address
        fleet capacity. Gradient synchronization applies only to training or fine-tuning.

      • MoE models (if chosen per Ch3) push toward EP, because the full expert set must be resident
        (the active count sets compute per token, not residency) and EP shards the experts across
        GPUs.

      • The canonical answer: the book’s ~70B/8×H100 baseline uses intra-host TP=8 to distribute
        the 140 GB weights and serving state. It requires model parallelism within the host, but not
        cross-host model parallelism. Eight ranks are the chosen baseline, not a minimum derived
        from weight bytes alone. TP, PP and independent replicas can then be composed according
        to measured capacity, communication and SLO constraints; their names do not establish a
        universal escalation order.

      Table 10-1 above consolidates the five parallelization strategies (plus the serving-only P/D
disaggregation): reading across a row gives one strategy’s full trade-off (what it splits, what it
replicates, what it communicates, when it fits), and reading down a column shows how each axis
varies across strategies. (Fig 10.1 illustrates the three canonical patterns — TP, PP, DP — side by side;
the table adds the specialist EP and CP rows.)


10.7. What We Still Don’t Know

      • Optimal split for very large MoE or long-context models is workload- and interconnect-
        dependent; the exact NVLink-vs-fabric crossover for a given model is unmeasured
        [UNRESOLVED] — measure on the target cluster.

      • 2026 MoE scaling has moved the specialist/EP frontier. Kimi K3 activates just 16 of
        896 routed experts per token (2.8T total / 104B active) via its Stable LatentMoE [1P: arXiv
        2607.24653]; Qwen3.8-Flash-Next routes 10+1 of 512 experts (125B total / 6B active) [1P: HF
Parallelism: Splitting the Model Across Machines                                                 168


      Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next]. These extreme sparsities (16/896 ≈ 1.8% expert activation) are
      why expert-parallel and fused cross-expert comm kernels (e.g. MoE expert parallelism with
      fused compute/communication, as in DeepSeek’s DeepEP/TileLang infra) are increasingly
      central to serving large MoE fleets [1P: arXiv 2606.19348]. For the architect this changes the
      serving calculus: a frontier MoE’s activated footprint (Kimi 104B, Qwen 6B) can be dramatically
      smaller than its total size, so the compute decision is made against active parameters — but
      the memory-bound EP decision (how many experts must be resident) is made against total
      parameters, since the full expert set occupies HBM even when only a fraction is routed per
      token.

    • Communication-overlap efficiency in real kernels is hard to predict from spec; sustained
      all-reduce throughput is a [HYPOTHESIS] until measured on the target cluster.

    • The right parallelism for mixed prefill/decode (P/D disaggregated) serving — where
      the prefill pool and decode pool may want different splits — is an active research area and a
      [HYPOTHESIS] for this book.


10.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: Diagnosing Why the Grown 400B MoE Is Slow

An architect inherits a deployment where the internal Q&A model (from Ch1’s mini-case) has
been fine-tuned and grown to a 400B-parameter MoE. The team reports “parallelism is killing us —
everything is slow.” The architect applies this chapter’s lens. First, weight residency: a 400B model
needs ~400e9 ×2 bytes = 800 GB even before KV — that is ~10×H100 for weights alone (~11
once KV/workspace is included), far beyond one node. The model necessarily spans nodes; the
architect must choose an inter-node decomposition — often PP and/or EP for MoE — while
avoiding expensive cross-node TP where possible (TP benefits from a tightly coupled NVLink-style
interconnect; across a slower network its per-layer all-reduce cost grows fast). Within each node,
the MoE active weights are small, so the team uses EP to shard experts + TP inside the node. The
architect measures the interconnect: the cross-node PP boundary runs over the cluster fabric (not
NVLink), so they minimize the number of PP stages to shrink the bubble, and they verify the DP
gradient-sync (if fine-tuning) stays under ~20% of step time. The result: a composed PP × EP × TP
configuration whose binding constraints (memory across nodes + expert routing) are each addressed
by the strategy that trades the right bandwidth. The team’s “parallelism is slow” becomes a precise,
diagnosed, and fixed split.
chapter 11.


Serving: From Model in Memory to Requests in
Flight



Serving is a small set of composable mechanisms — continuous batching, paged/blocked KV cache,
prefix caching, and prefill/decode disaggregation — that turn a static in-memory model into a live
multi-request system. The architecture choices that matter are which of these are adopted and how
they share the host’s KV budget, because the latency SLO is met by the batch and cache strategy
rather than by the model alone.


The Architect’s Question

After this chapter we should be able to answer the operational half of deployment: the model is
in memory and the requests are arriving at ~10 per second — how do we actually serve them without
violating our latency SLO? We will develop the serving mechanisms that turn a static model into
a live, multi-request system: how requests are batched, how KV cache memory is managed, how
repeated prefixes are reused, and when to split prefill from decode onto separate pools. After this
chapter, serving is not a black box — it is a sequence of explicit architectural choices, each with a
measurable consequence.


11.1. Concept

Serving is a small set of mechanisms, invented roughly in order:

   1. Batching — running multiple requests through the model together to amortize the weight
      reads. The key modern advance is continuous (iteration-level) batching introduced by



                                                169
Serving: From Model in Memory to Requests in Flight                                                 170


      Orca (OSDI 2022): instead of waiting for an entire batch to finish, the scheduler admits and
      evicts requests at every decoding step, filling the GPU’s idle slots as soon as they free up. [S1]
      [1P]

   2. PagedAttention / vLLM (SOSP 2023) — managing the KV cache in fixed-size blocks (like a
      virtual-memory page table) so that different requests’ KV caches no longer need contiguous
      memory, slashing fragmentation and letting the serving engine pack far more concurrent
      requests. [S2][1P]

   3. Prefix caching — recognizing that many requests share context (e.g. the same retrieved
      documents), and caching the KV of the common prefix so a new request does not re-prefill it.
      RadixAttention (SGLang) and Automatic Prefix Caching (vLLM APC) are the canonical
      implementations. [S3][1P]

   4. P/D disaggregation — splitting the compute-bound prefill stage from the bandwidth-bound
      decode stage onto separate pools, because they bottleneck on different resources. Pioneered by
      Splitwise (ISCA 2024) and DistServe (OSDI 2024); Mooncake takes the KV-centric view,
      transferring KV caches from the prefill pool to the decode pool (with CPU/DRAM/SSD offload)
      and reports up to 525% throughput lift in long-context simulation and 75% more requests
      on a real Kimi workload. [S4][1P]

    These mechanisms compose: continuous batching is the baseline, PagedAttention makes it
memory-efficient, prefix caching makes it cheaper, and P/D disaggregation makes it scale.
    Source keys [S1]–[S6]. The bracketed keys used throughout this book (and in the evidence
taxonomy of the Sources, Method, and Reproducibility chapter) point to the primary sources below.
Each is a [1P] first-party or peer-reviewed source; the book’s derived numbers cite the key plus a
[DERIVED] tag.

    • [S1] Orca — Yu et al., “Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative
      Models,” OSDI 2022. Continuous (iteration-level) batching.
    • [S2] PagedAttention / vLLM — Kwon et al., “Efficient Memory Management for Large
      Language Model Serving with PagedAttention,” SOSP 2023. Block-based KV cache.
    • [S3] Prefix caching — “Fast Inference from Transformers via Radix Attention” (SGLang, 2023)
      and vLLM Automatic Prefix Caching (APC). Caching shared-prefix KV.
    • [S4] P/D disaggregation — “Splitwise: Efficient Generative LLM Inference Using Phase
      Splitting” (ISCA 2024), “DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized
      Large Language Model Serving” (OSDI 2024), and Mooncake (KV-centric disaggregation, 2024).
    • [S5] DFlash — Chen et al., “DFlash: Block Diffusion for Flash Speculative Decoding,” ICML
      2026 (PMLR v306; arXiv:2602.06036). Speculative-decoding system reporting >6× lossless
      acceleration over autoregressive decoding (up to 6.1× on Qwen3-8B) and up to 2.5× faster than
      the prior state of the art, EAGLE-3.
171                                                    Serving: From Model in Memory to Requests in Flight


      • [S6] vLLM FP8-KV blog — the vLLM FP8-KV blog post’s ‘54%’ figure is a decode inter-token-
        latency (ITL) slope, a LATENCY metric, not a memory/residency ratio. Any reference to it
        (Chapters 1, 3, 6, 7, 15, 22, Appendix A and the glossary) is a latency reference only. The KV

        50% of BF16) [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]; any block-allocation/metadata overhead is NOT
        vendor-measured here and must be filled by a deployment benchmark.


11.2. Mental Model

      Serving is managing three precious resources against a stream of arrivals: GPU compute
(FLOPs, bound in prefill), GPU memory bandwidth (HBM, bound in decode), and GPU memory
capacity (HBM bytes, bound by KV cache). Each mechanism trades one of these:
    • Batching improves compute and bandwidth utilization by amortizing the fixed per-step weight
        reads across more requests.
      • PagedAttention improves memory capacity by eliminating KV fragmentation.
      • Prefix caching reduces memory capacity and prefill compute by reusing already-computed
        KV.
      • P/D disaggregation lets the prefill pool run at high compute utilization and the decode pool
        at high bandwidth utilization simultaneously, instead of one pool being starved.

      The mental model is a resource budget: a request arrives, consumes some FLOPs (prefill), some
bandwidth (decode), and some memory (its KV cache) for its lifetime. Serving architecture is about
sizing and scheduling those three budgets so the SLO holds across the burst.


11.3. Worked Example

11.3.1. The Canonical Workload in a Serving System

Recall the canonical enterprise-Q&A RAG workload (Ch 4, Table 4-2): ~10 rps average, ~40 rps peak;
each request carries ~9,200 input tokens and ~300 output tokens; TTFT budget 1.2 s, TPOT ~25
ms/token. [ASSUMPTION]

11.3.2. Discrete Batching Wastes the GPU

Naive discrete (static) batching accumulates requests until a batch fills, then runs them to comple­
tion, then starts the next batch. Problems compound at this workload’s 9.2K-input shape:

      • Requests arrive in bursts (recall the ~40 rps peak). Discrete batching forces early-arriving
        requests to wait for the batch to fill, inflating TTFT toward the 2 s SLO breach.
      • The batch is locked until its slowest member finishes (fits-all-in-one-run), so a short 100-token
        output tails behind the longest while the GPU finishes the whole batch — idle bubbles at the
        end of every batch.
Serving: From Model in Memory to Requests in Flight                                               172


    • Batch boundaries create periods where the GPU drains (no work) then floods — utilization is
      spiky around the mean. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]

11.3.3. Continuous Batching Fills the Bubbles

Continuous batching (Orca [S1][1P]) eliminates the batch boundary: at every decode step the
scheduler accepts any new prefill-ready request and evicts any finished one, so decode slots never
sit idle. In the canonical stream, a 300-token decode at ~25 ms/token occupies a slot for ~7.5 s;
while a long decode runs, the freed FLOPs are continuously refilled by new short requests. The
utilization gain is the difference between spiky discrete batches and a continuously-fed pipeline.
Rather than stipulate a single percent, the mechanism makes the GPU the steady bottleneck instead
of the scheduler. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]

11.3.4. PagedAttention: Killing the Fragmentation Tax

In re-packaged (naive) serving, each request’s KV cache for 9.2K input is ~24.1 GB (FP16, ~2.62 MB/to­
ken × 9,200, initial KV) [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]. If served contiguously, variable-length com­
pletions leave fragmented, unusable holes — exactly like a fragmented heap. PagedAttention/vLLM
[S2][1P] allocates KV in fixed blocks shared and evicted like page frames, so the ~24.1 GB per re­
quest is packed densely and more concurrent requests fit in the same 640 GB node [ILLUSTRATIVE]
[DERIVED]. The win is more concurrency under the same SLO, not faster single-request math.

11.3.5. Prefix Caching: Don’t Re-Prefill the Same Documents

The RAG request’s 8K retrieved-context tokens are largely shared across queries (same documents).
Without caching, every request re-runs the ~1.29 PFLOP prefill for those 8K tokens [ILLUSTRATIVE]
[DERIVED]. RadixAttention / APC [S3][1P] caches the KV of common prefixes, so a new request
reuses the shared-document KV and prefills only the unique query tail — cutting the dominant prefill
FLOPs and TTFT for repeated-context traffic [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]. Layout caveat: this reuse
requires the shared documents to sit at a fixed prefix position in the prompt (e.g. system prompt →
retrieved documents → unique query tail). If the unique query precedes the documents, the causal
K/V of the document span differs per query and no prefix is reusable — the savings above assume
the documents-then-query layout, which the architect must verify in the actual prompt template.
    Prefix reuse is also only one of the state-preservation requirements a serving system must meet:
preemption, speculative rollback, and adaptive-depth execution all constrain what a cache may evict
or reuse — see the serving qualification in §4.

11.3.6. When to Disaggregate: Prefill and Decode Want Different Pools

Recall from Ch2/Ch6: prefill is compute-bound (~1.29 PFLOP → ~1.19 PFLOPS required vs 0.989
PFLOPS peak), decode is bandwidth-bound (the whole-model weight-read rate of ~5.6 TB/s if served
by one device vs 3.35 TB/s per GPU; under the canonical 8×H100 host it is sharded to ~0.70 TB/s
per GPU, and the shard-invariant cause is the low ~1.0 FLOP/byte intensity, Ch 6) [1P][DERIVED].
Serving both from one pool forces a compromise: batch for prefill and it slows decode; optimize for
decode and prefill starves. P/D disaggregation (Splitwise/DistServe/Mooncake [S4][1P]) runs
prefill nodes at high FLOP-utilization and decode nodes at high bandwidth-utilization, transferring
KV across via the fabric (Fig 11.3 shows the two-pool topology and what moves between them).
Mooncake’s reported up to 525% long-context throughput and +75% request count are the quantitative
anchor [S4][1P]. For the canonical single-host (~10 rps) this disaggregation is premature; it pays off
only when the workload outgrows a node and the two phases’ resource conflicts become binding.
    The state crossing between prefill and decode pools is a different communication object from
a TP activation reduction. Its endpoints, ownership, block layout, and transfer frequency must be
stated independently. A KV-transfer path may use point-to-point or specialized transfer facilities
rather than a group collective. The service budget includes transfer and orchestration on the request’s
critical path; it does not count a whole KV cache again on every ordinary decode step. Ch 9 provides
the directional byte convention; this chapter determines when moving ownership is worthwhile.

11.4. Measurement

Good serving telemetry answers “are we meeting the SLO while keeping the GPU busy?”:

      1. Measure goodput, not raw throughput — tokens/s that arrive before their SLO deadline
        (Ch6). Continuous batching is only a win if it raises goodput.

      2. Measure KV utilization — fraction of the 640 GB node memory consumed by live KV vs
        weights. PagedAttention and prefix caching both raise the effective KV packing; track it.

      3. Measure prefill-vs-decode utilization separately — a FLOP-bound prefill core and a
        bandwidth-bound decode core running on one pool tells us when to disaggregate.

      4. Measure the scheduler’s real occupancy — idle decode slots, queue wait, and the tail of
        TTFT under load, not the average.

11.4.1. Serving qualification: model support is not serving capability

Model support is not a complete serving capability. A hybrid model can require both paged history
and bounded recurrent state. A looped-depth model can require iteration-specific caches. Prefix
reuse, preemption, and speculative rollback must preserve the state that the next execution actually
consumes. An early-exit interface also needs a runtime path that avoids the skipped work, rather
than selecting logits after all work has already run. A capability record can therefore identify the
exact model revision, engine revision, state representation, cache policy, precision, and supported
execution paths; kernel or module speedups remain separate from end-to-end goodput at the service
SLO. [DERIVED]
      Adaptive depth changes the scheduler’s unit of work. Requests that exit at different iterations can
leave an initially uniform batch with different amounts of remaining computation. A runtime may
compact active requests or group them by depth, but compaction, cache indexing, and synchronization
consume resources. Padding every request to the deepest active iteration can preserve batching
convenience while eliminating the hoped-for arithmetic saving. These are alternative implementation
choices, not measured features. [DERIVED]
      Latency evaluation must retain the depth distribution. Average passes per token does not deter­
mine p95 token latency: difficult tokens, long histories, and queueing can coincide. A comparison
Serving: From Model in Memory to Requests in Flight                                               176


therefore fixes the prompt population, output length, quality criterion, and SLO, then records actual
pass counts, state allocation, and elapsed time by phase. When prefill and decode use different cache
policies, one aggregate cache-reduction factor hides the capacity bottleneck. [DERIVED]
    The economic denominator is completed, quality-compliant work within the service target. A
reduced core-work budget is useful only if it increases that useful output or lowers the resources
required to produce it. Routing a difficult request to more depth can be rational even when its
per-token cost rises. Conversely, premature exits that can require retries can raise task cost despite
shorter first attempts. A training-time self-improvement loop and an inference-time depth loop
are different mechanisms; sharing the word “iteration” assigns no inference-time saving to either.
[DERIVED]


11.5. Common Mistakes

    • Assuming bigger batches always help. Bigger discrete batches raise raw tokens/s but push
      TTFT past the SLO, zeroing goodput (Ch6). Continuous batching exists precisely to uncouple
      batch size from wait.

    • Serving KV contiguous and watching fragmentation. PagedAttention removes the frag­
      mentation tax; skipping it wastes memory under concurrency.

    • Re-prefilling shared context. Without prefix caching, repeated RAG documents are recom­
      puted per request — one of the most wasteful failures for this workload.

    • Choosing P/D disaggregation too early. Splitting pools adds fabric + orchestration; for a
      single host it is overhead without the resource conflict that motivates it.

    • Believing speculative decoding (DFlash reports >6× lossless acceleration, up to 2.5×
      faster than EAGLE-3 [S5][1P]) is a serving baseline. These are paper-reported results
      under the paper’s evaluation setup, not portable serving-speed figures. Speculative decoding
      is an optimization for bandwidth-bound decode, not a requirement, and must be validated on
      the workload.


11.6. Architecture Consequence

    The serving mechanisms dictate the deployment choices:
    • Baseline (canonical single-host): continuous batching (vLLM/Orca) is near-mandatory to
      hold TTFT under the SLO (1.2 s, p95 ≤ 2 s) at 10 rps input-heavy load; PagedAttention ensures
      the ~24.1 GB-per-request KV pack fits; prefix caching is the highest-leverage optimization
      because the workload is repeated-context RAG. This matches the memory and compute
      conclusions of Ch4/Ch7 for the ~10 rps average baseline; at the ~40 rps peak the KV budget
      forces replication, which Chapter 17 sizes. [S1][S2][S3][1P]

figure 11.2: Serving is four orthogonal concerns, not a stack (request scheduling, state management,
reuse, resource specialisation). A concrete serving design that chooses one mechanism per concern:
request scheduling = continuous (Orca-style) batching; state management = PagedAttention
(fixed-size KV pages); reuse = prefix caching of shared context; resource specialisation = P/D
disaggregation (separate prefill and decode pools). The four are independent dials — a system can
combine any mechanism with any other — and the canonical baseline uses the first three; resource
specialisation joins when the workload outgrows a node (§11.3.6). [ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual]
 The design lever is what each concern trades: request scheduling exchanges latency for utilization,
 state management exchanges memory capacity for concurrency, reuse avoids re-prefill FLOPs, and
             resource specialisation matches two compute/memory regimes to two pools.


      • Scaling up: those three carry the workload far before disaggregation is justified. FP8 KV (raw
        tensor byte-halving = 1.31 MB/token, exactly 50% of BF16) [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] and
        KV offloading are memory levers available without restructuring.

      • Beyond a node: when prefill FLOPs and decode bandwidth fight on one pool, P/D disaggrega­
        tion (Splitwise/DistServe/Mooncake) is the architecture of choice, with Mooncake’s KV-transfer
        engine moving caches between pools. [S4][1P]

can erase the benefit — the transfer cost is the term that decides whether P/D disaggregation pays.

    The columns read as knobs on a common set of mechanisms, not as “which engine is best.” An
engine’s real value is which mechanisms it implements well for the deployed workload’s shape — e.g. a
repeated-context RAG workload cares most about the prefix-caching row (RadixAttention in SGLang
is a strong implementation), while a latency-critical single-stream deployment might care more about
the scheduler and structured-generation rows. Never conclude “X is the go-to engine” — that is
workload-independent and will be wrong. The only defensible statement is workload-specific: for
this request shape, this precision, and this hardware, engine Y implements the mechanism Z we need;
benchmark it against the alternative (Ch. 14).


11.6.2. What the capability table does not promise

A recognized quantization name is not an end-to-end support claim. A deployment needs
a chain of compatible choices: checkpoint schema, model graph, tensor layout, operator coverage,
runtime dependencies, and device instructions. “Supports four-bit weights” does not establish support
for a model’s grouped expert GEMMs, attention variant, modal branches, or KV format. A backend
may accept a checkpoint and select a different arithmetic path, reject a particular shape, or need
a temporary higher-precision representation; the serialized tensor layout and the kernel-required
runtime layout are different objects. A missing compatible path is a deployment failure, not a
guaranteed fallback. [1P][DERIVED] Implementation-specific examples are dated separately.
    The deployment record therefore includes the exact model and engine revision, device architec­
ture, driver/toolkit and library versions, quantized tensor inventory, selected kernels, and fallback
logs. It also records cold-load peak and steady HBM separately. This record determines whether the
configuration can be reproduced; a single support-table checkmark does not. Allocator or scheduling
limits then determine how much of the remaining memory can become usable KV capacity without
violating latency targets. Smaller weights do not justify increasing admitted concurrency until the
new operating point is measured. [DERIVED]
    A serving feature belongs to an algorithm path. The capability table is a map of mechanisms,
not a guarantee that every supported model can combine every row. Diffusion language models
181                                                           Serving: From Model in Memory to Requests in Flight


make this qualification especially important. A paged allocator can manage buffers without proving
that their contents remain valid across refinement. A prefix-cache key must describe finalized
token content and compatible state, not an unresolved mask canvas. Grammar constraints, quantized
loading, graph capture, and distributed parallelism also depend on the selected model implementation
and sampler. [1P][FACT]
      Requests can require different numbers of refinement rounds. A lockstep batch waits for its
slowest active member unless the scheduler can preserve unfinished state and admit or complete
requests independently. The SGLang diffusion scheduler inspected on 2026-10-28 (revision a1966e1)
implements a first-done-first-out path that retains partial block state.1 This is explicit iteration-aware
scheduling, not evidence that the autoregressive token loop works unchanged — an observation about
that inspected revision, dated 2026-10-28 and outside this edition’s 2026-08-30 evidence snapshot.
Tail latency depends on the distribution of rounds, block sizes, queueing, refresh, and cancellation,
not merely the average accepted tokens per round. [1P][FACT]; latency interpretation [DERIVED]
      A prefill/decode-style split must place context encoding, block refinement, and finalization on
explicit resources. Any transferred state, repeated attention to that state, and finalization work belong
in the service budget. The familiar principle survives: specialization is useful only when its benefit
exceeds transfer and orchestration costs. The objects being transferred cannot be inferred from an
autoregressive KV formula alone. [DERIVED]
      The complete backend path. A serving engine needs more than a visible accelerator. It needs
a compatible model implementation, numerical representation, attention path, cache management,
kernel set, runtime and driver. Distributed execution adds a collective backend and a supported
transport. Fig 11.4 separates these dependencies from the final qualification decision. Its columns are
alternatives, not interchangeable APIs.
      The distinction matters when an engine changes its implementation without failing the re­
quest. OpenVINO GenAI documentation inspected on 2026-10-28 states that LLMPipeline and
VLMPipeline can fall back to contiguous-cache SDPA if paged-attention initialization fails; explicit
paged-attention selection can instead make that failure visible.2 A service that still generates tokens
may therefore have lost the cache behavior assumed by its capacity calculation. The resulting con­
currency limit and queueing latency must be measured again. This CPU/GPU behavior does not
imply the same feature set on the NPU. [1P] (observed 2026-10-28, outside the 2026-08-30 snapshot)

      Graph execution provides a second example. Capturing work can reduce repeated launch over­
head, but it introduces startup work and constraints on supported shapes and operators. A compiler
transformation and graph replay are not the same mechanism. The SGLang XPU documentation
inspected on 2026-10-28 treats decode and prefill graphs separately and marks them experimental
and opt-in; the prefill breakable path uses segmented capture rather than torch.compile.3 More
capture is not automatically better when startup delay or shape diversity dominates. [1P] (observed
2026-10-28, outside the 2026-08-30 snapshot)
      A compact qualification record can contain seven gates:

      1. Exact device, checkpoint, tokenizer, engine, and dependency identities are fixed.
      2. Each rank fits weights, KV, workspace, and temporary conversion state.
      3. Required operators, weight/activation/KV formats, and attention layouts execute correctly.
      4. Scheduling, cache reuse, graph behavior, and any fallback are observable.
      5. Required collectives work on the deployed topology and message sizes.
      6. Long-context quality, concurrent-request isolation, and failure recovery pass.
      7. Measured tail latency and quality-qualified goodput satisfy the workload contract.

      A failure closes the proposed configuration. A different configuration can be evaluated, but a
reduced context, changed quality threshold, or disabled feature is a changed deployment — not an
unnoticed repair to the original result.


11.6.3. The serving concerns transfer; the text mechanisms do not transfer automatically

A video service still schedules requests, manages live state, reuses valid work, and chooses resource-
specialized pools. The mechanisms implementing those concerns differ. The inspected full-clip
Wan path does not emit a completed next frame at each denoising step.4 A step boundary can be a
scheduling or cancellation point if the runtime exposes it, but it is not automatically a text continuous-
batching boundary. Jobs with different shapes, samplers, guidance branches, and timestep sched­
ules may be difficult or wasteful to batch together. [1P][FACT] model execution; [ILLUSTRATIVE]
[HYPOTHESIS] scheduling consequence.
      A useful admission record therefore includes the checkpoint revision, task type, exact height
and width, frame count, audio/reference inputs, schedule, guidance method, precision, and parallel
layout. Shape-aware buckets limit padding and kernel recompilation. A deadline-aware dispatcher
can separate interactive previews from full-quality completion. It must include queue age and avoid

starving long jobs. A low-step preview is a separate quality contract unless the implementation
proves that its state can continue into the final recipe. A preview image, first decoded frame, and
finalized downloadable clip are three different completion events.
    Per-request memory limits follow measured peaks for each admitted configuration. The largest
VAE reconstruction, full-clip attention workspace, compiler workspace, and overlapping transfers
can bind even when the weight set fits. Offload and quantization change those peaks only where
the actual kernels support the chosen representation. A quantized checkpoint file alone does not
establish faster execution, adequate reconstruction quality, or a supported attention backend. [1P]
[FACT] documented offload paths; [ILLUSTRATIVE][HYPOTHESIS] deployment consequences.
    Parallelism also changes the cost of a step. Sequence or context parallelism partitions video
positions and exchanges attention data. Tensor parallelism partitions model operations and introduces
its own collectives. Weight sharding is a residency technique, not a synonym for either. Wan2.2’s
official multi-GPU path combines FSDP and Ulysses; the Ulysses strategy’s attention-head divisibility
requirement is part of the deployable configuration.5 More aggregate GPU memory does not establish
that an arbitrary partition or mixed-speed GPU group is valid or fast. Repeated synchronization
can make the slowest device or weakest link determine the step time. [1P][FACT] supported path;
[ILLUSTRATIVE][HYPOTHESIS] performance boundary.
    The end-to-end clock starts at request acceptance and ends only after the promised media artifact
is available. Model denoising, VAE decode, frame transfer, video encoding, audio muxing, safety
checks, storage upload, and delivery can all extend that clock. Encoder-heavy postprocessing may
merit a separate CPU or GPU pool, but the transfer and queue cost must be measured. A text
prefill/decode split does not prove that the same split is useful here.

11.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: Which Serving Mechanism to Reach For

This is an illustrative scenario, not a measured result. [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] An architect
examines one 8×H100 replica in the canonical internal Q&A service, whose aggregate service peak is
40 rps. Suppose that replica’s assigned load produces p95 TTFT of 2.2 s against a 2 s SLO. The first
checks are whether continuous batching and PagedAttention are active: the baseline KV for 9.2K
inputs is about 24.1 GB per request, so allocation behavior matters. Repeated RAG documents then
make prefix caching a candidate because valid shared-prefix KV can avoid repeated prefill work.
Suppose a controlled test at the same assigned load and request mix brings p95 TTFT below 1.8 s.
That assumed result would support the cache change for this replica; it would not establish service
capacity at 40 rps. P/D disaggregation and speculative decoding remain separate candidates, not
required steps in this diagnosis.
      Scope note: with the baseline mean service-time assumption of 8.6 s, the aggregate 40 rps peak
implies approximately 344 in-flight requests. The baseline unshared-KV capacity quotient is about
17.5 complete requests per host, conservatively floored to 17 integer slots. [canonical scenario]
[DERIVED] That baseline requires multiple replicas; a per-request TTFT result does not size the fleet.
Any capacity credit for sharing must follow measured prefix-cache occupancy, hit rates, service time,
and tail latency under the admitted workload. Chapter 17 applies joint residency and throughput
constraints, headroom, and failure reserve. The replica’s latency result and the service’s capacity
decision remain distinct.
    part IV.


The Architecture




       186
chapter 12.


Designing the AI System: From Constraints to
Candidates



Designing an AI system is constraint-driven generation, not menu-picking: the architect extracts
the hard constraints from a characterized workload — the three gates this chapter fixes: memory fit,
throughput at the SLO, and quality — then synthesizes candidate architectures that must clear them.
The payoff is a bounded set of two to three candidates that each fail a distinct, inspectable gate —
memory fit, throughput, or quality — which the measuring chapters then adjudicate.


The Architect’s Question

Designing an AI system means producing candidate architectures from the substrate — memory,
compute, communication, and parallelism — rather than selecting a canned stack. This chapter works
through a synthesis method: given a characterized workload from the six-dimension framework
(Ch. 4), generate two or three candidate architectures that each satisfy the hard constraints — the
three gates fixed here: memory fit, throughput at the SLO, and quality — then carry them forward
for evaluation in Chs. 14–16. The core thesis is that design is constraint-driven generation, not
menu-picking. This distinguishes our approach from the abstract meta-method presented in Ch. 22,
which operates at a level of generality that does not instantiate against concrete substrate constraints.
In the language of the book’s spine — the decision loop constrain → synthesize → measure → decide
→ refine — this chapter is the synthesize step: we turn a constraint-characterized workload into a
bounded set of candidate architectures that then enter the measure/decide stages in Chs. 14–16.




                                                  187
Designing the AI System: From Constraints to Candidates                                            188


12.1. Concept

The architect’s first step is to reverse-engineer the workload into its constituent constraints. From
the six dimensions — quality requirements, traffic profile, token profile, latency budget, economic
ceiling, and operational constraints — we extract the three hard constraints — the three gates used
throughout this chapter — that any candidate must satisfy: (1) memory fit — the weight memory plus
the KV-cache footprint must fit the target host’s aggregate memory; (2) throughput at the SLO —
sustained prefill and decode tokens-per-second, delivered within the latency budget (prefill + decode),
must meet the workload’s demand; and (3) quality — answer quality on the true evaluation set must
meet the quality requirement. Any architecture that violates any one of these is eliminated before
evaluation: a layout whose memory fits but whose throughput falls short of demand — as a single host
falls against the canonical ~92K input tokens/s — is not carried forward as-is; it returns to synthesis
for a larger layout or is dropped, and a smaller-model candidate whose quality is unmeasured is
gated, not promoted. (The economic ceiling is recorded but is not one of the three gates; §12.8 states
its consequence at fleet scale.) This constraint-first posture inverts the typical practice of browsing
vendor offerings and then hoping they fit; instead, we generate architectures that we know can
physically reside and operate within the specified substrate.


12.2. Mental Model

The substrate is a set of bounded resources, and the architecture design problem is essentially a
packing exercise. The resources are: GPU memory (weight residency + KV cache), memory bandwidth
(prefill throughput), inter-GPU communication volume (for parallelism schemes), and the latency
budget split between prefill and decode. A candidate architecture is a valid packing of the workload’s
weight memory and KV cache into the available GPU memory, paired with a parallelism and caching
strategy that delivers the required tokens-per-second throughput within the latency budget. The
architect alternates between squeezing the residency footprint (e.g., via KV quantization or precision
reduction) and adjusting the parallelism layout (e.g., parameter vs. data vs. pipeline) until all three
hard constraints are simultaneously satisfiable. This mental model — substrate as packing problem —
is what enables systematic candidate generation rather than ad hoc selection.


12.3. Worked Example

We generate three candidate architectures for the canonical enterprise-Q&A RAG workload: ~10
requests/s average, peak 40 rps, 70B FP16 model, 9.2K token input (1,200 prompt + 8K retrieved
context), 300-token output. The canonical weight memory is 140 GB (70B × 2 bytes FP16). The KV
cache for 9.2K context at FP16 precision ([ASSUMPTION] canonical (Ch 4, Table 4-2)) is approximately
24 GB (2 × num_layers × hidden_dim × 9,200 × 2 bytes per FP16 element), giving a total residency
189                                               Designing the AI System: From Constraints to Candidates


of 164 GB. A single 8×H100 host provides 640 GB aggregate memory (8 ×80 GB), leaving ample
headroom. Each candidate satisfies the three hard constraints differently.

      Candidate (a): single 8×H100 host with prefix caching (Ch. 11). This is the per-request-
latency baseline — the single 8×H100 host that the early book (Ch 2, 4, 7, 8) establishes as meeting one
request’s latency SLO. It is not a capacity baseline: a lone host cannot carry the arrival rate (~6 hosts
are needed for the canonical average, and ~21 at peak — see Ch 11, 13, 17), so its throughput-gate
failure below is expected and is not a reason to dismiss the host class itself. All 70B weights and
the full 24 GB KV cache reside on the 8-GPU host. Prefix caching from Ch. 11 amortizes the prefill
attention over repeated requests with the same prompt prefix, reducing effective prefill FLOPs by
~30% at 10 rps average and ~50% at peak 40 rps when many requests share common document roots.
(That 30–50% amortization range is a reasoned expectation, not a measured figure — it rests on the
untested premise about traffic overlap flagged in §12.7, so it is labeled [HYPOTHESIS] and should
be confirmed by measuring the actual prefix-hit rate before it is relied on.) The 8×H100 host fits the
full 164 GB residency easily, but on throughput we must be honest with the Chapter 8 arithmetic: a
single 8×H100 host sustains only ~19,800 prefill-tokens/s at the idealized 35%-MFU aggregate (8 ×
2,471; see the Ch. 8 scope note) — far below the ~92K input tokens/s the workload needs on average.
Even if prefix caching (~30% at average load) lifts effective prefill throughput toward ~28K tokens/s
[HYPOTHESIS], that is still well below 92K, so a single host fails the throughput gate too — prefill
is compute-bound at this operating point, and meeting it is exactly the scaling problem Chapters
15–17 take up. Memory fit and throughput fit are different gates: the memory gate passes with one
host; the throughput gate does not. Memory fit: 140 GB weights + 24 GB KV = 164 GB < 640 GB
aggregate ([ASSUMPTION] canonical (Ch 4, Table 4-2)). Throughput at the SLO: per-request prefill +
decode stay within the latency budget thanks to prefix caching and the high bandwidth of 8×H100,
but the sustained rate fails at one host, as shown above — the gate closes only when the host class
is replicated to ~5 hosts (Chs. 15–17). Quality: the 70B is itself the workload’s quality reference, so
this gate is met by construction. Economics (recorded, not one of the three gates — §12.8): one host
purchase, one software license tier.

      Candidate (b): P/D-disaggregated two-pool.
We keep the full 70B model in both pools and split by phase — which is what prefill/decode (P/D)
disaggregation actually means (Chapter 11): a compute-bound prefill pool and a bandwidth-bound
decode pool, each holding the complete 140 GB weights plus the in-flight KV, with the KV hidden-
state handed between them (Splitwise / DistServe / Mooncake). Each pool therefore needs its own
8×H100 host (residency ~164 GB — weights plus one request’s KV — comfortably under 640 GB). The
win is that prefill and decode no longer fight over the same host’s resources: the prefill pool runs
FLOPS-saturated on the 9.2K input, the decode pool runs bandwidth-saturated on the 300 output
tokens, and KV crosses between them. Crucially, P/D disaggregation does not raise per-host prefill
throughput: one 8×H100 prefill host still sustains only ~19,800 prefill-tokens/s (the same Chapter 8
arithmetic as Candidate (a)), far short of the ~92K input tokens/s the workload needs on average. So
Designing the AI System: From Constraints to Candidates                                                 190


Candidate (b) passes the memory gate per pool but still fails the throughput gate at a single prefill
host — its real advantage is that the prefill pool can be scaled independently of the decode pool, so
meeting the ~92K demand means scaling the prefill pool to ~5 hosts (92K ÷ 19.8K ≈ 4.65) plus the
decode pool, rather than forcing every host to serve both phases. Disaggregation buys the ability to
scale each phase separately, not the throughput itself. Economics: two hosts and added fabric as a
baseline, more as each pool scales; it is the right architecture at scale, not a two-host answer to the
canonical case.
    Candidate (c): KV-quantized smaller host.
We downgrade to a 7B-class model (7B × 2 bytes = 14 GB weights) with KV cache quantized to 4-bit.
The per-token KV depends on the model’s own attention shape (layers × KV heads × head dim ×
bytes, Chapter 7), NOT the 70B’s constant: a typical 32-layer, 4096-hidden, full-MHA 7B carries ~0.52
MB/token FP16, so ~0.13 MB/token at 4-bit → ~1.2 GB for the 9.2K context (vs the ~6 GB that comes
from naively reusing the 70B’s 2.62 MB/token ÷ 4). Total residency: 14 GB + ~1.2 GB ≈ ~15 GB, which
fits on a single H100 (80 GB) with large headroom. The trade-off is a quality question, and here we
must be careful not to assert an architectural theorem where one does not exist. Whether a 7B-class
model can match the 70B model’s answer quality on this workload is not derivable from parameter
count — a newer or task-specialized 7B can beat an older or general 70B on some tasks. It is an
empirical question answered only by running the actual evaluation set. The correct architectural
lesson is the quality gate: the smaller candidate must pass the capability/quality gate on the true
evaluation set; if it fails there, no amount of infrastructure optimization fixes that failure. So candidate
(c) is flagged for measurement against the quality gate, not dismissed by parameter counting. The
4-bit KV cache is a memory optimization, not a quality one; aggressive KV quantization can add its
own quality penalty that must also be validated on the target workload. Throughput is genuinely
much higher on the smaller model — a 7B prefill costs only ~14 GFLOP/token, so a single card sustains
tens of thousands of prefill tokens/s (vs ~2,471 per GPU for the 70B, Chapter 8) — but that throughput
advantage is only useful if the quality gate is first satisfied. The candidate is therefore provisional: its
fate depends on the measured quality gate, which Chapter 14 (the capability screen) administers.
This candidate illustrates the extreme end of the KV-quantization space: the memory footprint is
trivially small, but neither quality nor throughput makes it competitive for this workload.
    Memory/residency arithmetic summary. The canonical weights (140 GB) + KV (24 GB FP16 at
the 9.2K input context) = 164 GB fits 640 GB (8×H100). Candidate (a) uses the full host with room
to spare. Candidate (b) keeps the full model in each pool, so each 8×H100 host also holds ~164 GB.
Candidate (c) fits ~15 GB on one H100 and its throughput is high, but it is provisional — its fate
turns on the Ch 14 quality-gate measurement, not on parameter counting.


12.4. Measurement

    To validate a candidate architecture, the architect must derive three numbers from first principles
and verify them against the substrate: 1. Weight memory.
191                                                Designing the AI System: From Constraints to Candidates




                                      W = N × bytes-per-param

      where N is the parameter count and bytes-per-param is 2 for FP16 (replace 2 with bit-width/8 for
quantization). Derived fact [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]: 70 × 109 × 2 B = 140 GB. 2. KV cache
footprint.


                        KV = 2 × nlayers × dhidden × L × bytes-per-activation

      where L is the context length. For a 70B model with 8-bit KV caching, this is approximately
12.06 GB for 9.2K context (the raw tensor byte-halving bound: 2.62 MB/token FP16 ÷ 2 = 1.31
MB/token, exactly 50% of BF16; 9,200 × 1.31 MB ≈ 12.06 GB, Ch 7); at FP16 precision it is ~24.1 GB
[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]. The architect should compute this for the exact context length of the
workload, not assume a fixed value. 3. Throughput per device. Tokens-per-second that a single
device can sustain for prefill and decode, measured on the target hardware. This is the number that,
multiplied by the number of devices in the candidate layout, must exceed the workload’s tokens-
per-second demand (92K input tokens/s average, 3K output tokens/s average, 368K input tokens/s
peak, 12K output tokens/s peak). Vendors publish peak numbers; the architect should treat these as
benchmarks to be verified by measuring on equivalent hardware.
      All three numbers must be confirmed before a candidate is carried forward ([ASSUMPTION]
canonical (Ch 4, Table 4-2)). If any one fails, the candidate is returned to the synthesis step.
12.5. Common Mistakes
      • Menu-picking without constraint validation. Browsing vendor offerings and selecting the
        one that “feels right” rather than generating candidates against quantified hard constraints.
        This is the opposite of the constraint-driven method described here.
      • Ignoring the KV cache residency arithmetic. Assuming that the weight memory is the only
        memory budget item. In input-heavy workloads ([ASSUMPTION] canonical (Ch 4, Table 4-2):
        9.2K average context, 30× more input than output), the KV cache is ≈15% of total residency at
        the canonical 9.2K context (24.1/164.1; rising past 20% beyond ~13.4K) and is often the binding
        constraint.
      • Over-optimizing prefix caching. Assuming that prefix caching can amortize prefill across
        all requests. In practice, cache effectiveness depends on the overlap of prompt prefixes across
        the traffic workload; sparse prefix sharing reduces the realized savings.
      • Using KV-quantization as a free lunch. Quantizing the KV cache reduces memory footprint
        but introduces quality degradation that may be unacceptable for the target workload. The
        architect must measure the quality impact before committing to a quantized KV layout.
      • Forgetting the latency split. Treating the latency budget as a single number rather than a
        prefill/decode split. A candidate may meet the total latency budget by trading prefill for decode
        or vice versa, which may not satisfy the service-level objectives for either leg.
Designing the AI System: From Constraints to Candidates                                          192


12.6. Architecture Consequence

    The three candidates carry forward into the evaluation chapters (Chs. 14–16) with distinct test
plans, all written against the same three gates — memory fit, throughput at the SLO, and quality.
Candidate (a), the single 8×H100 host with prefix caching, is the baseline: we evaluate throughput at
the SLO (TTFT/TPOT compliance under load) on a single hardware configuration, with cost-per-
token recorded as an economic by-product rather than a gate. Candidate (b), the P/D-disaggregated
two-pool, is evaluated on the added complexity of inter-group communication and the pipeline
overlap efficacy; we measure whether the latency budget is maintained under the partitioned layout.
Candidate (c), the KV-quantized 7B model, is evaluated on the quality-degradation trade-off; we
compare answer quality against the 70B baseline and compute the economic break-even point
(number of hosts required) against the quality loss. The synthesis method produces these candidates
as a set from which the evaluation chapter selects based on quantitative results, not on gut feeling.
12.7. What We Still Don’t Know

    As of 2026-08, several questions remain open, each flagged [HYPOTHESIS]:
    • KV-quantization quality impact at 4-bit for enterprise Q&A. The quality loss from 4-bit
      KV quantization has not been systematically characterized across the diversity of enterprise
      prompts in the canonical workload [HYPOTHESIS].

    • Prefix-caching effectiveness under realistic traffic overlap. The assumed 30–50% prefill
      amortization rests on the premise that many requests share document-level prefixes. Empirical
      measurement of prefix overlap across a production enterprise traffic trace is needed to confirm
      these numbers [HYPOTHESIS].

    • P/D-disaggregation communication overhead in multi-host settings. The boundary
      between parameter-parallel and data-parallel placement is relatively unexplored at the 70B
      scale; the actual communication volume and its latency impact depend on the routing library
      and network topology [HYPOTHESIS].

    • Whether 8-bit KV caching is sufficient for 9.2K context at FP16-equivalent quality.
      The arithmetic in §12.4 assumes 8-bit KV reduces memory by 2× with minimal quality loss, but
      the interaction between 8-bit quantization and the retrieval-augmented generation pipeline
      has not been verified [HYPOTHESIS].

    These flags exist because home-lab measurements do not count as reference evidence per the
evidence taxonomy; each is an open empirical question a team should validate against its own target
workload, not a claim the handbook has settled.

12.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: From Vague Ask to Candidate Architectures

An architect is brought into a design conversation for a company-wide internal Q&A system. The
stakeholder states: “We need an AI system that can answer employee questions over our internal
documentation, with acceptable quality and within budget.” Before any architecture can be defended,
the architect applies the constraint-driven method from this chapter.
      First, the workload is characterized across the six dimensions. Quality requirements fix the model
class: the system must achieve ~70B-model answer quality on enterprise prompts. The traffic profile
is the canonical one (Ch. 4/5, canonical scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2)): ~2,000 registered users, ~5%
concurrent (~100), ~10 rps average / ~40 rps peak. The token profile is the canonical 1,200-token
prompt plus 8K retrieved context (~9.2K input) plus 300-token answers, with TTFT ≤ 1.2 s (p95
≤ 2 s) and TPOT ~25 ms/token. The economic ceiling is $15,000 monthly operating budget — a
per-host ceiling, expressed as the cloud-equivalent of one 8×H100 at ~$20/hr × 730 hr ≈ $14.6K/mo
(an on-premise host has no $/hr, so this is a budget cap, not a metered cost), which the reader should
note is far below what the full canonical workload costs once the multi-host fleet is sized (Ch 16): the
budget is a single-host cap, not the workload ceiling. The consequence must be stated, not dissolved:
the fleet the canonical workload requires costs ~$155.8K/mo ($155,816.93, ≈$24.97/1K; Ch 16 — the
cloud legs are $87,600 ≈ $14.04/1K at the default paid-occupancy input and $306,600 ≈ $49.13/1K at
21 hosts always-on) — ~10× the stakeholder’s stated $15,000 ceiling — so the economic constraint,
as stated, fails at fleet scale. Economics is therefore recorded as not yet passed (deferred), and the
architect’s first return-to-synthesis move is to renegotiate the budget, shape peak demand, or revisit
the model class. The operational constraint is that the system must run on existing on-premise GPU
infrastructure (no cloud add-ons).
      From the token profile, the architect computes: 9.2K input tokens + 300 output tokens ≈ 9.5K
tokens per request. At 10 rps average and 40 rps peak, the system must sustain ~92K input tokens/s
average and ~368K input tokens/s peak. Three hard constraints follow — the chapter’s three gates,
verbatim: memory fit (weight memory plus KV cache must fit within the on-premise GPU inventory),
throughput at the SLO (total tokens-per-second across the installed devices, delivered within the
TTFT/TPOT budget, must exceed the traffic demand), and quality (answer quality on the evaluation
set must meet the ~70B requirement).
      The architect generates three candidates using the method from §12.3. Candidate (a): a single
8×H100 host with 70B FP16 weights + 24 GB KV cache and prefix caching, which fits the memory
budget (164 GB < 640 GB aggregate ([ASSUMPTION] canonical (Ch 4, Table 4-2))) — but as Chapter
8 shows, one 8×H100 host sustains only ~19,800 prefill-tokens/s at the idealized aggregate (8 × 2,471
per GPU; the per-GPU figure is ~2,471, not per-host), far short of the ~92K input tokens/s the 10 rps
average demands, so the memory gate passes while the throughput gate already fails. Candidate (b):
a P/D-disaggregated two-pool design keeping the full 70B in each pool (prefill and decode pools,
each ~164 GB residency on its own 8×H100 host), which buys phase-splitting at the cost of a second
host plus the KV-transfer fabric. Candidate (c): a KV-quantized 7B model on a single H100, which fits
Designing the AI System: From Constraints to Candidates                                                 194


the memory budget (~15 GB total residency: 14 GB FP16 weights + ~1.2 GB 4-bit KV), but its quality
is provisional — whether a 7B-class model can reach the required answer quality is a hypothesis to be
measured against the quality gate (Chapter 14), not a settled fact — and it faces the same throughput
demand at peak, making it provisionally non-viable.
    The architect does not discard Candidate (c) by parameter counting alone: it is provisionally
moved to the quality-gate evaluation (Chapter 14) to measure whether a 7B-class model actually
meets the workload’s capability/quality threshold on its evaluation set. Its memory and economics
are trivially favorable; its fate turns on that measured gate. Because candidate (c) is strongly suspected
to fail the quality gate [HYPOTHESIS], it is not a finalist; the finalists are Candidates (a) and (b),
and the near-term decision falls between them. The decision between Candidates (a) and (b) hinges
on whether the doubled hardware cost of Candidate (b) is justified by its operational flexibility
(e.g., independent scaling of prefill and decode pools, fault isolation). The architect presents both
candidates, together with the honest throughput arithmetic of Chapter 8 (no canonical single host
meets the full prefill demand alone), to the stakeholder as the decision foundation.

    Two reading rules for this matrix. (1) Illustrative screen, not a fleet plan. The ~19 prefill hosts
at peak follows from the fixed, illustrative single-host prefill rate (~19,800 tok/s) divided into the peak
input-token demand (368K tok/s). This is a capacity screen that exposes the magnitude of the scaling
problem; it is not an operational recommendation, because real utilization, time-sharing/prefix reuse,
heterogeneous hardware, admission policy, and measured batch throughput differ. (2) Demand
to serve vs demand to shape. The matrix counts demand the system must serve at the SLO;
a system may instead queue, shed, or shape (off-peak, cap-and-queue, batch it) part of the peak,
which is an operational policy, not a throughput given. The architecture must state which it does
before the host counts mean anything. Until the gates in Chs. 14–17 are passed, no candidate is a
deployment-validated survivor; all three are conditional candidates with an open validation gate.

chapter 13.


Reference Architectures: From Local to
Hyperscale




The Architect’s Question

After this chapter we should be able to look at a characterized workload and place it on the right
archetype — the canonical deployment shapes that recur across the industry — without reinventing
a design from scratch. We will map the four tiers (local/edge, server, cluster, hyperscale), state what
each can serve in model size and traffic, and develop the decision rule for when a workload outgrows
a tier and must escalate. After this chapter, “we run on a server” or “we need a cluster” is a defensible,
quantified statement tied to the workload’s numbers — not a guess.


13.1. Concept

Architectures recur not because engineers lack imagination but because the constraints recur. Four
archetypes cover the vast majority of AI deployments, distinguished by how many GPUs are involved
and over what interconnect:

   1. Local / edge — a single GPU (or a laptop-class accelerator). Serves small models (up to ~7-
      13B at tight context) that must run on-device for privacy, latency, or connectivity reasons.
      Interconnect is not the question; memory capacity is.

   2. Server — one host with 1-8 GPUs, typically H100/H200, joined by NVLink/NVSwitch. Serves
      dense models up to ~70B-180B with real concurrency. This is the canonical enterprise-Q&A
      tier and the book’s 8×H100 baseline. [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] (the tier’s model-size



                                                   199
Reference Architectures: From Local to Hyperscale                                              200


      range is a book-defined characterization; the H100/H200 and NVLink/NVSwitch specs it cites
      are [1P] vendor datasheets)

   3. Cluster — multiple hosts (tens to hundreds of GPUs) joined by InfiniBand or high-speed
      Ethernet. Required when a model exceeds a node’s memory (so it must be split per Ch10) or
      when traffic outgrows one host (so P/D disaggregation per Ch11 applies).

   4. Hyperscale / data-center fleet — dedicated fleets of specialized inference/training clusters,
      often MoE or KV-centric (Mooncake-style disaggregation [S4][1P]), serving many tenants at
      enormous scale. The economics favor extreme specialization.

    These are a continuum, not hard categories; the useful question is always which tier does OUR
workload’s bounds demand?


13.2. Mental Model

    Each tier is a box with a fixed memory budget and a fixed cross-node bandwidth. A
workload fits a tier if (a) the model’s weight + KV residency fits the tier’s total GPU memory
(Ch7), and (b) the tier’s interconnect can carry the communication the chosen parallelism requires
(Ch9/Ch10), and (c) the resulting throughput + latency meets the SLO (Ch11).
    The mental model is a ladder with explicit rungs: we climb a rung when a binding constraint
can no longer be met. The three classic triggers for climbing:
    • Memory: model + KV no longer fits one node → cluster (split weights).
    • Traffic: one host’s throughput ceiling (goodput) below demand → more replicas (DP across
      nodes) or P/D disaggregation → cluster.
    • Latency/geography: SLO can’t be met due to distance or contention → move the serving
      edge closer (local) or split prefill/decode.

    We do not climb for fashion; we climb when a measured number crosses a threshold.


13.3. Worked Example

13.3.1. Placing the Canonical Workload

The canonical enterprise-Q&A RAG workload sits firmly on the server tier. We verify each bound:

    • Memory: 70B FP16 weights = 140 GB; KV for the 9.5K max context at FP16 ≈ 24.9 GB; inference
      residency ≈ 165 GB [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]. An 8×H100 host (640 GB) fits this with ample
      headroom for concurrency (Ch11 showed ~24 GB per request × concurrent requests still fits).
      ✓ [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]

    • Throughput/latency: ~10 rps average / 40 rps peak, input-heavy (9.2K in / 300 out). On the
      per-request latency axis, Ch11 showed continuous batching + prefix caching keeps p95 TTFT
201                                                         Reference Architectures: From Local to Hyperscale


        under the 2 s SLO on a single 8×H100 host. But on the capacity axis the single host does
        not carry the full arrival rate: with the canonical ~8.6 s service time, Little’s Law puts
        ≈40 × 8.6 ≈ 344 requests in flight at the peak, against ~17.5 KV-resident requests per host (an
        analytical continuous-occupancy figure; the conservative integer floor 17 is what hard host
        provisioning uses) — so a single host is a latency-feasible but not capacity-sufficient server
        (Ch16/17 size the fleet to ~21 hosts at the 40 rps peak). The tier choice here is about model
        residency and per-request latency, not about whether one host serves the entire peak arrival.
        [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]

      • Interconnect: no cross-host model parallelism is required (one node; intra-host TP=8 fits the
        140 GB model) — the interconnect question doesn’t bind. ✓

      So the server tier is the right model-residency archetype for the canonical workload — the model
and its KV fit a single 8×H100 node and the per-request TTFT SLO is met on one host. It does not
mean one host serves the whole arrival rate; a single host is latency-bound and the peak capacity is
a fleet-computing question (Ch17). [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]

13.3.2. Escalating: When 10×Traffic Forces the Cluster Tier

Now suppose the workload’s demand grows to ~100 rps average (a 10×). Recompute the ceiling:

      • Throughput ceiling of one host: continuous batching on 8×H100 at ~9.5K tokens/request
        sustained roughly tens of thousands of tokens/s; goodput against the SLO is the binding number.
        At ~100 rps × 9.5K tokens = ~950K tokens/s, one host’s goodput is exceeded. [ILLUSTRATIVE]
        [DERIVED]

      • Response: replicate the model across multiple servers (data parallelism at the serving layer —
        run N identical 8×H100 hosts behind a load balancer). At ~100 rps average with the canonical
        ~2.0 req/s per-host screen (Ch 16/17; C/W = KV-residency ÷ service time ≈ 17.5 ÷ 8.6 s — a
        KV/service-time screen, not an independently measured compute or goodput benchmark), the
        replica count is ~100 ÷ 2.0 ≈ 50 hosts — not a handful. The escalation is still the cluster tier:
        the model fits one node (no weight-splitting), but the fleet is a real cluster sized by the per-host
        goodput ceiling. The escalation is driven by traffic, not memory. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]

13.3.3. Dropping a Tier: When Privacy Forces Local

If the workload must run fully on-site without data leaving a facility, and the model can be distilled
to a 7-13B capable of the Q&A task, the local/edge tier applies: a single GPU runs the distilled model
at reduced (but acceptable) accuracy for privacy. The tier choice traded capability for the operational
constraint (privacy). [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]

13.4. Measurement

    The tier decision is only as good as the numbers that trigger it. We measure three things:
   1. Residency vs tier memory (Ch7): does weight + KV fit? If not, the floor is a cluster.
   2. Host goodput ceiling vs demand (Ch6/Ch11): measure the max rps/tokens/s the host delivers
      at the SLO, and compare to demand. When demand > ceiling, escalate.
   3. Communication fraction (Ch9/Ch10): if the parallelism the cluster requires spends >~20% of
      step time on collectives, the interconnect (not the GPU) is the binding tier constraint.

    These three numbers locate the workload on the ladder objectively.


13.5. Common Mistakes
    • Choosing hyperscale before measuring goodput. Most workloads never exceed one host’s
      latency budget; the mistake is building a fleet before measuring whether traffic actually
      outgrows one host’s capacity. (Note: the book’s own canonical workload does outgrow one
203                                                      Reference Architectures: From Local to Hyperscale


        host’s capacity at its 40 rps peak — ~21 hosts per Ch17 — so for that workload the fleet is
        warranted, not premature.)
      • Using model size as the only tier driver. A 70B model fits a server; traffic, not size, usually
        forces the cluster — an architect who only watches parameters escalates too early or too late.
      • Ignoring the operational constraint. Privacy/geography can force a lower tier regardless of
        what compute wants; the ladder is bounded by operations, not just performance.
      • Assuming a smaller model can’t serve the tier. Distilled small models on local GPUs can
        meet the goal when the capability suffices — don’t over-provision the tier.
      • Treating tiers as walls. They are a continuum; the correct answer can be a hybrid (edge
        cache + server generation) the measured numbers justify.


13.6. Architecture Consequence

      The archetype sets the entire downstream design vocabulary. On the server tier (canonical),
the consequences are already established: continuous batching + PagedAttention + prefix caching
(Ch11), KV quantization when residency binds (Ch7), no cross-host model parallelism (Ch10; intra-
host TP=8 fits the 140 GB model). Moving up to cluster introduces: DP/PP/TP replicas (Ch10), P/D
disaggregation (Ch11), and interconnect budgeting (Ch9). Moving down to local forces distillation
and on-device KV limits. The tier is the top-level decision; every other choice in the book slots
beneath it.
13.7. What We Still Don’t Know
      • Exact host goodput ceilings depend on the specific server, model, degree and batching; the
        representative numbers here are [UNRESOLVED] per deployment.
      • When P/D disaggregation’s benefit crosses its cost for mid-tier workloads is
        [HYPOTHESIS]; the breakpoint is workload- and fabric-specific.
      • Fleet-level economics (Ch16 TCO across a cluster) interact with the tier choice in ways that
        are [HYPOTHESIS] until a real cost model is applied.
