17.2. Mental Model

We visualize the fleet as a two-level hierarchy. At the top level, a load balancer — either hardware
(L7 switch) or software (NGINX, HAProxy, Cloud Load Balancer) — accepts inbound requests and
routes them to one of N backend hosts. Each backend host runs an identical copy of the model and
serves requests independently. At the bottom level, each host operates exactly as the single-server
model does: a model engine accepting prompts, producing completions, and returning tokens to the
load balancer, which forwards the response to the client.
               The mental model introduces two new invariants. First, the throughput invariant: total system
throughput ≈ N × throughput_per_host, reduced by a factor ρ that captures load‑balancer over­
head, health‑check traffic, and imperfect distribution (typically ρ ∈ [0.85, 0.98] depending on LB
sophistication). Second, the memory invariant: total GPU memory across the fleet is N × memory_
per_host, but the per-host memory available for model weights and KV cache remains the same as
the single-host case. The fleet does not increase the per-host model size; it increases the aggregate
number of concurrent requests the system can serve by parallelizing across hosts.
               A critical detail is the session-affinity decision. If user sessions must maintain conversation
From Server to Fleet                                                                                  248


state (KV cache, accumulated tool outputs, retrieval context), the load balancer must route subsequent
requests from the same user to the same host (sticky sessions). This reduces cross-host communication
but limits the effective parallelism, because a popular user can pin a single host to capacity while other
hosts stand underutilized. If sessions are stateless (the model is reloaded or KV cache is discarded
between requests), any host can serve any request, and load distribution becomes even. The architect
must choose between density (sticky sessions, higher per-host utilization) and evenness (stateless
routing, lower per-host utilization but better load balance).


17.3. Worked Example

    We continue from the canonical scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2): ~10 rps average / ~40 rps peak, prompt
~9,200 input tokens + ~300 output, 70B-class dense FP16 model, 8×H100 host with 640 GB GPU
memory. A single 8×H100 host’s capacity is set by the binding constraint among GPU compute,
HBM bandwidth, and KV cache memory. Let us verify with arithmetic, keeping the two quantities
distinct: aggregate HBM (640 GB) is not the same as KV-available memory (640 − 140 GB weights
− runtime/workspace reserve).
    Single-host concurrency capacity (KV-bound). The per-token KV footprint for the canonical
full-MHA reference geometry is 2 × layers × hidden × bytes = 2 ×80 ×8,192 ×2 = 2,621,440 B ≈ 2.62
MB/token (Chapter 7 canonical). Subtract the 140 GB FP16 weights and ~64 GB runtime/activa­
tions/workspace from the 640 GB pool, leaving ≈436 GB available for KV. Each request at 9,200 input
+ 300 output reserves a 9,500-token max KV of 9,500 ×2.62 MB ≈ 24.9 GB (the initial 9.2K residency
is 24.1 GB). A single host therefore holds C = 436 GB ÷ 24.9037 GB ≈ 17.5 concurrent requests
(byte-accurate; the conservative integer “requests that fit” floor is 17, not 18 — 17.51 cannot round
up for a hard fit) — using the canonical layer-complete κ. Computing κ from a single layer instead of
all 80 would overstate the concurrency figure by two orders of magnitude.
    Viability at peak. Peak traffic is 40 rps; with the canonical ~8.6 s per-request service time (1.08
s prefill + 7.5 s decode), Little’s Law puts ≈ 40 × 8.6 ≈ 344 requests in flight, against a KV capacity
of ~17.5 per host (conservative integer floor 17). A single host is not viable at peak even for the
non-agentic canonical workload — the fleet needs roughly ⌈344/17⌉ = 21 hosts at 40 rps (29
working hosts at the 70% utilization target, 30 total with N−1), and more for growth to 100 rps.
This flips the original conclusion: the fleet is not a distant luxury but a necessity at the canonical
peak, driven by the product of service time (8.6 s) and arrival rate.
    KV compression is the first lever. Switching KV to FP8 (κ ≈ 1.31 MB/token, raw byte-halving
— exactly 50% of BF16 [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]) cuts the 9.5K max per-request KV to ≈12.45
GB and raises C to ≈35.0 concurrent per host (436 ÷ 12.45 ≈ 35.0; conservative integer floor 35),
roughly doubling headroom before buying hardware. This is why the architect treats KV precision
as a first-class capacity dial, not a cosmetic detail.
    Threshold for fleet expansion. Suppose the agentic layer from Chapter 19 is added. Chapter
19’s illustrative turn distribution puts 68% of requests terminating in T=1, 25% in T=2, 5% in T=3, and
249                                                                                   From Server to Fleet


2% exceeding the turn limit (falling back to single-shot). That makes the median turn count T=1
(68% of requests finish on the first turn) and the 95th percentile T=3 (cumulative 68+25+5 = 98%
by T=3). Each turn adds ~800 tokens of retrieved context (delta) and ~65 tokens of model-generated
reasoning (gamma), so the effective per-request token count is

                      I(T ) = I0 + T (δ + γ) + Ofinal = 9,200 + T × 865 + 300

      • Median (T=1): I(1) = 9,200 + 1 × 800 + 1 × 65 + 300 = 10,365 tokens
      • 95th percentile (T=3): I(3) = 9,200 + 3 × 800 + 3 × 65 + 300 = 12,095 tokens
      • Hypothetical extension (T=4, if the turn limit were not enforced — per Ch 19 the >2% that exceed
        the limit fall back to single-shot, so no request actually reaches T=4): I(4) = 9,200 + 4 × 800 +
        4 × 65 + 300 = 12,960 tokens

      The KV cache per request rises proportionally, and per-host concurrency capacity follows from
the Ch 17 formula C = Mkv /(I(T )κ):

      • at T=1 (median): 10,365 × 2.62 MB ≈ 27.2 GB/request ⇒ C ≈ 16 concurrent (floor 16)
      • at T=3 (95th): 12,095 × 2.62 MB ≈ 31.7 GB/request ⇒ C ≈ 13.8 concurrent (floor 13)
      • at T=4 (hypothetical extension, turn limit not enforced): 12,960 × 2.62 MB                     ≈
        34.0 GB/request ⇒ C ≈ 12.8 concurrent (floor 12)

      Even the median agentic request already drops a single host below the peak in-flight demand (C
≈ 16 < 344 at 40 rps, or 860 at 100 rps), so the fleet is required under almost any agentic assumption.
Scaling forecast (service-time-aware). Because the canonical workload’s service time is ~8.6 s
— not a ~1 s latency — the in-flight concurrency at the 40 rps peak is λ_peak × W ≈ 40 × 8.6 ≈ 344
requests, not 40. With FP16 KV (baseline C≈17.5, conservative integer floor 17), the fleet needs
⌈344/17⌉ = 21 hosts at full utilization (29 at the 70% utilization target). Agentic turns make this
strictly worse: each additional turn adds ~800 tokens of context (lowering C) and more generated
tokens (raising W), so the agentic T=3 case needs a larger fleet still (C≈13.8 in the 95th-percentile
case and a longer W). The load balancer distributes λ/N rps per host and λ·W/N concurrent per host,
and each host’s per-host KV usage must stay comfortably under its C. This is the fleet point: hosts
are added because concurrency in flight × KV-per-request exceeds a single host’s residency — and
concurrency in flight must be computed from the full service time, not a target latency.
      Cross-host communication. In the canonical scenario, requests are independent — no user
session spans multiple hosts. If an agentic loop required retrieving results from a prior host (e.g.,
distributed retrieval), the system would need a coordination layer (Redis, gRPC, or message queue)
with added latency. We quantify this below in the measurement section.
From Server to Fleet                                                                              250


17.4. Measurement

    We derive three planning quantities from the worked example and Chapter 19’s illustrative
turn-count distribution. These are not measurements from production traffic. A deployment must
measure its own traffic distribution before using these quantities for provisioning.
17.4.1. Per-host throughput and KV cache budget

Let N be the number of hosts, λ the incoming rps peak, T the random variable for agent turn count
with distribution P(T), δ = 800 tokens per turn of retrieved context, γ = 65 tokens of model-generated
reasoning per turn, and O_final = 300 final output tokens. The per-request token count is


                                 I(T ) = I0 + T · δ + T · γ + Ofinal

    where I₀ = 9,200 is the baseline input tokens. The per-host concurrent‑request capacity in terms
of KV cache is

                                                   Mkv
                                           C=
                                                 I(T ) · κ
    where M_kv is the KV‑available memory — the portion of on‑host HBM left for KV after weights
and runtime — and κ = 2 × nlayers × dhidden × bytes ≈ 2.62 MB/token (2.5 MiB) is the per‑token
KV footprint (Chapter 7 canonical; κ includes all layers — omitting the layer factor understates KV
memory by orders of magnitude). For the canonical host, M_kv = 640 GB − 140 GB (FP16 weights)
− ~64 GB (runtime/activations/workspace/NCCL) ≈ 436 GB. Dividing memory by bytes (not the
byte‑divided‑by‑bytes collapse that trips unit analysis):

    • For T = 0 (baseline, I = 9,500): C = 436 GB / (9,500 ×2.62 MB) ≈ 436/24.9037 ≈ 17.5 concurrent
      requests per host (byte-accurate; the conservative integer “requests that fit” floor is 17, not
      18 — 17.51 cannot round up for a hard fit).
    • For T = 1 (median, per the Chapter 19 distribution; 68% terminate on turn 1): C = 436 GB /
      (10,365 ×2.62 MB) ≈ 436/27.17 ≈ 16 concurrent requests per host.
    • For T = 3 (95th percentile; cumulative 98% by T=3): C = 436 GB / (12,095 ×2.62 MB) ≈ 436/31.71
      ≈ 13.8 concurrent requests per host (floor 13).
    • For T = 4 (hypothetical extension beyond the enforced turn limit — Ch 19’s >2% tail falls back
      to single-shot, so no request reaches T=4): C = 436 GB / (12,960 ×2.62 MB) ≈ 436/33.97 ≈ 12.8
      concurrent requests per host (floor 12).


    These numbers are the KV-residency ceiling; measured concurrency may be lower if GPU
throughput or bandwidth binds first, so the architect takes the min of the KV, compute, and bandwidth
capacities.
251                                                                                      From Server to Fleet


        Reconciliation box — the four throughput rates in this book are different quan­
        tities, not a contradiction. (1) ~50 tok/s (Ch. 5) is a deliberately conservative single-
        stream, low-batch generation rate used to illustrate the tokens-per-dollar method; it is a
        floor, not the host’s serving throughput. (2) ~19,800 tok/s (Ch. 8) is the idealized prefill
        aggregate (8 × 2,471 at 35% MFU) before TP/system loss — an analytical upper bound on
        prefill, not a servable goodput. (3) ~35,000–70,000 tok/s (Ch. 15) is the batched serving
        decode+prefill range under FlashAttention + continuous batching — the multi-request
        serving throughput of the same host. (4) ~2.0 req/s (Ch. 17/20) is the KV/service-time
        bound on whole requests per host (C ÷ W), the quantity that sizes the fleet. The first
        three are token-rates at different batch/phase assumptions; the fourth is a request-rate
        bound. They reconcile only phase-by-phase, never as one fungible “total” rate. Do not
        set a summed 19K tok/s against any single-phase capacity. At ~2.0 req/s the request
        workload decomposes into two components that hit the hardware differently: 18,400
        input tokens/s (2.0 × 9,200 — the prefill phase, compute-bound) and 600 output
        tokens/s (2.0 × 300 — the decode phase, bandwidth-bound) — both first-order regime
        labels; see Ch 15/Ch 8 for the scope conditions. Compare the prefill component only
        against the prefill-only capacities (~19,800 tok/s, item 2; ~35–70K only if those figures
        are themselves phase-resolved) and the decode component only against decode-scale
        capacity — never the summed ~19,000 tok/s against a single-phase figure. The apparent
        near-equality of ~19,000 tok/s and ~19,800 tok/s is a numerical coincidence of units,
        not a physical equivalence: the two sit in different phases with different arithmetic
        intensity and different cost (compute-bound prefill vs. bandwidth-bound decode), so they
        cannot be added into one rate and compared to any single-phase number. Aggregate pre­
        fill + decode into a single “total” rate only after stating an explicit cost/phase-equivalence
        model (e.g., a weighted-FLOP or weighted-dollar basis). Use the token-rates for kernel
        and cost reasoning (keeping prefill and decode separate), and the request-rate for fleet
        sizing. [DERIVED]

    Which one drives KV residency? Only the model-execution occupancy (λWexec ) holds KV
slots — a queued request (λ·W_queue) is “in flight” from the user’s view but does not yet reserve
a KV block, and a request in the planning phase (λ·W_plan) has not reached the host at all. The
KV-residency ceiling C therefore bounds λWexec (the resident sequences), not λ·W_plan or λ·W_
queue. The end-to-end planning time (W_plan ≈ 10 s) is the workload-level Little’s-law basis used
to derive the arrival rate from the population (Chapter 4); the model-execution time (Wexec ≈ 8.6
s) is the capacity-level Little’s-law basis used to size the fleet (this chapter). The C/W shortcut is
thus an execution-residency screen, valid only when the serving system is the bottleneck and no
queue/planning backlog changes the resident count — state that scope, and never quote C/W as a
measured end-to-end goodput.
    If the peak traffic λ_peak = 40 rps, Little’s Law gives the number of requests in flight as λ_peak ×
W, where W must be the full per-request service time — for this canonical workload that is ~8.6
s (1.08 s prefill + ~7.5 s decode of 300 output tokens at ~25 ms/token, Chapter 8), NOT a sub-second
TTFT-type latency. Using a ~1 s “latency” here is the classic fleet-sizing error: it undercounts in-flight
concurrency by roughly the ratio of service time to target latency (here ~8.6×). The minimum number
of hosts is

                                              λpeak · W 1
                                                  ⌈︃             ⌉︃
                                       Nmin =          ·
                                                  C      u
    where u is the utilization target and W is the full service time (end-to-end: prefill + decode +
any tool/orchestration overhead). At the canonical peak:

    • KV-residency ceiling (C) is a per-host concurrency limit, not a fleet-size answer by
      itself. A host holds C ≈ 17.5 concurrent full-context requests (computed above; conservative
      integer floor 17). The fleet size is governed by how many requests are in flight at the peak,
      which is λ_peak × W.
253                                                                                     From Server to Fleet


      • At λ_peak = 40 rps and W ≈ 8.6 s, in-flight concurrency ≈ 40 × 8.6 ≈ 344 requests. With C ≈
        17.5 per host (FP16 KV) at full utilization, the minimum N = ⌈344/17⌉ = 21 hosts (29 working
        at the 70% utilization target, 30 total with N−1). This is the honest fleet size and matches the
        throughput/latency analysis in Chapter 20.
      • The 25 ms/token in W is the TPOT budget, not a measured per-step time. The decode-
        bandwidth floor for the canonical 8×H100 host is 140 GB ÷ (8 × 3.35 TB/s) ≈ 5.2 ms/step, so a
        well-tuned decode can run well under the 25 ms SLO. The fleet number above therefore uses
        the least-favourable (budget) pole of the service time. The sensitivity band, holding prefill at
        1.08 s and 300 output tokens: at 5.2 ms/step W ≈ 2.6 s (in-flight ≈ 106, ~7 hosts at full util); at
        10 ms/step W ≈ 4.1 s (in-flight ≈ 164, ~10 hosts); at the 25 ms budget W ≈ 8.6 s (in-flight ≈ 344,
        ~21 hosts). Sizing at the 25 ms budget is the conservative choice; a measured per-step time
        from a Chapter 14 benchmark should replace it before committing hardware.
      • Switching to FP8 KV (κ ≈ 1.31 MB/token, raw byte-halving — 50% of BF16, C ≈ 35.0 at T=0;
        conservative integer floor 35) raises per-host concurrency, cutting the fleet to a minimum N ≈
        ⌈344/35.0⌉ = 10 at full utilization → 15 working hosts at the 70% utilization target (16 total
        with N−1).

      Separate the two questions explicitly — they are not interchangeable, and mixing them is the
source of the under-sizing error:
      1. KV-only concurrency sizing (does one host’s KV budget hold the in-flight requests?):
        NKV = ⌈λW /(C · u)⌉. This uses C (KV-residency ceiling) and the full service time W.
      2. Full service-capacity sizing (does the fleet’s aggregate request rate clear the peak?): the
        same quantity when C/W is the per-host service rate — i.e. N = ⌈λ/(ρ · (C/W ))⌉. Because
        Little’s Law ties concurrency, service time and arrival rate, these two views coincide: λW /C =
        λ/(C/W ).

      KV residency provides one capacity ceiling, but it is not a fleet-size answer by itself. When the
canonical 300-token decode duration is included, Little’s Law raises in-flight concurrency from the
misleading “40 requests at 1 second” approximation to roughly 344 requests at 40 rps, and the fleet
must be sized to that.
      The fleet is governed by the minimum of several independent ceilings, not by KV alone.
C/W — and the KV-residency ceiling C that feeds it — is a necessary condition, not sufficient under
mixed prefill/decode scheduling. An architect must take min of: (a) KV-residency concurrency
C, (b) prefill compute capacity (the ~19,800 tok/s/host prefill screen of Ch. 8), (c) decode band­
width/compute capacity (the HBM-bound decode roofline), and (d) the observed p95-TTFT/TPOT
SLO goodput under a load test. A host may hold 17.5 KV-resident requests but never serve 17.5
at the quoted service time, because batch scheduling, prefill/decode interleaving, and tail latency
couple the two.
      Small queueing counterexample. Suppose a KV ceiling C = 17.5 and W = 8.6 s, so C/W ≈ 2.0
req/s. That is an average occupancy bound. If a burst of arrivals is shorter than the service-time
From Server to Fleet                                                                                  254


spread, or if the prefill of some requests monopolizes the GPU and stalls decode, the achieved goodput
can be well below 2.0 req/s even though the host holds 17.5 slots. Conversely, with prefix caching
and batch-friendly load, achieved can exceed the naive bound at higher batch. The upshot: C/W is
a planning lower-bound screen on the same order, and the fleet SLO-passing count comes from
the measured goodput at the target p95 — not from C/W. State the line’s assumptions (time-in-
KV occupancy, overlap of phases, admission policy) explicitly in the sizing summary rather than
presenting C/W as the achieved rate.

17.4.2. Simultaneous feasibility check (prefill + decode coexistence)

The ~2.0 req/s/host ceiling assumes prefill and decode run on the same host at the same time. We
check the prefill leg against the hardware.

    • (a) Prefill demand at 2 req/s. 2.0 req/s × 9,200 input tokens = 18,400 input tokens/s per
      host (2.0 × 9,200; the prefill leg of the ~2.0 req/s decomposition in the reconciliation box above).
    • (b) Idealized prefill ceiling. 8 × 0.989 PF/s × 35% / (2 × 70e9) ≈ 19,780 tokens/s (Chapter 8,
      35% MFU, prefill-only).
    • (c) The ratio. 18,400 ÷ 19,780 ≈ 93%. Prefill must run at ~93% of the idealized prefill ceiling.

    This result is [ANALYTICAL]. It is a prefill-load check, not a measured rate. The ~93% leaves
very little headroom. The host must also run decode. Prefill and decode coexist on the same hardware.
Batch scheduling, prefill/decode interleaving, and interference consume the same compute. The
idealized ceiling assumes no decode interference. The achieved MFU is below the 35% ideal. The real
headroom is smaller than ~93%.
    Therefore the ~2.0 req/s/host figure is an analytical upper bound. It is NOT a claim that a
host serves 2 req/s at SLO.
    Before treating 2 req/s/host as deployable, measure the p95 TTFT, p95 TPOT, and SLO-goodput
on a representative host. Bring a measured p95 TTFT/TPOT and SLO-goodput (Chapter 14) before
treating 2 req/s/host as a deployable service rate. Until then, the sizing in this chapter is a planning
bound.

17.4.3. Load‑balancer overhead factor

Let ρ be the effective throughput fraction after load‑balancer effects. These LB-efficiency val­
ues are [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] engineering thresholds, not universal vendor-
independent constants — a well‑configured software LB (NGINX) typically achieves ρ ≈ 0.95,
and a hardware L7 switch may achieve ρ ≈ 0.98, but both must be measured on the target topology,
workload, and sample duration before being trusted. The overhead comes from: health‑check traffic
(~1% of requests), session‑affinity hashing skew, and LB process CPU limits. The per-host throughput
itself must come from a benchmark on the actual workload (tokens/context/batch) — it is an ILLUS­
TRATIVE proxy until measured. What is derivable is the KV‑residency ceiling C from §17.3; the LB
255                                                                                     From Server to Fleet


overhead multiplies the schedulable fraction of that ceiling, and the ρ value should be replaced by a
measured figure from a load test before it is used as a capacity coefficient. In the worked example,
the fleet is currently sized by KV capacity (§17.3), not by a fabricated tokens/s number: at T=3 (the
95th-percentile sizing point, per the chapter’s own rule), FP16-KV C ≈ 13.8/host (436 GB ÷ (12,095 ×
2.62 MB ≈ 31.7 GB) ≈ 13.8; conservative integer floor 13) sets the continuous ceiling. The product
13.8 × 0.95 ≈ 13.1 is a continuous relaxation only, not usable additional-host capacity. The host can
admit at most 13 whole contexts. Applying the assumed throughput efficiency to that hard limit
gives 13 × 0.95 = 12.35 as the slot-equivalent schedulable fraction per added host, not an integer
admission count. Converting that coefficient to a request rate still requires the stated service time
and workload assumptions.

17.4.4. Cross-host interconnect budget

If a fraction φ of requests require cross-host data (e.g., distributed retrieval, shared vector index), each
such request incurs an additional network round‑trip latency t_net and moves data volume D over
the host‑to‑host network. Two distinct bandwidth quantities must be separated: the per‑request
burst a single cross‑host request draws during its round trip, and the fleet aggregate average across
all hosts. Assuming an intra‑rack 10 Gbps Ethernet backbone:

                                       D
                         Bper-req =        = 5 MB/0.02 s = 250 MB/s ≈ 2 Gbps
                                      tnet
      For D = 5 MB (top‑5 retrieval snippets), t_net = 20 ms (typical rack latency), the per‑request burst
is Bper-req = 5/0.02 = 250 MB/s ≈ 2 Gbps, while the fleet aggregate — the expected number of
concurrent cross‑host requests (ϕ · λ · tnet , by Little’s Law, where λ is the request arrival rate) times
that burst — is


                     Bagg = ϕ · λ · D = 0.1 × 40 × 5 MB = 20 MB/s = 0.16 Gbps

      Both are far inside the 10 Gbps link, so the base case appears benign (the burst leaves ~5×
headroom; the aggregate is even smaller). But if φ scales to 0.5 (many distributed queries) and D
grows to 50 MB, the per‑request burst becomes 50/0.02 = 2,500 MB/s ≈ 20 Gbps — exceeding a
single 10 Gbps link on its own — and the fleet aggregate becomes 0.5 × 40 × 50 = 1,000 MB/s = 1
GB/s, which is ~80% of the 10 Gbps (~1.25 GB/s) limit.
      This calculation shows that cross‑host communication must be dimensioned early on the per‑re­
quest burst (which can exceed a single link even before the aggregate does), and that both the burst
and the aggregate scale with φ and D, even if the base case appears benign.
From Server to Fleet                                                                                    256


17.4.5. Request traffic and model collectives are different populations

The retrieval budget above follows request arrivals: a fraction of requests moves a payload between
hosts. A distributed model introduces different events. Tensor-parallel participants exchange partial
results at layer boundaries; expert-parallel participants dispatch and combine routed tokens. Their
payload and frequency follow the actual TP or EP communication group and execution schedule, not
the total number of serving hosts. KV transfer follows a further boundary: ownership of a request’s
cached state. These populations need separate byte, frequency, and latency records before their loads
are combined on a shared link.1
    Independent inference replicas do not perform a cross-fleet gradient all-reduce merely because
more hosts are added. Conversely, request-driven retrieval traffic is not the whole network budget
when a model spans devices or hosts. The capacity check accounts for each group’s traffic, simul­
taneous schedules, and shared-link contention. Only exposed communication on the critical path
adds directly to request latency; adding every collective duration again after counting overlapped
execution would double-count time. The earlier retrieval arithmetic remains a request-traffic example,
not a budget for all distributed-model communication. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]


17.4.6. Counter-scenarios: KV is not always the driver

The canonical case is one regime — a mid-context, mid-rate RAG workload where the KV-residency
ceiling happens to be the binding constraint. Two counter-scenarios show that the method (compute
λ·W/C with the real service time) transfers while the conclusion (KV binds) does not. The formula
is the method; the binding term is per-workload.
    Counter-scenario A — short context, high batch: KV is not the host-count driver. A
code-completion-style workload is a clear case: ~500-token input, ~100-token output, but a very high
arrival rate (say 200 rps peak) and a small model (7B, so weights are ~14 GB and the KV footprint per
token is far lower). Here two things happen. First, per-request KV is tiny — a 600-token max-context
against a small per-token κ is well under 1 GB, so the host holds hundreds of concurrent requests
at the KV screen; C is not the ceiling. Second, the binding term becomes decode bandwidth: each
generated token re-reads the full ~14 GB of weights, so the per-host decode token rate is capped
by HBM bandwidth ÷ weight size, and at 200 rps × 100 output tokens the aggregate output-token
demand dwarfs what any one host’s bandwidth supplies. The host count is set by λ·O / (per-host
token rate), not by KV residency. The fleet formula is unchanged; the binding term is bandwidth, not
memory.
    Counter-scenario B — long context, low rate: memory dominates even below the KV
    1
     Implementation evidence inspected 28 October 2026, outside the 30 August snapshot: NVIDIA Megatron-LM,
tensor-parallel mappings at commit b9d4e2b2c899ef7a77b482ff81d020b3d328d8ab, https://raw.githubusercontent.
com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM/b9d4e2b2c899ef7a77b482ff81d020b3d328d8ab/megatron/core/tensor_parallel/mappings.py ;
DeepSeek, DeepEP dispatch/combine interface at commit f6aa38fe06cd4a0489e7730365d4e0114970a2f3, https://raw.
githubusercontent.com/deepseek-ai/DeepEP/f6aa38fe06cd4a0489e7730365d4e0114970a2f3/README.md . These sources
establish operation and group boundaries, not measured capacity or overlap for the book’s workload.
257                                                                                   From Server to Fleet


screen. A document-analysis workload is the opposite pole: ~128K-token input, ~50-token output,
but a low rate (say 2 rps). Here the per-request KV is enormous — 128K tokens against the canonical
κ is ~335 GB, which consumes most of the host’s ~436 GB KV budget (already net of the 140 GB
weights). Because even one request nearly fills the host, the fleet is sized almost one-request-per-host
despite the low rate. Here memory is not just a ceiling — it is the dominant term, and the canonical
brief-context C/W shorthand (which assumes many small requests share a host) does not apply at all.
      The transferable lesson. In the canonical regime the host is KV-bound and sized by λ·W/C;
in counter-scenario A it is bandwidth-bound and sized by output-token rate; in counter-scenario
B it is memory-dominated and sized by aggregate context. The architect must identify which term
binds for the specific workload before applying any single sizing formula — that is what makes the
canonical scenario a method rather than a template.


17.5. Common Mistakes

      1. Ignoring KV cache growth from agentic loops. A common mistake is to assume that
        adding an agentic layer barely changes per-request resource usage. As shown, each turn adds
        ~800 tokens of context, which linearly reduces concurrent‑request capacity. Forgetting this
        leads to under‑provisioning the fleet.

      2. Over‑relying on sticky sessions without load‑balance analysis. Sticky sessions simplify
        cross‑host communication but can create hot‑spot hosts if a few users generate disproportionate
        traffic. Always measure the session‑affinity distribution on the actual workload. A Gini coef­
        ficient exceeding 0.3 is an [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] example threshold, not
        a universal constant — the trigger to abandon sticky sessions depends on the workload, the
        tail-latency SLO, and the failure domain. Establish the skew threshold with a traffic replay/load
        test and tune it to the SLO, not to a fixed 0.3; measure per-host queueing, p95/p99 latency, and
        request drops to decide when stateless routing or session sharding is the appropriate response.

      3. Using raw rps to size the fleet. Requests‑per‑second is necessary but not sufficient; the
        product of rps × average latency gives concurrent load, which must fit within KV cache capacity.
        A host serving 40 rps at 0.5 s latency carries 20 concurrent requests, whereas at 2 s latency it
        carries 80 — the same rps, very different resource usage.

      4. Under‑estimating load‑balancer overhead. A 5% throughput reduction from ρ = 0.95 may
        seem small, but at the margin of capacity it can be the difference between fitting on N hosts
        and needing N+1. Always provision with ρ explicitly in the formula.

      5. Failing to model latency tail under spike traffic. GPU inference time is not constant;
        under sustained high load, kernel‑mode preemption, memory fragmentation, and concurrent
        kernel launches can increase per‑token latency by 20–50%. The linear model t = t_inference +
        t_tool is a lower bound; the architect should add a 20% safety margin.
From Server to Fleet                                                                                258


17.6. Architecture Consequence

    Transitioning from one host to a fleet reshapes every layer of the system.
    GPU fleet sizing. The number of hosts N must satisfy the service‑time‑augmented capacity
formula N = ⌈ λ_peak · W / (C · util_target) ⌉ (the minimum N — the provisioned fleet adds one
spare on top, the N−1 rule), where C depends on the agentic turn distribution and W is the full
per‑request service time (which rises with turns — each turn adds retrieval latency and generated
tokens). Two effects compound as turns grow: C falls (more tokens → more KV per request) and W
rises (more per‑turn latency), so in‑flight concurrency λ·W grows on both sides. For the canonical
customer‑facing peak (40 rps, W≈8.6 s), in‑flight ≈ 344 and N = ⌈344/17⌉ = 21 hosts at full utilization
(29 at 70% util, 30 total with N−1) with FP16 KV; FP8 KV cuts that to 15 working hosts (10 at
full utilization; 16 total with N−1). The lesson is honest: the binding term is λ·W/C, and W must
be the real service time, not a sub‑second target latency. Size for the 95th‑percentile latency and
token scenario, not the median, and treat KV precision as the cheapest way to shrink the fleet before
adding hardware.
    Load‑balancer selection and configuration. The choice between hardware (F5, Cloud LB) and
software (NGINX, HAProxy) affects ρ and the session‑affinity model. Hardware L7 switches offer
better ρ (≈0.98) but less fine‑grained traffic‑shaping; software LBs offer ρ ≈ 0.95 but can implement
consistent hashing for session affinity. The architect should match the LB capability to the session
model: sticky sessions → any LB; stateless → software LB with consistent hashing.
    Cross-host data infrastructure. If any request type requires cross‑host communication (dis­
tributed retrieval, multi‑model orchestration, state sync), a dedicated backend network must be
provisioned. The minimum bandwidth is B_min = φ · λ · D (the fleet aggregate derived in §17.4.4 —
the expected concurrent cross‑host requests φ·λ·t_net times the per‑request burst D/t_net, which
simplifies to φ·λ·D), and the fabric should provide at least 2×B_min for headroom. In the canonical
scenario with φ = 0.1, λ = 40 rps, D = 5 MB, B_min ≈ 0.16 Gbps (0.1 × 40 × 5 MB = 20 MB/s), so a 10 Gbps
intra-rack network has ample headroom for the aggregate; but as §17.4.4 notes, the per-request burst
itself (D / t_net = 250 MB/s ≈ 2 Gbps in the base case) must also fit a single link once a request is in
flight, which is the binding constraint when φ or D grows. But the architect should instrument φ
and D from production telemetry and revisit the bandwidth provisioning quarterly.
    Observability across the fleet. With N hosts, tracing a request end‑to‑end requires correlating
the LB routing decision, the selected host’s inference logs, and any cross‑host data calls. Structured
logging with a request‑ID field that propagates from the client through the LB to the host and back
is essential. Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry, Jaeger) should be enabled by default. Alerts should
trigger when per‑host concurrency exceeds 80% of C, when LB error rate exceeds 0.1%, or when
cross‑host bandwidth utilization exceeds 70%.
    Failover and redundancy. With N ≥ 2, the fleet provides automatic failover: if one host crashes,
the LB routes its traffic to the remaining N−1 hosts, reducing capacity by 1/N (N to N−1 hosts). For
N = 4, a single‑host loss reduces capacity from 100% to 75% (assuming equal load distribution). The
259                                                                                  From Server to Fleet


architect must decide whether this is acceptable or whether N must be larger (e.g., N = 6 for 83%
residual capacity after one failure). Health‑check frequency and graceful drain procedures affect the
real-world failover time, typically 5–15 seconds.
      Multi-region active-active availability is NOT priced in this chapter’s arithmetic. The
multi-region caveat of Ch 16 §16.3 applies verbatim to these host counts: every host count here — and
the N−1 failover/redundancy model above — is a single-region, N−1-only number (≈21 peak / 29
working / 30 with N−1), so the counts and the sizing arithmetic that hangs off them understate the
cost of the canonical workload’s own stated 99.9% availability requirement. Add a separate
multi-region capacity + replication cost line before the availability SLA can be considered met.
17.7. What We Still Don’t Know

      Despite the arithmetic above, several questions remain open and would benefit from targeted
research:
    • Turn-count distribution under fleet load. Do larger fleets (N > 4) change the observed T
        distribution? Intuitively, more hosts reduce per-host contention, potentially lowering latency
        and reducing the agentic loop depth, but empirical measurement is needed.
      • Latency amplification non-linearity. The agentic latency model from Chapter 19 frames
        the added orchestration overhead as β(T) = 1 + (T·L_agent / L_base), which assumes constant
        per‑turn orchestration overhead and a fixed base generation time. Under fleet scaling, GPU
        saturation may make per‑turn overhead grow with concurrent requests, introducing convexity.
        Empirical load‑testing across N = 1, 2, 4, 8 hosts is required.
      • Optimal fleet size for cost vs. latency. The cost of adding a host is roughly the cost of
        8×H100 (multi‑hundred-thousand dollars). The marginal latency improvement from the Nth
        host diminishes (diminishing returns). A cost‑per‑latency‑improved curve would help the
        architect justify fleet size to stakeholders.
      • Cross‑host communication patterns at scale. The φ = 0.1 assumption may not hold for all
        workloads (e.g., RAG over a shared index, distributed fine‑tuning). Real‑world measurement of
        cross‑host traffic patterns is needed to size the backbone accurately.
      • Context‑caching efficacy across a fleet. If many users query related topics, can a fleet‑wide
        KV cache or retrieval cache reduce the effective δ per request? The savings could be substantial
        but require cross-host cache-invalidation protocols that are not yet well understood.


17.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: Going Agentic: Service-Time-Aware Fleet Sizing

Scenario. An AI‑product company operates a fleet of 8×H100 hosts for the canonical traffic of 2,000
users at 10 rps average / 40 rps peak, 9,200 input + 300 output tokens, no agentic layer. After six
months, user growth pushes peak traffic to 100 rps, and the team introduces the agentic layer from
Chapter 19 with a maximum of 3 turns (median T = 1, 95th‑percentile T = 3, per the Ch 19 illustrative
turn-count distribution).
From Server to Fleet                                                                                   260


    Initial sizing analysis (service-time-aware). At T = 3 (the 95th‑percentile, and the honest
worst‑case sizing point), I(3) = 9,200 + 3·800 + 3·65 + 300 = 12,095 tokens. With FP16 KV (κ =
2.62 MB/token), per‑request KV ≈ 31.7 GB, so KV‑residency capacity C = 436 GB ÷ 31.7 GB ≈ 13.8
concurrent requests per host (conservative integer floor 13). But concurrency in flight is λ × W,
where W is the full service time, which here grows with the agentic turns: 1.08 s prefill (held at
the canonical 9.2K single‑shot representative; a 12,095‑token prefill would scale to ~1.42 s) + (~495
generated tokens × ~25 ms/token = ~12.4 s decode) + ~0.4 s of per‑turn tool/retrieval latency ≈ ~13.8
s (the tool/turn term here combines the per‑turn tool + retrieval latency; Chapter 19’s T·L_agent ≈
660 ms is the same class of overhead at a different per-turn rate (Ch 19: 220 ms/turn → 660 ms at
T=3; this case uses ~133 ms/turn → ~0.4 s) — a single model should use one rate consistently). (This
W is the full agentic service time — decode of all generated tokens plus the grown‑context prefill.
Because the prefill is held at the canonical 9.2K representative rather than the full 12,095‑token
context (which would scale it to ~1.42 s and give W ≈ 14.2 s), treat this ~13.8 s as a lower bound on
the agentic service time, and the resulting in‑flight counts and host totals as corresponding lower
bounds. It is not the incremental orchestration‑overhead figure of ~660 ms at T=3 that Chapter 19
reports as its T · Lagent ; the two are different quantities, and it is this full W that drives concurrency
and fleet size, per Chapter 19’s scope note.) So at the 100‑rps peak, in‑flight concurrency ≈ 100 × 13.8
≈ 1,380 requests, not 200. Against C ≈ 13.8 per host (conservative integer floor 13), N = ⌈1,380/(13
×0.7)⌉ ≈ 152 hosts on FP16 KV (≈107 at full utilization). This is the honest arithmetic the service-time
model produces — the naive “1–5 hosts” rps estimate is off by ~15–150× (about one to two orders of
magnitude) because it ignores both the decode duration and the added turn latency.

    KV compression changes the answer. Switching the KV cache to FP8 (κ ≈ 1.31 MB/token, raw
byte-halving — 50% of BF16) cuts per‑request KV at T=3 to ~15.85 GB and raises C to ≈27.5 per host
(436 ÷ 15.85 ≈ 27.5; conservative integer floor 27), giving N ≈ ⌈1,380/(27 ×0.7)⌉ ≈ 74 working hosts
(≈52 at full utilization). Prefix caching can reduce repeated prefill work and share identical cached
prefixes when the engine supports that representation. Its additional capacity benefit depends on
prefix reuse and cache allocation; no further host-count reduction is quantified here. KV precision
and prefix caching are the primary levers that make agentic fleets affordable, but even with both, an
agentic 70B workload at 100 rps is a multi‑dozen‑host fleet, not a handful.

    Decision. At the 100-rps sizing traffic, the integer-slot FP8 bound is 74 working hosts at 70%
utilization, plus one spare host for N−1 operation: 75 hosts in total. This is a KV-residency
planning minimum, not a validated deployment size. Prefix caching may reduce the requirement,
but no cache-hit ratio or additional host-count saving is assumed here. The proposed design uses
NGINX with consistent hashing for session affinity and OpenTelemetry tracing on each host. With
the illustrative φ = 0.05 and D = 5 MB, the network rule must also use the new 100-rps traffic: B_min
= φ·λ·D = 0.05 × 100 × 5 MB = 25 MB/s = 0.20 Gbps. The 2×B_min headroom screen is 0.40 Gbps,
below the existing 10 Gbps intra-rack link rate; the per-request burst must also fit (§17.4.4). At 74
working hosts, the planned KV-slot occupancy is 1,380/(74 × 27) ≈ 69%. This is not GPU compute
261                                                                                From Server to Fleet


utilization. A Chapter 14 deployment benchmark must validate service time, SLO-goodput, failover
behavior, and measured φ and D before hardware is committed. End-to-end latency including agentic
overhead remains an illustrative target until measured.
      Lesson. The fleet decision is driven by KV‑residency capacity vs. service‑time‑scaled con­
currency (λ·W) — not by raw rps, and not by a per‑layer KV constant. The architect’s checklist: (1)
compute I(T) for the expected turn distribution, (2) derive per‑host concurrent capacity C from the
canonical per‑token KV (2 × layers × hidden × bytes), and (3) convert peak rps into concurrency via
λ·W using the full service time. The full service time is prefill + decode of all generated tokens
plus per‑turn tool latency; with it, step (4) computes N = ⌈λ·W/(C·util_target)⌉. Steps (5) and (6):
apply the cheapest capacity levers first — KV precision (FP8), prefix caching, attention architecture
(GQA/MQA) — before buying hosts, and validate throughput and latency with a benchmark, not an
assumption. A multi‑dozen‑host FP8 fleet costs meaningful GPU capital, but avoids both wasteful
over‑provisioning and a costly re‑platform when traffic doubles.




      Minimum hosts N = ⌈λ·W / (C·u)⌉ at a 70% utilization ceiling, where the in-flight concurrency
must use the full per-request service time W — not a sub-second target latency. Two service times
apply: W ≈ 8.6 s for the non-agentic canonical request (1.08 s prefill + 7.5 s decode), and W ≈ 13.8 s
for the T=3 (95th-percentile) agentic request (the mini-case’s service-time-aware figure). These are
the in-flight counts the chapter derives in §17.3/§17.4.
      Table 17-1 — Fleet sizing matrix — KV-residency ceiling and minimum hosts (canonical

chapter 18.


Operating Multiple Models




The Architect’s Question

      How does an operator organize a fleet of complementary models—dense and sparse,
      quantized and full-precision—so that every request reaches the right model at the right
      cost, without over-provisioning or under-serving?

   This chapter answers that question with real arithmetic, routing logic, and operational judgment.


18.1. Concept

   A mixed-model fleet treats each model family as a resource with distinct cost, latency, and
capability profiles. Rather than running every request through a single 70B FP16 model on 8×H100,
we layer:
    • Dense FP16 (baseline, high-quality)
    • Dense 4-bit GGUF (lowest cost, edge-friendly; highest latency — see §18.3.2)
    • MoE sparse (selective activation, higher throughput per GPU)
    • Quantized variants (4-bit/8-bit trade-offs)

   The fleet operates on a routing function R(query) → model_id that maps incoming requests to
the cheapest model satisfying quality constraints.
   Key design principles:

   1. Cost-per-token is the primary unit of comparison across quantizations.
   2. Latency-per-token determines interactive vs. batch placement.
   3. Capability gaps (context window, tool-use, multilingual) dictate minimum model tiers.



                                                263
Operating Multiple Models                                                                          264


   4. Consolidation saves capex when overlap in workload profiles is high; separation preserves
      isolation when workloads have divergent SLA or security needs.


18.2. Mental Model

    The fleet operates as a cost-aware load balancer with three decision layers:
    Table 18-1 — Fleet routing decision hierarchy: capability filter → cost/SLO gate → fallthrough.

   Layer                    Question                           Decision

   Capability filter        Does any model in the fleet meet   Eliminate models that lack the
                            the request’s feature              feature (e.g., context window too
                            requirements?                      small, no tool-use).
   Cost/SLO gate            Among remaining models, which      Route to the cheapest suitable
                            minimizes weighted cost =          model; adjust α,β per deployment
                            α·token_cost + β·latency_cost?     mode (interactive vs. batch).
   Fallthrough              If all suitable models are at      Queue, degrade quantization, or
                            capacity, what is the next-best    escalate to the next tier.
                            alternative?


    The weighting (α,β) is deployment-context dependent. A chat UI tolerates ~200 ms of added
service latency per request; a batch ETL job tolerates ~2 s per request but demands lower token cost.
These are per-request service-latency thresholds for the short-prompt routing scenario — the chat
figure sits under the chapter’s ≤500 ms interactive threshold (§18.3.4) — not the canonical TTFT/TPOT
SLO (Ch 4); the canonical TPOT budget of ~25 ms is a per-token quantity and is not what these
per-request figures measure.


18.3. Worked Example

    Scenario: ~2,000 users, ~5% concurrent (≈100 simultaneous), ~10 rps average / ~40 rps peak. Total
token volume per request: ~9,200 in + ~300 out. Base hardware: 8×H100, 640 GB total VRAM. Model
families: a 70B dense FP16, a 70B MoE (16 experts, 2 active), and a family of 8-bit/4-bit quantized
models (70B equivalent).

    With 8×H100 (640 GB), we can simultaneously run the weights of:

    • One 70B dense FP16 (140 GB)
    • One 70B 8-bit dense (70 GB)
    • One 70B MoE 8-bit (~70 GB)
    • Two 70B 4-bit GGUF (≈70 GB total)

    That is ~350 GB of weights, leaving ~290 GB for KV cache and for smaller specialized models
(e.g., 22B, 8B) for classification or routing. KV, not weights, is the binding term: as the FP16 row
above notes, that tier’s KV alone uses the full 640 GB pool, so this co-residency holds only while the
resident tiers’ combined KV fits.

Qualification precedes placement and promotion

Placement starts with feasible configurations, not with a vendor label. A small local model can be a
candidate for an Intel GPU or an OpenVINO client path when its operators, memory budget and
service behavior pass the same gates as the central service.1 An integrated GPU and an NPU remain
separate choices even when they share a package and system memory. Their advertised compute
figures do not form one execution budget.2
    A routing policy also needs the cost of failure. If a local attempt misses its contract and falls back
to a central service, both attempts contribute resource use and end-to-end delay. The fallback route
must preserve the data policy and still meet any applicable deadline. Promotion therefore follows a
canary on the exact model/backend configuration, with monitored cache behavior, correctness, tail
latency and rollback. Replacing a driver, kernel package or graph mode can change that configuration
even when the model identifier is unchanged.3

18.3.3. Routing arithmetic

Each request carries its full token profile together: 9,200 input + 300 output = 9,500 tokens. Request-
level routing sends the entire request — input and output — to one model. A request cannot
have 70% of its input tokens answered by model A and the rest by model B, unless the architecture
explicitly supports model composition, cascade, or speculative decoding (a different mechanism we
do not assume here). Under ordinary routing, we therefore split by requests, not by in-tokens:
    For 1,000 requests/hour (≈0.28 rps — a light illustrative load; the arithmetic is scale-invariant in
tokens):

    • 70% of requests (700, ≈6.65M tokens) are routine → route to 70B 8-bit: 6.65M × $1.25 = $8.31
      / hr
    • 20% of requests (200, ≈1.9M tokens) need high-quality reasoning → route to 70B MoE 8-bit:
      1.9M × $1.00 = $1.90 / hr
    • 10% of requests (100, ≈0.95M tokens) are complex / multilingual → route to 70B dense FP16:
      0.95M × $2.50 = $2.38 / hr

    (Each request’s output tokens are generated by the same model that processed its input. Routing
output tokens to a different model would require an explicit cascade/composition stage — e.g., a
generator plus a separate rewriter — which is a distinct architecture, not a free assumption.) The
4-bit GGUF tier (800 ms) is listed for completeness but is not routed to in this 70/20/10 split: at 800
ms it would miss the 500 ms interactive threshold, so the bulk goes to the 8-bit GPU tier (250 ms)
instead — the same SLO constraint the §18.8 mini-case works out in full.
    Mixed-fleet hourly cost = $8.31 + $1.90 + $2.38 = $12.59 / hour vs. $23.75 / hour for single-FP16
(all 9.5M tokens at $2.50).
    Monthly savings ≈ ($23.75 − $12.59) × 730 hr ≈ $8,147 / month (≈ 47% reduction) with compa­
rable quality because the 8-bit model meets quality thresholds for ≥90% of requests.

18.3.4. Latency check

The per-request latency is that of the model serving it. The weighted-average request latency is

                    ∑︂
             L̄ =        pi · Li = 0.70 × 250 + 0.20 × 300 + 0.10 × 120 ≈ 247 ms/request
                    i

    (no separate output-routing term — output rides with its requesting model), where pi is the
fraction of requests routed to model i and Li its per-request service latency. Acceptable for interactive
chat (typical threshold: ≤500 ms).
    Scope note — the latency column is an illustrative routing-comparison input, not the
canonical service time. The 120/250/300/800 ms values are illustrative per-request latencies for a
short-prompt routing scenario (the kind of request a router triages in milliseconds), used only to
compare the four models against the interactive threshold (≤500 ms). They are not the ~8.6 s service
269                                                                               Operating Multiple Models


time of the 9.5K-token canonical RAG request (Ch 17), which is a multi-second, capacity-side number
that governs fleet sizing. The cost column, by contrast, is computed on the canonical 9.5K-token
request (6.65M tokens for 700 requests). Read the two columns on their own bases: cost on the
canonical request, latency as the illustrative routing input. A deployment benchmark (Ch 14) must
supply the real per-model service times before either column is used for a production decision.
      The latency and capacity must also reconcile with the canonical workload’s KV residency (Chapter
17): routing 70% of requests to an 8-bit model on 1×H100 changes the per-host KV ceiling accordingly,
and the fleet host count is set by the model each tier runs on. These are [ILLUSTRATIVE] pricing
and latency figures for Q4 2026; the architect re-runs the same arithmetic with measured per-model
cost/latency from a deployment benchmark (Chapter 14).

18.3.5. Consolidation vs. separation decision
      • Consolidate when: workload profile overlap ≥70%, latency tolerance ≥300 ms, and cost differ­
        ential >30%. Verified: our scenario sits exactly at the threshold — it consolidates ~70% of traffic
        to 8-bit (at the ≥70% boundary, not above it), saving ~$11.16/hr ($23.75 − $12.59, the §18.3.3
        derived figure).
      • Keep separate when: (a) security/classification policies require isolation, (b) workloads have
        bimodal latency needs (some ≤50 ms, others batch-tolerant), or (c) model versioning cadence
        differs (e.g., frequent fine-tuning on one family, stable other).

      In our example, consolidation wins because the MoE and 8-bit models capture the same request
classes at lower cost, and the FP16 tier handles the tail without contention. The FP16 tier has no
separate reserve in this worked example: per §18.3.1 it shares the 640 GB pool — 140 GB of weights
plus KV — and at the canonical 9.5K profile it cannot be a 2-GPU reserve, because a 2-GPU shard
holds 160 GB − 140 GB = 20 GB of KV headroom against the 24.9 GB that one 9,500-token request
needs (κ = 2.62 MB/token, Ch 17). Two reserved GPUs suffice only for the ~250-token support queries
of §18.8, not for the canonical 9.5K request.

    Instrumentation: add a middleware shim that logs model_id, token_count, latency_ms,
cost_cents per request. Export to Prometheus + Grafana for real-time dashboards.
    Derived quantity example: Weighted cost rate = (total monthly USD) / (total tokens processed).
Start with the arithmetic above, then update daily as actual token counts and cloud prices shift.


18.5. Common Mistakes
   1. Treating quantization as free. 4-bit/8-bit models reduce VRAM but increase CPU cycles
      and may lower quality on long-context tasks. Always measure the quality hit before routing
      en masse.
   2. One-size-fits-all routing. A static rule (“always use 8-bit”) fails when workload mix shifts
      (e.g., seasonal increase in multilingual queries that need FP16 precision). Use a dynamic router
      with feature-gate checks.
   3. Ignoring capital amortization. FP16 on 8×H100 has high upfront cost; spreading that cost
      across a mixed fleet improves effective cost/token. Don’t forget to annualize GPU capex in the
      per-token math.
   4. Over-provisioning the top tier. Keeping a full FP16 GPU idle “just in case” is expensive.
      Keep just enough capacity for the tail (≈10% of peak rps) and route the rest.
   5. No fallthrough plan. If the preferred model is at capacity, the router must have a next‑best
      alternative ready; otherwise requests time out or queue indefinitely.

    A routing candidate is a validated deployment variant, not only a model family. A lower-precision
variant can lower resource use, but its quality loss may appear selectively in reasoning, code, tool
arguments or long contexts. Retries and longer generations can consume the apparent savings. The
271                                                                          Operating Multiple Models


routing table therefore attaches quality and SLO evidence to the exact precision/backend combination,
and the fallback preserves the task’s acceptance conditions. A change to scales, excluded layers or
execution kernels creates a new candidate for validation; it does not inherit the previous candidate’s
quality curve automatically.


18.6. Architecture Consequence

       A mixed-model fleet changes the architecture in three ways:
      1. Router shim (HTTP middleware or gRPC interceptor) sits between the user API and the
        model execution layer. It evaluates feature requirements, reads current capacity, and selects
        model_id.
      2. Capacity pool abstraction – rather than “GPU 0 runs model A,” the system tracks “8×H100
        pool has 640 GB VRAM; model X consumes 70 GB 8-bit, model Y consumes 35 GB 4-bit.” The
        pool manager auto‑balances placements.
      3. Billing/telemetry pipeline – each request’s cost and latency are tagged with model_id,
        enabling downstream dashboards and alerting (e.g., “cost per token rising above $0.0025 (on
        the §18.8 mini-case per-token basis) for 3 consecutive hours”).

      The fleet operator becomes a cost‑latency steward rather than a single-model optimizer.


18.7. What We Still Don’t Know
      • Quality–cost curves for new quantizations. As 3-bit and sub-4-bit GGUF models emerge, the
        trade-off surface shifts; we need systematic human evals + automatic benchmarks (MT‑Bench,
        FLAN) across families.
      • Optimal router policy for non‑stationary workloads. Reinforcement‑learning–based
        routing that adapts α,β weights in real time is promising but underexplored in production
        fleets.
      • Cross-model distillation opportunities. Can a 70B 4-bit model be distilled from a 70B FP16
        teacher without quality loss, effectively lowering the cost floor? Empirical work needed.
      • Edge–cloud continuum effects. When users bring their own 4-bit‑quantized local models
        (via Ollama, etc.), the fleet routing must account for hybrid inbound/outbound token flows.


18.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: A Three-Tier Customer-Support Model Fleet

Deploy a three‑tier fleet for a customer‑support chatbot.

      • Tier 1 (4-bit GGUF): Handles 80% of queries (FAQ, account lookup). Runs on edge nodes
        (AMD Ryzen 7950X, 64 GB RAM). Cost: $0.0002/token, latency ~600 ms.
      • Tier 2 (70B 8-bit dense): Handles 15% of queries (order status, policy look-up). Runs on
        1×H100. Cost: $0.0015/token, latency ~250 ms.
Operating Multiple Models                                                                              272


    • Tier 3 (70B FP16): Handles 5% of queries (complex escalations, multilingual). Runs on 2 GPUs
      reserved. Cost: $0.003/token, latency ~120 ms.

    Arithmetic: A small pilot deployment serving ~1,000 registered users at a modest, deliberately
low volume — 5,000 tokens/hour (each request averaging ~250 tokens gives roughly 20 requests/hour,
a very light load chosen to make the per-token routing economics concrete rather than to model a
busy fleet; the traffic rate is not what drives this arithmetic, the per-token volume is). Hourly tokens:
~4,500 in + 500 out = 5,000. (Scope note: these tier per-token rates are illustrative scenario values that
differ from the §18.3.2 per-1M ledger — they are not the ledger’s $1.25 (8-bit) / $2.50 (FP16) / $0.15
(4-bit) per-1M rates converted, and the 4-bit tier’s ~600 ms latency differs from the ledger’s 800 ms. They
are on a per-token basis, distinct from — and not directly comparable to — the per-1M-token ledger; the
mini-case uses them to demonstrate the routing economics, and a real deployment would price from the
§18.3.2 per-1M basis.)

    • Tier 1 processes 4,000 tokens/hr → $0.80
    • Tier 2 processes 750 tokens/hr → $1.13
    • Tier 3 processes 250 tokens/hr → $0.75
    • Total hourly cost: $2.68 → $1,956 / month (× 730 hr).

    Check the SLO before the cost claim. If we had used a single 70B FP16 model: 5,000 tokens/hr
× $0.003 = $15/hr → $10,950 / month (× 730 hr). The three-tier split looks like an $8,994 / month
(≈82%) saving — but the SLO gates the cost claim, and here it fails. Tier 1 (the cheapest, 4-bit
GGUF on CPU, ~600 ms) serves 80% of queries, so the p95 per-request latency is ~600 ms,
which violates the 500 ms SLO for the dominant tier. The split saves cost by routing the bulk to
a slow-but-cheap model — precisely the mean-vs-tail trap: the average latency looks fine, yet the
majority tier misses the deadline. The $8,994 / month saving is therefore conditional on first making
Tier 1 feasible.
    Recalculated cost after substituting a feasible Tier 1. Replace the 4-bit GGUF (CPU, ~600
ms) with 8-bit quantization on a GPU (~250 ms, $0.0015/token — the same rate as Tier 2, which is
also 8-bit on 1×H100). The 80% of queries now route at $0.0015/token:

    • Tier 1 (8-bit on GPU) processes 4,000 tokens/hr → $6.00
    • Tier 2 (70B 8-bit dense) processes 750 tokens/hr → $1.13
    • Tier 3 (70B FP16) processes 250 tokens/hr → $0.75
    • Total hourly cost: $7.88 → $5,752 / month (× 730 hr).

    The p95 is now ~250 ms (all tiers under 500 ms), so the SLO is met. The saving narrows from
$8,994 / month (≈82%) to $5,198 / month (≈47%) — still a clear win, but the SLO-constrained figure,
not the raw 82%, is the honest number. The correct order within the cost/SLO gate is: check the SLO,
then size the cost (the capability filter still comes first, per Fig 18.1 and Table 18-1). The routing

chapter 19.


Agentic Systems




The Architect’s Question

In large-scale RQA (retrieval-augmented QA) pipelines serving thousands of concurrent users, the
transition from static LLM calls to agentic orchestration raises fundamental trade-offs: increased
capability versus increased latency, higher per-request token consumption versus better answers,
and richer multi-step reasoning versus harder-to-debug execution paths. This chapter addresses
the architect’s central question: how to design agentic layers that amplify intelligence without
unsustainably inflating cost and latency.
    We begin from the canonical deployment scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2): ~10 requests/second average
and ~40 requests/second peak. Each request carries ~9,200 input tokens and produces ~300 output
tokens. The base model is a 70B dense FP16 engine running on 8×H100 GPUs (640 GB total memory).
The agentic layer sits above this foundation, introducing tool use, retrieval, and multi-step reasoning.
The question we answer is how much additional overhead this layer introduces, whether the quality
gain justifies the cost, and how to size the infrastructure accordingly.


19.1. Concept

    An agentic system is one in which the LLM does not merely complete a single prompt but
iteratively decides which actions to take — calling tools, querying databases, running checks, and
then reasoning about the results before producing a final answer. The core idioms are:
    • Tool use: The model emits a structured call (often JSON) to invoke an external function — a
      search API, a database query, a code interpreter, or a guardrail validator.
    • Retrieval: Within each turn, the agent may trigger a vector search, re-rank results, and feed
      the top-k passages back into the prompt.



                                                  274
275                                                                                   Agentic Systems


      • Multi-step reasoning: The agent maintains an internal “thought” chain, appending each new
        observation and its interpretation before deciding on the next action.
      • Guardrails: Pre- and post-hoc checks that validate whether the model’s intended action is
        safe, on-topic, or within budget.

      The agent loop terminates when a stop condition is met: a final answer is emitted, a maximum
turn count is exceeded, or a guardrail blocks further progress. This design pattern replaces the
“single-shot” prompt — one LLM call, one response — with a dynamic sequence of calls whose length
is data-dependent.
      The architect must decide not only which tools the agent may call but also how to instrument
each call for latency and token accounting, and how to set termination thresholds so that the system
degrades gracefully under load.


19.2. Mental Model

      The mental model we adopt visualizes the agent as a state machine with four recurring states:
Plan, Execute, Observe, and Decide. In each cycle:
   1. Plan: The model reads the current context (original user query + accumulated observations)
        and emits a plan — either “proceed with final answer” or “call tool X with parameters Y.”
      2. Execute: The system routes the tool call to the appropriate backend, waits for results, and
        formats them back into text.
      3. Observe: The result text is appended to the conversation history, and the token count is
        updated.
      4. Decide: The model evaluates whether the observation resolves the user query or whether
        another cycle is needed.

      This loop is deterministic in structure but data-dependent in length. A simple query (“What is
the capital of France?”) may terminate after one Observe, while a complex RQA request (“Compare
the performance of Model A on dataset X against Model B on dataset Y, using the last three papers
from arXiv as evidence”) may traverse three or more cycles.
      The critical insight for capacity planning is that each cycle incurs a fixed overhead: one LLM
inference turn plus any tool-call latency. The variable portion is the number of cycles the model
chooses. Our mental model therefore separates fixed cost per turn from variable turn count, and we
will quantify both in the next section.


19.3. Worked Example

      Take a user query routed to an agentic RQA pipeline. The pipeline’s default policy is a maximum
of 4 turns; if the model has not terminated by then, the system returns a fallback answer “I’m
sorry, I couldn’t find a definitive answer within the allowed reasoning steps.” (Scope note on the

turn cap. This worked example uses a default cap of 4 to illustrate the binding worst case and the

mini-case and used for fleet sizing in Chapter 17 — caps turns at 3, per the §4 guidance and the

      Turn 0 (initial prompt):
      • Input: 9,200 tokens (user query + retrieved passages)
      • Model emits a tool-call: search(query="relevant concepts")
      • System routes the call to the search backend, returns top-5 passages (≈ 800 tokens of snippets)
      • Total tokens after Turn 0: 9,200 + 800 = 10,000

      Turn 1:

      • Input: 10,000 tokens (history + new passages)
      • Model emits a second tool-call: db_query(sql="SELECT ... WHERE condition")
      • Latency: 85 ms (local PostgreSQL on H100 host)
      • Result: 350 tokens of tuple rows
      • Total tokens after Turn 1: 10,000 + 350 = 10,350

      Turn 2:

      • Input: 10,350 tokens
      • Model decides to synthesize: emits a final answer
      • Output: 300 tokens
      • Conversation ends

      Token accounting:

      • Base single-shot: 9,200 input + 300 output = 9,500 tokens
      • Agentic: 10,350 input + 300 output = 10,650 tokens
      • Amplification factor: 10,650 / 9,500 ≈ 1.12×

      A harder query that exhausts all 4 turns is the upper-bound case. Using the chapter’s per-turn
convention (each turn adds δ≈800 tokens of retrieved context plus γ≈65 tokens of model-generated
reasoning), the token trajectory grows approximately linearly: after k turns, total input tokens ≈
9,200 + k·(800+65), and total output ≈ 300 (final answer) plus the intermediate reasoning (≈65 tokens
per turn). After 4 turns, input ≈ 9,200 + 4×800 + 4×65 = 12,660 tokens, output ≈ 300 tokens, giving a
total of ~12,960 tokens. The amplification factor vs. single-shot is 12,960 / 9,500 ≈ 1.36×.
      This worked example demonstrates that the cost increase is moderate for short reasoning paths
but compounds as the agent loops deeper. The architect must weigh the probability of deep loops
against the budget per request.
Agentic Systems                                                                                     278


19.4. Measurement

    To plan capacity and set budgets, we derive three quantities from the example above and the
illustrative turn distribution below. A production deployment must estimate these quantities from its
own telemetry.
    First, a scoping note that matters more than any single number: a production agent turn is not
guaranteed to be exactly “one LLM inference + one tool call.” A turn may contain zero or more
model invocations, parallel or chained tool calls, retrieval + reranking, model-generated reasoning,
tool output, context compaction, or cached prefixes. Treating “1 turn = 1 LLM call + 1 tool call” is a
simplified execution model, useful for first-pass arithmetic but not the general agent model. A more
faithful capacity model is an execution trace: request → model invocation(s) → tool invocation(s)
→ observation(s) → model invocation(s) → final response, with its own token and latency totals.
The amplification framework below (token α, latency β) is one concrete, simplified instantiation of
that trace — it is what an architect can compute before instrumenting a real system, and it must be
validated against measured traces afterwards.
19.4.1. Per-agent-turn token amplification

Let T be the number of agent turns and I₀ the initial input tokens (9,200 in our scenario). Each turn
adds δ tokens of retrieved context and γ tokens of model-generated reasoning. The total token count
after T turns is:


                               Total(T ) = (I0 + T · δ + T · γ) + Ofinal

    where Ofinal is the final output (≈300 tokens). The per-turn amplification α is the ratio of total
tokens to the single-shot baseline I0 + Ofinal :

                                           I0 + T · δ + T · γ + Ofinal
                                 α(T ) =
                                                   I0 + Ofinal
    With δ = 800, γ = 65, Ofinal = 300, and T = 3:


             9,200 + 3 · 800 + 3 · 65 + 300   9,200 + 2,400 + 195 + 300   12,095

    For T = 4: α(4) ≈ 1.36× as computed in the worked example. In production, the distribution of T
depends on query complexity. Consistent with the mini-case telemetry in §8 (68% T = 1, 25% T = 2,
5% T = 3, 2% fallback), the illustrative turn distribution here has median T = 1, 90th percentile T = 2,
and 95th percentile T = 3 [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] — derived from the §8 distribution.
    What α does and does not measure. α measures retained/accumulated task context under
the simplified turn model — the unique content that must be held (and, absent compaction, resent as
context) as the conversation grows. It is not the total model-processed or API-billed token multiplier:
