      The δ tokens are generated once (as retrieval/tool output), then retained as part of later turns’
input context — they are counted once as output-of-tool and again (as carried context) in each later
call’s input. That is correct and intended, but it means total tokens ≠ context size: the amplification
α (retained context) and the task totals (Σ per-call) are explicitly different, and neither is the billed
amount without a cache/billing rule.

19.4.2. Tool-call latency budget

Crucially, the agentic layer adds latency on top of the base answer generation, not instead of it. We
keep two terms rigidly separate:

      • Base inference latency Lbase — the time to generate the final answer itself. Under the
        canonical model this is ~8.6 s: 1.08 s prefill (Ch 8) + ~7.5 s decode of the 300-token answer at
        ~25 ms/token (Ch 8). Every agentic request pays this at least once, and usually again for the
        intermediate reasoning the loop generates (the T·γ tokens).
      • Agent orchestration / tool-call overhead Lagent — the per-turn cost of the loop around the
        model: the LLM’s short decision step to formulate the tool call, plus the tool backend round-trip.
        On 8×H100 the per-turn agent step averages ~120 ms for a 10,000-token context; tool backends
        (search, SQL) add 50–150 ms depending on data volume. So per-turn orchestration overhead
        Lagent ≈ 220 ms (median).



                                          Lagent = λstep + λtool

      where λstep ≈ 120 ms (the model’s tool-call decision step) and λtool ≈ 100 ms (median, tool
backend). For T turns the added orchestration overhead is T · Lagent ≈ 220 ms at the median T =
1, ≈ 440 ms at the 90th percentile T = 2, and ≈ 660 ms at the 95th-percentile T = 3 (consistent with
the §8 turn distribution and the §4 turn-distribution note; T is capped at 3, and the 2% fallback is
a zero-added-turn single-shot for this incremental expectation — its failed-attempt work is counted
unconditionally in the §8 fallback ledger). These are the incremental agent-orchestration numbers,
not the full request latency — see the next section.
Agentic Systems                                                                                           282


19.4.3. Multi-step reasoning cost

The “cost” of multi-step reasoning has two facets: token amplification (already quantified as α) and
latency. The incremental end-to-end latency — the base generation plus the added orchestration
overhead — is:


                                        LE2E (T ) = Lbase + T · Lagent

    where Lbase ≈ 8.6 s is the canonical full answer generation (1.08 s prefill + 7.5 s decode of 300
output tokens) and T · Lagent is the added agent-orchestration overhead (≈ 220 ms per turn). So the
agentic layer does not replace the ~8.6 s generation with ~440 ms — it adds a few hundred milliseconds
of orchestration/tool overhead on top of a request that already takes ~8.6 s to generate its answer.
    Scope note — two different quantities, separated in Table 19-1. The LE2E (T ) above holds the
base generation at the single-shot decode (300 output tokens) and adds only the per-turn orchestration
overhead; it deliberately isolates how much the agentic layer’s orchestration adds. The full agentic
service time — the quantity used for fleet sizing in Chapter 17 — must additionally account for (a)
the decode of the per-turn model-generated reasoning tokens (γ ≈ 65 tokens/turn, at ~25 ms/token
≈ 1.6 s/turn) and (b) the longer prefill of the grown context (I(T ) = 9,200 + T (800 + 65) + 300):


                  W (T ) = Tprefill (I(T )) + 25 ms/token · Ofinal + T · γ + T · λtool/retr
                                                           (︁             )︁


    Chapter 17 §8 derives that full service time as W ≈ 13.8 s at T = 3 (1.08 s prefill held at the
canonical 9.2K representative — the 12,095-token context would scale it to ~1.42 s, giving W ≈ 14.2 s,
so 13.8 s is a lower bound — plus ~12.4 s decode of ~495 generated tokens and ~0.4 s tool latency).
Applying the same formula to the other columns gives W(1) ≈ 10.3 s, W(2) ≈ 12.1 s, W(4) ≈ 15.6 s,
and W(0) = 8.6 s single-shot [DERIVED] — only W(3) ≈ 13.8 s is Chapter 17’s stated figure. So: the
incremental orchestration overhead is T · Lagent (~660 ms at T = 3, β ≈ 1.08×), while the full
end-to-end service time of an agentic request is ~13.8 s at T = 3 — the two are different quantities,
and the latter is what sets concurrency and fleet size. They are also not additive: T · Lagent is this
chapter’s 220 ms/turn orchestration budget (λstep + λtool ), whereas W’s tool leg is Chapter 17’s ~133
ms/turn tool/retrieval-only rate — Chapter 17 §8 itself notes that a single model should use one
rate consistently — and W already carries the per-turn model work inside the γ decode. Table 19-1
therefore reports them as two separate rows: Incremental orchestration (Lbase + T·L_agent) (~8.8 /
~9.0 / ~9.3 / ~9.5 s) and Full agentic service time W (Ch 17 §8) (~10.3 / ~12.1 / ~13.8 / ~15.6 s), the latter
matching Chapter 17’s fleet-sizing tables at the same T. The latency amplification is better expressed
as overhead, not a multiple of a sub-second single-shot number:

                                        Lbase + T · Lagent     T · 220 ms
                              β(T ) =                      ≈1+
                                              Lbase               8.6 s
    At T = 3, β(3) is 1 + 660 ms / 8.6 s ≈ 1.08×: the orchestration-only component adds ~8% — the
283                                                                                                       Agentic Systems


agent loop is not “2–6× slower” in the orchestration sense. But β measures only the incremental
orchestration overhead, not the full task slowdown. The full service time of a three-turn task
grows from ~8.6 s (single-shot) to at least ~13.8 s (~1.6×) once the per-turn reasoning decode (~65
γ tokens/turn) and grown-context prefill are counted — a full increase of ~5.2–5.6 s. So β is βorch
(orchestration-only), and the true task-level multiplier is Ltask E2E /Lbase ≈ 1.6–1.65× at T = 3. The
bound that actually matters: the added orchestration overhead is ~220 ms per turn (budget it), while
fleet sizing follows the total request time — the ~13.8 s full service time, not the ~8.6 s single-shot
generation.
      These derived quantities give the architect concrete numbers to set policies: cap T at 3 unless
the quality gain is statistically significant, and allocate ~220 ms per turn in the orchestration-latency
budget.


19.4.4. Internal depth, agent turns, and training rollouts

An internal depth iteration is not an agent turn. A recurrent model can repeat an internal block
within one model invocation without emitting a tool call. An agent turn can contain prefill, internal
computation, output generation, and tool interaction. A training rollout is a third object: a trajectory
collected for the training procedure, not a request-time turn budget. This distinction prevents a
training method or internal execution setting from being mistaken for the orchestration trace that
the fleet must serve.1
      Model qualification records the benchmark harness, context policy, reasoning effort, sampling
settings, and success metric with the model revision. A best-of-several-trials result is not inter­
changeable with pass-at-one. Averaging independent single-attempt success indicators can estimate
pass-at-one only under the declared sampling and task protocol. An advertised context window does
not establish useful long-context quality, target concurrency, or the cost of serving it. The deployment
decision follows measured task success, invocation traces, and SLO-goodput, not a model-family
label alone. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]


19.5. Common Mistakes

      1. Unbounded or miscalibrated turn limits. Setting the maximum number of agent turns too
          high for the task leads to runaway token consumption and latency spikes. A poorly scoped
          tool can let a model loop until token or deadline limits stop the request. [HYPOTHESIS] The
          right cap is task-calibrated: measure the distribution of useful completion turns, loop-failure
          turns, and marginal value per turn for the workload, then set the cap where marginal value
      1
      Geiping et al., Scaling up Test-Time Compute with Latent Reasoning: A Recurrent Depth Approach, arXiv:2502.05171v2,
17 February 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.05171v2; Ornith Team, Ornith-1.5: From Self-Scaffolding to Self-Improvement,
August 2026, https://ornith.ai/ornith_1_5.html. These primary accounts distinguish recurrent internal computation and
training trajectories; neither establishes the request-time turn count of the book’s hypothetical agent. Sources inspected 28
October 2026 as part of the separately dated addendum, not a refresh of the August comparison tables.
Agentic Systems                                                                                       284


      drops off (the canonical policy caps at 3, with a 2% fallback to single-shot — §4, §8); the number
      is a policy parameter, not a constant.

   2. Neglecting token accounting per turn. Many architects track only the initial input tokens
      and forget that each retrieval or tool call adds context that persists for all subsequent turns.
      Turn T therefore sees an input base that grows linearly with T . Concretely the append-only
      total is I₀ + T·δ + T·γ + O_final = 9,200 + 800T + 65T + 300, which at 2.62 MB/token takes FP16
      KV from 24.9 GB (single-shot, 9,500 tokens) to 34.0 GB (four turns, 12,960 tokens).

   3. Overlooking tool latency variance. A tool that typically responds in 30 ms may, under
      cache misses or lock contention, take 2 s. Without a timeout and fallback, the entire agent loop
      blocks. Always instrument timeouts and provide a “best-effort” fallback path.

   4. Confusing ‘agentic’ with ‘more prompts’. Adding extra prompts without a structured loop
      (Plan/Execute/Observe/Decide) does not give the model reasoning power; it just inflates token
      count. The agentic value comes from the model’s ability to reinterpret prior observations and
      decide the next action.

   5. Skipping guardrails. Without pre-call validation (e.g., query sanitization, budget checks)
      and post-call verification (answer relevance, hallucination detection), agentic systems can
      produce plausible but incorrect or unsafe outputs. Guardrails are not optional — they are the
      safety net that makes bounded loops safe in production. A production agent needs explicit
      termination, budget, recovery, and escalation policies: hard turn/token/cost/wall-time limits,
      tool timeouts, cancellation, idempotency/retry discipline, state checkpointing, and human
      escalation. A logical multi-step task may be resumed across bounded execution windows rather
      than granted unlimited resources — guardrails make the loop safe, not unbounded.


19.6. Architecture Consequence

    Introducing an agentic layer reshapes the system architecture in four ways:
    State-management policy sets the trajectory. Before quantifying context/KV growth, the
architect must decide the state-management policy, because that policy — not the model — determines
whether context grows unbounded. The quantitative path that follows (Fig 19.2/19.3) uses an append-
only bounding case with this exact retention policy: (i) the initial prompt is retained in full; (ii) each
turn’s tool outputs are retained in full (not externalized); (iii) the model’s per-turn reasoning tokens
are visible and retained in the context (not hidden); (iv) no prefix cache is assumed to be reused
across turns (each turn’s request is rebuilt from the full accumulated context); (v) no truncation or
compaction is applied. Under that policy the context is only ever appended and never evicted, so it
is the worst case — a deliberate upper bound, not the deployed design. Two token counts must be
kept distinct: the billable tokens (what the API charges, = the full accumulated context sent each
turn) and the KV-resident tokens (what occupies the cache, = the same accumulated context under
285                                                                                         Agentic Systems


this no-reuse policy); with prefix caching enabled the billable count can fall while the KV-resident
count stays, so the two diverge. The durable architectural lesson is that the growth rate is set by the
policy levers — summarization (compress the accumulated history each turn), truncation (drop the
oldest context beyond a budget), externalized tool state (store retrieval results out-of-band rather
than in-context), replay policy (re-derive rather than retain), and cache policy (prefix caching, KV
precision). A design that applies these levers can hold context roughly flat while an append-only
design grows it ~36% by turn 4; the append-only number is the stress case that bounds what the
system must tolerate if the levers fail, not the expected operating point.
      Inference scaling. The base model (70B FP16, 8×H100) must now serve variable-length contexts,
and — critically — the KV-residency conclusion is far more severe than a per-latency convenience
because the canonical per-token KV is ~2.62 MB/token (Chapter 7’s full-MHA reference geometry). A
request that triggers 4 agent turns carries ~12,960 tokens vs. 9,500 for single-shot (Table 19-1) — that
is not a “35% GPU memory” tweak but a move from ~24.9 GB KV per request (9,500 tokens × 2.62 MB)
to ~34.0 GB (12,960 ×2.62 MB) — roughly a 36% growth, on top of an already-large KV footprint. At
the canonical workload’s ~86 average in-flight requests at 10 rps (Lexec = λ × Wexec ≈ 10 × 8.6 per Ch
4; distinct from the ~100 active-user population) with the median single-turn profile (~27.2 GB/request
at 10,365 tokens), the aggregate KV alone is ~86 × 27.2 GB ≈ 2.3 TB — far beyond one host’s ~436 GB
KV budget, so agents do not just stress memory, they force a fleet (Chapter 17). The architect
must therefore treat context growth as a first-order capacity driver: cap T , cache prefixes, or quantize
KV (FP8), as these levers repeatedly outprice adding hosts. Note we must be precise: the per-request
KV is set by the model’s canonical per-token KV (all layers), not by per-layer figures; the honest
number is tens of GB per request, which is exactly why agentic depth is a fleet-sizing problem.
      Task economics. The deepest shift an agentic workload imposes is a change in what the architect
optimizes. For conventional inference, the unit of cost is the token: the architect optimizes token
economics — cost per token, latency per token, KV per token. For an agentic system, the unit of
value is the task: the architect optimizes task economics, because a task consumes a variable, data-
dependent number of model calls, tool calls, and tokens, and may fail. The right denominator is
therefore cost per successful task, not cost per token:

                                               model calls/task × tokens/call × $/token
                                               + tool calls/task × $/tool
                                               + retries/task × cost/retry
                  cost per successful task ≈
                                                                 psuccess
      where psuccess > 0 is the task success rate and tokens/call is itself inflated by the agentic amplifi­
cation α from Section 4. Two consequences follow. First, a more expensive model that completes
tasks in one turn can be cheaper per successful task than a cheap model that needs three turns —
the amplification term can dominate the base price. Second, the success rate is as important as the
unit cost: a 10% cheaper pipeline that fails 5% more often can be net more expensive once retries

and human intervention are counted. This is a genuinely different objective from cheapest tokens,
and it is why agentic workloads cannot be priced or capacity-planned with the single-shot token
arithmetic alone. An architect should instrument tasks (success, turns, calls, retries) and optimize cost
per successful task, exactly as an architect of a deterministic service optimizes cost per completed
request.
    Tool backend provisioning. Search indexes, SQL pools, and code interpreters become first-
class infrastructure components. Their capacity (concurrent queries, connection pool size, query
throughput) must be dimensioned alongside the LLM GPU pool. A bottleneck in the tool backend will
manifest as increased λtool , which directly inflates the per-turn latency L and therefore the overall
request latency.
    Observability requirements. Each turn generates a tuple of (turn number, model input tokens,
tool call, tool latency, tool output tokens, decision). Correlating these tuples across turns for a
single request, and across requests for the fleet, requires structured logging and tracing. Without it,
debugging why a request took 2 s and consumed 15,000 tokens is nearly impossible.
    Fallback & degradation pathways. Because the agentic layer introduces data-dependent depth,
the system must have graceful degradation: if the turn limit is reached, return the best partial answer
so far, or fall back to a simpler single-shot prompt. This preserves user experience even when the
agent fails to converge.

19.7. What We Still Don’t Know


    Despite the quantified arithmetic above, several questions remain open and would benefit from
targeted research:
    • Turn-count distribution shift with model scale. Do larger-context models (e.g., 405B FP16)
      exhibit different T distributions? Does the ability to “see more” reduce the need for multi-step
      loops, or does the model reason more deeply and actually increase T ?
    • Token amplification vs. answer quality curve. We can compute α(T) from the illustrative
      token counts, but we have not firmly established the marginal quality gain per additional turn.
      Is the 1.27× → 1.36× move from T = 3 to T = 4 worth the 7% token increase? A/B tests across
      query categories would help.
    • Latency tail under spike load. Our 95th-percentile added orchestration latency of ~660 ms
      (T = 3, the scenario turn cap; conditional on a completed agent run, with the fallback-inclusive
      ledger in §8 giving the same p95 but p99 = 860 ms) assumes GPU inference time is constant.
      Under traffic spikes, GPU saturation can increase inference latency non-linearly. Empirical
      measurement under controlled load is needed to validate the linear T·L model.
    • Optimal tool design for minimal turn count. Some tools could return more comprehensive
      results in a single call, reducing the need for multiple rounds. The design space of “rich
      vs. narrow” tools and its impact on T is underexplored.
    • Cross-user context caching. If many users ask related questions (e.g., “What does the policy
289                                                                                        Agentic Systems


        say about X?”), can we cache intermediate retrieval results and avoid redundant tool calls?
        The savings could be substantial but require careful invalidation logic.

still carries the full 800 tokens per turn (cached or not), so absent a concrete context-reduction policy

the added agent-orchestration latency is comfortably under 1 s, but the end-to-end request is ~9 s
because of the base generation. The architect therefore scopes the <1 s SLA to orchestration overhead
excluding final generation, and treats end-to-end as bounded by the ~8.6 s base generation in the
incremental view (or by the full service time W ≈ 10.3 s at the median T = 1 in the fleet-sizing view).
      Lesson. The agentic layer added an expected ~12% token overhead (distribution-weighted, §8)
and, at the median T = 1, ~220 ms of orchestration latency (on top of an ~8.6 s base generation), but
improved answer correctness on multi-step reasoning queries by an estimated 22% in an illustrative
human-eval reading [ILLUSTRATIVE] scenario result, not a reported production measurement. The
trade-off was acceptable — the added overhead is small relative to the base generation — and context
caching cut the retrieval re-fetch cost (transport only — the retained context is unchanged). The
architect’s key decisions were: (a) capping turns at 3, (b) adding a search cache, and (c) providing a
single-shot fallback when the limit is hit.

Fleet-Level Optimization




The Architect’s Question

As a RAG Q&A workload scales from a single host to a fleet of serving nodes, the architect must
confront a new set of trade-offs: how does aggregate throughput scale with added hardware, how
does scheduling latency affect user-perceived latency, and at what point does autoscaling cease to be
cost-effective? This chapter addresses these questions through concrete arithmetic, not hand-waving.


20.1. Concept

Fleet-level optimization treats the entire collection of serving hosts as a single resource pool rather
than independent islands. The central insight is that aggregate system throughput is not merely the
sum of individual host throughputs; it is modulated by scheduling overhead, network contention,
and the cost of moving data between hosts and storage. Two cost effects must be kept distinct. The
average cost per query declines only along a stated load path: as served demand grows and fixed
overhead (model loading, infrastructure, staff) is spread across more SLO-good requests, cost per
request may decline until additional capacity steps dominate; adding idle hosts at fixed demand
increases unit cost. The marginal cost of each added host, however, is roughly constant in this
model — one host buys ~2.0 req/s (17/8.6 = 1.977, [ANALYTICAL]) at ~$20/hr, so the marginal cost
stays near ~$10 per req/s per hour (Ch 17 §7 frames the Nth host as diminishing marginal benefit,
not falling marginal cost). The economic lever is amortizing the fixed term, not the marginal one.




                                                 293
Fleet-Level Optimization                                                                             294


    The key concepts are:

    • Aggregate throughput: The total queries-per-second the fleet can sustain before latency SLA
      violations.
    • Scheduling overhead: The per-request cost of dispatching a query to an available host,
      including placement decisions and data movement.
    • Autoscaling break-even: The point at which adding another host reduces marginal cost per
      query versus the fixed cost of provisioning and maintaining that host.


20.2. Mental Model

    The mental model for fleet optimization replaces the single-host query pipeline with a two-level
hierarchy. At the lower level, each host processes queries using its GPU/CPU pipeline. At the upper
level, a scheduler routes incoming requests across hosts, handling load balancing, model parallelism
where needed, and graceful degradation under overload.
    The scheduler’s decisions have direct impact on the tail of the latency distribution. Poor placement
can cause some hosts to saturate while others remain underutilized, inflating the 99th-percentile
latency even when aggregate throughput is ample. Conversely, intelligent scheduling—such as
consistent hashing for session affinity or predictive placement based on historical patterns—keeps
utilization flat across the fleet and minimizes tail latency.
    A critical assumption in this model is that the workload follows a known arrival process. For the
canonical scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2): ~10 rps average and ~40 rps peak. With ~9,200 in-tokens and
~300 out-tokens per query, a ~8.6 s service time per request (1.08 s prefill + ~7.5 s decode), and a 70B
dense FP16 model running on 8×H100 (640 GB total HBM3), the fleet must sustain ~40 requests/s
at peak, which — by Little’s law — corresponds to λ·W ≈ 40 × 8.6 ≈ 344 requests in flight, not
merely the ~100 concurrent users or the nominal 40 rps. The distinction between “concurrent users”
(a population), the arrival rate (rps), and in-flight requests (λ·W) is exactly what Chapter 17 develops;
it is the difference between sizing for a population and sizing a fleet against a latency bound.
20.3. Worked Example

    Take a fleet of N hosts, each with 8×H100 running a single 70B FP16 model instance. Two
capacities must be reconciled — throughput (tokens/s) and KV residency (concurrent requests) —
and neither can be reduced to a single “rps” constant, because rps is workload-specific (per-request
input/output tokens, context length, batch).
    Latency floor first, then reconcile the two capacity bounds. A 300-output-token request at
a ~25 ms/token decode rate (Chapter 8) takes ~7.5 s of generation alone, plus 1.08 s prefill, so the
service time is ~8.6 s per request (before tool calls). Two separate ceilings bound how many requests
a host can serve per second, and they must be reconciled — they are not interchangeable:
    • Throughput bound (tokens/s). A host sustains an illustrative ~35,000 tokens/s of total
      (prefill+decode) serving throughput — the conservative low end of the ~35,000–70,000 tokens/s
295                                                                                  Fleet-Level Optimization


        range in Chapter 15 [ILLUSTRATIVE] achievable range — distinct from the ~19,800 tok/s
        prefill-only ideal in Chapter 8 (8 × 2,471 at 35% MFU), which counts prefill compute alone.
        These two are not directly comparable as single numbers: ~35,000 is a phase-mixed
        prefill+decode total and ~19,800 is a prefill-only figure. To compare them one must
        first phase-resolve both, then compare prefill with prefill (the presented workload’s
        prefill leg is 2.0 req/s × 9,200 = 18,400 input tok/s) and decode with decode (2.0 ×
        300 = 600 output tok/s); aggregating the two phases into one “total” rate requires an
        explicit cost/phase-equivalence model. Dividing the total by the ~9,500 tokens/request
        gives ~3.7 requests/s — but this is not achievable here, because it would require ~3.7 × 8.6
        ≈ 32 concurrent requests in flight, roughly double the host’s KV-residency ceiling (C ≈ 17.5,
        conservative integer floor 17, Chapter 17). The token-throughput figure is thus a non-binding
        upper edge for this canonical workload.
      • KV-residency / latency bound (Little’s law). The real ceiling is set by concurrency and
        service time together: a host holds 17 whole concurrent full-context requests (the ~17.5 KV
        ceiling, Chapter 17, floored to whole contexts — no fractional admission) each for ~8.6 s, so it
        serves C/W = 17 / 8.6 = 1.977 ≈ 2.0 requests/s [ANALYTICAL] at steady state.

      The binding per-host rate is the minimum of the two — here the KV/latency bound. This is
exactly why a token-throughput number must not be divided by tokens-per-request to manufacture
an “rps” here: the units do cancel (tokens/s ÷ tokens/request = requests/s), but the numerator is a
phase-mixed prefill+decode total with no cost/phase-equivalence model, and the ~3.7 req/s answer
would need ~32 concurrent requests against the 17-slot host capacity. The per-host request rate is a
concurrency × service-time quantity — what makes the division wrong here is what its numerator
mixes and its answer assumes, not its units.
      Call this quantity what it is. The ~2.0 req/s figure is a KV-residency / service-time analytical
planning bound under the canonical W assumption — not a measured serving throughput. It is
achievable only if serving C concurrent sequences does not inflate W beyond the assumed ~8.6 s, and
neither a compute, bandwidth, nor scheduler constraint binds first. In real continuous batching, W
is a function of batch occupancy, scheduler policy, prefill interference, decode batching, the arrival
process, tensor-parallel communication, and the context distribution — so C and W are not always
independent constants. Treat ~2.0 req/s as an upper-bound model, and require benchmarked goodput
(Chapter 14) under the target arrival process for actual fleet sizing. Planning-bound caveat: like
the ~19,800 prefill tok/s/host figure (Ch. 8, idealized prefill only), the ~2.0 req/s/host figure is an upper-
order planning bound — model-derived, not an implied deployed rate. No p95/p99 performance
guarantee has been shown for any of the host counts in this chapter; the p95/p99 tail latency and
achieved goodput must be measured on the target deployment (Chapter 14) before the 21/22-host
sizing is treated as validated.
      Simultaneous feasibility check (prefill + decode coexistence). The ~2.0 req/s/host bound
assumes prefill and decode run on the same host at the same time. Evaluated at the displayed ~2.0 rps
Fleet-Level Optimization                                                                            296


— a deliberate stress screen, slightly above the unrounded 17/8.6 = 1.977 — the prefill demand is 2.0 ×
9,200 = 18,400 input tokens/s per host (§3). The idealized prefill ceiling is 8 × 0.989 PF/s × 35% / (2
× 70e9) ≈ 19,780 tokens/s (Chapter 8, 35% MFU, prefill-only). The ratio is 18,400 ÷ 19,780 ≈ 93%.
Prefill must run at ~93% of the idealized prefill ceiling. This is [ANALYTICAL] (Axis-3 measurement
status; defined with the evidence taxonomy in the Sources, Method, and Reproducibility chapter)
— a prefill-load check, not a measured rate. The ~93% leaves very little headroom before decode
coexistence, interference, and the actual achieved MFU. Prefill and decode share the same hardware.
Batch scheduling and decode interleaving compete for the same compute. The achieved MFU is
below the 35% ideal. Therefore ~2.0 req/s/host is an analytical upper bound, NOT a claim that a
host serves 2 req/s at SLO. Before treating 2 req/s/host as deployable, measure the p95 TTFT, p95
TPOT, and SLO-goodput on a representative host (Chapter 14).
    Fleet aggregate throughput (illustrative form). Keeping the illustrative per-host rps = Q for
the algebra, aggregate throughput is


                                           Λfleet = N × Q

    At the canonical peak of 40 rps, fleet size must satisfy both the KV-residency and the through­
put/latency bounds and whichever binds first. With the per-host rate at ~2.0 req/s (17/8.6 = 1.977, the
binding Little bound above), a fleet for 40 rps starts at 21 hosts on the Little-bound — ⌈40 × 8.6 / 17⌉
= ⌈344/17⌉ = ⌈20.24⌉ = 21. The KV-residency bound coincides here — by Little’s law, the in-flight
count at 40 rps is λ·W = 40 × 8.6 ≈ 344, and ⌈344/17⌉ = 21 hosts (17 whole contexts per host, no
fractional admission) — so the two bounds are co-binding at the peak, exactly as Chapter 17 notes
(the two views are the same identity, λW/C = λ/(C/W)); the ρ ≈ 0.95 fractional-throughput derate
raises the requirement to 344 / (0.95 × 17) = 344/16.15 ≈ 21.3 → 22 hosts. The “far fewer hosts (~6)”
figure applies only to the 10-rps average (⌈86/17⌉ = 6), not the 40-rps peak. The correct statement is:
the fleet must satisfy both, and the larger requirement wins. Reading Fig 20.1’s two gaps: below
saturation the ~5% gap between C_analytic(N) = N × 17/8.6 and C_eff(N) = 0.95 × C_analytic is the
assumed throughput-efficiency derate; above saturation C_eff − S, with S = min(40, C_eff), is unused
capacity from insufficient offered demand — not scheduling overhead. Queueing and tail-latency
penalties are not determined by this two-line calculation and must be shown separately if claimed.
    Scheduling overhead. A lightweight round-robin scheduler adds ~0.5 ms of dispatch latency
per request — negligible next to a real 7.5 s decode, but it must stay under ~5% of the measured
per-request time.
    Autoscaling economics. Each 8×H100 host costs ~$20/hour (cloud, $2.50/GPU-hr canonical)
or ~$8/hour amortized (owned) — [ILLUSTRATIVE]. The marginal cost per additional rps is $20 ÷
(rps gained per host); the economic lesson (diminishing cost of a marginal host once fixed costs
dominate) is sound, but the exact per-rps figure is only meaningful after the real per-host throughput
is benchmarked.

20.4. Measurement

      To validate fleet-level optimization claims, five core metrics should be measured at regular
intervals:
      Table 20-1 — Fleet-level measurement metrics

      Metric                          Definition                        Target

      Aggregate rps                   Total queries processed per       ≥ 2× peak rps for comfort
                                      second across all hosts           margin

      latency                         request waits in the fleet

      Note: end-to-end median/p99 latency is deliberately not a fleet-level target for this canonical 9.5K-
token workload — a request takes ~8.6 s in service (1.08 s prefill + ~7.5 s decode), so an end-to-end <100
ms p99 is infeasible (see the mini-case). Table 20-1 therefore qualifies these as scheduler-added (dispatch)
latency targets only.
      Measurement methodology: use a distributed load generator (e.g., Locust or a custom gRPC-driven
pump) that sends queries at the target rps while instrumenting each host’s internal metrics—GPU
occupancy, kernel launch time, scheduler dispatch timestamp, and queue depth. Aggregate these
via a time-series database (InfluxDB or Prometheus) and compute the above metrics over sliding
1-minute windows.
      A practical pitfall: measuring only aggregate rps without tracking per-host variance can mask
saturation in individual nodes. Always report both the fleet-wide and per-host metrics.
      Placement also determines the communication and failure domain. A slow or failed participant
can delay an entire model-parallel group while other replicas remain healthy. Group-level completion
tails, asynchronous failures and the affected requests therefore accompany per-host utilization. A
Fleet-Level Optimization                                                                           298


placement that improves average utilization but increases cross-group contention can reduce SLO-
goodput; replica isolation and group recovery require measurement before they become fleet-capacity
assumptions.
    The qualification gate in Chapter 18 applies before a configuration enters any capacity pool. A
fallback route consumes capacity too; its quality, deadline and data-policy constraints remain part of
the placement contract.


20.5. Common Mistakes

    • Treating hosts as independent: Optimizing each host in isolation (e.g., tuning batch size per
      host) ignores the scheduling overhead that becomes dominant when the fleet is viewed as a
      unit. A suboptimal batch size on one host can increase dispatch frequency for the entire fleet.

    • Overlooking data movement cost: In RAG workloads, the ~9,200 in-tokens and ~300 out-
      tokens per query must be fetched from a vector database or cache. If every host pulls data
      independently, the network cost scales linearly with fleet size. A better approach is to colocate
      vector stores with serving hosts or use a shared cache layer that amortizes fetch cost across
      concurrent queries.

    • Autoscaling too aggressively: Adding hosts at the first sign of latency increase can be
      suboptimal if the bottleneck is scheduler throughput or cache contention, not compute capacity.
      Measure the marginal cost of adding a host before triggering a scale-out event.

    • Ignoring cold-start cost: When a host is freshly provisioned or re-warmed after idle, load­
      ing the full model weights into HBM takes 30–120 seconds [ILLUSTRATIVE] (a load-path
      assumption for a ~140 GB model over a ~10–40 Gb/s path — 140 GB ÷ 30–120 s ≈ 4.7–1.2
      GB/s — not a hardware benchmark; distinct from the much shorter KV-cache warm-up of ~2 s
      discussed in Chapter 15, which re-populates only the retained KV state). Autoscaling policies
      must account for this weight-load warm-up window when scaling out a fresh host; otherwise
      the fleet experiences a spike in error rate or timeout during scale-out events.


20.6. Architecture Consequence

    Fleet-level optimization reshapes the serving architecture in three ways:
   1. Centralized scheduler: A lightweight service (e.g., based on etcd or a custom placement
      engine) maintains real-time view of per-host utilization and makes dispatch decisions. This
      service must be highly available, and its dispatch overhead should stay a small fraction of
      the per-request SLO — for the canonical ~8.6 s service time, a sub-millisecond decision is
      a comfortable target (the round-robin baseline adds ~0.5 ms, §3), not a universal necessity:
      the binding constraint is that dispatch overhead not consume a meaningful share of the
      request/turn SLO, which depends on routing frequency and scheduling architecture.
299                                                                               Fleet-Level Optimization


      2. Data colocation: Vector indexes and model weights are stored close to the hosts that consume
        them. This may mean running a local Qdrant or Milvus instance per host, or using a shared
        object store (e.g., MinIO) with read-replicas per availability zone. The goal is to minimize the
        distance—measured in network hops—between the scheduler’s placement decision and the
        data fetch. But colocation is a trade, not a free win: a per-host index multiplies memory/storage,
        consistency, ingestion, and operational cost across the fleet, and model-weight locality is a
        different problem from vector-index locality. The right placement depends on the workload —
        compare centralized retrieval, AZ-local retrieval, replicated indexes, and cached results, and
        identify the traffic/latency point at which colocation’s access-latency saving outweighs its
        replication cost. Do not conflate the two locality questions.

      3. Graceful degradation: The fleet should have a mode where, under extreme overload, it serves
        stale or truncated answers rather than failing entirely. This could mean returning the top-k
        results from a cached embedding rather than recomputing, or surfacing a “try again” message
        with an estimated wait time. The architectural contract must make this trade-off explicit so
        product teams can set appropriate SLOs.

20.6.1. The useful completion is an accepted clip

For a fixed output contract, a video fleet can report completed clips/s and generated frames/s together.
Frames/s alone is ambiguous: larger frame counts can increase reported output work while reducing
completed jobs. Across changing durations and frame rates, generated clip-seconds/s also needs a
stated denominator and does not normalize the nonlinear attention cost.
      A useful goodput definition counts clips that satisfy the completion deadline, output-integrity
checks, quality gate, and safety requirements in the same observation window. Rejections, OOMs,
cancellations, retries, and unusable outputs remain visible as separate counters. The cost per accepted
clip divides the total allocated cost of that window—including idle capacity and failed attempts—
by the accepted-clip count. Storage, delivery, encoding, and license costs enter explicitly rather
than disappearing into a GPU-seconds estimate. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] proposed service
accounting.
      If no clips pass, accepted-clip goodput is zero and cost per accepted clip is undefined; the report
retains the total cost and rejection counters rather than reporting zero unit cost.
      Shape-specific measured service time and peak memory determine placement. Warm replicas
trade idle cost for avoiding checkpoint downloads, initialization, compilation, and encoder loading on
the request path. Heterogeneous pools can separate preview, denoising, and reconstruction contracts
where measurement justifies the transfer. Replicas add independent job capacity; sequence-parallel
groups can make a larger job feasible or reduce its service time at a communication cost. These are
different scaling actions. The existing distinction between analytical capacity bounds and measured
SLO-goodput remains unchanged.
Fleet-Level Optimization                                                                          300


20.7. What We Still Don’t Know


    Several open questions remain at the fleet level:
    • Heterogeneous hardware: What happens when hosts mix H100, A100, and CPU-only nodes?
      The scheduler must handle different throughput ceilings and memory capacities, and the
      aggregate throughput calculation becomes a weighted sum rather than a simple multiple.
      Real-world measurements of mixed-device fleets are scarce; most published benchmarking
      uses homogeneous hardware, so the crossover point where heterogeneity hurts versus helps is
      not well quantified.



    • Multi-model serving: When multiple model sizes coexist (e.g., 70B for complex queries, 7B
      for quick ones), the scheduling problem gains a new dimension—placement must balance
      model size against query urgency and host memory. Mixed-precision serving (FP16, FP8, INT4)
      adds another layer: lower precision increases throughput but may degrade answer quality on
      subtle reasoning tasks, and the quality-throughput trade-off curve is model-specific.



    • Economic auto-scaling: The break-even point between owning hardware versus cloud-
      on-demand depends on utilization patterns that are workload-specific. A fleet that runs at
      20% utilization on average may be cheaper in the cloud; one at 80% utilization favors owned
      hardware. The transition point is a function of capital expenditure amortization period, elec­
      tricity cost, and the volatility of user demand. Published TCO analyses typically assume steady
      utilization, but bursty workloads with short-lived spikes can make ownership risky unless
      over-provisioned.



    • Tail-latency arbitration: When two queries compete for the same GPU HBM bandwidth,
      the 99th-percentile latency can spike disproportionately. We lack a general-purpose scheduler
      policy that guarantees a target tail latency under arbitrary arrival patterns; this remains an
      area of active research. Some systems use priority queues or token buckets to cap per-query
      bandwidth, but these mechanisms add scheduling complexity and can increase median latency.



    • Cross-query caching effects: In RAG workloads, the ~9,200 in-tokens and ~300 out-tokens
      per query overlap significantly across users asking related questions. The potential for caching
      intermediate embeddings or partial KV caches is substantial, but the cost of cache management
      (invalidation, coherence, metadata overhead) must be quantified against the compute savings.
      We lack large-scale measurements of caching efficiency across diverse query populations.
301                                                                                Fleet-Level Optimization

Scenario: A RAG Q&A fleet serves 2,000 users with the canonical parameters: 5% concurrent, 10 rps
average / 40 rps peak, ~9,200 in-tokens + ~300 out-tokens per query, 70B dense FP16 model, 8×H100
per host, 8 hosts total.
      Question: What is the fleet’s aggregate rps capacity under the canonical KV/latency bound, and
what is the marginal cost per rps when scaling from 8 to 16 hosts? Is an end-to-end 99th-percentile
latency under 100 ms even feasible for this workload — and if not, what can the scheduler bound?
      Solution (illustrative algebra — the per-host figure is an [ILLUSTRATIVE] estimate for showing
the fleet math; the real per-host rps must come from a Chapter 14 deployment benchmark, bounded
by KV residency per Chapter 17):

      • Per-host request rate — the KV/latency bound (Ch. 17 basis). A host holds 17 whole
        concurrent full-context requests (the KV-residency ceiling, Chapter 17; byte-accurate 17.51,
        floored to 17 — no fractional admission) and each request is in service ~8.6 s (1.08 s prefill +
        ~7.5 s decode of 300 output tokens at ~25 ms/token, Chapter 8). So a host serves C/W = 17 / 8.6
        = 1.977 ≈ 2.0 requests/s [ANALYTICAL] at steady state — the defensible capacity number,
        from concurrency × service time (Little’s law), not a token throughput ÷ tokens per request
        (§3: ~35,000 tok/s ÷ ~9,500 needs ~32 in flight — 17 slots cannot hold).
      • Fleet aggregate (8 hosts): 8 × (17/8.6) = 15.8 ≈ 16 req/s, below the canonical 40-rps peak. The
        idealized minimum is ⌈344/17⌉ = 21 hosts; the ρ ≈ 0.95 factor used in this chapter and Ch 17 —
        a fractional-throughput efficiency derate on the rate, not a second slot floor and not a failure
        spare — raises it to 344/(0.95 × 17) = 344/16.15 ≈ 21.3 → 22 hosts. (The KV-residency bound,
        Chapter 17, needs far fewer — ⌈86/17⌉ = 6 at the 10-rps average — but the throughput/latency
        bound binds here, so the larger requirement governs.)
      • Marginal cost (real basis): adding one host at ~$20/hr (cloud, [ILLUSTRATIVE]) buys ~2.0
        req/s, so marginal cost = $20 ÷ (17/8.6) = $20 × 8.6 / 17 = $10.12 ≈ $10 per req/s per hour. (The
        ~$0.012 figure from Chapter 4 is a per-request managed-API price, not a per-req/s-per-hour
        rate — Chapter 4’s own basis note says the two cost bases are not interchangeable — and with
        a real multi-second service time per request the per-host rate is ~2.0, not a hypothetical 250.)
      • Algebra practice (kept [ILLUSTRATIVE]): the per-host 250 rps / fleet 2,000 rps arithmetic
        is kept only to show the structure of the fleet math (marginal host cost ÷ marginal capacity):
        $20 ÷ 250 = $0.08 per rps per hour. The 250 rps is hypothetical and unachievable for this
        9.2K-in/300-out workload; substitute the measured per-host rate from a Chapter 14 deployment
        benchmark, or the ~2.0 req/s bound derived here — which gives the $10 above.
      • The 100-ms end-to-end p99 is infeasible under the stated workload, and that is the
        honest answer. A request here takes ~7.5 s of decode alone (300 output tokens × ~25 ms/token,
        Chapter 8), so no scheduler-overhead percentage can bring end-to-end p99 under 100 ms —
Fleet-Level Optimization                                                                      302


      model execution already exceeds the budget by two orders of magnitude. What the scheduler
      can bound is the overhead it adds on top of model execution: a round-robin dispatcher adds
      ~0.5 ms per request and a <=5% scheduler-added p99 is comfortably achievable.
    • Planning-bound caveat (sizing tail). §3’s caveat governs: upper-order planning bounds, not

The AI Factory: Turning Inference Into an
Industrial Process




The Architect’s Question

After this chapter we should be able to treat AI delivery as an industrial process rather than a one-off
project: a repeatable factory with automated pipelines for data, evaluation, promotion, and rollback.
We will separate the three layers of the factory (the model lifecycle, the serving pipeline, and the
operations loop), then build the economics of promotion gating and retraining cadence for the
canonical workload. After this chapter, “we ship a better model” is a gated, measurable, reversible
event — not a risky redeploy.


21.1. Concept

The AI Factory is the discipline of making model delivery routine. We use the term as a generic
architectural concept — the idea that model delivery can be run as an industrial, gate-driven
process — not as any one vendor’s marketing vocabulary. It rests on three pillars:

   1. Data pipeline — the automated intake, cleaning, versioning, and labelling of the data that
      trains or evaluates the model. For a RAG system this includes the retrieval corpus, its freshness,
      and its quality gates. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]

   2. Evaluation & promotion gate — a systematic process that scores a candidate model or
      configuration against defined metrics (quality, latency, cost) on a held-out benchmark before
      it can replace the incumbent in production. This is where Ch14’s deployment benchmarking
      becomes a recurring gate rather than a one-time event.



                                                  304
305                                              The AI Factory: Turning Inference Into an Industrial Process


      3. Serve + observe + rollback — the serving layer (Ch11) plus a feedback loop that mea­
        sures real traffic, detects drift or regression, and can roll the production model back safely.
        [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]

      The factory converts the architect’s recurring question from “should we adopt this model?” (a
one-off decision) into “does this candidate pass the automated gate?” (a routine, repeatable decision
with the same rigor every time).


21.2. Mental Model

      The AI Factory is best read as a release pipeline with a quality gate placed before every
promotion, mirroring how software CI/CD gated deployments decades ago. Three mental moves:
   • Models are artifacts like code. They get versioned, tested, reviewed, and promoted through
        environments (staging → canary → production) with automated checks at each step — not
        dropped into prod on a hunch.
      • The gate is the memory of the factory. The evaluation suite and its thresholds encode
        everything we’ve learned about what “good enough” means (Ch4 capability, Ch14 deployment).
        If the gate is weak, the factory has no standards.
      • Everything is reversible. A promotion that regresses metrics must be rollback-able in minutes.
        The factory’s value is not eliminating errors but making them cheap and safe.

      The factory’s shape is a pipeline with decisions: data in → train/fine-tune → evaluate →
push to canary → observe → promote or rollback → serve. Each arrow is a decision point, and each
decision point is where an architect has influence.


21.3. Worked Example

      The example below works the economics of promotion gating on the canonical 70B RAG workload.
21.3.1. The Economics of Promotion Gating for the Canonical Workload

We show the factory’s value by comparing ungated and gated adoption of a candidate model on the
canonical 70B RAG workload (~10 rps average, 9.2K-in/ 300-out). [canonical scenario] (Ch 4, Table 4-2)
      Setup. Suppose a new model candidate claims better retrieval-QA quality but no one has measured
its serving behavior. Two adoption paths:

      • Ungated: deploy the candidate to all production traffic immediately. If it regresses (say p95
        TTFT degrades because of a slower tokenizer, or quality drops on a subset), the service suffers
        until rollback.
      • Gated: run the candidate on a 5% canary for N hours, measure TTFT/goodput/quality against
        the incumbent, promote only if it beats every threshold.
The AI Factory: Turning Inference Into an Industrial Process                                           306


    Cost of a bad ungated release. The canonical service does ~288,000 requests/workday (10

Suppose a regression raises p95 TTFT from 1.9 s to 2.8 s (breaching the 2 s SLO) for 6 hours before
discovery and rollback. That is 6/8 ×288,000 ≈ 216,000 requests served at a broken SLO. At the Ch16
canonical self-hosted rate of ~$24.97/1K requests (active business-hours volume, Ch 4), the direct
cost is 216,000 × 24.97066185897436 ÷ 1,000 ≈ $5,394, and it is ≈ $3,032 on the Ch16 cloud-scaled
~$14.04/1K basis (216,000 × 14.038461538461538 ÷ 1,000 = 3,032.31) — modest relative to the business
cost, but the dominant term is users experiencing a 47% latency regression, trust erosion, and the fire
drill. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] (worked example, not reference)
    Cost of a good gated release. A canary at 5% traffic for 2 hours serves 5% × 288,000 ×2/8 ≈
3,600 requests through the candidate while it is measured against a full evaluation suite. If it passes,
promotion is low-risk; if it fails, no users beyond canary were exposed. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
    Reading the result. Gating turns a risky 216K-request exposure (ungated) into a controlled
~3.6K-request canary — a ~60× reduction in blast radius for the cost of a 2-hour evaluation. The
factory makes this routine. [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]

21.4. Measurement

    The configuration qualification in Chapter 18 supplies the candidate identity for these gates:
model, precision, backend and relevant runtime versions. A changed execution path needs new
evidence; a previous model-level approval does not establish that the new configuration is safe to
promote.
    The factory is only as trustworthy as its gates. We measure four things continuously:
   1. Gate pass rate / false-promotion rate — how often a gated change later regresses in
       production; a rising value means the evaluation suite is losing fidelity.
307                                              The AI Factory: Turning Inference Into an Industrial Process


      2. Canary-to-production time and rollback time — the speed of promotion and escape; both
        should be minutes, not days.
      3. Model freshness / data staleness — time since the retrieval corpus or model was last validated;
        drift detection feeds the retraining decision.
      4. MTTR for a bad release — mean time to detect + rollback; the factory’s core reliability
        number.


21.5. Common Mistakes
      • No gate, or a decorative gate. An evaluation that always passes is worse than none because
        it grants false confidence.
      • Promoting on quality only. Quality passing but serving (Ch14) regressing still breaks the
        service; the gate must include deployment metrics.
      • Assuming retraining cadence is “as often as possible.” More frequent retraining is not
        free — it consumes compute, risk, and evaluation effort; the right cadence balances drift against
        churn (see Ch7-8 for training economics).
      • Skipping rollback rehearsal. A rollback that has never been exercised will fail precisely
        when it is needed.
      • Treating the factory as a build-once artifact. It is a living process that must absorb new
        models, new metrics, and new data sources continuously.


21.6. Architecture Consequence

      The AI Factory is the operational backbone that makes the book’s whole loop durable. Every
architectural decision recomputes through it: model selection (Ch3/5) feeds the evaluation gate,
serving choices (Ch11) determine canary mechanics, benchmarking (Ch14) becomes the recurring
gate, TCO (Ch16) sets how much gating overhead is affordable, and fleet operations (Ch17-20) provide
the rollout/rollback surfaces. Without the factory, each chapter’s decision is a one-off; with it, they
compound into a system that gets better and safer every cycle.
21.7. What We Still Don’t Know
      • The true cost of model churn (retraining + reeval + redeploy) per productivity gain is (a
        hypothesis) and workload-specific; there is no universal cadence.
      • How well evaluation suites generalize across distribution shifts in real traffic is (to be
        verified); a suite tuned on last quarter’s data may misjudge this quarter’s model.
      • The right canary size for a given risk posture is to be verified per service; 5% worked here
        but high-risk systems may need smaller, staged canaries.

21.8. End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: The Vendor’s ‘Better Bench’: Canary and Roll­
      back

A vendor pitches the architect a newer, cheaper model: “just swap it in — it scores better on the
bench.” A year ago the architect might have, and watched p95 TTFT silently drift past the SLO for a
week. Now the AI Factory is in place. The architect drops the candidate into the pipeline: the data
pipeline versions it, the evaluation gate scores it against quality AND the deployment benchmark
(TTFT/goodput/cost) on the canonical workload, and a 5% canary serves it for two hours. The gate
flags a quality regression on the legal-document subset the benchmark suite specifically covers —
a subset the vendor’s “better bench” never measured. The candidate is rejected automatically, the
incumbent stays, and the legal subset keeps working. No fire drill, no user-visible regression, no
manual heroics — the factory made the wrong vendor claim cost nothing to the business, which is
precisely what industrializing the delivery loop is for.

21.9. Transition to Part VI

Parts I–V traced one engagement: token accounting defines workload demand; model architecture
sets compute and memory costs; parallelism adds communication; serving schedules shared resources;
fleet design determines capacity and cost; the AI Factory governs changes. These mechanisms connect
request-level behavior to operational decisions.
      Part VI applies these mechanisms to decisions under uncertainty rather than introducing another
subsystem. It makes the decision process explicit: state workload assumptions, compare alternatives
against resource bounds, and identify the measurements needed to resolve uncertainty. The next
chapters provide a worksheet for recording the decision, its assumptions, and its validation criteria.

How to Think Like an AI Solution Architect




The Architect’s Question

Before any model is selected, any GPU is counted, any latency budget is allocated, the architect must
answer one question: what is the actual token-scale cost of delivering the stakeholder’s request? This
chapter exists to make that question automatic. We do not reach for vendor marketing numbers or
rule-of-thumb heuristics. Instead we trace a vague stakeholder ask — “we need a Q&A system over
our internal documents” — through a canonical loop that turns it into concrete architectural bounds.
The output is a set of derived quantities (token throughput, KV cache memory, prefill FLOPs, decode
bandwidth) that are verifiable, derived from first principles, and grounded in the canonical ~2,000
user, ~10 rps / ~40 rps peak, RAG Q&A, 70B dense FP16 scenario that every other chapter in this
handbook cites. The reasoning is traced by the architect and the system investigating together.


22.1. Concept

The unit we price, size, and optimize is the token. We established what a token is in Chapter 1
— not a word, character, or byte, but whatever the model’s tokenizer carves text into via learned
byte-pair merging; that token counts are never proportional to character counts; and that “one token
≈ 4 characters” is a rough rule for general-English prose, to be confirmed against the actual tokenizer
before pricing anything (Ch. 1 §1). We do not restate that here; this chapter builds on it.
   What Chapter 22 adds is not a re-derivation of the token but a re-framing of it as the input to
a decision loop. The architect treats a token as a metered unit of thought — the way a kilowatt-hour
meters electricity — not because one token is meaningful by itself, but because every downstream
cost and capacity number is denominated in it. The durable mental model, unchanged from Chapter



                                                 311
How to Think Like an AI Solution Architect                                                           312


1’s: tokens are the interface between a human’s request and a machine’s arithmetic, and anything we
are asked to size or price reduces to “how many tokens, in what context, with what precision.” The loop
below turns that unit into concrete bounds.



22.2. Mental Model

    The prefill/decode split is the figure the rest of the book builds on, and it was established in Ch 2
§2 (in the canonical operating point, long-prompt prefill is compute-bound — a large burst of FLOPs
once per request — while low-batch decode is bandwidth-bound — a small amount of work repeated
for every output token). Ch 22 does not re-derive that distinction; it uses it. What this chapter adds
is the reasoning loop: the architect does not have to hold every quantity in their head, because the
loop turns a vague ask into a small, ordered set of token-scale bounds that the downstream chapters
price against. The mental model, distilled, is that the loop is the discipline — derive the unit, then
the traffic, then the split, in that order, so every later number is anchored rather than guessed.
22.3. Worked Example — The Canonical Loop

    We now demonstrate the canonical loop: turning a vague stakeholder ask into concrete bounds.
The stakeholder says: “We need a Q&A system over our internal documents. About 2,000 employees will
use it, they’ll ask questions throughout the day, and the answers should be accurate and fast.” From this
single sentence we will derive a full set of token-scale quantities that every downstream chapter will
price against.
    Step 1 — Identify the unit. The ask mentions “Q&A over internal documents.” We do not assume
“one question = one page” or “one question = 500 words.” We go to the model’s tokenizer and ask: how
many tokens does a typical prompt contain? We extract representative prompts from the documented
corpus, run them through the tokenizer, and measure. In the canonical scenario, the prompt consists
of ~1,200 tokens of query text plus ~8,000 tokens of retrieved RAG context, yielding ~9,200 input
tokens. The answer generated is ~300 tokens. These are the book’s [canonical scenario] inputs
(Ch 4, Table 4-2) — an author-defined illustrative workload, not a vendor-reported [1P] figure, so
they are labeled [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION], not [1P].
    Step 2 — Establish the traffic profile. The ask says “about 2,000 employees” and “throughout
the day.” We instrument or survey to find the per-user rate. The canonical scenario settles on ~10
requests/s average, with peaks of ~40 rps. These are derived quantities [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED],
not stipulated.
    Step 3 — Compute the token throughput. With I = 9,200 input tokens and O = 300 output
tokens per request, and λ = 10 req/s average:


                       input tokens/s = I · λ = 9,200 × 10 = 92,000 tokens/s

[DERIVED]
      Step 4 — Derive architecture-relevant quantities. The 30× input/output ratio is one of the
most important derived quantities here. It means this workload is input-heavy: the token budget is
dominated by prefill (processing the 9.2K prompt), not decode (generating the 300 answer tokens).
Combined with the canonical model, precision, serving, and SLO assumptions, this 30× ratio pushes
the design toward high prefill compute and KV-capacity pressure. The ratio alone does not settle
which resource dominates — that also depends on model architecture, attention/KV-head count,
precision, batching, hardware, kernel efficiency, prefix caching, and output-generation speed — but
under the canonical assumptions the prefill-compute and KV-capacity terms are where the pressure
lands, not decode bandwidth. Every downstream chapter (memory, compute, cost) will price against
these derived numbers.
      Step 5 — Record in Table 22-1. The full table of derived quantities appears below.
      This loop — stakeholder ask → measured token counts → traffic profile → token throughput →
architecture-relevant derived quantities — is the canonical thought process an AI solution architect
runs, every time, before a single architecture decision is made. It is how we move from “we need a
Q&A system” to “at the canonical operating point our prefill will be compute-bound at ~1.29 PFLOP
per request, and our decode will be bandwidth-bound at a required weight-read rate of ~5.6 TB/s
over each ~25 ms token interval.” The loop is the chapter’s central contribution; the quantities that
issue from it are the evidence [1P]/[2°]/(to be verified) that every following chapter trades on.
