    Three efficiency levers every 2026 frontier family pulled:

   1. Hybrid attention as the new KV lever — an efficiency lever, not (by itself) a capability
      lever. Every frontier model re-engineered attention to shrink long-context cost at the mecha­
      nism level — compressed/sparse hybrids (DeepSeek CSA+HCA), delta+sparse (Qwen Gated
      DeltaNet + QSA), delta/residual (Kimi KDA + AttnRes), sparse+linear (GLM). KV cache is no
      longer a fixed per-token constant we only quantize; it is a design surface the model vendor
      already optimized. The intended benefit is to preserve useful model capability while reducing
      long-context inference cost and/or extending practical context length — indispensable, but it
      does not by itself make the model smarter. Capability gains come from the post-training/rea­
      soning stack in A.8.
   2. MoE sparsity went extreme — the capacity-per-FLOP lever. Active-parameter fractions
      fell to single digits (Kimi 104B of 2.8T; Qwen 6B of 125B). In our reading, one could argue
      MoE is a larger architectural innovation than attention: it lets a lab grow knowledge/capacity
      without proportionally growing FLOPs per token. That is why the 2026 open landscape is
      heavily MoE-oriented. Expert parallelism and fused cross-expert communication moved from
      a footnote to a serving-critical capability.
   3. Efficiency is a first-class result, not an afterthought. Training-stable optimizers (Muon)
      and post-training RL (GRPO, async RL) are now reported as core architecture, not tooling.

    These three form the cost/context ledger of the frontier. The capability ledger — reasoning, post-
training, test-time compute, agent harness — is where most of the qualitative improvement actually
lives (A.8). Distinguishing efficiency levers from capability levers is the architect’s first move when
reading any new model card.
365                         Appendix A — 2026 Frontier Architecture Signals: Four Open-Weight Model Families


A.2. How to read this appendix: Observed, Interpretation, Hypothesis

This appendix surveys vendor-reported material, so we are careful to separate three layers of
statement that are easy to blur — especially in a fast-moving field full of first/“most-efficient”/3T-
class claims:

      • Observed — what the vendor’s technical report or model card actually states (e.g., “DeepSeek-
        V4 reports a reduced KV footprint”). This is [1P] fact about the claim, not the same as the third
         layer.
      • Interpretation — our read of what architectural mechanism the report demonstrates (e.g.,
       “the KV reduction suggests the model changes how attention stores state”). This is analysis,
         ours, and could be wrong.
      • Hypothesis — a prediction about consequence we draw for serving architecture (e.g., “we
         expect long-context serving to become more memory-comfortable at equal context”). This is a
         testable (a hypothesis), not a fact.

      When we write “a number of frontier models converge” or “one could argue MoE is a larger
architectural innovation,” read those as Interpretation / Hypothesis — defensible reads of the
frontier signal, not independent measurements. Vendor numbers stay tagged [1P] and flagged verify-
on-own-hardware; our reads sit one register lower and should be read with the same skepticism we
ask of any vendor claim. The practical rule: if it’s a percentage from a report, it’s Observed [1P]; if it’s
a claim about what the industry trend means, it’s ours — treat it as analysis, tune it against the reader’s
real workload.
      Mapping onto the book’s evidence taxonomy. These three reader-friendly layers are an
on-ramp to, not a replacement for, the three-axis taxonomy used throughout the book (provenance ×
epistemic status × measurement status): Axis 1 provenance [1P]/[2°]/[LAB]/[ILLUSTRATIVE] × Axis
2 status [FACT]/[DERIVED]/[ASSUMPTION]/[HYPOTHESIS]/[UNRESOLVED], with Axis 3 riding
along.

      • Observed ↔ [1P] · [FACT] — the vendor’s stated claim, a fact about the claim.
      • Interpretation ↔ [DERIVED] — the book’s own analysis, a derivation from the evidence.
        (Where the book’s taxonomy would label it [ILLUSTRATIVE], note that; the appendix uses
       “interpretation” only as plain prose for a derived read, never a separate sanctioned status.)
      • Hypothesis ↔ [HYPOTHESIS] — a testable prediction, exactly the taxonomy’s
         [HYPOTHESIS].
      • Measurement status ↔ Axis 3 — ANALYTICAL / ILLUSTRATIVE / MODELED / MEASURED
        (or [UNMEASURED] where the stage is not yet determined): how far the number has climbed
         the measurement-status hierarchy, defined in the Sources, Method, and Reproducibility chapter.

      The appendix’s labels are the human-friendly framing; the three-axis labels are the precise
book-wide convention. They should never conflict.
Appendix A — 2026 Frontier Architecture Signals: Four Open-Weight Model Families                          366


    This is a dated field guide, not an evergreen ranking. The four-family comparison is a
snapshot as of the 2026-08-30 cutoff (with separately dated September and October observations
outside the comparison). A later edition re-verifies the vendor reports and may change the families,
numbers, or the comparison; the ranking here is not a permanent verdict. Reproduction status is
recorded per family in the First-hand Sources list (A.10): each entry carries its source URL/identifier,
the version and release date where known, and the verification status (whether the claim is vendor-
reported [1P] pending independent check, or independently verified). Where a number has not been
independently validated, it is flagged — do not treat a model-card figure as an audited measurement.
The vendor-fact / author-interpretation / hypothesis layers above, plus the per-family reproduction
status, are the four columns a reader needs; a sources.csv manifest (source URL, accessed date,
model variant, reported baseline, verification status) accompanies the repository’s render/ material
for the fast-changing Appendix A claims.


A.3. DeepSeek-V4 — Making Long Context Cheap by Re-Architecting Attention

Decisive fact [1P] — arXiv 2606.19348; HF deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro: V4-Pro is 1.6 T total
/ 49 B activated, V4-Flash 284 B / 13 B activated, both 1M-token context, MIT-licensed. Its hybrid
attention combines Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) and Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA).
At 1M context, DeepSeek reports ~27% (Pro) / ~10% (Flash) of V3.2’s single-token inference
FLOPs and ~10% / ~7% of its KV cache.
    What this means for the architect (ties to Ch7 Memory, Ch8 Compute). In our reading of
the vendor reports, this is a strong confirmation that KV-per-token is a moving target. Chapter 7’s
arithmetic (per-token × context) is a floor for a given architecture; DeepSeek shows the constant factor
itself can be cut ~10× without changing the model’s parameter count. The architectural decision
shifts from “how much KV memory does this context need?” to “which KV scheme does this model
use, and is its vendor-published saving reproducible on my serving stack?”


A.4. Kimi K3 — Vendor-Reported First Open 3T-Class Model, and the MoE-Sparsity
     Extreme

Decisive fact [1P] — arXiv 2607.24653; HF moonshotai/Kimi-K3: 2.8 T total / 104 B activated,
native vision, 1M context. Built on Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) + Attention Residuals (AttnRes),
with Stable LatentMoE activating just 16 of 896 routed experts per token. Claims ~2.5× scaling
efficiency over Kimi K2. Weights are QAT-trained from SFT onward with MXFP4 weights / MXFP8
activations. Full weights are released — per the vendor, the first open 3T-class model.
    What this means for the architect (ties to Ch3 Model, Ch10 Parallelism). A model whose
total size is 2.8 T but whose activated footprint is 104 B is a clear illustration of Ch3’s total-vs-activated
distinction and Ch10’s expert-parallelism doctrine. Serving Kimi K3 requires accommodating the 2.8
T total parameter fabric across the serving system (the full expert set must reside somewhere unless
367                      Appendix A — 2026 Frontier Architecture Signals: Four Open-Weight Model Families


an explicit offload/load-on-demand architecture is used) while only ~104 B parameters participate in
the computation of a given token. The architectural problem is therefore simultaneously one of total
weight residency/distribution and active-weight communication/computation — sharding
and scheduling the expert fabric, plus the KV for our context. The decision surface is expert-parallel
communication and fused cross-expert kernels, not raw capacity.


A.5. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next — A Vendor-Framed Qwen4 Architecture Preview, Pri­
     oritizing Cost-Performance

Decisive fact [1P] — HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next; GitHub QwenLM/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:
125 B total / 6 B activated, plus a separate 51 B of N-gram embedding parameters (offloadable to
host memory). Native 262 K context (YaRN to 1M). Hybrid attention: Gated DeltaNet (GDN) +
Qwen Sparse Attention (QSA), where QSA operates at the micro-block level; Gated Residual
widens the residual stream; 512 MoE experts (10 routed + 1 shared per token); Muon + AdamW.
Reported training cost ~1/9 of Qwen3.7-Plus.
      What this means for the architect (ties to Ch3, Ch5 Model Selection, Ch16 TCO). Qwen’s
technical report, 26 August 2026, describes the n-gram tables as held off the accelerator and prefetched
from host memory. This is a vendor-reported mechanism, not only an architectural inference. Its effect
on a particular deployment still depends on placement, bandwidth, overlap and engine support; the
report does not establish a general serving-performance result for every backend. The 125B backbone,
separate 51B n-gram tables and separately listed MTP module remain distinct parts of the residency
inventory. Model selection therefore weighs heterogeneous memory and the supported transfer path
alongside total and active parameters. [1P][FACT] mechanism; deployment consequence [DERIVED].


A.6. GLM-5.3-Flash — Vendor-Reported First Natively Multimodal GLM,
     Efficiency-Branded

Decisive fact [1P] — HF zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash; Z.ai release article, 2026-08-26: 320 B total / 18
B activated, 1M native context, 131 K output. Per the vendor, the first natively multimodal model in
the GLM-5 series (text/image/video). It combines sparse+linear attention (first in the series per the
vendor), Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), W8A8 quantization with mixed-cache
(INT8/FP8/BF16), and Encode-Prefill-Decode serving. The release article compares it with GLM-5.3
using attention compute per head per layer and average BF16 KV cache per layer. On those
normalized measures, it reports 3.0× less attention compute and a 4.4× smaller KV cache. These are
not whole-model FLOP or total-cache ratios, and they do not establish an end-to-end speedup. The
February GLM-5 parent report, arXiv:2602.15763, is not the source of these Flash-specific ratios. MIT
weights. Z.ai positions it as approaching Claude Opus 4.8 on coding/agentic at ~1/10 the price.
      What this means for the architect (ties to Ch7 Memory, Ch8 Compute, Ch19 Agentic).
GLM’s coupling of hybrid attention with native multimodality shows the model border is remaking:
Appendix A — 2026 Frontier Architecture Signals: Four Open-Weight Model Families                  368


“LLM” and “vision/audio model” are converging in a single weight set, which changes workload
characterization (Ch4) — a multimodal prompt has a different token/KV profile than text-only. And
mHC + attention-mixing being reported as scaling-efficiency results reinforces Ch8’s point that
compute arithmetic is architecture-specific, not universal.
    Post-snapshot observation (recorded 2026-09-27; outside the 2026-08-30 compile-date
envelope). Beyond the four families above, Ornith-1.5-397B (released 2026-08-19 by DeepReinforce /
ornith-ai) ships as another natively multimodal frontier model: 397 B MoE, ~262 K context, MIT
weights, image-input via the inherited Qwen3.5 vision tower. We verified the image-input path
end-to-end with a live API call carrying a base64-encoded PNG as image_url content: the model’s
own reasoning trace referenced the rendered pixels (a white-square test and a red/blue half-image test
both answered correctly). This is a [LAB] author observation — a single first-person capability
probe: one API call, one ad-hoc image fixture, which establishes only that one function
path (image input) is reachable. It is not a benchmark, not comparable across models,
and not reproducible without re-running the call: the exact model/API ID, sampling settings,
prompt/image fixtures, and (credential-redacted) API response are not published as a reproducibility
capsule, and the probe says nothing about benchmark quality, throughput, or cost. It must not be
read as evidence for any comparative claim about Ornith-1.5-397B relative to the four families (which
it is not a part of), nor as a measurement of capability or quality. It is recorded as a single-path
capability hint and cited as an observational sidebar, not promoted into the four-family comparative
figures or the First-hand Sources list above, both of which retain the 2026-08-30 compile-date stamp.
Treat as a hint that the natively multimodal frontier continues to widen between snapshots — exactly
the trajectory the four-family narrative above predicts.



A.7. What This Means for the Handbook’s Canonical Arithmetic

      bound: ~1.31 MB/token, exactly 50% of BF16, which is what the fleet-sizing chapters use.

      3 — a latency metric, not a memory ratio; there is no vendor-measured FP8 memory footprint,
      and any allocator block/metadata overhead is not vendor-measured. The 8-bit KV constants
      are [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED].) Hybrid-attention models cut it 4–10× at the mechanism, so
      “context fits on N GPUs” must be re-derived per model, not looked up once. [1P]
    • The roofline (Ch8) still holds; what changed is where a frontier model’s prefill/decode ride it.

A.8. Where 2026 Capability Actually Comes From (beyond Architecture)

A recurring error — easy to fall into after reading four new model cards — is to attribute frontier
gains to the attention mechanism splashed across the front page. The industry is converging not just
on architectures (MoE + efficient attention + very long context) but on a multi-layered recipe in which
architecture is one ingredient, and arguably not the dominant one. A qualitative decomposition of
the recipe:


   Lever                                              Primary effect

   Post-training / RL / reasoning                     Capability (a major source in current frontier
                                                      systems)
   Test-time compute                                  Capability on hard tasks (more compute on
                                                      hard problems)
   Training data + optimization                       General capability
   MoE / parameter scaling                            Capacity per FLOP
   Attention innovation                               Context + efficiency (makes the above
                                                      affordable)
   Inference / runtime optimization                   Cost + latency
   Agent harness / tool use                           Real-world task completion
   Multimodal architecture                            New modalities


    A frequently underestimated layer is the one the model card almost never shows: post-
training. Two models with broadly similar architectures and pre-training can end up materially
different when one went through mediocre post-training and the other excellent. The recipe — the
same families every lab now runs — is what carries much of the qualitative gap:
371                        Appendix A — 2026 Frontier Architecture Signals: Four Open-Weight Model Families


      • RLVR / reinforcement learning for reasoning
      • synthetic reasoning data
      • verifier-based training
      • preference optimization
      • curriculum learning
      • tool-use training and agent trajectories
      • coding-specific trajectories
      • multimodal reasoning
      • long-horizon interaction training

      This is why architecture alone never tells an architect how good a frontier model is, and why the
decision can no longer stop at “which model” — the marginal capability may live in the post-training
and the runtime that wraps it.
      From a single model to a whole system. The earlier stages (Transformer, Efficient, MoE) are
efficiency-led — they make inference affordable and raise capacity-per-FLOP. The later stages (Rea­
soning, Test-Time Compute, Tool-Using, Agent, Agent System, Agent Fleet) are capability-led — they
raise effective intelligence. [DERIVED]
      This chain is the spine of this handbook — from a single model’s tokens (Ch1–9) to parallelism
(Ch10), serving (Ch11–16), and finally the fleet of specialized models and agents (Ch17–26). It also
explains why two models with broadly similar base architectures can have very different practical
intelligence (post-training/reasoning), and why an agent runtime can lift real-world performance
without changing model weights at all: model intelligence ≠ system intelligence anymore.


A.9. The Frontier Question: Where Should Intelligence Live?

The most useful lens for an AI Solution Architect in 2026 is not “which attention mechanism does
the model card list?” but where the intelligence and the compute budget should be placed:
      The placement ladder. Every host layer that can carry intelligence is a place the architect may
choose to push capability or cost; this book gives the arithmetic and decision framework for each
(Ch3/7/8 weights & attention, Ch10 MoE routing, Ch19/21 post-training, Ch8/20 test-time, Ch19/24
tools, Ch17–20 runtime, Ch18/20 fleet). [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
      Every host layer maps to chapters in this book:

      • Inside weights (dense capacity) — Ch3 Model, Ch8 Compute
      • Inside attention (context / efficiency) — Ch7 Memory, Ch8 Compute
      • Inside MoE routing (capacity per FLOP) — Ch10 Parallelism
      • Inside post-training (reasoning, RL, verification) — Ch19 Agentic, Ch21 AI Factory
      • Inside test-time search (adaptive inference, more compute on hard tasks) — Ch8 Compute,
        Ch20 Fleet-Level Optimization
      • Inside tools (compute allocated via a harness) — Ch19 Agentic, Ch24 Red/Green Team

Post-snapshot technology notes — 2026-10-28

Architecture dimensions and executed depth — 2026-10-28

This update is separate from the four-family comparison compiled through 30 August 2026. A retrieval
date is not a release date. Some examples below were available before that comparison; others are later
releases or later paper revisions. The purpose is to examine mechanisms that change a deployment
decision, not to extend a model ranking.


Three independent dimensions

A model description now needs at least three independent dimensions: parameter allocation, history-
state representation, and execution depth. Dense feed-forward layers can coexist with recurrent
token mixing. Sparse experts can coexist with global attention. Shared weights can execute repeatedly
within one token prediction. None of these properties determines the others.
    Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B is a useful counterexample to the idea that a dense model must use conven­
tional full attention throughout. Its card describes dense feed-forward layers and native image/video
understanding. Its language configuration contains 48 Gated DeltaNet layers and 16 full-attention
layers. DeltaNet updates a recurrent history state; the full-attention layers retain a separate history-
dependent KV component. Dense parameter allocation therefore does not imply a full-MHA cache
formula.1
    A different form of recurrence repeats a shared core over the current representation. Huginn and
Ouro provide public research examples. Their shared weights reduce the unique parameter inventory
    1
      Qwen, Qwen3.8-27B model card, “Model Overview,” “Benchmark Results,” and long-context guidance:

Phase and storage tier matter

deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash changes more than one constant. Its vendor report describes
a Causal Encoder-Decoder with 552B backbone parameters and a separate 196B Engram component.
It reports 8B activated parameters per token during prefill and 16B during decode. A single active-
parameter figure would obscure this phase difference. These counts describe the vendor’s computation
paths; they do not establish an elapsed-time ratio.4
    The report also separates memory objects. Cross-layer reuse and FP4 main-KV storage produce a
reported global HBM KV footprint of 890 bytes per token. This is not total request memory. Bounded
sliding-window state, weights, workspaces, and allocation overhead remain separate. The reported
persistent-cache reduction to approximately one-eighth of DeepSeek-V4-Flash concerns host or SSD
storage under SWA Bounded Replay. It is not the same metric as global HBM KV.
    The transferable rule is to account for each independently stored state, its update rule, and
its location. Sparse attention that reads selected history entries need not store only those entries.
Cross-layer consumers can share one stored object. A local window can bound live state while prefix
restoration still incurs storage or recomputation. Capacity across several accelerators also does not
establish that each rank fits its assigned weights and state.



A stopping rule is not yet a runtime saving

Huginn’s model card requires a recurrence-aware cache so that later core passes do not overwrite
earlier KV entries. It also labels its per-token adaptive-compute facility a zero-shot proof of concept.
Its stopping criteria include changes in latent state, output distributions, and prediction stability.5
    Ouro’s revised paper studies learned exit decisions and cache sharing. It reports that prefill needs
distinct iteration caches in the evaluated setting, while selected decode-only sharing strategies can
reduce the cache component. These are phase-specific experiments, not a universal reduction in
whole-request memory.6
    The released runtime path also matters. In the Ouro implementation retrieved for this update,
the core loop computes all configured iterations before the language-model wrapper selects an exit
representation. That path does not demonstrate skipped core computation merely because an earlier
representation is selected. The model card separately states that its vLLM path does not support

adaptive exit. A paper’s stopping policy, a reference implementation, and an optimized serving engine
are different evidence objects.7,8
      A deployment evaluation would therefore record actual core executions, state bytes, and per-
stage time alongside quality. Variable-depth scheduling could change batch efficiency and latency
tails. That consequence remains a testable hypothesis until measured on the intended engine and
workload.
      Figure A.5 separates the parameter object from its invocations and the invocations from their
cached histories. The lower lanes make the stopping boundary explicit. Only the upper lane avoids
the final pass. The exit index in the drawing is illustrative; it does not prescribe a quality-preserving
stopping rule for either research model.
      With separate caches, an iteration index is part of the state identity. Reusing the same weight
pointer does not make different hidden representations interchangeable. A cache-sharing policy
changes that assumption and needs its own phase-specific evidence. An adaptive stopping rule also
needs an accuracy target: stable logits or a small latent-state change is a stopping signal, not proof
of correct reasoning. These distinctions keep a research mechanism from being promoted into a
production efficiency claim without the intervening engine and workload evidence.9,10

Training loops are not inference loops

Ornith-1.5 provides a useful boundary case. Its report describes joint improvement of training tasks,
scaffolds, and solution rollouts. The released family builds on existing architectures with additional
training. This is evidence about the training and evaluation system, not proof of shared-depth
recurrence or online weight updates during a user request.11
      The same distinction applies within a vendor’s product family. Z.ai describes GLM-5.3 as using
the GLM-5.2 base with post-training gains, while GLM-5.3-Flash starts from a newly trained base
and a redesigned hybrid architecture. The exact variant determines which explanation applies.12
      “Flash” does not identify a common architecture or a small resident model. The open-weight
examples combine different expert layouts, compressed or local attention, multimodal encoders,
and drafting mechanisms. For gemini-3.8-flash, the public documentation establishes a service

Quantization implementation observations — 2026-10-28

These observations concern pinned October implementations, not support at the August cutoff. No
backend performance was measured for this note.
      Current implementations illustrate why representation and execution are separate. At vLLM
commit 41dd82e6a7392ead33b1e8a7d175442511e488ca, NVFP4 has a CUTLASS low-bit path, a
Marlin W4A16 path and a higher-precision emulation path. Its MXFP4 Marlin code explicitly ignores
a requested activation-quantization configuration because that kernel is weight-only. These are
different execution experiments even when the stored weights use the same named representation.
They are code observations, not benchmarks or proof that a particular installed release selects the
native path. [1P][FACT] (NVFP4 CUTLASS; NVFP4 Marlin; MXFP4 Marlin.)
      The same separation appears in GGML/llama.cpp. At the pinned revision in the source ledger,
block_q4_K occupies 144 bytes for 256 values: 4.5 effective bits/value. Q4_K_M, however, selects a
mixture of tensor encodings and can promote selected tensors to Q6_K. IQ encodings have their
own grid, sign, lookup and scale layouts; their imatrix requirements are type-specific. The complete
model’s average precision therefore follows a tensor inventory, not one block’s byte rate. GGML’s
block_nvfp4 also has a specific scale layout; the name alone does not establish interoperability with
NVIDIA’s tensor-global-scale representation. [1P][DERIVED][ANALYTICAL] (block definitions;
tensor selection.)
      Post-training calibration and training-based recovery also describe different work. PTQ estimates
quantization parameters without a full model-training run; the particular algorithm can search scales
or compensate weight errors. QAT updates model parameters while accounting for quantization
effects. QAD additionally uses teacher targets to recover behavior. That recovery consumes training
compute and memory, and a favorable fake-quant evaluation still needs confirmation after export
through the real serving kernels. Calibration, recovery and inference therefore receive separate
resource ledgers and separate quality records. [1P][DERIVED] (Model Optimizer QAT/QAD example,
pinned revision.)
      An NVFP4 training recipe need not have the same storage arrangement as a one-dimensional
inference storage budget. Transformer Engine documents two-dimensional 16×16 weight scaling,
as well as gradient-specific stochastic rounding, transformations for weight-gradient computation
and high-precision treatment of sensitive layers. These are additional recipe choices, not properties
supplied by the four-bit value code. Training can also require multiple tensor orientations, higher-
precision state and temporary buffers. The unique scale information of a 2D block is therefore not a

Diffusion language generation — 2026-10-28

This observation is outside Appendix A’s frozen 2026-08-30 comparison. It does not update that
four-family table or treat a present-day source as proof of its historical contents.
    Public artifacts now support more than one diffusion-language deployment pattern. LLaDA
and Dream provide open checkpoints and generation code for masked/refinement-based language
generation. Their announcements, paper dates and later checkpoint revisions are separate provenance
events. LLaDA2.2 adds bounded block editing and block-level expert routing. DiffusionGemma is an
explicitly experimental open release with an encoded context cache and a separately refined canvas;
its uniform-state renoising does not require MASK. Mercury 3 is a vendor-documented closed API
release dated 2026-10-19. Its internal schedule, precision and hardware allocation have not been
independently established here. Gemini Diffusion’s official page describes an experimental demo.
These records establish different release and support boundaries, not a common production-readiness
level. [1P][FACT]14
    The inspected SGLang revision, a1966e1b5d8b750b494d7e53cca1d2464f960038, illustrates
why engine names are insufficient. Its Gemma4Renoise path disables radix caching and chunked
prefill, rejects quantized loading and pipeline/context parallelism, and accepts only specified attention
backends. Its recipe rejects grammar/logit-bias requests. Vendor low-precision performance claims

      Wan-Animate-2 also demonstrates why the attention boundary must follow the exact variant.
Its Base path separates reference and denoising branches and uses sparse reference attention. Its
Lite path instead applies causal chunk dependencies; the report illustrates eight-frame segments
of the driving stream. Tokens in a current noisy chunk attend to preceding clean context and to
one another. This is chunk-wise autoregression around iterative generation, not a single-token text
decode loop. Earlier chunk delivery can change the latency contract, but accumulated errors and
retained history still require a budget. The report does not establish a particular KV-cache layout
or an unlimited constant-memory stream. [1P][FACT] architecture; [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]
serving boundaries.26
      Versioned implementation evidence is also narrower than production validation. Diffusers v0.35.0
documents Wan2.2; v0.37.0 introduces LTX-2; v0.40.0 documents Wan-Animate-2; v0.42.0 contains
LTX-2.5 and HunyuanVideo-1.5 pipeline documentation. Their published release dates are 19 August
2025, 5 March 2026, 20 August 2026, and 23 October 2026 respectively. The last is outside the book
cutoff. The existence of a pipeline does not establish a validated queueing service, multi-tenant
isolation, every kernel backend, or a latency SLA. [1P][FACT]27
      Two evidence limits remain material. LTX-2’s report uses 14B+5B in its abstract and 13B+3B in
its conclusion; this note does not choose an exact total from that conflict. LTX-2.5’s official release
notes date it to 11 August 2026, but raw gated configuration requests were not accessible in this
investigation. Its official 22B label is not a tensor-count audit. The license text is accessible and must
be considered separately. [1P][FACT]28,29

Apache-2.0, while LTX-2.5 and HunyuanVideo-1.5 use community licenses with commercial or
territorial conditions. Input-image, audio, likeness, music, and output-use permissions are separate
questions. Provenance records can retain checkpoint revision, recipe, seed, source-asset rights,
moderation decisions, and output hashes. Such records support investigation; they do not establish

Glossary of Acronyms and Common Terms



Model fundamentals

   • tokenization / tokenizer — splitting text into the model’s vocabulary of integer IDs; a token
     is whatever the model’s tokenizer decided to carve the text into (learned BPE-style merges),
     so token counts are tokenizer-dependent — run the model’s own tokenizer on representative
     traffic rather than a characters-per-token rule of thumb (Ch 1).
   • embedding — the lookup that maps each discrete token ID to the dense vector the model
     actually operates on; the pipeline is text → tokenizer → IDs → embedding → attention → KV
     cache (Ch 1).
   • attention — the mechanism that compares each token’s query (Q) against every prior key (K)
     and blends the values (V) by those scores; a processed token’s K/V never change, which is why
     they are cached (the KV cache) rather than recomputed each step (Ch 2).
   • logits — the model’s raw, unnormalized per-vocabulary scores at a generation step; the sampler
     turns them into the next token (Ch 2).


Inference and serving

   • TTFT — time to first token: latency from request to the first output token (prefill-dominated).
   • TPOT — time per output token: steady-state decode latency per token.
   • ITL — inter-token latency: the decode phase’s per-token lag; the book treats TPOT (steady-
     state) and ITL (per-token, incl. any measured inter-token gap) as the same canonical per-token
     metric and writes them “TPOT/ITL.” Where a measurement distinguishes them, treat ITL as
     the per-token value that includes any queueing/scheduling gap between emitted tokens, i.e. a
     tail-sensitive complement to bounded TPOT.
   • tail latency — latency at the high percentiles of the distribution (p95/p99), set by the slow­
     est requests rather than the typical one; the SLOs in this book are written against the tail
     (TTFT/TPOT p95/p99), so a median that meets its budget says nothing about the tail (Ch 20).
   • prefill — the pass that processes the prompt tokens and builds the KV cache/state. Often the



                                               387
Glossary                                                                                                388


      compute-bound pass in high-arithmetic-intensity regimes, but the compute- vs bandwidth-
      bound classification is a function of model, sequence length, batch, kernel, and device operating
      point (Ch 8, §8.2). Long-context and large-batch regimes can shift where it sits on the roofline.
    • decode — the autoregressive pass that generates the output one token at a time from the built
      state. Often memory-bandwidth-bound at low batch (small arithmetic intensity per emitted
      token), but not invariably so; large-batch and bandwidth-friendly regimes can move it. Refer to
      the operating-point discussion in Ch 8, §8.2 for the conditional, not unconditional, classification.
    • goodput — useful throughput: throughput that meets the latency/quality bar, discounting
      failures.
    • P/D disaggregation — running prefill (P) and decode (D) on separate pools/services.
    • continuous batching — scheduling new requests into a running decode batch so the GPU is
      kept busy token-by-token rather than waiting for an entire batch to finish; raises throughput
      at some latency cost.
    • chunked prefill — splitting a long prompt’s prefill into sub-blocks interleaved with decode
      work, so a long prompt does not monopolize the GPU and stall latency-sensitive decode.
    • FlashAttention — an I/O-aware attention kernel that tiles/fuses the Q·K·V computation
      through fast on-chip storage, reducing HBM traffic while preserving the same attention
      mathematics.
    • PagedAttention — a memory-management strategy for the KV cache that allocates key/value
      blocks in non-contiguous pages, reducing fragmentation and enabling near-full memory
      utilization.
    • speculative decoding — a draft model proposes a candidate sequence that the target model
      verifies in parallel, accepting matching tokens to raise effective throughput at the cost of draft
      + verification compute.
    • MFU — model FLOPs utilization: achieved FLOPs as a fraction of hardware peak.
    • RPS / QPS — requests per second / queries per second: a rate of incoming work, the primary
      input to a capacity model.
    • concurrency — the number of requests in flight (being served) at the same time; distinct from
      concurrent users, which is a population measure, and related to the arrival rate by Little’s law
      (in-flight ≈ λW ) (Ch 17, 20).

Memory and attention
    • KV cache — the keys/values of past tokens retained so attention need not recompute.
    • KV quantization — reducing the bytes per K/V element (e.g. FP16 → FP8), not the number of
      K/V entries; the canonical raw byte-halving is 2.62 → 1.31 MB/token (exactly 50%), a raw-array
      figure that is not a vendor-measured engine footprint, and the vLLM FP8-KV blog’s 54% is a
      decode-ITL latency slope, not a memory ratio (Ch 2, 6, 7; S6).
    • KV offloading — moving some KV state out of GPU HBM (to host DRAM/SSD), trading
      capacity against transfer latency; it does not shrink the state itself (that is quantization), and the
389                                                                                             Glossary


        cited 2–22× TTFT range is a particular warm-cache reuse benchmark, not a generic cold-cache
        improvement (Ch 2, 6; S7).
      • GQA — grouped-query attention; MQA — multi-query attention; MHA — multi-head attention;
        MLA — multi-head latent attention: a compressed per-token KV (K/V stored in a low-rank
        latent space), so KV per token still grows with context but at fewer bytes/token than full MHA
        (Ch 1, 8; App. A).
      • APC / RadixAttention / prefix cache — caching of shared prompt prefixes to avoid recom­
        putation.
      • prompt caching — the broader system/provider term; the book uses it to mean reusing the KV
        of a shared prompt prefix across requests, so it is not a separate mechanism from prefix caching
        above (Ch 2) — the provider-facing name for the same reuse, kept as its own entry because
        providers document and bill it as a feature.
      • cache hit / miss — a cache hit serves a request (or a shared prefix) from cached state without
        recomputing it; a miss must be computed (or re-prefilled); the hit ratio (hits ÷ requests) is the
        FACT that the prefix- and semantic-cache arithmetic starts from (Ch 15, 19, 26).
      • TTL — time-to-live: how long a cached entry stays valid before it must be refreshed or evicted;
        the semantic response cache uses a 5-min TTL, and its hit ratio is measured at TTL=T (Ch 26).
      • LRU — least-recently-used: the eviction policy that discards the least recently used cache entry
        first (Ch 26, Table 26-2).
      • HBM — high-bandwidth memory: the large, relatively slow-capacity memory attached to a
        GPU (distinct from fast on-chip SRAM).
      • arithmetic intensity — FLOPs moved per byte read from memory (FLOP/byte); the quantity
        that determines whether a kernel is compute-bound or memory-bound.
      • MoE — mixture of experts: a sparse model that routes each token to a subset of expert layers,
        cutting compute-per-token without reducing the parameter count or (necessarily) the KV
        cache.

Parallelism and flows
      • TP — tensor parallelism; PP — pipeline parallelism; DP — data parallelism; EP — expert
        parallelism; FSDP — fully sharded data parallelism (shards the model weights, gradients and
        optimizer state across ranks, reducing per-rank memory vs full-replica DP); CP — context
        parallelism (shards the sequence dimension across ranks when a single context is too long for
        one rank).
      • all-reduce — the collective that aggregates (e.g. sums) a tensor across ranks so every rank
        ends with the same reduced value; used to share gradients, activations, or states.
      • RQO — Reasoned Quality Optimization: the discipline of improving the quality of an architec­
        ture decision by forcing the articulation of alternatives and evidence, so the trade-off surface
        is explicit and the reasons are verifiable; ADRs are where it is recorded (Ch 25 §6).

System and economics
Glossary                                                                                           390


    • SLO — service-level objective (the latency/availability target committed to); SLA — service-level
      agreement.
    • TCO — total cost of ownership (capex + opex + staff + energy over a horizon).
    • PUE — power usage effectiveness: total facility power over IT equipment power.
    • ADR — architecture decision record: a short write-up of a design choice and its rationale.
    • RAG — retrieval-augmented generation: augment generation with retrieved context.
    • PIES — prompt-injection exposure surface: the count of distinct prompt-pattern classes an
      adversary can submit through all user-facing entry points, with “distinct” fixed by an author-
      chosen normalized-edit-distance threshold stated before any number appears; a local, author-
      defined operational proxy for one deployment, not a standardized or portable security metric
      (Ch 24).
    • NED / normalized Levenshtein (normalized edit distance, NLE) — string distance scaled
      to [0,1] by the longer string’s length; it is the deduplication criterion behind PIES (two probe
      patterns count as the same class within NLE ≤ 0.25) (Ch 24).
    • MTTR — mean time to recover from a bad release: mean time to detect + roll back; the factory
      loop’s core reliability number (Ch 21).
    • FAISS — a vector-similarity index library for nearest-neighbor embedding retrieval; the RAG
      corpus-policy example moves the retrieval index from a pure FAISS index to a provenance-
      aware store (Ch 24).


Notation used in the arithmetic

    • PFLOP — peta-FLOPs; FLOP/param — floating-point operations per parameter per forward
      pass (≈2 for a matmul).
    • roofline — a capacity model that plots achievable performance (FLOP/s) against arithmetic
      intensity; a kernel sits on a bandwidth-bound line below the ridge point and a compute-bound
      plateau above it. The ridge point is the arithmetic intensity at which a machine transitions
      from memory-bound to compute-bound (peak FLOP/s ÷ peak bandwidth).
    • GB vs GiB — decimal vs binary units: 1 GB = 109 , 1 GiB = 230 . The book uses decimal GB
      unless stated.
    • CDF — cumulative distribution function: F (x) is the probability a draw is at most x; the
      capstone’s two-point latency model gives F (50) = 0.35 and F (250) = 1.0, which separates
      the 180 ms mean from the 250 ms p99 (Ch 26).
    • tokens/s — throughput in tokens per second; token/request — average tokens per request (a
      workload property).
    • κ (kappa) — per-token KV cache footprint in bytes/token (e.g. ≈2.62 MB/token FP16 for the
      canonical full-MHA 70B; κ = 2 × nlayers × dhidden × bytes). Used in the KV-residency and
      concurrency arithmetic (Ch 7, 17).
    • ρ (rho) — the effective throughput fraction after load-balancer and scheduling effects (the
391                                                                                             Glossary


      fraction of theoretical peak a host actually sustains under the chosen LB/fleet configuration);
      used with the capacity formula (Ch 17).

Where an acronym is ambiguous or its definition is load-bearing, the body defines it at first use and the
relevant chapter develops the consequence.

      al., “GPipe: Efficient Training of Giant Neural Networks using Pipeline Parallelism,” in NeurIPS
      32, 2019. arXiv:1811.06965.
    • Quantization. B. Jacob et al., “Quantization and Training of Neural Networks for
      Efficient Integer-Arithmetic-Only Inference,” in Proc. IEEE/CVF Conference on Com­
      puter Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), 2018, pp. 2704–2713, arXiv:1712.05877.
      (Leading author is Benoit Jacob, not the author of the binary-network paper of
      the same period; https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_cvpr_2018/html/Jacob_
      Quantization_and_Training_CVPR_2018_paper.html.) Also E. Frantar et al., “GPTQ: Ac­
      curate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers,” in ICLR, 2023.
      arXiv:2210.17323; and T. Dettmers, A. Pagnoni, A. Holtzman, and L. Zettlemoyer, “QLoRA:
      Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs,” in NeurIPS 36, 2023. arXiv:2305.14314.
    • Speculative decoding (canonical). Y. Leviathan, M. Kalman, and Y. Matias, “Fast Infer­

      Chen et al., “Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling,” 2023.

Sources, Method, and Reproducibility



This handbook marks every number with an evidence label so a reader never has to guess the
provenance, the epistemic status, or the measurement status of a figure. The book publishes exactly
one authoritative taxonomy, and it has three orthogonal axes: Axis 1 source provenance (where
the number comes from), Axis 2 epistemic status (what the number claims to be), and Axis 3
measurement status (how far the number has climbed the measurement-status hierarchy). Labels
of the form [provenance][epistemic-status] combine one item from each of Axes 1 and 2; the
Axis-3 measurement status rides with that pair (e.g. [LAB][MEASURED]) or stands alone (e.g. a bare
[ANALYTICAL]). The axes are orthogonal — each answers a different question, so an item from one
axis never substitutes for an item from another, and the measurement-status hierarchy below is Axis
3 of this taxonomy, not a second, competing scheme.

Axis 1 — Source provenance: where the number comes from.

    • [1P] First-party / primary source. A vendor technical report, model card, or official docu­
      mentation. These are the model’s own stated parameters, benchmarks, and limits.
    • [canonical scenario] The book’s own internally-defined canonical workload and model
      (Ch 4, Table 4-2). This is an internal source the book sets up so its arithmetic is anchored and
      reproducible; it is author-defined, not external first-party evidence. Used to distinguish ”where
      this number comes from inside the book” from ”[1P]” (a real vendor source).
    • [2°] Secondary source. A third-party measurement, survey, or synthesis (e.g. an independent
      benchmark or a community write-up). Requires independent verification.
    • [LAB] Measured on the author’s own hardware. These are home-lab measurements, not
      production hardware, and are used to illustrate mechanisms and orders of magnitude.
    • [ILLUSTRATIVE] A worked-example or scenario input chosen to demonstrate a calculation,
      not a reported measurement. It is a number we assumed so the arithmetic would be concrete.


Axis 2 — Epistemic status: what the number claims to be.

    • [FACT] Stated by the source as a fact (e.g. a parameter count or a vendor benchmark).



                                                 395
Sources, Method, and Reproducibility                                                                 396


    • [DERIVED] Computed by arithmetic from stated inputs. The derivation is our work; the
        inputs come from a source item.
    • [ASSUMPTION] A deliberately chosen scenario input (a number we picked so a worked
        example would be concrete), distinct from a hypothesis because it is not a claim about the real
        workload at all. It pairs with a provenance of [ILLUSTRATIVE]: [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMP-
        TION].
    • [HYPOTHESIS] A reasoned expectation that has not yet been validated. Deliberately kept,
        because it distinguishes what we know from what we only expect.
    • [UNRESOLVED] An open item that could not be pinned to a first-party source at the time
        of writing. Such items are flagged in the text and must be re-checked against current vendor
        documentation before any procurement or deployment decision; they are precisely the numbers
        most likely to have drifted. In evidence-label lines and copy-ready templates, the parenthetical
        “(to be verified)” is the plain-language form of [UNRESOLVED] and means exactly the same
        thing.


Axis 3 — Measurement status (the measurement-status hierarchy). Where Axis 1 says where
a number came from and Axis 2 says what it claims to be, Axis 3 says how far it has climbed the
measurement-status hierarchy — a third, orthogonal axis, folded into this one authoritative taxonomy
rather than published as a separate scheme. A number in this book can fall into one of four stages,
and they are not interchangeable. Reading “ceiling” as “achieved” is the single most consequential
mistake an architect can make with these figures. The same convention is applied in the fleet and
TCO synthesis tables (Chs. 12, 17, 20, 22).

Stage                             What it is / what it is not

ANALYTICAL                        an arithmetic or physical upper bound from stated inputs (e.g. KV
                                  occupancy ceiling C, or the per-host prefill rate). Valid for planning;
                                  not an achieved rate.
ILLUSTRATIVE                      a worked-example value on stated assumptions, chosen to make the
                                  method concrete; not a measurement or a vendor claim.
MODELED (offered-load)            the result of a simulation or queueing model on a synthetic or
                                  recorded load curve; reflects the model, not a measured system.
MEASURED                          the only stage that demonstrates a deployed system meets a rate and
(SLO-goodput)                     a tail-latency SLO on real hardware. Requires a load test with a
                                  recorded trace.
In the text and figures, an [ANALYTICAL], [ILLUSTRATIVE], [MODELED], or [MEASURED] tag
states the stage; where the stage is not yet determined, the value is marked [UNMEASURED] and
cannot be treated as achieved throughput. A capacity ceiling becomes a deployment claim only after
the [MEASURED] stage is reached. Author-run probes (a one-off API call to probe a capability) are
397                                                                 Sources, Method, and Reproducibility


labeled [LAB] and are evidence of one functional path, not a model benchmark or an [1P] vendor
claim; they never double as a vendor validation.
Why [ILLUSTRATIVE] appears on two axes. It is the same worked-example number viewed from
two axes that answer different questions: on Axis 1 it is the provenance (an input we chose so the
arithmetic would be concrete), on Axis 3 it is the stage (a worked-example value, not a measurement
or a vendor claim). The two uses never conflict — a worked-example input is by definition at the
ILLUSTRATIVE stage — so [ILLUSTRATIVE] is one token shared by two orthogonal axes, not an
ambiguity.

Scope of the labeling. The label is mandatory for every load-bearing quantitative claim — a number
that a later calculation, sizing decision, or comparison depends on; the Axis-3 stage rides with every
load-bearing claim whose stage is known. Such a claim carries the labels directly (inline) or via an
identified table or section that states them for every row. Purely illustrative or rhetorical numbers
that no later calculation depends on (e.g. a round figure used only to make a sentence concrete) may
carry the labels in the surrounding prose rather than inline. This is the unambiguous exception the
preface refers to: the test is whether a downstream number depends on it.

Reading a label. [1P][FACT] means a vendor-stated fact; [1P][DERIVED] means arithmetic we
computed from a first-party input; [LAB][FACT] means a home-lab measurement; [ILLUSTRA-
TIVE][ASSUMPTION] means a number we chose so the worked example would be concrete — it is
not evidence of anything about the real workload. The Axis-3 measurement status reads alongside
them: a bare [ANALYTICAL] means an arithmetic upper bound from stated inputs (valid for planning,
not an achieved rate); [MODELED] means the result of a simulation or queueing model (it reflects
the model, not a measured system); [MEASURED] means a load test with a recorded trace that
demonstrates an achieved rate and tail-latency SLO on real hardware; [UNMEASURED] means the
stage is not yet determined, so the value cannot be treated as achieved throughput; and the combined
[LAB][MEASURED] pairs the Axis-1 provenance (our own hardware) with that Axis-3 stage. When
only one axis is shown, the other is implied by the surrounding sentence (e.g. a bare [DERIVED]
carries the status, with the provenance stated in prose).
The [S#] keys are a bibliography index, not a provenance. A label such as [S6][1P] combines
a source reference key ([S6], pointing to an entry in the References chapter) with a provenance
on that source ([1P]). The [S#] key is not a fifth provenance item; it merely says which reference
the first-party or secondary evidence comes from. A composite label always carries at least one
provenance item in addition to any [S#] key.
Prices, models, and benchmarks are a moving target. The model names, parameter counts,
context limits, prices, and throughput figures in this book are a dated snapshot. They vary with
the provider, region, commit/on-demand/spot status, hardware SKU, precision and sparsity mode,
quantization, batch and concurrency, software stack, GPU count and topology, kernel version, warmup
procedure, and percentile method used. Re-verify before acting.
Sources, Method, and Reproducibility                                                              398


Reproducibility. The book’s quantitative examples are worked from the stated inputs in the sur­
rounding text; the home-lab measurements were made on the author’s own hardware under the
configuration described in the chapter. Where a number is flagged as unresolved, the workspace did
not have a first-party source at hand, and we say so rather than present an estimate as fact.



Home-lab scope. The author’s lab is a CPU-only workstation (Intel i5-3210M, two cores (four
threads), 15 GB RAM). Measurements reflect that environment and the reduced-precision / small-
model regime; they are used to illustrate mechanisms and orders of magnitude, not to characterize
production hardware. Kernel-performance and throughput figures from public sources are to be
treated as vendor-reported until re-measured on the target cluster. No H100/H200 production-
performance claim in this book should be interpreted as a home-lab measurement unless
explicitly labeled as such.



Code and data availability. The build scripts that produce this book (text → LaTeX → PDF, plus
the figure generators) are in the accompanying repository. The figures are generated where possible
(matplotlib and a hand-drawn diagram pipeline), so the arithmetic and layouts are inspectable rather
than opaque artifacts.



Claim-to-source ledger. Every load-bearing number traces to a source by a fixed path, so a reader
can re-derive it without guessing: (1) a [S#] key resolves to the matching entry in the References
chapter, which gives the work, venue, and a stable identifier (arXiv id or first-party URL); all such
sources were accessed as of the build date (v20260913). (2) a number derived from the canonical
scenario traces to Ch 4, Table 4-2 (the single set of inputs every chapter cites). (3) the calculation
itself is either the in-text arithmetic (stated with its operands) or the figure’s generator script in
the repository (render/fig_*.py), which is reproducible from the stated inputs. A [1P] first-party
claim is cited to its source but is a vendor statement, not an independent re-measurement; per the
“moving target” note above, re-verify it against the current source before acting. This ledger is the
mechanism; it does not substitute for the independent re-derivation and print proof that the release
gates require.



Canonical parameter-and-unit ledger. Every derivative fleet/TCO/memory table cites this single
ledger for its geometry, precision, and byte conventions, so a number is never silently re-based
between the raw tensor overhead, the cache-block allocation, and the serving-engine observed
footprint. The canonical scenario (Ch 4, Table 4-2) is full multi-head attention (MHA), 80 layers,
hidden width 8192, BF16/FP16 KV, on an 8 × H100 host. The ledger is split into two blocks: the
geometry and byte arithmetic and the planning and engine observations.

Reference-geometry convention. Any isolated per-token KV or memory figure in this book
(e.g. ‘2.62 MB/token’, the raw FP8 ‘1.31 MB/token’, or a GB figure) refers to the canonical reference
geometry — full multi-head attention (MHA), 80 layers, hidden width 8192, BF16/FP16 — unless the
surrounding text or caption names a different geometry. This is the deliberately pessimistic upper
bound from Ch. 1/7. It is not a typical 70B-model KV footprint: a real 70B model may use GQA, MLA,
or hybrid attention, which reduce KV per token, so an architecture-specific figure must be derived
for that model’s own attention shape rather than inheriting the MHA number. A decimal GB/binary
GiB distinction is stated wherever a precise mount depends on it; where only an order of magnitude
matters, the base is given explicitly.

Three conventions apply throughout. (1) “KV raw per token” always means the un-allocated array
product, stated in base-2 (MiB) and base-10 (MB) as appropriate; “KV allocated” or “measured
footprint” includes the metadata and cache-block overhead. Do not conflate them. (2) A precision
adjective is always attached to its subject (“FP16 weights” vs “FP8 KV ”), never implied. (3) An
architecture-specific advantage (GQA ∼8×, MLA, hybrid) is a sensitivity for that configuration only
and is not inherited by a different model.

Caption style convention. A figure caption follows a three-part order — (1) a one-sentence takeaway
of what the figure shows, (2) a succinct ‘Scope/source:‘ line naming the geometry, assumptions, and
evidence basis, and (3) any measurement warning — intended to make the figure scannable without
deleting a qualification. A detailed derivation or cross-chapter reconciliation lives in the section
body or a nearby note, not in the caption. Where a caption is observed to repeat a body paragraph at
length, it is shortened to this convention rather than stripped of its provenance/scope condition.
Presentation of evidence tags. Load-bearing numbers carry provenance and status labels inline or
through an identified table or section note. A shared note can govern contiguous values with the
same labels; a value with a different status retains its own inline labels. Grouping repeated labels
improves readability without removing evidence controls.
The Architecture Worksheet




How to use this



Every chapter of this book turns a vague ask into a defensible number. This worksheet is the reverse:
a single reusable worksheet that applies the whole loop to the architect’s own workload. Fill it in
row by row; each row is a decision in Chapters 1–26. When a row is empty, that is precisely the gap
to investigate next. The canonical workload box (Chapter 4) shows what a fully-filled row looks like;
the two derived rates most often needed are given under its table.

   All quantities are the architect’s own — traceable, verifiable, and stated in the evidence tax­
onomy (provenance: [1P ] first-party, [canonical scenario] the book’s own workload, [2◦ ] reputable
secondary, [LAB] home-lab, [ILLUSTRATIVE] worked-example; epistemic status: FACT / DERIVED /
ASSUMPTION / HYPOTHESIS / UNRESOLVED; measurement status — the third, orthogonal axis
— ANALYTICAL / ILLUSTRATIVE / MODELED / MEASURED / UNMEASURED). See the Sources,
Method, and Reproducibility chapter for the full three-axis definition.

Following up

Keep one sheet per significant architecture decision, and re-check it when the workload’s numbers
change. A machine-readable (Markdown) companion to this worksheet ships in the repository
(render/architecture_worksheet.md), so a practitioner can copy, fill, and version it alongside
the corresponding ADR rather than transcribing the printed page. The worksheet’s sequence —
requirement, workload, model, compute/memory, architecture, decision, validation & operations —
is the same loop Chapter 22 makes explicit, and the same reason the Patterns Library in Chapter 26
exists: a decision recorded with its evidence can be reused, while a decision recorded without it must
be re-derived every time. Rows 7–8 close the loop by pinning what was measured, at what load, the
economics and failure policy assumed, and when it must be re-verified.
